posts.t: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, November Week 2, 2026: Crew Wi-Fi as a Way In, Insurers Ask for Proof, and Korea's Cyber Test Ship
c: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, November Week 2, 2026: Crew Wi-Fi as a Way In, Insurers Ask for Proof, and Korea's Cyber Test Ship The incidents, CVEs and threat intelligence that matter to ships, ports and shipping companies, as of 8 November 2026 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn Every ship has two kinds of network. One runs the ship: engines, cargo, navigation. The other lets the crew call home after a long watch. Everyone agrees there should be a wall between them, and almost everyone says theirs is there. The harder question is who has actually checked it.

Let me say it plainly: this was a quiet week , with no new confirmed attack on a ship, port or shipping company in the sources I could read. But the few solid stories all come back to that wall. An offshore connectivity provider warned that crew internet is becoming a way in. A Korean insurer and a maritime security company agreed to tie cover to proof of security. And Korea showed off a real ship built so that people can attack it on purpose. There are also two short updates: the Le Havre terminal is reported back to normal, and the n0n leak listings have not grown.

At a Glance Date Where What Status 5 Nov 2026 UAE / offshore IEC Telecom warns that crew "welfare" internet on offshore sites can expose operations systems Expert view, reported by press 23 Oct 2026 Korea Hanwha General Insurance and CYTUR sign an MOU to link ship cyber cover to security assessments Company announcement; pilot planned for December 27 Oct 2026 Busan, Korea KISA and Korea Maritime & Ocean University unveil a test ship for cyberattack and response trials at sea Confirmed by the agencies, reported by press 27 Oct–3 Nov 2026 Le Havre, France Update: TNMSC terminal reported back to normal operations Reported by a forwarder; cause still not confirmed by the operator 3 Nov 2026 Global Update: all 38 n0n maritime listings still up, no new shipping or port names since 26 October Leak-site claims, unverified Week to 30 Oct 2026 UKMTO reporting area GNSS interference: four ship reports to UKMTO, thousands of anomalous AIS positions Reported, via a newsletter 3 Nov 2026 Global CVEs: one new CISA ICS advisory, for a power-utility product; nothing marine-specific Published advisory Ⅰ.

The Crew's Internet: From Welfare to a Way In Not long ago a seafarer's link to home was a satellite phone and a few minutes a week. Today crews on ships and offshore platforms expect video calls, messaging and social media, and the rules now support them: The National notes that amendments to the ILO Maritime Labour Convention in force since December 2024 give seafarers access to social connectivity on board. That is good for people at sea. It also means that a network full of personal phones and laptops, which the company does not control, now sits on the same platform as the systems that run the operation.

That was the warning in a report from the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi, published by The National on 5 November. Alaa Alsadi of IEC Telecom, a satellite connectivity provider, said companies must keep workers' internet separate from the systems that control critical operations. He described crew internet as something companies have run as a "welfare system" over the last five or six years; before that, connectivity was mainly for operations. The same article says the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency, in guidance from March 2026, recognised that messaging and social media can reduce loneliness at sea, and also warned that less secure connections give criminals an opportunity.

I have read this guidance only as The National reports it. Why does a crew phone matter to an engine room? Because attackers rarely break through the strongest door. They look for the easiest one, and a personal device that clicks a bad link or installs a fake app is an easy door. Once inside a network, an intruder looks for the next connection. If the crew network and the operations network are truly separate, that search ends at the wall. If they share a switch, a satellite router or a "temporary" cable someone added during a repair, it may not. In plain words: segregation Think of a ship's accommodation and its engine room.

Both are on the same hull, but you would not let every visitor walk from the mess room into the engine control room. Network segregation is the same idea in cables and settings: the crew network and the control network share the ship, but traffic between them is blocked, or allowed only through one watched door. The point is not that the door exists on a drawing. The point is that someone has tested it and keeps checking that nobody has propped it open. This blog has met the same idea recently.

In the November Week 1 brief , H-Line was quoted by TheElec as saying that the engine and measurement control equipment on Vivit Africa LNG is separated from the crew's internet network, while the company that is taking the ship over plans its own OT review. Nobody in this week's report links the two stories, and I am not suggesting a link. The common point is the claim itself: "it is separated" is a statement, and someone has to check it. Captain Paul's reading Crew connectivity is not the enemy, and cutting it would be the wrong answer: a rested, connected crew is a safer crew. The right answer is to treat the crew network as what it is, an untrusted network that happens to be on board.

If I were a superintendent, I would ask one simple question at the next visit: show me, on this ship, where the crew Wi-Fi ends and what stops it going further. A drawing from the yard is a start. A test result from this year is better. Ⅱ. Insurance: Cover That Depends on Proof Ask most owners whether their ships are insured against a cyber incident, and many will assume the answer is yes because the hull is insured. That is often not the case. Marine Insight , reporting a new Korean partnership on 29 October, puts it bluntly: "existing vessel insurance policies exclude general cyber-related losses," which leaves shipping companies with significant gaps in cover.

The partnership is a memorandum of understanding signed on 23 October between Hanwha General Insurance and CYTUR, a Busan-based maritime cybersecurity company. As described, the roles are split. CYTUR assesses a vessel's security across its life, from design and construction to operation, and gives the insurer technical analysis for underwriting. After a ship is covered, CYTUR keeps monitoring it and supports reassessment at renewal. If something happens, it carries out remote analysis and onboard forensics and writes the technical report for the claim. Hanwha designs the products, and plans to link assessment results to whether a ship can be insured and on what terms.

A pilot with Korean shipping companies and owners is planned for December 2026. No premiums, limits or wording have been published, so this is still a plan, not a product. Why would an insurer want this? Because an underwriter cannot price what it cannot see. For fire, there are surveys, class records and drills. For cyber, until now there has been little more than a questionnaire. An assessment, ongoing monitoring and forensic support give the insurer something closer to a survey report and a voyage data recorder for the network: evidence before the policy, and evidence after a loss.

Captain Paul's reading This is how security usually becomes real in shipping: not when a rule says so, but when someone puts a price on it. If cover and terms start to depend on assessment results, the wall between crew and control networks from item Ⅰ stops being an IT preference and becomes a commercial fact. Two things to watch when the pilot reports: who checks the assessor's work, and whether the forensic report written for the insurer is also shared with the owner. Evidence that only one party sees is weaker than evidence everyone can check. Ⅲ.

Korea Builds a Ship to Be Attacked There is a problem at the heart of ship cybersecurity: you cannot safely test an attack on a ship that is carrying cargo. A laboratory testbed helps, but a lab does not roll, does not lose its satellite link in bad weather, and does not have an engineer who switches a pump over by hand in the middle of the test. Somewhere between the lab and a working ship, there has to be a real ship where breaking things is allowed. On 27 October, as Byline Network reported , the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and Korea Maritime & Ocean University publicly showed such a facility for the first time, with a joint demonstration at the university in Busan.

A dedicated demonstration ship was built to verify cybersecurity technology across navigation, communications and engine systems. The team simulated cyberattacks and tested detection and response in a real sea area. The university provides the sea area, mooring and safety management. The research is part of a KISA project supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT and IITP. The report does not name the vessel or describe the specific attacks or tools, so I cannot say more about what was tested. KISA's Park Hae-ryong, head of its AI Security Technology Division, said that as ships become more digital, it is important to verify cybersecurity technology in the actual operating environment.

The partners also plan to discuss extending the research to autonomous ships and smart ports. KISA is not new to real cases either: in the November Week 1 brief, H-Line said its Vivit Africa LNG investigation was carried out with KISA and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries. Captain Paul's reading A test ship is the closest thing our industry has to a fire-training ground: a place where you can light the fire on purpose and watch who reaches for the right extinguisher. It answers the question this whole brief keeps asking, "how do you know the wall holds?", in the most honest way, by trying to get through it.

I hope the results are published in enough detail for yards and equipment makers to learn from them. A demonstration that stays inside the project helps far fewer people than one that ends in a public report. Ⅳ. Updates: Le Havre Back at Work, n0n's List Unchanged Update · Le Havre The November Week 1 brief left the TNMSC terminal at Le Havre closed, with no confirmed restart date after the IT disruption of 13–14 October. Kuehne+Nagel's port update for 27 October to 3 November now says that "TNMSC has returned to normal operations following the cyberattack, but vessel arrivals are affected by the strike", with an average vessel waiting time of about one day at Le Havre. Two cautions.

This is a forwarder's operational note, not a statement by the terminal or the port. And Kuehne+Nagel's word "cyberattack" is the same wording it used before: we still have not seen the terminal operator or HAROPA Port confirm the cause, so this brief keeps it as "not established". It took roughly two to three weeks, by this account, to get from failure to normal working. Update · n0n The Maritime Cyber Weekly newsletter of 3 November reports that, three weeks after the deadline, all 38 shipping and port entries are still on n0n's leak site, and that no new shipping or port names have appeared since 26 October.

This is one newsletter's monitoring, and the listings themselves remain claims: we have not seen any listed organisation confirm an intrusion. The same newsletter mentions two other leak-site listings from late October, one of a shipyard and one of a logistics company, each from a single source with no statement from the company. Following this blog's rule, we do not name them. Captain Paul's reading Le Havre gives us a rough number worth remembering: a terminal that loses its systems can be out for weeks, not hours. That is the figure to put in a business continuity plan, not the optimistic "back up by tomorrow". On n0n, a quiet list is not good news by itself.

The data that was published stays published, and anyone named should assume their partners have read it. Ⅴ. GNSS Interference: Why the Counts Disagree If you ask "how bad is GPS jamming this week?", you will get very different numbers depending on who you ask, and they are not necessarily contradicting each other. The 3 November Maritime Cyber Weekly laid three counts side by side. Ships sent UKMTO four reports of GNSS interference in the week ending 30 October, up from one the week before. In the same seven days, UKMTO logged 15,714 anomalous AIS positions, against 18,049 the week before.

And Windward, as summarised there, counted 124,235 vessels touched by interference worldwide in the third quarter of 2026. I have not read UKMTO's or Windward's own figures, so treat these numbers as reported by the newsletter. Windward's own Q3 report summary separately says that 52% of September's Hormuz transits were "dark convoy passages". In plain words: three ways of counting A ship's report to UKMTO is a crew noticing a problem and taking the time to tell someone, so it is the smallest number.

An anomalous AIS position is a computer noticing that a ship's reported position makes no sense, for example a jump onto land, so it counts every bad position, whether or not anyone on board noticed. A quarterly count of affected vessels counts each ship once, however many bad positions it had. Each number answers a different question. Four reports against thousands of anomalies mostly tells us how few interference events are reported by the people living through them. Captain Paul's reading The gap between four reports and thousands of anomalies is the part I would take to the bridge. Interference has become so normal in some waters that crews stop reporting it.

That is understandable, and it is also how a pattern goes unseen until a ship touches bottom, as the Georgia Tech work on Port Sudan in last week's brief suggested. A short report costs a few minutes and makes the picture better for everyone. Ⅵ. CVEs: A Quiet List Since the last brief, CISA's ICS advisory list shows only one new item, on 3 November: ICSA-26-307-01 for SUBNET Solutions PowerSYSTEM Center, a product for the energy and critical manufacturing sectors. It covers two flaws, CVE-2026-63017 (incorrect authorization) and CVE-2026-63774 (SQL injection), each scored 9.0 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.4 under v4.0 by CISA.

CISA lists fixes in the 2026 Update 1.1 for the 2024 and 2026 product lines; for the 2020 line, Update 30 is listed only for the first CVE. Nothing in the advisory mentions ships or ports, and we have no information that the product is used on board. If your port or terminal runs its own power distribution and uses this software, follow the advisory; otherwise there is nothing marine-specific to act on this week. Ⅶ. How This Connects to IACS UR E26/E27 None of this week's stories is a UR E26 or E27 failure, and none of the sources says whether these rules applied to any particular ship. The link is practical. posts.t: NIS2 for Shipping Companies: Essential or Important Entity? From Status Assessment to Governance Design
c: NIS2 for Shipping Companies: Essential or Important Entity? From Status Assessment to Governance Design Questions every shipping company should settle before NIS2 settles them for it: scope, classification, the owner–manager split, and the governance that has to sit behind the answer. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity NIS2 adds a layer on top of the IMO and IACS cyber requirements that shipping companies already know, and that layer is aimed at the company rather than the ship.

This post sets out how to think about NIS2 status, what really separates essential from important entities, and why the more useful question is not "are we in scope?" but "would our structure hold up under any status?" NIS2 regulates the company, not the ship Same duties, different supervision Out of scope is not out of reach Owner or manager: who is the entity? Liability cannot be outsourced Design for the highest status 1. Why shipping companies need to understand NIS2 EU cybersecurity regulation began with the 2016 NIS Directive (Directive (EU) 2016/1148, NIS1) and expanded considerably with the 2022 NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555).

NIS1 covered operators of essential services, which each Member State identified one by one, and digital service providers. NIS2 instead defines its scope by sector and company size. Maritime transport sits in Annex I, the list of "sectors of high criticality." Cybersecurity is not new to shipping. IMO Resolution MSC.428(98) encouraged Administrations to ensure that cyber risks are appropriately addressed in safety management systems (SMS) under the ISM Code, and MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3, since revised several times, set out a framework for maritime cyber risk management.

The resolution itself is a recommendation, but flag states and class societies have checked cyber risk in the SMS during ISM audits. Newbuildings now also fall under IACS UR E26 and E27. Shipping companies already meet cyber requirements through ISM audits, ISPS security plans and class surveys. NIS2 adds one more layer, and the difference is what it regulates. The IMO and IACS frameworks look at ships and their operation. NIS2 looks at the company . Management approval and oversight, incident reporting, supply chain security and dealing with supervisors are all required at company level. So the question cannot stop at "are we subject to NIS2?" It has to continue: if we are, what changes?

And if we are not, what should we still prepare? This post takes those questions in order. 2. NIS2 at a glance What NIS2 asks of in-scope entities can be grouped into four pillars. ▸ Cybersecurity risk-management measures (Article 21): ten areas, covering risk analysis and security policies, incident handling, business continuity, supply chain security, security in system acquisition, development and maintenance, assessing the effectiveness of measures, basic cyber hygiene and training, cryptography, personnel security, access control and asset management, and multi-factor authentication with secured communications.

▸ Incident reporting (Article 23): incidents with a significant impact on service provision must be reported to the competent CSIRT or authority in stages: an early warning, an incident notification, an intermediate report on request, and a final report. ▸ Management accountability (Article 20): the management body approves the risk-management measures, oversees their implementation and can be held liable for infringements. Its members must follow training. ▸ Supervision and enforcement (Articles 31–34): the supervisory powers of competent authorities and the system of administrative sanctions. In-scope entities fall into two categories, essential entities and important entities (Article 3).

Both carry the same risk-management and reporting duties, but they are supervised differently and face different levels of sanctions. One point matters from the start. NIS2 is a directive, not a regulation. It takes effect through each Member State's national transposition law, and details can differ along the way. An analysis comparing Greece's transposing law (Law 5160/2024) with the Directive, for example, notes that Greece set more specific requirements, such as appointing a dedicated security officer, submitting a cybersecurity policy to the authority periodically and keeping an asset inventory.

Transposition has also been uneven: in July 2026 the European Commission referred several Member States that had not completed it to the Court of Justice of the EU. A note on numbers. Reporting deadlines, maximum fines and size thresholds should be checked against both the Directive text and the national law of the Member State concerned. National law can be stricter or more specific than the Directive. 3. Status assessment: where does a shipping company fall? Whether a shipping company is in scope generally turns on four factors. Sector.

In Annex I, the water transport subsector covers "inland, sea and coastal passenger and freight water transport companies," as defined for maritime transport in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 725/2004 on ship and port facility security. The same entry adds that this does not include the individual vessels operated by those companies . NIS2 looks at the company, not the ship. Port managing bodies and port facilities, and vessel traffic service (VTS) operators, are in the same subsector. Size. As a rule, NIS2 applies to entities that are at least medium-sized under the EU SME definition (Article 2(1)).

There are exceptions that apply regardless of size, for example where an entity is the sole provider of an essential service in a Member State, or where a disruption could significantly affect public safety or cause systemic risk (Article 2(2)). Member State identification. On these grounds, Member States can identify particular entities as essential, and they compile and update a list of in-scope entities (Article 3). Two companies of the same size can end up with different status depending on the Member State's view. Establishment in the EU.

NIS2 applies to entities that provide services or carry out activities in the Union, and jurisdiction generally lies with the Member State where the entity is established (Article 26(1)). Certain digital service providers, such as cloud and data centre providers, must designate an EU representative if they are based outside the Union, but shipping companies are not on that list. What about non-EU shipping companies? For a company headquartered outside the EU, such as a Korean operator, the starting point is what form its EU presence takes and what it does.

According to a general guide to Belgium's NIS2 rules published by BDK Advokati, a Serbia-based regional law firm, a branch that is not a separate legal entity can bring the foreign company itself under the Member State's obligations. A subsidiary that is in scope does not automatically pull a non-EU parent into scope, but if the two share IT infrastructure, or the parent sits in the subsidiary's supply chain, the parent will in practice be expected to apply equivalent measures. This guidance is not shipping-specific, so actual decisions should be confirmed against the relevant national law and with legal counsel. In a group, assess each legal entity separately.

Where owning companies, ship managers, agencies and terminal operators sit in one group, each entity's sector, size and location can lead to a different status. The bottom line: status assessment is a legal question , and it is not a one-off. Mergers and acquisitions, setting up an EU entity, business growth or a change in Member State identification all call for a fresh look. 4. Essential vs important: what is the same, and what differs? For Annex I sectors, the basic dividing line is size. Large enterprises above the medium-sized ceiling are essential entities; other in-scope entities are important entities. Member State identification can change this (Article 3).

What is the same ▸ The risk-management duties under Article 21 ▸ The incident reporting system under Article 23 (early warning, notification, final report) ▸ Management approval, oversight and training under Article 20 ▸ Submitting registration information under Article 3(4) What differs ▸ Supervision. Essential entities are subject to proactive (often described as ex ante) supervision: the authority can proactively carry out on-site inspections, random checks, regular and targeted security audits, security scans and information requests (Article 32).

Important entities are subject to ex post supervision, which starts when the authority receives evidence, indications or information of possible non-compliance (Article 33). ▸ Sanctions. Both categories can face administrative fines, but the maximum is higher for essential entities (Article 34). ▸ Personal accountability. For essential entities, if other enforcement measures prove ineffective, the authority can request a temporary ban on a person at chief executive or legal representative level from exercising managerial functions (Article 32(5)). Article 33, which governs important entities, contains no such measure.

Essential entity Important entity Out of scope Risk-management measures Legal duty Legal duty No duty (contractual or voluntary) Incident reporting Legal duty Legal duty No duty (contractual notice possible) Management accountability and training Legal duty Legal duty No duty Supervision Ex ante and ongoing Ex post None (customer due diligence instead) Sanction level Relatively higher Relatively lower Not applicable Temporary ban on managers Available Not available Not applicable The difference between essential and important lies less in how much you must do than in how you are supervised. The list of required measures is the same.

What changes is when the supervisor looks, and how heavy the consequences are when something goes wrong. That has a practical implication. An important entity may never be inspected in normal times, but after an incident it will have to prove what it had been doing all along. If that evidence has not been built up in advance, the burden lands at the worst possible moment, right after an incident. 5. If you are out of scope, can you ignore NIS2? Concluding that a company is out of scope does not mean nothing needs doing. NIS2 reaches such companies in three ways. Through contracts.

In-scope entities must manage security in their relationships with direct suppliers and service providers (Article 21(2)(d)). If EU cargo owners, charterers, ports or terminals are in scope, they have reason to require incident notification, security standards and audit cooperation from their counterparties by contract. An out-of-scope shipping company can therefore face NIS2-level requirements indirectly, through the supply chain. Through a change of status. Business growth, mergers and acquisitions, a new EU entity or a Member State identification can all change status. Starting to build a framework after the change is too late. Through information sharing.

NIS2 encourages voluntary cyber threat information-sharing arrangements among in-scope entities, and entities outside the scope can take part where relevant (Article 29). For an out-of-scope company, voluntary alignment is a realistic option. Running NIS2-level risk management and reporting as internal standards makes customer due diligence easier and lowers the cost of switching if status changes. Steps that apply only where there is a legal obligation, such as external reporting, are best marked "where applicable" to avoid confusion. 6. A shipping-specific issue: owner or manager, who is the NIS2 entity?

Shipping has a structure few other industries share: the company that owns a ship and the company that operates and manages it are often different. The ISM Code treats as the "Company" not only the shipowner but also any organisation, such as a manager or bareboat charterer, that has assumed responsibility for operating the ship from the owner, and that company holds the Document of Compliance (DOC). NIS2 takes its definition of water transport companies from the EU regulation that transposes the ISPS Code, but its wording does not say directly whether the owner or the manager is the entity. That judgment is left to national law and to supervisors' interpretation.

A flowchart for maritime shipping companies published on Germany's flag state portal (Deutsche Flagge) shows one approach. Alongside a size test, it asks whether the company is the company responsible under the ISM Code (the DOC holder) . If both conditions are met, the onshore part of that company is to be classified as an essential or important entity. This reflects German national law (the BSI Act), and it cannot be assumed that other Member States will do the same. But it points in a clear direction: the NIS2 entity is the company that actually operates and manages the ship. This structure raises practical issues. ▸ The ISM company and the NIS2 entity may differ.

A ship manager may hold the DOC, while the owning company is separately in scope because of national rules or group structure. ▸ Reporting responsibility blurs. Who reports the same incident? If both are in scope, the incident may be reported twice. If neither believes it is the reporting entity, it may not be reported at all. ▸ The notification chain gets longer. As notice passes from ship to manager to owner, contractual notice periods stack up and can make the NIS2 early-warning deadline hard to meet. The fix is contractual.

Ship management agreements should spell out mutual notification periods for cyber incidents, who reports under NIS2 and who may report on the other's behalf, cost allocation and responsibility for preserving evidence. Notice periods between the parties should be set well inside the NIS2 deadlines so the end of the chain can still meet them. 7. How status shapes governance NIS2 status feeds directly into organisational design. Five points deserve attention. Records of management approval and oversight. Article 20 requires the management body to approve the risk-management measures and oversee their implementation.

Doing so is not enough; there must be records a supervisor can see, such as board or executive committee minutes, regular reporting records and annual approval documents. Management training should also leave completion records. An accountable executive and the CISO's reporting line. If the CISO reports through an IT executive, the record of direct management approval and oversight easily breaks in the middle. For an in-scope company, it helps to name an accountable executive who puts the risk-management measures to the management body and oversees them, and to give the CISO a direct line to management. The limits of an outsourced CISO (vCISO).
Smaller shipping companies often hand the CISO function to an outside expert. Technical advice

posts.t: ShipPaulJobs Weekly AI Brief, November Week 2, 2026: Ports Wait for AI Returns, Windward Adds Cameras, and the AI Trade Wobbles
c: ShipPaulJobs Weekly AI Brief, November Week 2, 2026: Ports Wait for AI Returns, Windward Adds Cameras, and the AI Trade Wobbles AI in shipping, ports and shipyards, and the AI industry news that will reach them, as of 7 November 2026 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn Ask a terminal manager today whether the port uses AI, and the answer is usually yes. Ask what that AI has added to the bottom line, and the room goes quiet. That gap between using AI and earning from it ran through this week's news. A port survey put a number on it. Maritime AI companies kept buying and launching anyway. A Korean shipyard found a way to get class societies to trust an AI inspector.

And on Wall Street a $2.5 trillion selloff asked the same question about the whole AI industry, on the very day Maersk said AI is helping to fill its ships. This is the first ShipPaulJobs Weekly AI Brief. Each week it takes a handful of stories and explains what is going on underneath them, and what they mean for people who run ships, ports and yards.

At a Glance Date Where What Status 3 & 6 Nov 2026 Global ports BCG and TIC4.0 survey: only 4% of container port respondents report measurable earnings gains from AI Survey, reported by press 5 Nov 2026 Global Windward acquires Azimut.ai to add camera-based vessel identification to its maritime AI platform Company announcement 5 Nov 2026 Greece / global AskChief opens its AI tool for technical and compliance teams to the wider market Company announcement 29 Oct 2026 Korea HD Hyundai Heavy Industries' AI coating inspector; MOU with LR, ABS, DNV and KR on AI inspection procedures Company announcement, reported by press 5 Nov 2026 USA / global A $2.5 trillion tech selloff questions the AI buildout that is lifting container demand Market data, reported by press Now → 2 Dec 2026 EU EU AI Act: what already applies, and the next date for generative-AI marking Regulation in force Part 1 · Maritime AI Ⅰ.

Ports: AI Is Spreading, Returns Are Not Picture a container terminal that has spent two years on AI. One model reads bills of lading and customs papers so clerks no longer retype them. Another watches the cranes and warns before a gearbox fails. The pilots worked, people like them, and now the board asks a simple question: how much money has this made us? A survey published this week suggests most terminals cannot answer it. Boston Consulting Group and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) asked 103 experts from terminal operators, port authorities, shipping lines and technology vendors on five continents in August 2026.

The results were reported by FreightWaves on 3 November and by WorldCargo News on 6 November . AI is clearly past the experiment stage: 44% said their organisation has reached the scaling stage or later. But only 4% reported measurable earnings gains. Why such a gap? The survey itself points to the first reason. Only 11% of respondents systematically track what AI does to their efficiency or margins. A terminal that does not measure cannot report a gain, even if one exists.

The other reasons are familiar to anyone who has tried to put software into an operation: when asked about barriers, 41% named an unclear return on investment, 32% named data quality and 30% named integration with existing systems. An AI model can only be as good as the data it is fed, and in a port that data sits in a terminal operating system, crane controllers and paper that were never designed to talk to each other. Where AI is earning its place is less glamorous than the headlines. The two leading use cases are extracting data from shipping documents, which 62% are exploring or implementing, and predicting failures of cranes and straddle carriers, at 48%.

The benefits people cite follow the same pattern: operational efficiency (74%) and faster decisions (44%) come well ahead of cost reductions (41%) and customer experience (18%). There is one more detail worth noticing. Unclear return was named by 44% of staff below the C-suite but by only 21% of senior leaders. Captain Paul's reading The number I would hang on the wall is 11%, not 4%. If only one in nine organisations measures what AI does for it, the 4% says as much about measurement as about results. And when the people closest to the work are twice as doubtful as the people who approved the budget, that is usually a sign the measuring needs to start on the quay, not in the boardroom. Ⅱ.

Windward Buys Azimut.ai: From What Ships Say to What Cameras See Most of what the world knows about where a ship is comes from the ship itself. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) is a transponder that broadcasts a vessel's identity, position and course to anyone listening. It is, in effect, a self-report. A ship that does not want to be seen can switch it off or broadcast a false position, and that weakness sits at the heart of the sanctions-evasion problem often called the dark fleet. That is the background to an acquisition Windward announced on 5 November . The maritime AI company has bought Azimut.ai, a maritime visual intelligence company, for an undisclosed price.

Azimut.ai uses optical sensing to identify and "fingerprint" vessels in real time at chokepoints and ports, including vessels whose AIS is off. Windward says it will place cameras at key chokepoints and combine what they see with the ownership, sanctions, cargo and behavioural data it already holds. A simple way to think about it: AIS is the boarding pass a passenger shows; the camera is the one at the gate. Windward's customers will not receive raw images or video, and the company says the system analyses vessel activity, not individuals. CEO Ami Daniel called the deal "our first step in building a proprietary visual intelligence layer".

Captain Paul's reading For ordinary operators the practical effect arrives through compliance. When a charterer or bank screens a counterparty, it will increasingly have a second, harder-to-fake signal next to AIS. A vessel with a gap in its AIS track may now also have, or lack, a camera sighting that explains the gap. Ⅲ. AskChief Opens to the Market: AI That Reads the Company's Own Manuals Think of a superintendent answering a vetting observation late in the evening, or a chief engineer chasing an alarm on a sister ship's purifier. They rarely lack knowledge.

What they lack is time to find the right page: the maker's manual, the procedure in the safety management system (SMS), the record of the last time the same thing happened. AskChief's co-founder Vassilis Mavrogiannis put it this way: "The bottleneck is getting the right evidence in front of the right person". AskChief, an AI platform for ship technical and HSQE teams, opened to the wider market on 5 November after nearly a year of live use with shipowners and managers. It has two applications, AskChief Technical and AskChief Compliance.

Both answer questions from a company's own technical manuals, SMS, vessel records and past cases, and both show the sources behind each answer so staff can check them. Seanergy Maritime, Castor Ships, Iblea, Delia and IMECS (part of the ITOCHU Group) worked with the company on the tools. In plain words A general-purpose chatbot answers from what it learned during training, which can be out of date or simply wrong about your ship. A tool that answers from your own documents works more like a fast librarian: it finds the relevant pages first, then writes the answer from them. If it shows which page it used, a person can check the answer in seconds instead of trusting it.

Captain Paul's reading Showing the source is the right design, because on a ship an unverifiable answer is worse than no answer. The question an operator should ask before rolling out any tool like this is where its manuals and SMS will be stored and processed, and who can see them. Those documents describe how the company's ships are built and run, which is exactly what an attacker would like to read. Ⅳ. Shipyards: HD Hyundai Brings the Class Societies In Coating inspection is one of the oldest crafts in a shipyard. An inspector walks a block, looks closely at the paint film and decides whether a defect needs repair.

It depends heavily on the individual's eye and experience, and the yard's result is later looked at again by the owner's and the class society's surveyors. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries announced on 29 October an AI system for this job, AI CIP (AI Coating InsPector). It uses vision AI trained on large sets of coating-quality data from the group's own yards to find defects, replacing judgement that depended on the individual inspector. Development began in 2024 with HD KSOE's AX Center, and the company says the system has passed technical review by major classification societies. No accuracy figures were published. The more interesting part came the same day.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, HD KSOE and HD Hyundai Samho signed an MOU with Lloyd's Register, ABS, DNV and Korean Register. The yards will apply the system and improve how inspection data is collected; the class societies will support technical review and work on standard inspection procedures for AI-based inspection. Captain Paul's reading Why bring the class societies in? Because in shipbuilding an inspection only counts when the people who sign the certificates accept it. A yard can use any tool it likes for internal quality control, but for AI to replace part of a survey, the surveyor has to be able to trust and audit it.

The open questions are about evidence: how the model's decision is recorded, and how a disputed result is settled between yard, owner and class. Part 2 · The AI Industry, and What It Means for Shipping Ⅴ. A $2.5 Trillion Selloff Meets AI Cargo In shipping we usually talk about AI as software, on board or in the office. This week was a reminder that it is also cargo. A data centre needs servers, chips, transformers and power equipment, and a great deal of that moves by sea. So when investors start doubting the AI buildout, it is not only a technology story.

On 5 November the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, about $2.5 trillion in market value and its biggest one-day percentage drop since April 2025 according to Reuters, as reported by Gizmodo . The Philadelphia semiconductor index had its worst day since early 2020. Reports linked the fall to weak AI-sector earnings and to the US midterm results, with investors expecting tougher scrutiny of the AI industry. UBS estimates, per Reuters, that about 30% of the US data-centre capacity expansion expected in 2028 may be at risk of construction pauses.

On the same day, Maersk raised its 2026 profit guidance for the third time , to an underlying EBITDA of $14–14.5 billion, on the back of higher freight rates rather than more cargo. Its shares still fell 11%. CEO Vincent Clerc said demand is "increasingly" driven by investment in electrification, energy and AI infrastructure, which generates significant industrial cargo flows. Captain Paul's reading Put the two stories side by side and the link is plain. Part of today's demand for ships rests on a building programme that markets are now questioning. If even part of the data-centre pipeline pauses, as UBS warns, project and breakbulk cargo tied to it softens.

Owners and charterers exposed to that trade should watch AI spending numbers as closely as freight indices. Ⅵ. Rules: What the EU AI Act Already Requires Recent headlines said the EU had delayed its AI Act. That is true for only part of it. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved the dates for high-risk systems but did not pause the rest, according to a 5 November summary and law-firm analysis . It helps to think of the Act as a fleet delivery schedule: some ships are already in service, one is due next month, and the largest have had their delivery dates pushed back.

Already in service: the bans on prohibited practices and the duty to give staff adequate AI literacy (since 2 February 2025); the obligations on general-purpose AI models (since 2 August 2025); and most of the Article 50 transparency duties, such as telling people they are talking to a chatbot and labelling deepfakes (since 2 August 2026). Due next: on 2 December 2026, machine-readable marking of AI-generated content (Article 50(2)) applies to generative systems already on the market before 2 August 2026, and new bans take effect on AI that generates non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material.

Delayed: stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III) move to 2 December 2027, and high-risk AI built into regulated products (Annex I) to 2 August 2028. Commentators describe the Article 50(2) timing slightly differently, so check the Official Journal text before relying on a date. In plain words: where marine equipment fits The delayed Annex I date does not work the same way for every product. Annex I of the Act lists existing EU product laws in two groups. For products under the laws in Section A, such as machinery, the AI Act's high-risk requirements apply directly. The Marine Equipment Directive (2014/90/EU) is in Section B, alongside the laws for civil aviation, vehicles and rail.

For Section B products, Article 2(2) says that only a few articles of the AI Act apply. Instead, Article 105 amended the Marine Equipment Directive itself: when the Commission sets technical specifications and testing standards for AI systems that are safety components, it must take into account the high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act. Put simply, a maker of type-approved marine equipment will meet these AI rules through future MED specifications and testing standards, not through a separate AI Act certificate. (Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on EUR-Lex , Article 2(2), Article 105 and Annex I.) What are those requirements?

Chapter III, Section 2 is the core of the high-risk rules: a risk management system, data and data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping (logs), information for the people using the system, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Whichever route the rules take to a product, the AI Act directly or the Marine Equipment Directive, the questions will be of the same kind: show how this system was tested, on what data, how often it is wrong, and how a person can step in when it is.

Captain Paul's reading For a shipping company in the EU, the duties that bite now are the unglamorous ones: staff who use AI tools need adequate AI literacy, and a customer-facing chatbot must say it is a chatbot. For equipment makers, neither the delay nor the MED route is a reason to wait. The evidence those rules will ask for, what data a model was trained and tested on, how accurate it was, how it fails and how a person overrides it, can only be collected while the system is being built. A file put together in 2028 cannot describe tests that nobody wrote down in 2026. And as the HD Hyundai MOU shows, yards and class societies are already asking f

posts.t: Three Pages for an Entire Ship: Why I Rejected a Shipyard's E26 Vessel Asset Inventory
c: Three Pages for an Entire Ship: Why I Rejected a Shipyard's E26 Vessel Asset Inventory First : Vessel Asset Inventory [E26, 5.1.3] ※ The shipyard and SI company names are anonymized (H*, M*). Jack Superintendent · M** (M** Shipping Company) I want to share some of the problems I have experienced with cyber security documents for ships being built in China. The first document I want to talk about is the Vessel Asset Inventory under E26, Section 5.1.3. I have a strong message for Chinese shipyards and shipowners: Hire a competent cyber security SI company of Korea. I am writing this as a ship superintendent, not to blame any particular shipyard or company.

The owner's side will live with these documents for the entire service life of the vessel, long after the shipyard has delivered it. What I want to see is not perfect paperwork on the first submission, but a shipyard that takes ownership of the problem and works with us to solve it. 1 What the Shipyard Submitted A vessel is currently under construction at H*, one of the largest shipyards in China. M* is responsible for the cyber security SI work. They are known as one of the most technically advanced SI companies in China. So, what did shipyard submit for approval? Just three pages, with around 50 entries with so many pending. Yes, only three pages for the Vessel Asset Inventory. Surprised.

Of course, fewer pages do not always mean a bad document. But the assets on board must be properly identified, and the important information about each system and its connections must be included. However, the document I received was little more than a list of system names. In my view, it was nowhere near sufficient to provide a proper understanding of the vessel's cyber-related assets or to support the subsequent risk assessment and selection of appropriate security measures.

A modern ocean-going vessel carries a large number of computer-based systems: integrated automation, power management, navigation, communication, fire detection, cargo and ballast control, and the network switches, gateways, and workstations that connect them.

For a reviewer, each entry in the inventory should answer at least the following: What the system or device is, and what function it serves on board Manufacturer, model, and supplier Physical location on the vessel Hardware, operating system, firmware, and software versions Network connections, interfaces, and communication protocols Which security zone it belongs to, and how critical it is to the safety of the ship Whether it has any remote access, wireless, or external connection An inventory with "TBD" in most of these fields is not yet an inventory. It is a placeholder.

2 "What Is the Problem?" I raised the following question with the shipyard: "Do you really consider this a reliable document that adequately identifies the cyber-related assets on board? Is this why you submitted it for approval?" The shipyard's answer was quite straightforward: "This document was prepared by M*, one of the leading cyber security SI companies in China. We simply submitted what they provided. What is the problem?" OMG. Really? Is that supposed to be enough? Just because a company is well known, does that mean its documents are always good? Is that really a reason to approve them? Outsourcing the work does not outsource the responsibility.

The shipyard, as the party submitting the document and integrating the systems on board, is still accountable for what it submits. A reputable SI company is a reason to expect a good document, not a reason to skip checking one. My decision was clear. REJECT. The problem was not the number of pages. The problem was that the document did not meet the basic requirements for properly identifying and managing the vessel's cyber-related assets. What is even more surprising is that the shipyard did not seem to understand what was wrong with the document. They simply forwarded the material they had received from the SI company to the shipowner without any proper review.

To make matters worse, some of my fellow colleagues on the owner's side also seem unsure whether the document is acceptable or completely inadequate, or whether they should approve it as submitted or raise comments. 3 A Vessel Asset Inventory Is Not Just a List of System Names A Vessel Asset Inventory is not just a list of system names. It should help us understand what assets are installed on board, how they are connected, and which assets need to be considered from a cyber security perspective. It is one of the basic documents needed to support the risk assessment and the development of appropriate security measures.

Every other cyber security document for the vessel is built on top of it: Vessel Asset Inventory → Zones & Conduit Diagram → Risk Assessment → Security Measures → Test Procedures → Operation & Surveys If the inventory itself is incomplete or unreliable, how can we have confidence in the risk assessment and other cyber security documents built on top of it? 4 What I Expect from Shipyards: A Problem-Solving Attitude Chinese shipyards build some of the largest and most advanced vessels in the world. Their cyber security documentation should meet the same standard as their steel and machinery.

From the superintendent's side, this is what I would like to see when a document is rejected: 1 Own the document, even when an SI prepares it Assign a responsible engineer at the shipyard who reviews every SI deliverable against the actual vessel before it is submitted, and who can answer technical questions about it. 2 Answer comments with substance, not with a company name A reply such as "M* prepared it" does not resolve a comment. A revised document with the missing information does. 3 Collect equipment data from makers early Versions, interfaces, ports, and protocols come from the equipment makers. Request them at the purchase-specification stage, not one month before delivery.

4 Check the inventory against the real ship Compare the document with the as-built configuration on board. Anything marked "pending" should have an owner and a date. 5 Keep all cyber documents consistent The inventory, Zones and Conduit Diagram, and test procedures must describe the same ship. When one changes, the others must be updated. 6 Treat comments as joint work, not as an obstacle Regular technical meetings among the shipyard, SI company, owner, and class society will close issues faster than exchanging rejected documents. 7 Hand over a document we can maintain After delivery, the owner must keep the inventory up to date for the life of the vessel.

Deliver it in a form that can actually be maintained. 5 What Will Happen If We Let It Pass A weak inventory rarely causes a problem on the day it is approved. The problems appear later, when they are more expensive and harder to fix: ! Risk assessment and security zones built on the wrong baseline Assets that are missing from the inventory are missing from the risk assessment too, so they receive no protection. ! Late findings at commissioning, sea trials, or class survey Equipment that was never documented is discovered during testing. That means rework, retesting, and pressure on the delivery schedule. !

Repeated across sister vessels In a series project, the same incomplete document is copied to every ship in the series, and so is every gap. ! No baseline for vulnerability and patch management When a vulnerability is announced for a particular firmware version, the owner cannot tell which ships or systems are affected. ! Slower incident response During a cyber incident, the crew cannot isolate devices or connections that nobody knew were there. ! Hidden remote access and external connections Undocumented remote-maintenance links or vendor connections remain open as attack paths into the ship's systems. !

Responsibility disputes after delivery When an issue appears in operation, nobody can say whether it was in the scope of the original approval, and the cost moves to the owner. By then, fixing the problem means work on a ship in service, not a revision on paper. 6 To Shipowners and Classification Societies To shipowners and classification societies involved in newbuilding projects in China, I would like to make one point very clear. Do not approve cyber security documents simply because they have been submitted by the shipyard or prepared by a well-known SI company.

Check whether the documents properly reflect the actual vessel, whether the required technical information is included, and whether the contents are consistent with the other cyber security documents. If something is missing or inadequate, raise your comments and ask for proper revisions. You may also receive a Vessel Asset Inventory that is only three pages long. If such a document is approved without a proper technical review, important asset information may remain unidentified or undocumented. This can create serious problems later when assessing cyber risks and determining the security measures needed to protect the vessel. Approval should not be just a formality.

Someone needs to check the document properly and make sure it meets the actual requirements. Our responsibility does not end when we put an approval stamp on a document. If the document has not been properly reviewed, its shortcomings may only become apparent later, when the vessel is in operation. Raising comments is not about being difficult. A clear, early comment costs the shipyard a revision; a missed issue costs everyone much more after delivery. This is the first issue I have encountered while reviewing cyber security documentation for ships being built in China.

My hope is simple: when a document comes back with comments, the shipyard asks "what is missing, and how do we fix it?" instead of "what is the problem?" Cyber security requirements for newbuildings are only getting stricter, and the shipyards that build this capability now will be the ones owners trust with their next projects. If that capability is not yet available in-house or locally, bring in people who have it. I have a strong message for Chinese shipyards and shipowners: Hire a competent cyber security SI company of Korea. More to come. ps. I'm going absolutely crazy dealing with the cyber security issues between Chinese shipyards and Chinese SI companies. It's driving me insane!

If the class society approves this document without raising a single comment, I'm seriously going to lose my mind! Related Reading: OT Asset Management for Ships Zones and Conduit Diagram: Establishing the Vessel's Security-Zone Architecture (IACS UR E26 Compliance Series · Article 2 of 7) IACS UR E26/E27: Two Years of Survey Practice — A Class Surveyor's Inside View Why Most Ship ZCDs Fail — Seven Common Mistakes in IACS UR E26/E27 Projects About the Author Jack Superintendent · M** (M** Shipping Company) Marine electrical & automation specialist: from equipment maker and shipyard design offices to the shipowner's side of newbuilding approval.

20+ Years in marine electrical & automation 8 Shipyards in Korea & China 5 Organizations: maker, yards, aerospace, owner Career Timeline 201* – Present M** · Superintendent Specification, new technology review & application, drawing approval, electrical & machinery survey on newbuildings at Hyundai, Hyundai Samho, DSME (Hanwha), Samsung, Hanjin, STX, SPP, and DSIC (China). Projects include the DSIC 16K series and fixed fire-fighting systems during 24K container ship sea trials. 201* – 201* Ko** · Principal Researcher AFCS (Automatic Flight Control System) control research and airworthiness certification. 201* – 201* SP** · Deputy General Manager Electrical design and specification.

201* – 201* ST** · Manager · Part Leader Led the electrical basic design part for ST** Dalian (China); electrical design and specification. 200* – 201* Ha** · Assistant Manager Electrical basic design: control and fire system design; specification. 200* – 200* Ko** · Assistant Manager Integrated automation: ICMS, PMS, CLMS, and related vessel control systems. Core Expertise Electrical Design (Basic Design) Specification ICMS / PMS / CLMS Control · Navigation · Fire Systems Drawing Approval Electrical & Machinery Survey New Technology Review Airworthiness Certification Naval Architecture Safety Management 👤 Author Profile ↗

posts.t: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, November Week 1, 2026: A Terminal Down at Le Havre, n0n's Exposed Server, and a US Deadline for Cyber Plans
c: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, November Week 1, 2026: A Terminal Down at Le Havre, n0n's Exposed Server, and a US Deadline for Cyber Plans The incidents, CVEs and threat intelligence that matter to ships, ports and shipping companies, as of 2 November 2026 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn This week's brief has one new event, one unverified claim added on 3 November, and two useful updates. The common thread: the hard questions are about recovery and basic access, not exotic attacks.

A container terminal in Le Havre stopped handling boxes for reasons nobody has publicly established, new research suggests the n0n group got in with weak or stolen passwords, and US-regulated operators now have a dated requirement to put their cyber plans on paper.

At a Glance Date Where What Status 13–14 Oct 2026 Le Havre, France Terminaux de Normandie suspends container handling after an IT disruption Cause not established 22 Oct 2026 At sea, bound for Texas Tasnim, citing Neftegaz, claims a cyberattack on the LPG carrier Botan Unverified claim 4 Nov 2026 Korea Update: Vivit Africa LNG moves to K-LNG; H-Line says its investigation is closed, K-LNG plans its own OT check Reported; cause not published 14 Oct 2026 France M-CERT warns the maritime sector of DDoS attacks Reported; no major outage confirmed 30 Oct 2026 Global Update: SOCRadar finds n0n's exposed server Researcher findings 20 Oct 2026 USA USCG NVIC 02-26: Cybersecurity Plans due 16 July 2027 Published guidance 29 Sep 2026 Global Georgia Tech study of GPS spoofing across 367,000+ vessels Research, reported by press Ⅰ.

Incident: A Container Terminal Stops at Le Havre On the evening of 13 October 2026, according to local press, systems at Terminaux de Normandie , the Le Havre container operation that Kuehne+Nagel refers to as the TNMSC terminal, began failing. One logistics firm dates the incident to 14 October. Management is reported to have confirmed a disruption to its information systems that caused a temporary suspension of handling operations. Impact Receiving and delivering goods stopped, and data exchange with partners was not working normally. Storage and monitoring of refrigerated containers continued, as reported on 16 October . Cause Not established. HAROPA Port did not confirm the origin .

Kuehne+Nagel calls it a "cyber attack", and dockworkers are reported to suspect one, but no ransomware, claim of responsibility or data leak has been tied to the terminal in the sources reviewed here. Status Kuehne+Nagel's update for 14–20 October said the terminal "remains closed", with no container gate-in or gate-out and no confirmed restart timeline. Its 21–27 October update says only that TNMSC suspended operations during Storm Austen and does not mention the cyber event. We could not confirm a reopening date as of 2 November. Workaround Empty containers could still be collected and returned through private depots, and significant congestion was expected once operations resume.

Captain Paul's reading Whatever the cause turns out to be, the operational picture is the same. When a terminal system stops, gate and transhipment work stop with it. The detail I would keep is that reefer monitoring reportedly continued, which shows someone had thought about what must keep running. Ship operators calling at any single-terminal port should ask what their booking and cargo plan looks like if that terminal is dark for days. And please don't repeat "cyberattack" as fact yet: nobody with the evidence has said so publicly. Ⅱ. Claim: A Reported Attack on an LPG Carrier, and What Is Unverified Added 3 November 2026.

On 2 November Tasnim , the Iranian outlet that Maritime Executive describes as associated with the IRGC, published a report citing the Russian-language outlet Neftegaz. It says the Marshall Islands-flagged LPG carrier Botan was targeted on 22 October while sailing from Singapore to the Nederland terminal in Texas. We found no independent confirmation, and we have not read the Neftegaz original. Claimed impact "Serious disruption" of cargo monitoring and control systems, attributed to unnamed "informed sources". Claimed response The captain and owner reportedly told the US Coast Guard confidentially and were reportedly told not to go public.

No official is quoted, and we found no US government statement on this vessel. Claimed pattern Tasnim calls the series a targeted campaign against US-owned vessels. That does not match earlier reporting: Bloomberg, via Insurance Journal reports Vivit Africa LNG as owned by South Korea's H-Line Shipping, and our VL Prosperity review records Hyundai Glovis as owner and HMM Ocean Service as manager, under a Liberian flag. The Coast Guard described the two ships it boarded as foreign-flagged. What these cases share is a voyage or cargo connected to the US, not US ownership. Stronger than the record Tasnim says US agencies "confirmed" an intrusion on VL Prosperity.

Their joint statement, as reported , cites "indications" that networks were compromised by foreign actors, and reports no operational disruption. Its Vivit Africa account also goes beyond the record: the cause is not established . Kohaku Tasnim lists this ship without details. Cybernews, citing the Wall Street Journal , earlier named it as a second Texas-bound tanker reportedly targeted. No official source we read names it. Korean link The ships with public build records share a Korean connection. Hyundai Economic News reports VL Prosperity and Vivit Africa LNG as built by HD Hyundai Samho, and Kohaku by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, all contracted before UR E26/E27 took effect on 1 July 2024.

VL Prosperity and Vivit Africa LNG are also Korean-owned or Korean-managed . We could not establish Kohaku's operator. For Botan, public vessel data shows a 2023-built LPG carrier. Registry-style listings for Botan (IMO 9940966) and Kohaku (IMO 9932608) give both the same length (227 m) and gross tonnage (51,931), which suggests a similar design, but the builder, owner and manager names are not visible on those public pages. A Korean link for Botan is only a possibility. Wider context US agencies were reported in September to be tracking cyber threats against nearly 20 vessels worldwide. No responsible party has been officially named.

Captain Paul's reading Treat this as a lead, not a finding. An IRGC-associated outlet has reasons to present these events as a campaign against the US, and at least two of its details do not survive a check against other sources. It also should not be dismissed outright, since Iranian media named VL Prosperity before US agencies said anything about their boardings. The useful point for a ship operator does not depend on who is right: cargo monitoring and control are named again, so those are the logs to protect and the anomalies to report. The Korean connection deserves attention from Korean owners, yards and class, and it is not proof of targeting.

Korea builds a large share of these ship types, so the pattern could simply reflect the market. Nothing published so far points to a shipyard or to a shared onboard system as the cause, so I would not draw that conclusion. If a confirmed list ever shows a common builder, integrator or vendor, that would change the picture. Update, 4 November 2026 Vivit Africa LNG changes hands while its cause stays unpublished TheElec (디일렉) reported on 4 November that Vivit Africa LNG, the ship covered in our October article , is one of 16 LNG carriers that K-LNG, formerly SK Shipping, is taking over from H-Line Shipping.

The ship 174,103 m³ LNG carrier built by HD Hyundai Samho in 2023, owned by H-Line's special-purpose company KAISER 3 S.A. The deal Hahn & Co., the major shareholder of both companies, is regrouping the fleets: LNG carriers to K-LNG, tankers and bulk carriers to H-Line. K-LNG takes 16 LNG carriers and hands over 11 VLCCs and one product tanker. Long-term contracts and crews move with the ships. Closing is targeted within the year, subject to cargo owners' and lenders' consent. H-Line's account As quoted by TheElec: it has finished the investigation with KISA and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and the hacking and data theft described in the media were not confirmed.

An H-Line official said the company has worked out how the malware operated after it got in, and that the measurement and engine-control equipment is separated from the crew's internet network and unrelated to the attack. The ship is said to be operating normally. K-LNG's concern K-LNG did not take part in that investigation and is concerned that OT security was not examined. TheElec reports it is preparing its own OT security review of the ship within the year. Status The investigation findings have not been published. H-Line's statements are the company's account as reported by one outlet. The cause of the September cargo-system problem is still not publicly established.

Captain Paul's reading This is the first time the operator side has been quoted as saying malware got in, while also saying the control side was isolated. That goes further than anything public when we wrote in October, but it is still a statement without published findings, so the ship stays in the "cause not established" column. K-LNG's question is the right one for any buyer: an investigation of the crew and office network does not by itself show the state of the cargo monitoring and control systems.

This ship was contracted before UR E26 took effect, so the rule does not apply to it as a class requirement, but its steps make a sensible handover checklist: an up-to-date asset inventory of the cargo and measurement systems, a check that the boundary between crew network and OT really is enforced, a review of logs from the September window, and the incident records handed over with the ship. Ⅲ. France: DDoS Warning, Limited Confirmed Effect On 14 October the French maritime cyber incident response centre, M-CERT, warned the sector of ongoing or imminent DDoS attacks, reportedly attributing the campaign to the pro-Russian collective NoName057(16).

Stratégies Logistique lists French ports and maritime companies as targets about 48 hours after the Le Havre failure, and states that no major interruption is publicly confirmed for any of them other than Le Havre. No public source links the DDoS campaign to the terminal outage. We have not read the M-CERT alert itself, and because the listed organisations have not confirmed an impact, this brief does not name them. Captain Paul's reading The timing invites a neat story, and that is exactly why to be careful with it. DDoS usually hurts websites and availability for a while, which is a very different event from a terminal losing its operating systems for days.

Treat them as two separate things until someone shows they are connected. Ⅳ. Update: What n0n's Exposed Server Shows The October Week 4 brief covered n0n listing 38 maritime organisations on 12 October. On 30 October The Register reported that SOCRadar had found the operator's own server left open, with 1,719 files including attack scripts and ransomware source code. Access SOCRadar's CISO is quoted: "In every documented compromise in this investigation, access relied on weak or stolen credentials." Methods included RDP scanning, FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing, an exposed AWS key and reused hosting portal sessions.

It found no evidence of vulnerability exploitation in the cases examined. Scale The group has claimed 108 victims since appearing in September. The server shows attempts against 23 organisations in 14 countries. Maritime listings The report says none of the 38 were marked settled, no payment addresses showed transactions, and all the data was published. It links at least 21 to customers of the maritime software provider CyberLogitec, which has not confirmed an intrusion. Demands Now reported as USD 400 thousand to USD 28 million. The October Week 4 brief carried two other ranges (USD 400 thousand–400 million from Cydome and USD 2.4–14 million from SOCRadar via trade press).

The figures remain unreconciled. AI use More than USD 7,216 on AI services by 22 October, using an open-source coding agent. Attribution is not settled: the group is believed to be Russia-based, but the server gave no definitive evidence. Captain Paul's reading Note the limit: these findings describe the cases on that server, and they do not tell us how the maritime data was obtained. The single-vendor theory remains unconfirmed. Still, the practical lesson is plain. Spending on AI did not make this actor sophisticated, and strong authentication on VPN and remote access would have made most of the routes it documents much harder. That work costs far less than a new security product. Ⅴ.

Rules: USCG Puts a Date on Cybersecurity Plans The US Coast Guard released NVIC 02-26 , implementation guidance for its 2025 cyber rule (33 CFR Part 101, Subpart F), republished by Maritime Executive on 20 October . It applies to owners and operators of US-flagged vessels, facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities regulated under MTSA. Deadline Cybersecurity Officer designations, Cybersecurity Assessments and Cybersecurity Plans completed and submitted by 16 July 2027 . Enclosures Plan development, a sample officer designation letter, penetration testing guidance, and an optional NIST CSF-based scoping method.

Worth noting Penetration testing is not required in the initial plan submission. There is no requirement to hire a third party for the assessment or plan. The requirements are performance-based. Captain Paul's reading Eight months sounds comfortable, but inventory and network documentation take longer than expected on a working fleet. Those records overlap with UR E26 work, so owners with ships under both regimes should try to build them once. I read this from the Coast Guard text as republished, so check the circular itself before relying on the details. Ⅵ.

Threat Intelligence: Measuring GPS Spoofing at Scale A Georgia Tech study published on 29 September, reported by Hackread , examined AIS data from more than 367,000 vessels between late November 2024 and early February 2025. It found 17,936 abnormal episodes involving 2,663 vessels and 31 persistent zones: 13 corroborated as spoofing, 9 newly identified, and 9 suggestive only. One finding links to a case this blog has covered. Near Port Sudan in January 2025, about five months before the MSC Antonia grounding , the researchers found vessels showing the same type of displacement, with false tracks reportedly matching the later MSC Antonia pattern in latitude to the fifth decimal place.

Captain Paul's reading The authors call their numbers a lower bound, since short or single-ship events fall outside the method, and AIS cannot identify who is transmitting.
