posts.t: Are ships safe in the era of AI hacking?
c: From Cybersecurity to the Era of Cyber Resilience The question now isn't "how do we block it" — it's "how do we survive it." Richard Principal Maritime Engineering Leader · Digital Ship Innovation & Cyber Security On August 12, I attended the Maritime Cybersecurity Conference 2026 (co-hosted by CYTUR and SecurityNews, held concurrently with ISEC 2026) at the COEX ASEM Ballroom in Seoul. Listening to Hanwha Ocean's presentation, "AI-Era Vessels' New Challenges and Responses," I realized the industry's front line is wrestling with exactly the same questions. This article is a write-up of what that talk left me thinking about.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is accelerating digital transformation across the shipbuilding and shipping industries. Smart ships, digital twins, remote maintenance, predictive maintenance, and autonomous navigation technologies have become core tools for improving vessel efficiency and safety. But technological progress brings new threats along with it. In cybersecurity, AI has recently begun to be used as an attack tool, fundamentally changing the security landscape . Hacking is no longer the domain of a few specialists — it is expanding into something anyone who can use AI can attempt. Ⅰ.

AI Has Changed the Paradigm of Hacking In the past, cyberattacks demanded a high level of technical skill. An attacker had to understand a system's architecture, analyze its vulnerabilities, and write attack code by hand. This technical barrier to entry naturally limited attackers to specific nation-state organizations, criminal groups, and professional hacker crews. But that changed dramatically with the arrival of generative AI. AI can now automatically carry out tasks like network reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, exploit-code generation, and attack-path discovery. Work that once took months of study and experience is now achievable with natural-language instructions alone.

An attacker can acquire a meaningful level of offensive capability simply by describing a goal to AI — without understanding the technical details underneath it. There have already been reported cases of AI services being used to carry out real intrusions against government agencies and financial institutions. Attackers used AI to automate the entire attack chain — reconnaissance, vulnerability analysis, account takeover, and data exfiltration — resulting in large volumes of personal and administrative data leaking outside the organization. Cases like this show that AI can be used as more than a productivity tool — it can amplify an attacker's own capability . Ⅱ.

What the Shift in Who Attacks Actually Means The biggest change in the AI era isn't the attack method — it's who is attacking . In the past, an attacker's expertise determined the level of threat. Now, with AI performing a large share of the attack tradecraft itself, an environment is emerging where even people without much technical skill can attempt an attack. The core element of hacking is shifting from skill to intent. This means an explosive increase in attempted attacks.

Where a small number of specialized groups once targeted a limited set of objectives, going forward it's likely that a much broader, unspecified range of actors will attempt attacks against a much broader range of targets. It's not just the quality of attacks that rises — it's the sheer volume. Because AI can attack multiple targets simultaneously, mass, automated attacks are expected to increase more than narrowly targeted attacks against a specific company or a specific vessel. An even more concerning point is that AI can now understand the specialized protocols used in the maritime domain.

In the past, a lack of knowledge about shipboard communication systems and automation systems made this domain genuinely hard to access — but AI is now reaching a level where it can analyze these protocols and generate attack code from publicly available technical documentation alone. Ⅲ. Why Hacking a Ship Is Dangerous In a typical enterprise environment, a cyberattack often leads to data leakage, service disruption, or financial loss. That's serious enough on its own — but a ship is a different situation. A ship's digital systems are directly connected to the operational technology (OT) environment that controls its physical equipment.

Navigation systems, engine automation systems, power management systems, and cargo management systems are all connected over the network — and if any of these systems is attacked, it can turn into a physical accident. For example, if a navigation system is manipulated, a ship could follow the wrong course or run aground. If an engine system is compromised, the vessel could lose propulsion and drift at sea. If a power system is disabled, the entire ship could lose electrical power. If a cargo management system is attacked, cargo damage or a stability problem could trigger a safety incident. In the end, onshore you lose data — but on a ship, you can lose propulsion, steering, and power.

That's a fundamentally different kind of risk. The defining feature of ship security is that a cyberattack can turn directly into a safety incident. Ⅳ. Main Attack Paths That Target Ships Most attacks against ships follow a fairly consistent process.

Initial intrusion — remote maintenance channels, satellite communication links, USB storage devices, crew members' personal devices ↓ Lateral movement onboard — from the information technology (IT) domain into the operational technology (OT) domain ↓ Privilege escalation and bypassing security controls ↓ Taking over automation and control systems — manipulating sensor data/control signals, disabling alarm systems ↓ Physical impact — reduced propulsion, steering abnormalities, unstable power supply These outcomes can escalate into serious incidents such as collisions, groundings, or disruption to port operations. Ⅴ.

New Security Threats in the AI Era As AI begins to be used in ship operations, new kinds of attacks are emerging as well. Prompt Injection — an attack technique that feeds malicious instructions to an AI system to make it bypass existing security policies. As AI becomes more deeply embedded in ship operations, this could become a very significant threat. Data Poisoning — a method where an attacker deliberately manipulates sensor or voyage data so that AI learns from corrupted information. If location or navigation-related data is poisoned, AI becomes far more likely to make a dangerous decision.

Errors in AI-Generated Control Logic — as equipment manufacturers increasingly use AI to develop control software, there is a real possibility that unverified code ends up running actual ship operations. There is also a growing concern that multiple AI agents operating independently could create unauthorized data exchanges or hidden communication channels. Ⅵ. From Cybersecurity to Cyber Resilience In the AI era, a defense-only security strategy is no longer enough. Blocking attacks still matters, but the ability to keep operating safely and recover quickly once an attack has already happened is becoming just as important. This is what's known as Cyber Resilience .

Building cyber resilience requires the following, in parallel: Incorporating AI-driven attack scenarios into risk-analysis processes Defining AI agents themselves as managed assets and continuously monitoring them Building a Human-in-the-Loop framework that requires human approval for critical control commands Verifying the integrity of AI training data, building anomaly-based detection capability, and strengthening supply-chain security Security needs to go beyond simply blocking outside intrusions — it has to be designed so a ship's core functions keep working even under attack. Ⅶ. Conclusion AI is a core technology that will determine the future competitiveness of the shipping industry.

But at the same time, AI is becoming a new threat that lowers the barrier to hacking and expands the scale of attacks. Attackers are no longer only professional hackers — anyone who can use AI is a potential threat actor. The shipping industry can no longer afford to think only about "how do we block an attack." It also has to think about "how do we keep operating safely even after an attack happens." Going forward, competitiveness won't be decided by the company with the strongest shield — it will be decided by the company with the resilience to survive safely, no matter what kind of attack it faces.

posts.t: How Can a Functional Description in a Manual Be Converted into a Reproducible Test Procedure?
c: How Can a Functional Description in a Manual Be Converted into a Reproducible Test Procedure? Article 8 of a 12-Part Series on UR E27 Strategies for Marine Equipment Suppliers ※ The product examples, Test Case IDs, setting values, and file names described in this article are illustrative examples created to explain how a reproducible UR E27 Test Procedure can be structured. Blue Horizonist (Lew) Maritime & Cyber Security Consultant · ISP Consultant The previous article examined how a statement that a function has been implemented in a product can be converted into verifiable Evidence by linking the applicable requirement, product design, Configuration, and test results.

Among these elements, the Test Procedure is one of the areas that generates the most rework in actual projects. Equipment manufacturers may assume that cybersecurity tests can be prepared without significant difficulty by referring to existing FAT procedures or user manuals. A manual, however, explains how to use a product, while an FAT procedure is primarily intended to confirm that the product's operational functions perform normally. UR E27-related cybersecurity tests may need to verify not only normal operation but also access denial, failure handling, potential bypasses, Event logging, and recovery behavior.

How Can a Functional Description in a Manual Be Converted into a Reproducible Test Procedure? For example, assume that the manual includes the following statement: "Users can log in to the system by entering an ID and Password." Testing this statement should not end with confirming that a valid user can log in successfully. It may also be necessary to verify whether accessible functions are differentiated by user role, what restrictions are applied after repeated incorrect Password entries, whether changes in account status are recorded in the Log, and which privileges are required to recover a locked account.

Preparing a Test Procedure is therefore not a matter of converting sentences from a manual into a sequence of test steps. It requires translating requirements into verification objectives and then defining those objectives as repeatable actions and observable results. This article examines how to define Test Case preconditions, test steps, expected results, acceptance criteria, failure conditions, restoration procedures, and objective test records based on the Product Baseline and the Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix.

※ In this article, a Test Procedure means a procedure that defines the test target, test environment, preconditions, test steps, expected results, acceptance criteria, and restoration method. A Test Record means a record of the actual actions performed, results obtained, Screenshots, Logs, and determinations made in accordance with that procedure. The specific test scope and classification society witnessing requirements should be confirmed against the applicable classification society's Rules and Guidance and the project-specific approval conditions.

1 The Purpose of a Test Procedure Is to Enable Another Tester to Confirm the Same Result A good Test Procedure should allow a person who did not develop the product to perform the same actions under defined conditions and confirm the same results. A procedure that can be understood only by its author or that depends heavily on the tester's experience lacks reproducibility. The following statements indicate the general direction of a test but are not sufficient for actual execution. Verify the user authentication function. Test whether unnecessary Ports are blocked. Confirm that Backup and Restore are performed correctly. Confirm that Remote Access is securely controlled.

Confirm that security Events are recorded in the Log. For example, the statement "test whether unnecessary Ports are blocked" does not identify which Interface on which equipment should be tested, which Ports should be permitted or blocked, which Tool should be used, or whether a lack of response can be interpreted as evidence that the Port has been blocked. A reproducible procedure should define at least the following information.

Test equipment and Network Interface Source equipment and IP address used to perform the test Ports and Protocols to be checked Tool and Version used for the test Firewall and Service status before testing Communications that should be permitted and those that should be blocked Acceptance criteria for responses, Timeouts, Resets, and other outcomes Logs and Screenshots used to demonstrate the test result Settings that must be restored after the test The quality of a Test Procedure should be judged not by the amount of detail it contains, but by whether another tester can repeat the same test without having to make additional assumptions.

2 A Requirement Should First Be Converted into a Verification Objective Rather Than Tested Directly UR E27 requirements define the capabilities or controls that a product should provide, but a requirement statement does not automatically constitute a single Test Case. One requirement may contain several controls. Some may be confirmed through document review or analysis, while others may require product testing or vessel integration testing. The test target should therefore be developed through the following sequence in the Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix.

Requirement → Control Implemented in the Product → Verification Objective → Verification Method → Test Case → Result Evidence For example, requirements related to accounts and privileges may be divided as follows.

Control Implemented in the Product Verification Objective Appropriate Verification Method Creation of individual user accounts Confirm that users are individually identifiable and do not share the same common account Functional test and account-list review Separation of role-based privileges Confirm that an Operator cannot use administrator-only functions Positive and Negative Tests Modification of Default accounts Confirm that the initial authentication information used at shipment does not remain in the delivery Configuration Configuration review and access test Restriction after repeated login failures Confirm that further access is restricted after the configured number of authentication failures Failure-condition test Recording of account changes Confirm that account creation, deletion, and privilege changes are recorded in the Security Log Functional test and Log review Defining the verification objective first reduces the risk of treating an entire requirement as one vague test.

3 Each Test Case Should Include at Least the Following Information The Test Case format may vary by manufacturer and project. To ensure reproducibility and traceability, however, it should include at least the following fields.

Field Information to Be Recorded Test Case ID Unique identifier that can be linked to other documents Related Requirement Applicable Rule or Requirement ID Verification Objective Control to be confirmed through the test Test Target Product name, equipment ID, and Product Baseline Preconditions Account, Network, setting, and operating status before testing Test Tools Equipment, Software, and Tool Version used Test Data Accounts, files, setting values, and input information Test Steps Specific actions to be performed by the tester in sequence Expected Results Product response that should be observed at each step Acceptance Criteria Objective conditions for determining Pass or Fail Result Records Screenshots, Logs, Configuration Exports, and measured values Restoration Procedure Method for returning the product to its normal state after testing Related Evidence Identification of the Test Record and supporting attachments Not every Test Case requires a lengthy explanation.

However, the conditions and criteria required to evaluate the result should not be omitted. 4 Preconditions Should Include Enough Information to Reproduce the State of the Test Target Even when the same test procedure is used, the result may differ if the pre-test Configuration is different.

Preconditions should therefore record the states that may affect the test rather than merely state that "the system shall be operating normally." Product Baseline ID Hardware, Software, and Firmware Versions Applied Patches and Builds Network connection status and IP addresses Enabled Ports, Protocols, and Services Firewall Rules User accounts and roles Password Policy and login-failure restriction values Time-synchronization status Log storage location and remaining capacity Backup files and test data Activation status of Remote Access and optional functions For example, if a repeated-login-failure test is performed without first confirming that the account lockout threshold is set to five attempts, blocking the sixth login attempt does not necessarily demonstrate that the designed control operated correctly.

Preconditions are not only a preparation checklist for starting the test. They are also Evidence of the Configuration in which the test result was generated. 5 Test Steps Should Separate the Action Performed from the Result to Be Confirmed A common problem in Test Procedures is combining the action and the result in a single sentence. For example, the following statement is difficult to use as a specific test step: "Confirm that a general user cannot access the administrator menu." It is better to separate the action and the result into individual steps, as follows. 1 Log in using a test account assigned the Operator role. 2 Select the user-management menu.

3 Confirm that the system restricts the display or execution of the menu. 4 Attempt to access the same function through a direct URL or shortcut. 5 Confirm the access-denial message and the corresponding Security Log. 6 Log in using an Administrator account and confirm that the same menu can be accessed normally. This procedure verifies both the Operator's denied access and the Administrator's authorized access. If only access denial is tested, a function that is disabled for all users could be incorrectly interpreted as a correctly implemented privilege control.

6 Expected Results and Acceptance Criteria Should Be Defined Separately An expected result describes how the product should respond at each test step. An acceptance criterion defines the condition used to determine whether that result constitutes a Pass or Fail.

If these two elements are not distinguished, the test may be left with a subjective determination such as "operates normally." Category Insufficient Expression Specific Expression Login-failure restriction Access is blocked after repeated failures Further login attempts for the account are restricted for 10 minutes after five consecutive failures Remote Access Connection is permitted only when approved No Session is created without a registered approval number, and the connection attempt is recorded in the Security Log Log generation The relevant Event is recorded The designated Log records the user ID, Event type, result, Source equipment, and Timestamp Backup The Backup is created successfully A Backup file containing the designated configuration files and Application data is created, and its Hash is recorded Restore The previous state is restored The previous accounts, settings, and communication status are restored, and the main operational-function tests are passed Software Update Only approved Software is installed Installation of a Package that fails integrity verification is rejected, and the failure Event is recorded Acceptance criteria should, where possible, be expressed in terms of observable states, setting values, times, attempt counts, or recorded information.

7 Cybersecurity Testing Should Verify Failure, Bypass, and Recovery Behavior as Well as Normal Operation A conventional functional test focuses on whether the intended function is performed under normal inputs and conditions. Cybersecurity testing should also determine whether the control remains effective under unexpected conditions. Test Direction What the Test Confirms Account-Management Example Positive Test Does the function operate normally for an authorized user under permitted conditions? An Administrator creates a user account Negative Test Is an unauthorized user or input rejected?

An Operator's attempt to create an account is denied Bypass Test Can the control be bypassed through another path or method? Access to an administrator function is attempted through a direct URL or Engineering Tool Failure Test Does the product maintain a secure state during a communication failure, storage-capacity shortage, or authentication failure? Unauthorized access is not permitted when the central authentication Server connection is lost Recovery Test Can the product be restored safely to its normal state after a failure?

An authorized administrator unlocks a locked account and confirms the associated records It is not necessary to apply all five test directions mechanically to every security function. The necessary directions should be selected based on the product architecture and associated risks. However, if the test scope covers only normal usage scenarios, it may not be possible to determine how the control behaves during an actual incident or failure. 8 Account and Privilege Tests Should Verify Privilege Boundaries Rather Than Merely Successful Login Account-management testing often ends after confirming that a valid account can log in successfully and an incorrect Password is rejected.

The more important objective, however, is to verify that permitted and restricted functions are correctly differentiated by user role. For example, if the product has Operator and Administrator roles, the following items may be tested together. Screens and commands permitted for each role Privileges to change setting values User-account management privileges Software Update privileges Privileges to delete Logs or change Log settings Backup and Restore privileges Engineering Tool access privileges Recording of attempts to exceed assigned privileges In actual testing, the privileges defined in the User and Privilege Matrix should be linked to the relevant Test Cases.

Functions permitted to an Operator should execute normally, while Administrator-only functions should be restricted through menus, direct paths, and external Tools. This approach verifies the privilege Matrix through actual product behavior rather than leaving it as a role table that exists only in the documentation. 9 Remote Access Testing Should Verify the States Before, During, and After the Connection If a Remote Access test is limited to confirming that a connection can be established, it cannot verify the approval, recording, and termination controls. The full Remote Access flow should therefore be tested in three stages. Before Connection Is Remote Access disabled by default?
Is it impossible to create a Session without prior approval? Are the authorized user, equipment, and access path defined? Are the permitted connect

posts.t: ClassNK Puts GNSS Interference Detection on the Class Certificate — What It Means Beside IACS UR E26/E27
c: ClassNK Puts GNSS Interference Detection on the Class Certificate — What It Means Beside IACS UR E26/E27 A new notation for ships that can detect jamming and spoofing — the gap it fills, what it does not promise, and why other class societies are likely to follow Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn Japan's ClassNK has added a class notation for ships fitted with systems that detect the effects of GNSS interference and alert the bridge . It is a small line in a rulebook, but it is the first time a major class society has put GPS jamming and spoofing on the class certificate itself.

For anyone working with IACS UR E26 and E27 , it is also a clear signal: the cyber-resilience rules we are all implementing do not cover attacks that arrive through the antenna instead of the network. Ⅰ. What ClassNK Announced According to trade reports published in October 2026, ClassNK revised its Guidelines for Advanced Safety Measures and issued Edition 1.1 . The revision lets ships that carry onboard systems for detecting GNSS interference and alerting the bridge receive formal class recognition through a notation, after surveyors evaluate the detection and alerting arrangement.

The Guidelines for Advanced Safety Measures are the framework behind ClassNK's "Advanced Safety (a-SAFE)" notations, first published in 2022 for technologies such as collision-risk display and berthing support. The GNSS item extends that same voluntary, technology-based approach to navigation-signal threats. ✔ What the notation recognises A shipboard capability to notice that GNSS input is being jammed or spoofed and to tell the bridge team — evaluated by the class surveyor. ✖ What it does not promise It does not mean the ship is immune to interference, nor that reliable satellite positioning can be restored during an attack. Detection buys time; seamanship still decides the outcome.

Note: at the time of writing, the Edition 1.1 text itself was not publicly available. Owners and yards should confirm the exact notation designation and survey requirements directly with ClassNK. Ⅱ. Why GNSS Interference Became a Class Issue Jamming and spoofing are no longer rare events in a few hotspots. P&I clubs now ask members to treat GNSS disruption as a foreseeable risk, and other class societies have issued circulars telling bridge teams to cross-check GNSS positions against independent means.

The two attacks behave very differently on the bridge: Attack What the receiver does Why it is dangerous Jamming Loses the fix — alarms usually sound Loud but obvious; ECDIS, AIS position and time-dependent systems degrade at once Spoofing Keeps a "valid" fix — at a false position or time Quiet; often no alarm at all. Every system fed by GNSS trusts the false data GNSS is not just "the GPS on the bridge". The same position and time feed ECDIS, AIS, radar ground-stabilisation, the VDR, GMDSS position reporting, dynamic positioning on offshore units, and time synchronisation across shipboard networks.

A spoofed GNSS input is, in effect, false data injected into many computer-based systems at once — without anyone touching the ship's network. Ⅲ. The Gap Beside IACS UR E26 and E27 ClassNK has reportedly clarified that the IACS cyber-resilience requirements UR E26 and UR E27 do not directly require protection against GPS spoofing or jamming — which is why the new notation is a separate addition rather than an E26/E27 interpretation.

This matches the design of the two URs: IACS UR E26 IACS UR E27 ClassNK GNSS notation Level Ship (whole vessel) System / equipment Ship capability (navigation) Status Mandatory — newbuilds contracted on/after 1 Jul 2024 Mandatory for CBS supplied to those ships Voluntary class notation Threat path Networks, interfaces, remote access, removable media Security capabilities of the CBS (access control, authentication, logging…) Radio signal in space — the antenna Question answered "Can an attacker get into the ship's systems?" "Is this equipment built securely?" "Will the bridge know when the position it trusts is false?" Captain Paul's reading A ship can be fully E26/E27-compliant — segmented networks, hardened ECDIS, type-approved equipment — and still be steered off course by a spoofed signal, because the attack never touches the network .

E26 and E27 protect the integrity of the systems; they cannot vouch for the truth of the data those systems receive from space. The GNSS notation is the first class-level answer to that blind spot. That said, the two worlds connect in practice. A GNSS-interference detector is itself a computer-based system on the bridge . On an E26 ship it belongs in the CBS asset inventory, in a security zone, with its alert interface to the bridge documented — and, depending on the class society's categorisation, the supplier may need to show E27 capabilities for it. In other words, the notation does not replace E26/E27 work; it adds one more system that must be integrated the E26/E27 way . Ⅳ.

What Each Stakeholder Should Expect ⚓ Shipowners & managers A verifiable way to show charterers, insurers and port states that the bridge can recognise interference. Pair it with SMS procedures: who acts on the alert, which independent references (radar, visual, terrestrial) are used, how events are logged and reported. 🏗️ Shipyards A new specification item for newbuilds trading in high-risk waters: antenna and detector placement, integration with bridge alert management, and the E26 paperwork — inventory, zones and conduits, test records — for one more bridge CBS. 🔧 Equipment makers A market for maritime-grade interference detection and multi-source integrity checking.

Expect buyers to ask two questions together: "Will class accept this for the notation?" and "Can you document E27 security capabilities for it?" Ⅴ. Will Other Class Societies Follow? My expectation is yes — and faster than E26/E27 did . Class notations tend to spread when three forces line up, and all three are already moving: 1 Risk owners are already asking. P&I clubs describe GNSS disruption as a foreseeable risk; charterers and insurers will want a recognisable mark that a ship can detect it — a class notation is the easiest proof to put in a contract or a vetting form. 2 Other class societies are already issuing guidance.

Operational circulars on spoofing and jamming (for example IRClass's 2026 technical circular) are the usual first step; a voluntary notation is the natural second step, as it was for cyber notations before UR E26/E27. 3 The technology is maturing. Multi-constellation receivers, cross-checks against independent sensors, and signal-authentication services such as Galileo OSNMA give class something concrete to evaluate. The risk to watch If every society writes its own GNSS notation with different criteria, makers will face the same fragmentation they faced with cyber notations before IACS unified them.

The better path is the one E26/E27 eventually took: individual notations first, then an IACS Recommendation that sets common expectations for detection, alerting and crew response — and, in time, a link from E26's "Detect" and "Respond" functions to navigation-signal integrity. Ⅵ. A Practical Checklist for Now Map every system on board that consumes GNSS position or time — not only ECDIS and AIS. Check whether your E26 CBS inventory and zone diagram already show those dependencies. Write the bridge procedure first: what the OOW does in the first five minutes after a GNSS-integrity alert. For newbuilds with ClassNK, ask the yard to price the detection system and notation as an option.

For ships with other class, ask your society now whether an equivalent notation or guidance is planned. Ask makers for both answers in one document: notation acceptance and E27 security documentation. Closing Remarks UR E26 and E27 taught the industry to protect the ship's systems. ClassNK's GNSS notation starts the next lesson: protecting the ship's sense of where it is . It is voluntary today and it promises detection, not immunity — but it gives owners, yards and makers a common language for a threat that has been treated as "the bridge team's problem" for too long. I expect other class societies to follow, and I hope IACS will bring them together before the notations drift apart.

Until then, the safest assumption on any bridge is simple: a GNSS fix is a claim, not a fact — check it. 012/2026 on GNSS spoofing and jamming UK P&I Club — GNSS disruption at sea: what bridge teams need to know ShipPaulJobs — Class Society Cyber Guidelines: IACS UR E26 & E27 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security Specialises in OT/IT cyber security and IACS regulatory analysis for the shipping and shipbuilding industries. Tracks how class societies interpret UR E26/E27 and turns new class rules into practical guidance for owners, shipyards and equipment makers. 📋 More Compliance Articles ↗

posts.t: Paper Review: Agentic Software - How AI Agents Are Restructuring the Software Paradigm (Cao, 2026)
c: Agentic Software: How AI Agents Are Restructuring the Software Paradigm Paper review · Zhenfeng Cao · arXiv preprint, June 2026 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security Most articles about AI coding tools ask how much faster programmers can work. This paper asks something bigger: if an AI can decide what to do while it runs, is it still the kind of software we have known for fifty years? The answer is interesting, but the most useful part for our industry is a warning buried in the evidence. AI agents that do well on a single task become much less reliable when the work carries on over time, and ship systems stay in service for decades.

Paper Details Title Agentic Software: How AI Agents Are Restructuring the Software Paradigm Version 1, shown here, was titled "The End of Software Engineering". Author Zhenfeng Cao, Lingxi Intelligent Investment (Shenzhen) Development Co., Ltd. Status arXiv preprint, cs.SE and cs.AI. Submitted 4 June 2026, revised 10 June 2026 (v2). 15 pages. License CC BY 4.0 Source arXiv:2606.05608 ↗ 🔍 (1) The Big Idea in Plain Words Think of traditional software as a procedure manual written ashore. Programmers think through the situations in advance and write down the rules, and the computer follows those rules exactly.

If something happens that the manual does not cover, a person has to come back and rewrite it. An AI agent works more like a duty officer who is given a goal and some equipment, then decides the next step as the situation unfolds. Technically, Zhenfeng Cao describes an agent as four parts working together: a large language model (the kind of AI behind today's chatbots) that does the reasoning, tools it can use, a memory, and a planner. It may even write a small piece of code to get a job done and then throw that code away. That comparison with a manual and a duty officer is ours, not the author's, but it captures the paper's main point. In traditional software the code holds the decisions.

In agentic software the decisions are made while the system is running, and code becomes something closer to a disposable tool. Cao argues that this is a change in what software is, and not merely a faster way of writing it. The paper proposes a name for the new field, "Agentic Engineering", a term the paper credits to LangChain, a company that builds tools for AI agents. ⚙️ (2) Why the Author Sees This Change as Unavoidable The argument begins with complexity. Every time you add a component to a system, the number of ways the components can interact grows much faster than the number of components. The paper gives a mathematical upper limit for this.

With only 10 components, there could in theory be 2 to the power of 45 different interaction patterns, which is more than 35 trillion. Human ability to understand a system, meanwhile, stays roughly the same. Cao's conclusion is that people will eventually hit a ceiling, while an AI's capacity can keep growing as more computing power goes into training it. The paper then places this in a short history of how software reaches its users. First we bought licensed programs and ran them ourselves, so the user carried the burden of keeping them working. Then came online subscription services (SaaS), where the vendor took on that burden.

Cao now sees a third step, called Agent-as-a-Service, where the agent itself does the work and the customer pays for the result. Each step moves more of the complexity away from the customer. People do not disappear in this picture, but their job changes. Instead of writing every instruction, they explain clearly what they want, oversee the overall design, judge the quality of the result and take responsibility for the ethical decisions. In the paper's framing, the human states the intent, the agent does the work and the human audits it. 📊 (3) What the Evidence Really Says This is the part of the paper most worth reading, because the results point in different directions.

Note that these numbers come from other researchers' studies, which the paper brings together. Start with the good news. In a pilot reported from LangChain, a team of cooperating agents was applied to more than 20 enterprise debugging workflows. The time needed to find the root cause of a problem fell by 93%, saving over 200 engineering hours in one month. That is impressive, but debugging is a clearly bounded job, and a pilot is not the same as an independent test. Next comes a more modest result. SWE-bench Verified is a widely used test that checks whether AI systems can fix real software issues.

The paper reports that one model, Lingma SWE-GPT 72B, solved 30.20% of them, close to GPT-4o at 31.80%. Progress is real, but about seven out of ten issues remained unsolved, even though each one is a separate task. Then comes the sobering number. A study called EvoClaw looked at what happens when agents keep working on software over time, the way a real product is maintained, instead of handling one isolated task. Across 12 leading AI models and 4 agent frameworks, success fell from above 80% on isolated tasks to at most 38% in continuous work. An agent can look excellent in a demonstration and still struggle when asked to look after the same system month after month.

The paper gives four reasons for this drop. The first is that agents lose track as a codebase grows beyond what they can keep in view at once, which the paper calls context drift. The second is that a small mistake in one change can spread through later changes. The third is that agents do not think about the long-term cost of maintaining what they build. The fourth is perhaps the most worrying: an agent can pass all its tests while still introducing a subtle error in what the software actually means or does.

Cao sees these as limits of today's memory and verification methods and not as permanent barriers, but also accepts that fully autonomous development is still several years of research away. 🧭 (4) Where the Author Thinks This Is Heading Cao sketches four stages. In the first, from 2023 to 2025, AI is a helper that completes code and fixes single issues while the person remains the author. In the second, from 2025 to 2027, an agent can build a feature or debug a problem from start to finish, and the person becomes the one who sets the intent and checks the result.

In the third, from 2026 to 2029, teams of agents cooperate across the whole life of a software product, and people act more like project managers, architects and auditors. In the fourth, from 2028 onward, agents discover, learn and modify themselves, while people set the goals and govern the ethics. These dates deserve some caution. The paper says the roadmap is based on current capabilities and trends, and it labels the fourth stage as prospective. It is better read as a thoughtful guess about direction than as a schedule to plan a fleet's technology around. 🏆 (5) How Far Should We Trust It? The paper's great strength is its clarity.

It gives us simple language for the difference between rules fixed in advance and decisions made at runtime, and it reports the drop in continuous work openly when it could have shown only the best numbers. Still, it should be read for what it is: a preprint by a single author, built as a conceptual argument on other people's studies. Preprints are shared publicly without having to pass peer review first, and the listing we checked shows no journal or conference. A theoretical limit on complexity does not prove that agents are required, because real systems never use every possible interaction.

The paper also cites more than 179,000 GitHub stars for a project called Hermes Agent, but stars show popularity and say little about whether something works. Finally, it does not deal with safety-critical or regulated equipment, so its conclusions cannot simply be carried over to ships. ⚓ (6) What This Means for Ships The paper never mentions ships, so what follows is this review's own reading. Even so, the four weaknesses above sound very familiar at sea. Sister vessels slowly drift apart in their configuration, so what an agent believes about "the system" may not match the ship in front of it.

One flawed change, repeated as a template, could reach several integrated systems or a whole fleet. A shortcut taken at delivery can become the owner's burden for the rest of the vessel's life. And a passed test procedure does not prove that equipment will behave correctly in every operating condition. For teams working under IACS UR E26 and E27, a cautious path follows. These are this review's suggestions, not requirements from the rules. The sensible place to begin is shore-side work with clear limits, such as helping to investigate a fault or preparing a first draft of a document. That is where the evidence above is strongest.

Anyone using an agent to draft a Vessel Asset Inventory or a Zones and Conduit Diagram should still check it against the actual ship. Agents should not be given direct write access to onboard operational systems. Whatever they propose should go through the existing management of change process, with a named person approving it. It also makes sense to keep a record of what the agent saw and did, because when decisions are made at runtime, that record may be the only evidence available to an audit or investigation. And since agents can pass tests while still being wrong, their changes need a person to review the intended behaviour as well as the test results.

🎯 (7) The Takeaway The paper's title promises a new era of software, but the number to remember is the fall from above 80% to at most 38%. For an industry that keeps its systems running for decades, the real question is not whether an agent can finish a task. It is whether anyone can still trust the system after the hundredth change. posts.t: EU CRA Series, Part 4 of 5: Proving Security, Function and Recovery by Test
c: EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers · Part 4 of 5 Proving Security, Function and Recovery by Test Turning CRA requirements into test conditions, pass criteria and evidence for marine equipment Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 For a marine equipment maker, the hardest CRA question is not "does the product have a password?" but "when someone attacks it, does it refuse, keep doing its job, and come back cleanly?" Answering that needs tests built for each product, with conditions, pass criteria and records that hold up in front of an authority.

This part sets out five test groups, a step-by-step test flow using a networked monitoring panel as the example, and what it takes to run such tests repeatedly. EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers: the series What the CRA is and how it differs from IACS UR E26/E27 The CRA in numbers: fines, deadlines and the reporting clock From E27 evidence to CRA evidence: what suppliers must add Proving security, function and recovery by test (this article) A CRA roadmap for marine equipment suppliers 1.

Why Paper Evidence Is Not Enough The CRA asks for effective and regular tests and reviews of product security (Annex I, Part II(3)), and for products that protect the availability of essential and basic functions, also after an incident, including resilience against denial-of-service attacks (Annex I, Part I(2)(h)). UR E27 makes a parallel demand from the ship's side: security measures shall not adversely affect the availability of essential systems, and shall not cause loss of safety, control or monitoring functions (E27 2.3). Both point to the same thing. It is not enough to show that a security function exists.

The supplier has to show what the equipment does when the function is triggered and when something goes wrong: whether readings still update, alarms still raise, outputs stay safe and the unit returns to normal. That means turning each requirement into concrete test conditions and pass criteria for the specific product, then analysing the results, fixing what falls short and testing again. 2. Five Test Groups These five groups cover most of what a networked marine product needs to demonstrate. The CRA references show which requirement each group supports.

Test group and basis What is done to the product What is measured or observed Pass criteria and evidence Unauthorised access and commands Annex I, Part I(2)(d) Wrong accounts, commands outside a user's rights and unauthorised connection attempts on management and control interfaces Whether access or commands are accepted; changes in settings or outputs; audit records Refused as the role definitions and access policy say. Keep the requests, responses, settings and logs.

Malformed input and traffic load Annex I, Part I(2)(f), (h), (j) Messages of wrong length, format or order; repeated connections; rising traffic and request rates Error handling, CPU and memory, response time, restarts, loss or degradation of function Compared against the protocol specification, availability requirements and risk assessment. Keep the input data, load conditions and product response. Communication loss and reconnection Availability and resilience Delay, packet loss and disconnection, then recovery Data refresh, communication-failure alarm, output state, automatic or manual return to normal Compared against the behaviour defined for loss and return of communication.

Keep the time of failure, inputs and outputs, alarms and recovery time. Update authenticity and integrity Annex I, Part II(7) Tampered files, unauthorised updates, packages for the wrong product or version Whether the package is verified and rejected; whether it installs; effect on existing version and settings Handled as the approved-package and compatibility policy says. Keep package identifiers and the verification and installation records.

Update interruption and recovery Updates and availability, risk-based Power or communication cut at each stage of download and installation, then recovery Boot state, running version, preserved settings, recovery of functions and interfaces Compared against the product's update and recovery design and functional specification. Keep the stage interrupted, boot result, version and recovery outcome. 3. A Worked Example: Losing Communication on a Monitoring Panel Take a networked measuring and monitoring panel, the kind that displays tank levels, temperatures or pressures received over a fieldbus or Ethernet link and raises alarms.

A single test run follows four steps, and each step leaves a record. STEP 1 Confirm normal state Feed known measured values and normal messages. Check displayed values, outputs and alarm states against specification. Record: product version, settings, normal values STEP 2 Inject an abnormal condition Send malformed messages, then cut the communication link or load it. Record: input conditions and the time each starts STEP 3 Check function and recovery Watch value refresh, the communication-failure alarm and output states. Restore the link and supply new values; confirm the latest values appear and alarms clear or hold as specified.

Record: product response, order of events, recovery time STEP 4 Judge and retest Line up conditions and observations on one timeline, compare with the specification, list shortfalls, fix and retest the affected scope. Record: basis of judgement, corrective action, retest result What makes the evidence convincing is that every observation sits on the same timeline as the condition that caused it. A log that says "alarm raised" is weak; a record showing the link was cut at 10:02:15, the alarm raised at 10:02:17 and values resumed 3 seconds after reconnection is strong. 4. Where It Gets Difficult 1 Deciding the test scope.

Separating what existing evidence already proves from what needs a new test, for each product variant. 2 Setting product-specific criteria. Defining test conditions, acceptable behaviour and recovery criteria for each model, configuration and operating condition. A two-second alarm delay may be fine for one panel and unacceptable for another. 3 Interpreting results and confirming fixes. Combining communication captures, logs and input/output records to find the real cause of a failure, then proving the fix worked without breaking something else. Suppliers that lack in-house test expertise often find these three steps, rather than running the test itself, the main bottleneck. 5.

Making It Repeatable: A Test Bench Because the CRA expects testing again whenever the product or its software changes, a one-off test campaign is not enough. Suppliers with several product lines should consider a reusable bench that can inject faults and measure the product's response automatically.

A typical bench has five modules: Module What it does Communication and fault injection Generates normal and malformed messages; creates delay, loss, disconnection and reconnection Signal generation and measurement Produces analogue, contact and digital input signals; measures the product's outputs Power control Cuts and restores power at defined test steps and records the actual power state Observation and logging Captures data refresh, alarms, contact outputs, boot and recovery states Test execution and reporting Runs scenarios, aligns all records on one timeline, helps judge pass or fail and produces the report Once connections, measurements and records are set up for one product, they can be adjusted for similar equipment from other makers, so the effort pays back across a product range.

※ This article describes a general testing approach. The exact tests and criteria for a product depend on its risk assessment, its specification and, once published, the harmonised standards under the CRA. ⚓ Captain Paul's Take Ship engineers already know how to test equipment for function: commissioning and FAT are built on it. The CRA asks for the same discipline applied to the moment security and function collide. A firewall rule that blocks an attack but also blocks the alarm feed is a failure, not a success. The suppliers who will find the CRA easiest are those who treat security tests as part of functional testing, recorded on the same timeline, rather than as a separate box to tick.

posts.t: EU CRA Series, Part 3 of 5: From E27 Evidence to CRA Evidence: What Marine Equipment Suppliers Must Add
c: EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers · Part 3 of 5 From E27 Evidence to CRA Evidence: What Marine Equipment Suppliers Must Add Reusing what UR E27 already asked for, and closing the gaps the CRA opens Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 A supplier that has prepared for IACS UR E27 already holds much of what the EU Cyber Resilience Act asks for: an asset inventory, security-function tests, a secure development lifecycle, update procedures. But E27 evidence was built to show a class surveyor that a system is secure at delivery. The CRA asks the maker to prove a product stays secure for its whole support period, for every version it sells.

This part maps E27 evidence onto the CRA requirements, area by area, and sets out what has to be added. EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers: the series What the CRA is and how it differs from IACS UR E26/E27 The CRA in numbers: fines, deadlines and the reporting clock From E27 evidence to CRA evidence: what suppliers must add (this article) Proving security, function and recovery by test A CRA roadmap for marine equipment suppliers 1. Start From What You Already Have UR E27 is not only about security functions.

It also requires a secure development lifecycle (section 5, based on IEC 62443-4-1), a plan for maintenance and verification of the system (3.1.7), a management of change plan (3.1.9), and processes for security update documentation and testing updates before release (5.2–5.4). Those are exactly the areas where the CRA goes further. Check this before you start. Because E27 already covers secure development, update QA, maintenance and change management, how much a supplier has to add depends heavily on how seriously it implemented those sections. Two suppliers with the same E27 type approval can face very different amounts of CRA work. 2.

Five Areas, Side by Side The table compares what an E27-ready supplier will typically hold with what the CRA requires, and names the work in between. Area Evidence prepared for E27 (typical) What the CRA requires What the supplier must add Product security functions Description of security capabilities, test procedure and test results (E27 3.1.3, 3.1.4; capabilities in 4.1, 4.2) Products meet the security properties of Annex I, Part I Compare the models, firmware versions, settings and use conditions that were tested with the products actually sold in the EU. Where existing results do not prove a requirement, add tests or analysis.

Components and vulnerabilities CBS asset inventory: hardware, system software and versions, software components (E27 3.1.1); dependent component update documentation (5.3) Identify and document components and vulnerabilities, including a machine-readable SBOM of at least top-level dependencies (Annex I, Part II(1)) Check that the inventory names every software component; define each component's version and dependencies; keep data that lets you judge how a new vulnerability affects the product.

Security testing and change Security capability tests at FAT (6.3.2); maintenance and verification plan (3.1.7); management of change plan (3.1.9) Effective and regular tests and reviews of product security (Annex I, Part II(3)) Set the scope and interval for periodic reviews and for retesting after changes; keep records per version of test results, defects found and retests.

Security updates Security update documentation, dependent-component updates, QA testing of updates before release (5.2–5.4) Secure distribution of updates; vulnerabilities fixed without delay; updates free of charge, with advice to users (Annex I, Part II(2), (7), (8)) Check how far the current release process already meets this; add verification of distribution, installation, failure detection and recovery suited to the product.

Support and reporting after sale Secure development lifecycle documents, update and maintenance guidance, user guidance including incident reporting (3.1.6, 5.7) Declared support period, public disclosure of fixed vulnerabilities, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, a contact for reports, legal reporting (Arts. 13, 14; Annex I, Part II(4)–(6)) Rebuild the reasoning for the support period, how affected versions are identified, and who fixes, discloses and reports, by when, as procedures the company can actually run. 3.

Three Pieces of Evidence E27 Does Not Give You (1) A machine-readable SBOM E27's asset inventory lists software components and their versions, but as a document for a class review. The CRA wants a software bill of materials in a commonly used, machine-readable format, covering at least the top-level dependencies (Annex I, Part II(1)). It is part of the technical documentation and does not have to be published, but authorities can ask for it. Formats such as SPDX and CycloneDX are widely used. The real value comes from linking it to vulnerability data, so that when a library vulnerability is published the supplier can tell within hours which products and versions are affected.

(2) A working vulnerability-handling process Annex I, Part II asks for a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, a contact address for reports, public disclosure of fixed vulnerabilities once an update is available, and fixes without delay. In practice that means a product security incident response team (PSIRT) function, even if it is two people: someone receives reports, someone judges severity and exploitation, someone owns the fix and the advisory. E27 asks the supplier to inform users about security updates (5.2); it does not ask for any of this machinery. (3) A support period you can defend E27 does not ask a supplier to commit to a support period. The CRA does (Art.

13(8)): at least five years unless the product is expected to be used for less, chosen with regard to how long users can reasonably expect to use it. For marine equipment, the reasoning behind that number, and what happens when it ends, belongs in the evidence. Part 2 covers the figures. 4. Where Suppliers Will Struggle Three issues come up repeatedly for marine equipment. None of them can be judged from documents alone, because whether the evidence is sufficient depends on how the product behaves. Issue What the supplier faces Product life longer than software support The equipment stays in service, but support for its embedded OS or third-party libraries can end first.

The supplier has to show, over a long period, that it can still fix vulnerabilities or swap in replacement components. Test results that do not transfer across products and settings Security behaviour and function can change with the model, firmware, communication options and ship-specific configuration. It is hard to judge how far an existing test result can be claimed for a different variant. Security measures that affect operation Updates, stronger authentication or communication limits can change response time, data refresh, alarms and control outputs. The supplier has to show both that the security function works and that the equipment keeps working and recovers.

The third issue is not new to marine engineers: E27 itself says security measures shall not adversely affect the availability of essential systems (2.3). The CRA adds the expectation that this is demonstrated, not assumed. How to do that by test is the subject of Part 4. 5. A Practical Way to Map the Two 1 List the products and variants sold into the EU , with model, firmware and configuration options, not just the product family. 2 Build one cross-mapping matrix : each Annex I requirement in a row, the E27 section and the existing evidence that addresses it in the next columns. 3 Mark each row as covered, partly covered (for example, tested on a different variant) or not covered.

4 Turn every partial or missing row into a task with an owner: a test, an analysis, a document or a process change. 5 Keep the matrix alive. Each new firmware release or variant re-opens the rows it touches, which is how the CRA's "regular tests and reviews" becomes routine work. ※ Harmonised standards for the CRA are still being developed. When they are published, the mapping should be updated to show conformity against them rather than against Annex I alone. ⚓ Captain Paul's Take E27 gave many suppliers their first real security file. The mistake now would be to start a second, separate CRA file. Map once, and let each piece of evidence serve both the class surveyor and the EU authority.

The harder part is not documents but behaviour over time: a process that notices a vulnerability in a library shipped five years ago, decides fast, and pushes a fix that does not stop the equipment working. That is where suppliers should spend their effort. Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner?

posts.t: Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner? The Gaps Shipbuilding and Equipment Contracts Must Close
c: Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner? The Gaps Shipbuilding and Equipment Contracts Must Close Equipment makers now report to EU authorities. Whether that information ever reaches the shipowner, and the ship, depends on the contracts in between. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity The EU Cyber Resilience Act now requires manufacturers to report actively exploited vulnerabilities to EU authorities and to inform their users. On a ship, the "user" is hard to pin down, part of the equipment sits outside the Act, and the timelines do not match a ship's life.

This post looks at those three gaps from the owner's side and sets out what contracts need to cover so the information actually reaches the ship. Reporting covers equipment already in service The yard, not the owner, is the buyer Marine equipment sits outside the CRA Three clocks that do not match Contracts close the gaps A notice needs someone to receive it 1. CRA reporting has started On 11 September 2026, the reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, the CRA) began to apply. The CRA's core product security requirements apply from 11 December 2027, but Article 14, which sets out manufacturers' reporting obligations, applies earlier.

This obligation is not limited to products launched from now on. The CRA states that Article 14 also applies to products placed on the market before December 2027 (Article 69(3)). In other words, if a piece of equipment already installed on a ship in service falls within the CRA's scope, its manufacturer already has reporting duties. That raises the question a shipowner should ask: does vulnerability information that an equipment maker reports to the authorities actually reach our ships? This post identifies three gaps along that path and how contracts can close them. 2. CRA reporting at a glance Article 14 places two kinds of obligation on manufacturers. Reporting to authorities.

When a manufacturer becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability in its product, or a severe incident affecting the product's security, it must notify the designated coordinating CSIRT and ENISA at the same time. Notifications go through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform (SRP) in stages: an early warning, a notification and a final report. Informing users. The manufacturer must also inform the impacted users, and where appropriate all users, of the vulnerability or incident and, where necessary, of the mitigation and corrective measures users can take, where appropriate in a structured, machine-readable format.

If the manufacturer does not inform users in time, the CSIRT that received the notification may provide the information to users itself (Article 14(8)). For a shipowner, the second obligation is the one that matters directly. Reporting to authorities serves supervision; informing users is the path to action. How this differs from NIS2. NIS2 places risk-management and incident-reporting duties on organisations that operate services. The CRA places duties on manufacturers that put digital products on the market.

A shipping company in scope of NIS2 must manage security in its relationships with direct suppliers (NIS2 Article 21(2)(d)), and the information it receives from manufacturers under the CRA becomes material for meeting that duty. The two regimes look at the same incident from opposite ends. 3. Why ships are a special case CRA user notification assumes that the manufacturer knows who its users are. Ships are an environment where that assumption weakens. The purchasing chain is long. On a newbuilding, the owner does not buy the equipment. The owner contracts with the yard, the yard buys from equipment makers, and the makers use parts and software from their own suppliers.

Apart from owner-supplied items, the buyer of record until delivery is usually the yard. Ships are not always connected. Satellite bandwidth and cost are limited, and it is hard to take equipment offline and patch it at sea. Patching follows a process. For remote maintenance, IACS UR E26 requires security patches and software updates to be tested and evaluated before installation, and requires suppliers to provide plans for, and make available, security updates to the shipowner, referring to UR E27.

In the related survey requirements, the owner must show the class society at the first annual survey evidence that patches and updates were installed in line with management of change (MoC) procedures and in cooperation with the supplier. So there is real distance between "the manufacturer informed its users" and "the fix is in place on board." Three gaps sit along that distance. 4. Gap 1: Who receives the notice? The CRA tells manufacturers to inform "impacted users," but on a newbuilding the counterparty a manufacturer knows is usually the yard. The owner or ship manager, who will actually use the equipment, may not appear in the manufacturer's customer records at all.

That can lead to the following: ▸ During construction: the notice reaches the yard and stops there if the yard has no contractual duty to pass it on. ▸ At delivery: the party using the equipment changes from the yard to the owner, but the manufacturer's notification contact does not. ▸ After delivery: a change of manager, a sale or a change of flag can break the contact again each time. The CRA does give manufacturers the option of informing all users, and provides the CSIRT as a fallback, but neither guarantees that the notice lands on the chief engineer's desk on a particular ship.

To make notices reach the real user, the user side needs to register, and that registration needs to be handed over at delivery. 5. Gap 2: Equipment the CRA does not reach The CRA does not apply to equipment within the scope of the Marine Equipment Directive (Directive 2014/90/EU, the MED) (Article 2(4)). The MED covers equipment for which flag state approval is required by the international instruments (IMO conventions and related resolutions and testing standards), and its implementing regulation lists categories such as life-saving appliances, marine pollution prevention, fire protection, navigation and radio communication equipment.

As a result, two kinds of equipment sit side by side on the same ship. MED equipment falls outside CRA reporting and user-notification duties, while non-MED IT equipment, communication terminals, remote monitoring gateways and software may fall within the CRA. Some of the equipment that matters most for a ship's cyber risk may therefore sit outside the CRA notification path. There is also an interpretive point. The MED applies to equipment "placed or to be placed on board an EU ship" (MED Article 3(1)). In my reading, whether the CRA exclusion applies in the same way when the same equipment goes on a non-EU-flagged ship is open to differing interpretations.

An owner of, say, Korean-flagged ships is better off confirming with equipment makers and legal counsel than assuming either answer. The practical conclusion is simple: regardless of whether the CRA applies, require the same level of vulnerability notification by contract for all cyber-relevant equipment on board. UR E27 already requires suppliers of newbuilding equipment to have a process for making security update documentation available to users, for example through a cyber security point of contact or periodic publication (UR E27 5.2). That is a natural starting point. 6. Gap 3: Guarantee period, support period and ship life Three clocks run at once for the security of ship equipment.

▸ The shipbuilding guarantee period: the period after delivery during which the yard is responsible for defects. It is usually short. ▸ The CRA support period: the period during which the manufacturer must handle vulnerabilities and provide security updates. Manufacturers must set it to reflect how long the product is expected to be in use, subject to a legal minimum, and must state its end date at the time of purchase (Article 13(8) and (19)). ▸ The ship's operating life: decades. These three do not line up. Who handles a vulnerability found after the guarantee period ends? Who manages the risk when equipment past its support period is still on board?

Because the CRA asks manufacturers to consider "reasonable user expectations" and the nature of the product when setting the support period, there is a basis to ask for longer support for equipment supplied for ships, given how ships are used. But that is a basis for negotiation, not a guarantee. 7. Closing the gaps by contract: a stage-by-stage checklist Contracts are the tool for closing these gaps. The table below lists the items to put on the negotiating table at each stage. It is a list of topics, not model wording.

Contract stage Items to cover Shipbuilding contract (owner–yard) Yard's duty to pass on equipment vulnerability and incident notices received during construction; transfer of manufacturers' notification registrations to the owner (or nominated manager) at delivery; how security defects are handled during the guarantee period; delivery documents stating CRA applicability and support end date for each item Equipment purchase specification (yard–maker) Declaration of whether the CRA applies; equivalent vulnerability notification for equipment outside the CRA; support period and end date; security documentation such as update documentation and SBOM; cooperation in registering the end user (owner) for notices Post-delivery service agreement (owner–maker) Where notices are sent (ship and shore contacts) and how contacts are kept current; how patches are delivered (remote or on site) and test results shared; support for class approval and MoC; advance notice of end of support and replacement options This checklist connects with an earlier post on the cyber security clause (Clause 23) of SHIP25, the Norwegian standard newbuilding contract: SHIP25 Clause 23 Cyber Security .

Clause 23 deals with the yard's own digital environment. The items here deal with security information for the equipment that passes through the yard onto the ship. Looking at both together narrows the cyber gaps in a newbuilding contract. 8. What the owner needs in place internally A notice that arrives with no one ready to receive it achieves nothing. ▸ A receiving point. Name a shore-side contact (for example, the cybersecurity function) for manufacturer notices, and link it to each ship's equipment list. ▸ Inventory matching.

Record manufacturer, model, software version and support end date in the asset inventory, so that when a notice arrives you can tell at once which equipment on which ship is affected. ▸ Patching and change management. Set the flow in advance: assess the notice, test, and apply in line with class requirements and MoC procedures. ▸ Link to incident reporting. If a notified vulnerability leads to a significant incident, and the company is in scope of NIS2, it moves into the company's incident reporting process. It should sit in the same flow as the company's external reporting matrix. 9. Closing The CRA sets out manufacturers' duties.

Getting that information onto the ship depends on contracts and on the owner's own operating framework. Regulation does not close the three gaps: the notice path, the scope and the timelines. Treat the CRA as the floor, and fill the rest of what a ship needs through contracts. That is a realistic starting point for owners on equipment security. This article is a general framework overview, not legal advice. Interpretation of the CRA, in particular the reach of the marine equipment exclusion, and the specific wording of contract clauses should be reviewed by legal professionals.

posts.t: Vivit Africa LNG: What Is Known About the Suspected Cyber Incident on an H-Line LNG Carrier
c: Vivit Africa LNG: What Is Known About the Suspected Cyber Incident on an H-Line LNG Carrier A crew reported a cyber attack, the coast guard recorded a malfunction, and the cause is still not established. Why that gap is itself the lesson. Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn In early September 2026 the LNG carrier Vivit Africa LNG , owned by South Korea's H-Line Shipping , lost access to some of its control systems while approaching Italy with a US cargo. The crew reported a suspected cyber attack. The Italian Coast Guard recorded a malfunction whose cause could not be identified. The ship left without discharging.

As of 30 October 2026 I could find no published finding, so this is an unconfirmed incident, and it should be read that way. Ⅰ. What Happened Vessel Vivit Africa LNG, LNG carrier, reported as Liberia-registered Owner / charterer H-Line Shipping Co. Ltd.

(South Korea) / Vitol Group, long-term time charter Voyage Loaded at Cameron LNG, Louisiana, for the Adriatic LNG terminal near Rovigo, Italy Early September Crew suddenly lost access to some internal control systems as the ship neared its destination, and reported a suspected cyber attack to Korean Register Off Italy Chioggia Coast Guard issued an urgent notice to mariners to keep clear; company technicians intervened 16 September After idling without discharging, the ship turned west toward Algeciras, Spain, and was later tracked near Tunisia Attribution None. Reports say there are no indications of who a perpetrator might be. Ⅱ.

Confirmed, Reported, Alleged The accounts differ, so it helps to separate them by how strong each one is. Level Claim Source Official The master reported "a malfunction in the systems used to monitor cargo parameters". The cause "couldn't be identified". The Coast Guard "intervened solely for navigation safety purposes". Italian Coast Guard, Capt. Roberto D'Arrigo, via Bloomberg Reported Crew lost access to some internal control systems and reported a suspected cyber attack. Investigations are ongoing. Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter Alleged Attackers "gained temporary control of the steam pressure and safety valve systems" during the Strait of Gibraltar transit.

Later interference with tank-pressure controls and boil-off gas management is also alleged. Crew members, via Splash247. Not independently verified. Vendor "It is too early to draw conclusions regarding the cause or any potential security implications." Kongsberg Maritime, supplier of some positioning, navigation and propulsion equipment No comment Vitol confirmed the charter and declined further comment. H-Line and Korean Register did not immediately respond to Bloomberg. Bloomberg Not established No investigator has publicly confirmed that a cyber attack took place. A control-system fault with a non-malicious cause remains possible, and the crew's account remains possible.

This article does not conclude either way. One open point: a Korean press report of 26 October ( Asia Economy ) describes an LNG carrier built by HD Hyundai Samho and managed by H-Line as hit by a suspected hack "early this month", without naming the ship. I could not confirm whether that is this same event with a different date, or a separate one. Ⅲ.

The Wider Pattern, and Its Limits Vivit Africa LNG was reported as the third suspected tanker incident in about a month: Ship Type Event Status VL Prosperity VLCC Crew-reported events during the Strait of Gibraltar transit on 7 Aug; boarded by USCG and FBI on 21 Aug USCG confirmed malicious cyber activity; no public attribution Kohaku LPG carrier Boarded three days after VL Prosperity under similar circumstances No operational disruption or physical danger reported by US authorities Vivit Africa LNG LNG carrier Control access lost in early Sep; Italian discharge not completed Cause not established US officials are also reported to be monitoring nearly 20 ships worldwide for similar threats.

See also my earlier analysis of the VL Prosperity attack . Captain Paul's reading It is tempting to connect these because two crew accounts mention Gibraltar and both ships have Korean links. I would be careful. Gibraltar is the gate for almost all traffic entering the Mediterranean from the Atlantic, so a shared location is weak evidence, and nothing public links the three technically. What the cluster does justify is a practical precaution: treat this as a live risk for your fleet while the investigations continue. Ⅳ.

Why the Disputed Cause Is the Real Lesson Whatever the investigators conclude, this case shows a problem every operator shares: when a control system fails at sea, the crew often cannot tell quickly whether it is a fault or an attack.

That answer changes what they should do next: Decision If it is a fault If it may be an attack Restart / reboot Often the first fix May destroy evidence, and may reinfect Vendor remote support Normally helpful The remote link may be part of the problem Isolate networks Rarely needed May be essential, but can affect other systems Who to call Technical superintendent Also the cyber response lead, class and flag A ship cannot wait for a forensic report to make those decisions. It needs a default it can act on while the cause is unknown. On an LNG carrier the stakes are higher, because cargo pressure and boil-off have to be managed continuously, whatever the cause of the fault.

Losing monitoring is an operational problem well before anyone proves a cyber attack. The planned discharge in Italy was also not completed. The reason the ship turned back has not been explained, but the outcome shows how much disruption is possible without any confirmed takeover. Ⅴ. Where IACS UR E26/E27 Fits The public reports do not give this ship's contract date, so I cannot say whether UR E26 and E27 apply to her, and nothing here suggests any failure against them.

As a reference for any operator, though, UR E26's Detect, Respond and Recover requirements speak directly to this scenario: Detect: could the crew distinguish abnormal network activity from a sensor or controller fault, using logs they can actually reach? Respond: E26 expects an incident response plan, local independent or manual operation, network isolation, and a fallback to a minimal risk condition. Has your crew drilled these for cargo systems, not only for navigation? Recover: are there tested backups and a recovery plan that a technician can use on board? Ships outside E26 scope have no such class requirement, but the same questions apply under their ISM-based cyber risk management. Ⅵ.

What Operators Can Do Now Write a one-page "fault or attack?" card for the ECR and CCR: what to record before any restart. Define who may authorise network isolation, and which systems must stay running if it happens. Drill loss of cargo monitoring with manual readings and local control, with a time target. Confirm that logs from cargo and automation systems are retained on board long enough to be useful. Agree in advance how vendor remote support is approved during a suspected incident. Decide who reports to class, flag, charterer and coastal state, and what they say while the cause is unknown. Closing Remarks We may learn that Vivit Africa LNG was attacked, or that it was not.

Either way, a crew faced a failing control system and had to act without knowing which. Preparing for that moment does not depend on the investigation's result. I will update this article if Korean Register, H-Line or the authorities publish findings.
