posts.t: Assessing the USCG's Unmanned Systems Test Area Policy: Three Reasons to Add Cybersecurity
c: Assessing the USCG's Unmanned Systems Test Area Policy: Three Reasons to Add Cybersecurity Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Summary. The U.S. Coast Guard's policy on designated test areas for unmanned systems (WWM 26-05) is a timely measure that pursues innovation support and maritime safety management together. Centered on physical navigation safety, it lays the foundation for a risk assessment and management framework. Extending that framework to cybersecurity, in light of the distinctive characteristics of unmanned systems, would make the policy considerably more effective.

This article sets out three reasons to add cybersecurity to the policy: for unmanned systems, a cyber incident is an operationally fatal event; their cyber resilience and recoverability can be verified only to a limited extent in the private sector because of technical and regulatory constraints; and, from the perspective of unmanned weapon systems, cybersecurity bears directly on the operational reliability of national security assets. The article assesses the policy from three perspectives, fitness for purpose, operational structure, and extensibility , and then explains why it should be extended to cybersecurity and in which direction. 1.

Fitness for Purpose: A Timely Measure Balancing Innovation and Maritime Safety On October 15, 2026, the USCG issued Policy Letter WWM 26-05. The document instructs field units on establishing designated test areas for testing unmanned, autonomous, and remotely operated maritime systems and other novel maritime technologies. It aligns with America's Maritime Action Plan , released by the White House in February of the same year, and reflects a broader view of unmanned maritime systems as a strategic sector for both commerce and national security. The policy is timely because it addresses two objectives at once. ▸ Supporting innovation.

Developers no longer face the uncertainty of seeking permission case by case and can test new technologies in a predictable environment. ▸ Managing maritime safety. Concentrating test activity in waters away from major shipping lanes and fishing grounds reduces the risk of conflict with general shipping, fishing, and recreational activity. As an example of a regulator opening the way first in order to keep pace with innovation, the policy offers a useful reference for other countries. 2. Operational Structure: A Foundation Built Around Physical Navigation Safety The policy establishes the foundation of a risk assessment and management framework centered on physical navigation safety.

Its main elements are as follows. ▸ Advance designation. Each Captain of the Port (COTP) designates test areas in advance, avoiding high-traffic routes and major fishing grounds. ▸ Extended waters. Test areas may extend beyond the territorial sea into the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), with candidate sites recommended on the basis of vessel traffic data and port access route studies. ▸ Risk assessment. A navigation safety risk assessment is conducted that reflects the operator's concept of operations (CONOPS). ▸ Records and notification.

Assessment results and measures are recorded in USCG record systems and communicated to waterway users through navigational warnings and local stakeholder forums. ▸ Operator responsibility. The USCG does not approve or certify individual systems, and it makes clear that responsibility for safe operation rests with the operator. This structure is well suited to managing physical hazards such as collision, grounding, and interference with traffic routes in a systematic way. Moreover, as operational guidance rather than binding regulation, the policy leaves room for further guidance . It provides a flexible base on which the scope of oversight can be broadened as technology evolves. 3.

Extensibility: A Structure That Can Absorb Cybersecurity Without a New Regime In terms of extensibility, the policy's greatest strength is that cybersecurity can be added without creating a separate regime. Extension does not mean building a new system. It means adding a cyber perspective to the foundation already in place. Operators would address cyber risks in their CONOPS, the COTP's risk assessment would review them alongside navigational risks, and the results would be kept in the same record systems. In this way, test areas would evolve from "places to test navigational capability" into "places to verify safety comprehensively." Why cybersecurity, then? There are three reasons. 4.

Three Reasons to Add Cybersecurity Reason 1. For unmanned systems, a cyber incident is operationally fatal Unmanned systems are operated not by people but through communication links, positioning data, sensors, and software. On a crewed vessel, if a cyber incident occurs, the crew can switch to manual operation and continue the mission. Unmanned systems have no such fallback. The very means of controlling the operation lie in the cyber domain. A cyber incident on an unmanned system therefore directly affects the entire operation. ▸ Loss of control. If remote control is lost or hijacked, the vessel cannot be operated at all. ▸ Mission disruption.

If positioning or sensor data are manipulated, the mission either cannot continue or is distorted by erroneous decisions. For an unmanned system, then, a cyber incident is not collateral damage such as a data leak; it is a fatal event that halts or neutralizes the operation itself . Cybersecurity is a precondition for operating unmanned systems. The failure of an operation, moreover, does not stay the operator's problem. An unmanned system that has lost control can cross the boundary of the test area and become a hazard in general waters. The guidance itself states that use of a test area does not relieve operators of their responsibility for safe operation.

In this respect, the cybersecurity of unmanned systems goes beyond the operator's business risk and touches the safety of the marine transportation system that the policy seeks to protect. If what a test area ultimately seeks to confirm is "whether an unmanned system can operate safely," the policy's objective can be fully achieved only when the cyber dimension is addressed as well. Reason 2. Technical and regulatory constraints limit private-sector verification of cyber resilience and recoverability Developers can verify physical navigation performance themselves in a test area.

Resilience to cyberattack, and the ability to recover to normal operation after an attack, are far harder for the private sector to verify on its own. ▸ Technical constraints. The security of an unmanned system extends beyond the hull to the shore-based remote operations center, satellite and cellular links, and the cloud. For small and mid-sized developers, building a test environment that reproduces realistic attack scenarios across this entire chain imposes a heavy burden of cost and expertise. ▸ Regulatory constraints. The tests that matter most for unmanned systems, such as communications jamming and position spoofing, cannot lawfully be conducted at sea by private parties at will.

In the United States, federal communications law prohibits private use of jamming equipment altogether ( FCC Enforcement Advisory ). Without government control and authorization, such tests cannot take place at all. ▸ Absence of standards. IACS UR E26/E27, the existing cyber requirements for ships, define their scope of application by ship type and size ( IACS ), which makes them difficult to apply as they stand to small unmanned systems. Without common test criteria, regulators, insurers, and buyers find it hard to compare or trust the test results of individual developers.

Verifying cyber resilience and recoverability is therefore an area that the market alone is unlikely to address , and one where a public role is needed. Reason 3. For unmanned weapon systems, cybersecurity bears directly on the operational reliability of national security assets The guidance explicitly lists national security applications alongside commercial ones among the intended uses of unmanned systems. Unmanned weapon systems, such as unmanned warships and swarming unmanned surface vessels, typically undergo final verification at navy test ranges.

However, the defense contractors and dual-use technology companies that develop them are likely to use civilian test areas in early development. If cyber verification is missing at the civilian testing stage, that gap carries through to the point of military acquisition. For unmanned weapon systems, cyber and electronic warfare threats are not a risk that might materialize but an operating environment they will certainly face . Recent cases make this clear. ▸ Black Sea. Ukraine's uncrewed surface vessels have significantly constrained the operating range of Russia's Black Sea Fleet, demonstrating that unmanned systems can change the balance of maritime power ( RUSI ).

At the same time, this means unmanned systems become prime targets for an adversary's concentrated interference and countermeasures. ▸ Baltic Sea. A 2025 shipborne measurement study identified attacks that went beyond simple jamming, combining counterfeit GPS signals with interference against other satellite navigation systems ( UK Defence Journal ). For unmanned systems that depend on positioning data, this is a direct threat. In such an environment, an unmanned weapon system whose minimum level of cyber warfare readiness has not been verified will struggle to establish confidence in its ability to carry out operations.

Swarm assets in particular are exposed: when a single control system is neutralized, many platforms are affected simultaneously, so the impact is far greater than for a single platform. Verifying cyber resilience and recoverability from the civilian test area stage onward is therefore the starting point for assuring the operational reliability of national security assets. 5. Direction of Extension and Participating Agencies This extension is not something the USCG's waterways management organization can take on alone. A realistic approach is to use the test areas established under WWM 26-05 as a common platform, with the agencies responsible for each domain participating together.

Direction Content Key participants Cyber test criteria Develop common criteria, adapting existing international standards to the testing stage of unmanned systems, in phases starting at the advisory level USCG cyber organizations, CISA, classification societies Cyber test infrastructure Authorize communications jamming and position spoofing tests on a per-test-area basis, and support shared test facilities that emulate shore-based remote operation environments Spectrum authorities (FCC, NTIA), Maritime Administration (MARAD) Civil-military cooperation Defense authorities with electronic warfare test capabilities support private-sector testing Department of Defense, defense and commercial developers Civil-military cooperation in particular benefits both sides.

The private sector gains verification opportunities it could not obtain on its own, and the military can confirm early the cyber resilience of assets it plans to acquire. With a single infrastructure serving both civilian and military users, the public value and effectiveness of the infrastructure itself also grow. 6. Anticipated Objections and Responses Objection 1. Cyber requirements conflict with the policy's intent to streamline. The core of the guidance is to simplify testing procedures to support innovation. One might worry that adding cyber requirements would raise barriers to entry and slow innovation instead. Response.

What is proposed here is not mandatory requirements but advisory-level criteria and optional testing opportunities . At the testing stage, it is enough to start with basic checks such as "does the system detect anomalies and come to a safe stop?" Confirming this early in testing reduces developers' overall cost and schedule burden compared with facing security requirements for the first time just before commercialization. Objection 2. Cyber test infrastructure is expensive. Who will bear the cost? Response. That is precisely why a public role is needed. Having every developer build its own test environment amounts to duplicated investment from the standpoint of society as a whole.

Bundling authorizations by test area and having civilian and military users share a single infrastructure lowers individual burdens and increases the infrastructure's public value. Objection 3. Cybersecurity is outside the remit of USCG waterways management. Response. This is a fair point. For that reason, this article does not ask the waterways management organization to take on every role. It proposes a structure in which the test areas established under WWM 26-05 serve as a common platform, on which the agencies responsible for cyber, spectrum, defense, and other domains cooperate. 7. Implications for South Korea South Korea already has a similar institutional framework in place.

The Act on the Promotion of Development and Commercialization of Autonomous Ships, which took effect in January 2025, grants exemptions from the Ship Safety Act, the Ship Officers Act, and other laws once a safety assessment has been passed within separately designated operating waters ( News Seoul ). The area around Ulsan Port has been designated as the first such operating waters, and in June 2026 the first approval for real-sea demonstration operations under the Act was granted ( Newswire ). The U.S. designated test areas and South Korea's operating waters rest on the same idea: demonstrating safely within defined waters .

The extension tasks raised in this article therefore apply equally to South Korea. ▸ Add cyber items to the operating-waters assessment. Consideration could be given to including a review of cyber risks in the safety assessments for designating operating waters and approving demonstrations. ▸ Add cyber testing capabilities to public demonstration platforms. Combining communications jamming and position spoofing test environments with public demonstration infrastructure, such as performance demonstration centers, would substantially reduce the verification burden on domestic developers. ▸ Build on the foundation for civil-military cooperation.

Linking the defense sector, which is developing maritime unmanned systems, with the civilian demonstration framework would allow a single infrastructure to meet both civilian and defense needs. Now that the United States has just launched its test area program, if South Korea is first to combine a cyber verification framework with its operating-waters program, it could also take the lead in international norm-setting discussions on autonomous ships and unmanned systems. 8. Conclusion WWM 26-05 is a meaningful first step in which a regulator has opened the way for innovati

posts.t: Maritime AI & Tech Summit 2026 Why I'm Heading to Busan on 28 October
c: 📅 Event Preview MATS 2026 · Busan Maritime AI Cybersecurity Maritime AI & Tech Summit 2026 Why I'm Heading to Busan on 28 October An innovation advisor's preview — what I expect, and what I'll be asking in every session Iaan 伊恩 Head of Maritime Innovation Division · ShipPaulJobs Technical Advisor 📍 Hyatt Place Busan Yeonsan · Oct 28, 2026 For years my work has been about moving smart-ship architecture, digital twins and autonomy off the slide deck and onto real ships and ports across the Asia-Pacific.

Every one of those projects eventually hits the same wall: the ship becomes a node on a network, and the question is no longer whether AI comes aboard but how we keep it safe, accountable and compliant once it does . That is exactly the question the Maritime AI & Tech Summit 2026 (MATS2026) , hosted by Rakuten Maritime in Busan, sets out to answer. Here is my preview: why I think this one is worth a day out of the office, and my take on every announced session. 📅 Date Wed, 28 Oct 2026 09:30 – 18:00 KST 📍 Venue Hyatt Place Busan Yeonsan Ballroom II (7F) 🏢 Host Rakuten Maritime KR–EN interpretation 🎟️ Entry Pre-registration Invitation e-mail required 1.

Why This Summit Caught My Attention I attend a lot of maritime events. Most of them treat AI and cybersecurity as two separate tracks in two separate rooms. MATS2026 is built on the opposite premise — its own tagline is “Navigating a Safe Path to the Future of Maritime” , with cybersecurity framed as the thing that guides AI safely to its destination. That framing is exactly right, and here are the four reasons I'm looking forward to it: ⚓ Three classification societies in one room ClassNK, ABS and RINA all on one programme is rare. Anyone who has worked an IACS UR E26/E27 project knows the rules are unified, but the interpretations are not.

Hearing three societies side by side — and then in the same panel — is the fastest way to see where they converge and where they still differ. 🏭 Busan is the right city for this conversation Korea builds a large share of the world's newbuildings, and the shipyards, equipment makers and owners who actually implement E26/E27 are a short drive from the venue. This is a summit held where the steel is cut — not a theoretical discussion. 🎓 Academia, vendors and class — the full chain The line-up runs from university research (Plymouth) to security vendors (Fortinet, CYTUR) to class societies and a system integrator's own R&D team. That is the whole value chain from research to rule to deployment.

⏱️ Timing: E26/E27 ships are now in service E26/E27 became mandatory for ships contracted from 1 July 2024. Those ships are now delivering, which means the industry is moving from “how do we pass the survey?” to “how do we operate and keep this secure for 25 years?” — while AI systems are being added on top. This summit lands right in that transition. 2. The Programme at a Glance The day is split into three parts: Part 1 — Building a Resilient Maritime Future (morning), Part 2 — Navigating the AI Era: Intelligence, Security & Trust at Sea (afternoon), and Part 3 — a Panel Discussion to close. Korean–English interpretation is provided throughout. Official programme (image: Rakuten Maritime).

Programme and speakers are subject to change. 3. Session by Session — My Take For each announced session: what I expect to hear, and the one question I'll bring from smart-ship projects and class discussions. The “Iaan's Pick” rating is simply how strongly I'd tell a colleague not to miss it. PART 1 · Building a Resilient Maritime Future — Morning 09:40 – 10:00 KEYNOTE Iaan's Pick ★★★★☆ The AI Transition: In Search of New Standards for the Shipbuilding and Maritime Industries Speaker to be announced · Opening remarks by Ryan Son, Head of Rakuten Maritime (09:30) The title says “ in search of ” new standards — an honest admission that we don't have them yet.

For cybersecurity we have E26/E27 and IEC 62443; for AI on board there is no equivalent single rulebook. I hope the keynote maps the current landscape (class AI guidance, the IMO MASS Code for autonomous ships, national rules) instead of just announcing that “AI is the future.” ❓ My question: Should AI assurance be bolted onto E26 as a new “system category,” or does it need its own unified requirement? 10:00 – 10:40 SESSION 1 · ACADEMIA Iaan's Pick ★★★★★ AI in Maritime Operations: Research from the Alan Turing Institute and AI as a Double-Edged Sword Tam, Kimberly · Professor, University of Plymouth My must-see session of the morning.

Plymouth has been one of the leading academic voices on maritime cyber risk, and “double-edged sword” is the right framing: the same AI that helps detect anomalies can be fooled by manipulated sensor data, and the same models that help defenders also help attackers write convincing phishing for crew. Independent research — with no product to sell — is exactly what this agenda needs at the top. ❓ My question: When an AI navigation or decision-support tool is wrong, how should the officer of the watch be trained to recognise it — and who carries the accountability?

10:50 – 11:30 SESSION 2 · CYBERSECURITY Iaan's Pick ★★★★☆ Fortinet Maritime 4.0 Infrastructure for Cyber Resilience of Ships and On-board Systems Neo Moon · Senior OT BDM / Ph.D, Fortinet Korea A vendor session, and I'll judge it by one standard: does it map to the ship, not the office? E26 asks for security zones and conduits, network segregation and protection of OT systems that can't be patched on a weekly cycle. I want to see how the architecture handles limited and expensive satellite bandwidth, a crew that is not a SOC team, and equipment from dozens of different makers.

❓ My question: With LEO connectivity now on many ships, how does the reference design keep the IT/OT boundary from quietly eroding after delivery? 11:30 – 12:10 SESSION 3 · CLASS Iaan's Pick ★★★★★ The Next Phase of Maritime Digitalization: Physical AI, Cybersecurity and Trust Kaoru Shimamoto · Project Manager, ClassNK “Physical AI” is the phrase I most want unpacked this year. Once AI stops recommending and starts acting — controlling machinery, steering, mooring, inspection robots — a cyber incident is no longer a data breach, it's a safety event. A class society talking about trust means talking about verification: how do you survey something that learns?

Coming from smart-ship and MASS projects, this is the gap I run into most: autonomy needs a trust model that class can actually verify. ClassNK's view here could set the tone for the whole afternoon. ❓ My question: If a model is updated after delivery, is that a “management of change” event under E26 — and what evidence would class expect? 🍱 12:10 – 13:20 · Lunch & Networking — honestly, often the most valuable 70 minutes of any summit. Come with business cards. PART 2 · Navigating the AI Era: Intelligence, Security & Trust at Sea — Afternoon Sessions 4 & 5 (13:20 – 14:40) and Session 9 (16:50 – 17:20) are still marked “Coming Soon,” and the organiser says more speakers will be announced.

I'll update this post when they are confirmed. 14:50 – 15:30 SESSION 6 · CLASS Iaan's Pick ★★★★☆ Floating Data Center Jung-Kyu Park · Vendor Lead, North Pacific Region, American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) The wildcard of the programme — and the one I'm most curious about. AI demand is driving huge need for compute, power and cooling, and a floating data center turns the ocean itself into infrastructure. For a classification society, it raises new questions: is it a ship, an offshore unit, or critical digital infrastructure? And a data center afloat is an attractive cyber target in its own right.

❓ My question: Which rulebook applies to the cyber resilience of a floating data center — E26, IEC 62443, data-center standards, or a new combination? 15:30 – 16:10 SESSION 7 · MARITIME CYBER Iaan's Pick ★★★★★ Maritime Cybersecurity in the AI Era: From Design to Operation Enjay Kim · Lead of Business Planning Team, CYTUR (Partner) “From design to operation” is precisely the gap I see most often. E26 deliverables are produced during design and construction — asset inventories, zone and conduit diagrams, test procedures — and then too often sit in a folder after delivery.

A Korean maritime-cyber specialist talking about the full lifecycle, including what happens once the ship leaves the yard, is directly relevant to every owner and yard in the room. ❓ My question: What is the practical hand-over package from shipyard to owner that keeps the cyber resilience program alive for the next 25 years? 16:20 – 16:50 SESSION 8 · HOST R&D Iaan's Pick ★★★★☆ AI and Cybersecurity R&D Team · Rakuten Maritime The host's own R&D session.

There are two halves to “AI and cybersecurity” and I hope both are covered: AI for security (anomaly detection, alert triage for a fleet with no onboard security staff) and security for AI (protecting the models, data and update pipelines themselves). Seeing real R&D results rather than slideware would be the best outcome. ❓ My question: How do you keep false positives low enough that a ship's officer actually trusts and acts on an AI security alert?

PART 3 · Panel Discussion — 17:30 – 18:00 17:30 – 18:00 PANEL Iaan's Pick ★★★★★ Industry–Academia–Government Collaboration for Compliance with Maritime AI and Cybersecurity Standards and Regulations Moderator: Enzo Di Capua · Marine Korea & Japan Area Operations Director, RINA Stay until the end for this one. A RINA moderator, with class, academia and industry voices on stage, is the right set-up to talk honestly about where compliance breaks down in practice: inconsistent interpretations, equipment makers struggling with E27 evidence, and owners caught in the middle. Thirty minutes is short — I hope the moderator keeps it to concrete actions rather than general agreement.

❓ My question: What is one thing each sector — industry, academia and government — can commit to in the next 12 months to make compliance easier for small and mid-sized equipment suppliers? 4. Who Should Go — and What to Bring Home The organiser lists its target attendees as shipowners and shipping companies, shipyards, marine and offshore equipment suppliers, R&D institutes and academia, ICT/AI/cyber companies, and government and public bodies. My short guide by role: 🚢 Shipowners & managers Don't miss Sessions 1, 7 and the panel. Bring back: how to operate (not just certify) an E26 ship with AI aboard. 🏗️ Shipyards Sessions 2, 3 and 7.

Bring back: architecture patterns and class expectations for AI-enabled systems. 🔧 Equipment suppliers Session 3 and the panel. Bring back: how class views AI features in E27 type approval. 💻 ICT, AI & cyber firms Sessions 6 and 8. Bring back: where maritime is genuinely different from shore-side IT. 5. How to Attend ⚠️ Important: seating is limited. Entry is reserved for people who pre-register and then receive an invitation e-mail . Submitting the form is a request, not a confirmed seat — the organiser reviews submissions and contacts each applicant individually. Register early.

● Address: Hyatt Place Busan Yeonsan, Ballroom II (7F), 1121 Jungang-daero, Yeonje-gu, Busan — a short walk from Yeonsan Station (Busan Metro Lines 1 & 3) ● Map: Naver Map → ● Inquiry: is-rs_maritime@rakuten.com 📄 View the official summit overview & speaker line-up (image) Image: Rakuten Maritime ⚓ Advisor's Closing Note In every smart-ship and digital-twin project I have worked on, the lesson is the same: a model is only as trustworthy as the data and the network behind it. AI on board deserves that discipline — useful, powerful, and never trusted blindly.

What makes MATS2026 worth the trip is that it puts the people who build the AI, the people who secure it and the people who certify it in the same room for a full day. I'll be there with my questions. I hope to see you in Ballroom II. Register for MATS2026 → Related Reading on ShipPaulJobs Prepare for the summit with these posts, matched to the sessions above. Session 1 · AI double-edged sword AI Cyber Threats (3/3): How Ship Systems Defend Against Algorithmic Risks How onboard systems can defend against AI-driven attacks — the “other edge” of the sword.

Session 2 · Ship network architecture Zones and Conduit Diagram: Establishing the Vessel's Security-Zone Architecture The E26 zone & conduit foundation any Maritime 4.0 security infrastructure has to map onto. Session 3 · Physical AI & trust From AI to Trusted Autonomy: Smart Ships, Cyber Resilience and Global Regulations Why autonomy only scales once trust, cyber resilience and regulation move together. Session 6 · Floating data center Floating Data Centers: Why the AI Revolution Is Creating an Entirely New Ship Market Background reading for the ABS session — the market and engineering case for compute at sea.

Session 7 · Design to operation Beyond E26 Paperwork: Building Sustainable Ship Cybersecurity Engineering (Ch.9) How to keep E26 deliverables alive after delivery instead of leaving them in a folder. Disclosure: this is an event preview that links to the organiser's registration page. Event details, programme and images are from Rakuten Maritime's official MATS2026 page and are subject to change. The opinions and session commentary are my own (Iaan, Technical Advisor to ShipPaulJobs).

posts.t: The Missing Layer in IACS UR E26/E27: Why Maritime Cyber Resilience Needs HSM and KMS
c: The Missing Layer in IACS UR E26/E27 — Why Maritime Cyber Resilience Needs HSM and KMS Protecting the cryptographic keys behind ship identity, secure communications and software integrity — before AI and quantum computing meet. Kevin CK Lee President & Co-Founder, Keypair, Inc. · PKI · HSM/KMS · Secure Elements A recent article on this site by a class surveyor summarised the first two years of UR E26/E27 as a shift in the centre of gravity of class survey — from verifying physical objects to verifying system behaviour. Reviewers now ask whether a security capability described in a CSDD (Cyber Security Design Description) is a catalogue phrase or an actually configured setting.

I would like to add one question that remains after the zones and conduits are drawn and the firewalls and VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) are in place: where are the cryptographic keys that those systems rely on for trust — and what happens to them when a system is compromised? 1. When the Perimeter Falls, the Keys Go With It The past two years of edge-device incidents tell a consistent story. In early 2024, chained authentication-bypass and command-injection flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure led to more than 2,100 compromised appliances identified by external scanning; attackers harvested stored credentials, moved laterally, and evaded the vendor's own integrity checking tool.

Fortinet's FortiGate — one of the most widely deployed firewall and SSL-VPN (Secure Sockets Layer Virtual Private Network) platforms, including on board commercial vessels — illustrates the same problem from three angles: Stolen configurations outlive the vulnerability. In January 2025, a threat actor published configuration files, including administrator and VPN user credentials, for more than 15,000 FortiGate devices — data believed to have been extracted years earlier through an authentication-bypass flaw that had long since been patched. Persistence survives patching.

In April 2025, Fortinet disclosed that attackers had planted a symbolic link in the SSL-VPN file system that kept read-only access to device files, including configurations, even after the original flaws were fixed. The Shadowserver Foundation counted over 16,000 affected internet-facing devices, and CERT-FR (France's national Computer Emergency Response Team) advised resetting all secrets — credentials, certificates, identity tokens and cryptographic keys. AI removes the skill barrier.

Between January and February 2026, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed a low-to-medium-skilled, financially motivated actor use commercial generative AI tools to compromise more than 600 FortiGate devices in 55 countries. No vulnerability was exploited — only exposed management interfaces and weak single-factor credentials. The actor extracted full configurations containing VPN and administrative credentials, and used AI-generated scripts to parse and decrypt them. This is not a criticism of one vendor; every edge platform faces the same structural issue.

As long as keys and credentials live inside the device's software, compromising the device means compromising the keys — and a patch closes the hole but never recalls a key that has already left. Ships face this under worse conditions: patches wait for voyage schedules and satellite bandwidth, there is no security specialist on board to judge an alert, and IT (Information Technology) compromise can propagate into machinery and navigation systems. An environment that detects late and patches late needs a design in which keys cannot leave in the first place. 2. AI and Quantum Computing: Two Halves of One Attack Chain AI and quantum computing are usually discussed as separate threats.

For maritime operators they should be seen as the front and back ends of the same chain, and both converge on one target: keys and identity . Today, AI lowers the cost of attack to the point where small operators and equipment suppliers who assumed they were "not a target" now are; the FortiGate campaign above is a live example. Tomorrow's risk is Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) : adversaries record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer can run Shor's algorithm against RSA (a widely used public-key encryption algorithm) and elliptic-curve cryptography.

No such machine exists yet and timelines are debated — but AI changes the economics of harvesting, because it can automatically triage vast volumes of intercepted data and keep what is worth decrypting later. Figure 1. AI accelerates theft of keys stored in software today; combined with quantum computing, it enables retroactive decryption of traffic harvested today Shipping meets both HNDL preconditions unusually well.

Nearly all ship–shore traffic — operational data, remote maintenance sessions, software updates — travels over satellite links whose signals are broadcast over wide areas, and voyage and cargo data for energy carriers, naval auxiliaries or major charterers keeps its value for years. Where the attack target is a signing key or a control channel, the consequence in OT (Operational Technology) is not just disclosure but forgery: an attacker who holds a trusted key does not need to break in; they are let in. 3. UR E27 Already Talks About Keys UR E26/E27 are goal-based and do not mandate any specific product, and nothing in this article should be read as claiming otherwise.

It is sometimes said, however, that E27 never mentions HSMs (Hardware Security Modules). The text says otherwise. Section 6.3.4.1 (IEC 62443-4-1, the IEC's industrial/OT cybersecurity product-security standard — requirement SM-8) requires suppliers of digitally signed software to show policies, procedures and technical controls protecting the generation, storage and use of code-signing private keys, and gives cryptographic hardware such as a hardware security module as an example of such a technical control. An example is not an obligation — but when a surveyor asks what the technical control actually is, it is the most demonstrable answer.
Table 1 lists the E27 items that touch keys directly. Table 1.

UR E27 Rev.1 requirements directly related to cryptographic keys UR E27 Rev.1 Requirement What It Asks For (Summary) What It Means for Key Management §4.1 #4 Authenticator management Protect authenticators from unauthorised disclosure and modification when stored and transmitted Keep credentials and keys inside a secure element or HSM, not in files §4.1 #22 Use of cryptography Algorithms, key sizes and mechanisms per commonly accepted industry practice KMS (Key Management System)-based crypto agility so algorithms can change as practice changes §4.2 #31, #32 MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication); device authentication MFA over untrusted networks; identify and authenticate software processes and devices Hardware tokens for remote maintainers; per-device certificates (device ID) §4.2 #38 Cryptographic integrity Cryptographic mechanisms to recognise changes in communication via untrusted networks SATCOM (Satellite Communications) VPN/TLS (Transport Layer Security) keys issued, rotated and revoked via HSM + KMS §5.1 / §6.3.4.1 Private keys for code signing (SM-8) Policies and technical controls for generation, storage and use of signing keys; HSM cited as an example Signing keys non-exportable in an HSM, with role separation and audit logs §5.4 / §6.3.4.4 Update authenticity (SUM-4) Users must be able to verify that security updates are authentic Signature verification chain anchored i

But a single ship carries dozens of computer-based systems, manufacturer signing keys, remote-maintainer certificates and SATCOM gateway keys. Who issues them, when are they rotated, and how is a maintenance contractor's certificate revoked when the contract ends? Governing that lifecycle is the job of a KMS; physically protecting its root of trust is the job of an HSM. E26's expectation that cyber resilience is maintained across the operational life of the ship is difficult to demonstrate without it. 4. HSM Protects the Key; KMS Governs Its Life Keys on a ship are not only on the ship. The most dangerous keys are often ashore.

If one equipment maker's firmware-signing key leaks, correctly signed malicious updates can reach every vessel carrying that equipment. Figure 2 maps where keys sit across shore, link and onboard layers, what protects them, and which requirements they relate to. Figure 2. Three layers of maritime cryptographic trust — existing firewalls, VPNs and detection tools stay in place; only the key layer beneath them changes Equipment manufacturers : moving code-signing keys into an HSM is the clearest way to evidence SM-8 during E27 type approval.

Shipowners and managers : a fleet KMS and PKI (Public Key Infrastructure) to issue, rotate and revoke remote-access certificates, VPN keys and device certificates across vessels and vendors. This also helps with the grey zone around owner-supplied systems raised in the surveyor's article: if owner-supplied CBS (Computer Based System) must obtain certificates from the owner's PKI before connecting, responsibility at the interface becomes explicit. Onboard equipment : designed for unattended operation, with device identity held in a tamper-resistant secure element that erases keys on physical intrusion. 5.

A Moving Baseline: The Post-Quantum Transition E27 item #22 does not name algorithms; it requires "commonly accepted security industry practices". Not naming them means the baseline moves. NSA's (U.S. National Security Agency) CNSA 2.0 (Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0) requires software and firmware signing to use quantum-resistant algorithms exclusively by 2030; NIST's (U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology) draft transition guidance (IR 8547) proposes deprecating RSA and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035; Korea's national migration master plan also targets 2035.

NIST has already standardised ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 204). Figure 3. Service life of a late-2024 newbuild against published cryptographic transition milestones Servers ashore are replaced every three to five years; a ship contracted in late 2024 will trade into the 2050s. This does not mean replacing every system with post-quantum cryptography tomorrow — most onboard equipment cannot support it yet.

It means designing crypto agility in now : hybrid classical-plus-PQC (Post-Quantum Cryptography) schemes on ship–shore links, and an architecture in which algorithms can change without replacing equipment. The practical switching point for that change is the HSM and KMS layer. 6. Five Questions for Shipowners and Security Managers at RFQ Stage 1 Where are your code-signing private keys stored, and to what standard (e.g. FIPS 140-3 — a U.S. cryptographic-module security standard, or KCMVP — Korea's Cryptographic Module Validation Program) is that HSM validated? (E27 SM-8) 2 Are device credentials and identity keys in the file system, or inside a secure element?

(E27 #4, #32) 3 Who issues and revokes remote-maintainer certificates — the manufacturer or the owner? 4 Can cryptographic algorithms be changed through a firmware update, and what is your post-quantum roadmap? (E27 #22) 5 Is there a cryptographic bill of materials (CBOM) for the whole ship, including owner-supplied systems? Closing: Firewalls Guard the Door; HSMs Guard the Keys Strengthening the key layer does not require dry-docking a ship. Existing firewalls, VPNs and detection tools remain in service; only the keys they trust move behind a hardware boundary.

The sequence is straightforward: inventory where cryptography is used (CBOM); move shore-side signing keys and PKI roots into HSM/KMS, which protects the whole fleet without touching a vessel; write crypto agility into newbuild specifications; and build secure elements into the next generation of onboard equipment. UR E26/E27 have taught the industry to demonstrate cyber resilience. The next question is who is responsible for the keys that underpin that demonstration — where they are held, and for how long. When that question appears in shipbuilding contracts and equipment purchase specifications, cyber resilience will stop being a set of documents and become part of the ship's structure.

Related Reading: IACS UR E26/E27: Two Years of Survey Practice — A Class Surveyor's Inside View UR E27 Is Already in Effect — So Why Do Marine Equipment Manufacturers Still Feel So Little Urgency? Is Our Product Actually Subject to UR E27? , a Seoul-based company he has led since January 2014 that developed the world's first NFC (Near-Field Communication)-enabled OTP (One-Time Password) & HSM smart IC card for PKI and electronic authentication, later extending into AMI (Advanced Metering Infrastructure), Smart Grid and access-control security. Keypair's current lineup includes the KeyWallet series of NFC and biometric-token crypto cold wallets. He also advises Pharmaonex, and previously served as President of Insprit (developer and manufacturer of Korea's first tablet), CEO of Reakosys Inc.

(MPEG4 (Moving Picture Experts Group-4) streaming and video compression for early feature phones), and Regional Director at Alcatel-Lucent (ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode)/IP (Internet Protocol) product marketing for telecom and broadband carriers). posts.t: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, October Week 4, 2026: A Claim Against 38 Maritime Firms, Critical Flaws in Wärtsilä FOS, and Two Port Outages
c: ShipPaulJobs Weekly Cyber Brief, October Week 4, 2026: A Claim Against 38 Maritime Firms, Critical Flaws in Wärtsilä FOS, and Two Port Outages The incidents, CVEs and threat intelligence that matter to ships, ports and shipping companies, as of 30 October 2026 Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security · LinkedIn This is the first ShipPaulJobs weekly brief. The common thread this time: the exposure sits with the vendor and the shore-side system, not on the bridge. One extortion group may have reached dozens of maritime companies through a single software supplier, a fleet-optimisation product shipped with hard-coded keys, and two ports fell back to manual work after IT outages.

Because this is the first issue, it also catches up on events from August and September. At a Glance Date Where What Status 12 Oct 2026 Global, 18 countries n0n lists 38 maritime organisations Unverified claim 26 Oct 2026 Global Blue Initiative maritime vulnerability database launched Public resource 15 Sep 2026 Global (vendor: Finland) Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard: CVE-2026-78225, CVE-2026-81855 Patch available Sep 2026 Malaysia Port of Tanjung Pelepas terminal operations halted Phased restart from 10 Sep 4 Aug 2026 North Carolina, USA NC Ports IT outage; manual gate processing Actor not identified Ⅰ.

Incident: n0n Names 38 Maritime Organisations On 12 October 2026 the extortion group n0n , which only appeared in mid-September, posted a single batch of maritime organisations on its leak site: shipping companies, port terminal operators, logistics firms, ship managers and agents across 18 countries. Listed 38 organisations in 18 countries (some reports say 37 or 40+) Demands Cydome reports USD 400 thousand to USD 400 million per listing, about USD 1.22 billion in total. SOCRadar's review, as reported in the trade press, put them at USD 2.4–14 million. The figures have not been reconciled. Deadline 19 October 2026. Risky Bulletin reports most victims refused to pay and their data was posted.

Suspected source Cydome assesses the data is likely linked to one CyberLogitec support and project archive, split into per-customer listings. At least 21 of the 38 are documented CyberLogitec customers. Cydome states this is "not confirmed". Vendor According to Cydome, citing Korean press, CyberLogitec confirmed the named Korean companies are its customers, sent them a precautionary notice and reported their systems operating normally. It has not confirmed an incident. Everything here should be read as alleged. Being named on a leak site does not mean a company's own network was breached, and some of the data is reported to be years old.

For that reason this brief does not list the named companies. Captain Paul's reading If the single-archive theory holds, this is 38 listings from one breach, and that is the lesson. Support tickets, project files and EDI samples held by a vendor can describe a company's systems in detail, and that company's own security controls never see them. Even if nothing on board was touched, the leaked detail makes very convincing material for phishing the fleet. Ⅱ. CVE: Hard-Coded Keys in Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard CISA published advisory ICSA-26-258-02 on 15 September 2026 and updated it on 24 September, after Cydome reported two flaws to Wärtsilä and CISA.

CVEs CVE-2026-78225 (server key, deployer-ng Update Controller) and CVE-2026-81855 (client authentication key, robot testing framework). Both CWE-321. Severity (CISA) CVSS v3.1 8.3 High; CVSS v4 9.0 Critical. Cydome's coverage cites 9.5 and 9.3, so check which score your process uses. Impact An attacker could deliver an unauthorised update, execute code, or extract credentials to impersonate a privileged client. Affected / fixed FOS-Onboard 5.07.0923.01 → fixed in 5.08.4052.01 Exploitation None known to CISA at publication. The attack vector is adjacent network, not internet. Vendor position Wärtsilä says the flaws "are not exploitable when the product is installed as recommended".

Captain Paul's reading The vendor's qualifier only helps if you know how your ship was actually installed, so verify it on board. An update channel is an especially sensitive place for a hard-coded key, because it is designed to change what runs on the system. If FOS is on your ships, confirm the version, confirm the network it sits on, and record both. Ⅲ. Ports: Two Outages, Same Fallback Port of Tanjung Pelepas, Malaysia. The port confirmed a cybersecurity incident affecting its operating systems that temporarily halted container terminal operations, with a controlled, phased restart from 10 September 2026.

The port handled over 14 million TEU in 2025 and is a main hub for the Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd Gemini network. A group called "direwolf" has reportedly claimed the attack on its leak site; no official source confirms that or says it was ransomware. North Carolina Ports, USA. An attack detected on 4 August 2026 caused a systems-wide IT outage at Wilmington, Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. The authority activated its cybersecurity contingency plan and moved gates to manual processing; normal gate hours returned on 6 August while processing stayed manual. It said the breach was contained with "no indication that sensitive data was compromised". No actor has been identified.

Captain Paul's reading In both cases what kept cargo moving was a manual procedure, so that is the thing to rehearse. For ship operators, a port outage is also an operational event: expect berthing delays and changed gate procedures, and be wary of "urgent" emails about them, since an outage is an easy pretext for phishing. Ⅳ. Threat Intelligence: A Public Maritime CVE Database On 26 October 2026 BankInfoSecurity reported the launch of the Blue Initiative , a public database of vulnerabilities affecting maritime systems, founded by companies including Cydome, Rakuten Maritime, ClassNK and Bureau Veritas, with MTS-ISAC participating.

It draws on vendor advisories, the CVE database and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, grouped by navigation, propulsion, communications, industrial controls and onboard IT. The most useful number is the split: of 29,505 vulnerabilities tracked, only 37 are in maritime-only systems. The rest are mostly ordinary fleet IT such as email and web servers. Captain Paul's reading Read that way, most of a fleet's vulnerability exposure is ordinary IT, which ordinary patch discipline can reach. For teams maintaining UR E26 CBS inventories, a shared catalogue like this could make vulnerability review far less manual. I will be watching how well it matches real shipboard product versions.

Ⅴ. How This Connects to IACS UR E26/E27 None of this week's main stories is a rule failure. UR E26 and E27 focus on the ship and its computer-based systems, while a vendor's support archive or a port's terminal system sits outside that scope. Two practical links are worth making: Inventory: if a product like FOS-Onboard runs on board, it belongs in your asset records with its version, so an advisory can be answered in minutes. Check with your class society how it is treated in your CBS scope. Supplier assurance: a type-approved product does not tell you what the supplier keeps about you. Ask what customer data vendors hold, for how long, and how they will notify you of a breach. Ⅵ.

What to Do This Week List vendor support and remote-access accounts; rotate shared or long-lived credentials. If you use CyberLogitec products, review admin and integration accounts first, and account activity from July 2026 onward (Cydome's recommendation). Warn staff and crews about targeted phishing that quotes realistic ticket, EDI or invoice details. Check whether FOS-Onboard 5.07.0923.01 is on your fleet; plan the update to 5.08.4052.01. Add breach-notification terms and MFA requirements to vendor contracts at the next renewal. If your company is named: verify where the data came from before responding to any demand.

Sources Cydome: n0n extortion incident likely traces back to a single vendor (15 Oct 2026) Risky Bulletin: supply chain attack and shipping companies (23 Oct 2026) Financial Ports: 38 maritime firms face $14m ransom deadline (SOCRadar figures) CISA ICSA-26-258-02: Wärtsilä FOS-Onboard (Update A) Cydome: CISA publishes its first Wärtsilä advisory Lloyd's List: Cyber attack disrupts operations at Port of Tanjung Pelepas OODAloop brief on Tanjung Pelepas (11 Sep 2026) BleepingComputer: North Carolina Ports confirms cyberattack WECT: NC Ports operating manually after cyberattack (6 Aug 2026) BankInfoSecurity: Maritime sector to catalog nautical software vulnerabilities (26 Oct 2026) Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security Specialises in OT/IT cyber security and IACS regulatory analysis for the shipping and shipbuilding industries.
