posts.t: Zero Trust for OT in the Age of AI: Concept and Execution through NIST SP 800-207 and the NSA OT CSI
c: Zero Trust for OT in the Age of AI: Concept and Execution through NIST SP 800-207 and the NSA OT CSI NIST SP 800-207 defines what zero trust is. NSA's new OT guidance says what legacy OT should do first. Read together, they show what OT defense should accelerate in the age of AI, and what it should keep under human control, especially on a ship that loses its link to shore.

Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity On 8 October 2026, the NSA released a Cybersecurity Information Sheet (CSI) titled "Hardening Department of War (DoW) Critical Operational Technology (OT) Environments with Zero Trust (ZT) Principles." It frames the urgency around AI. Adversaries, it says, are using super intelligence (SI) to automate reconnaissance, speed up exploit development and run campaigns at unprecedented speed and scale.

NSA CSI, October 2026 26 of 84 OT activities 0 from Automation & Orchestration NIST SP 800-207, August 2020 Fast judgment, approved action Policy decisions belong onboard AI is speeding up attacks. So why leave out automation? Something in the CSI stands out. DoW guidance for zero trust in OT lists 84 activities, and the CSI picks 26 of them for immediate impact. None of the 26 come from the Automation & Orchestration pillar. Attacks are moving toward machine speed, yet where the CSI does let automation change enforcement policy, it puts human approval first.

To make sense of that, the CSI has to be read alongside NIST SP 800-207, the zero trust architecture standard it cites for its definition of zero trust. 800-207 defines what zero trust is and how it is structured. The CSI turns that concept into what to do first in legacy OT. Read together, they show what OT defense should accelerate in the age of AI, and what it should keep a firm hand on. That matters most in OT that runs for decades and loses its connection, like a ship at sea. The two documents at a glance In one line: 800-207 is the design language, and the CSI is the execution checklist.

Item NSA CSI (Oct 2026) NIST SP 800-207 (Aug 2020) Type Implementation guidance (Cybersecurity Information Sheet) Architecture standard (Special Publication) Core question What should legacy OT do first? What is zero trust and how is it structured?

Audience Primarily NSS, DoW and Defense Industrial Base system owners and operators Enterprise architects at federal agencies Scope Legacy OT/ICS Primarily IT enterprise Length 25 pages, 26 priority activities 59 pages, 7 tenets and a logical model Parent framework DoW ZT Framework (7 pillars, 45 capabilities); DoW ZT for OT guidance (84 activities) Self-defined (PE, PA, PEP; 4 deployment models) Threat picture 2026 (SI, Volt Typhoon, AA26-097A) 2020 (how AI agents authenticate is an open issue) The 26 CSI activities break down as User 8, Device 5, Application & Workload 2, Data 4, Network & Environment 4, and Visibility & Analytics 3. Automation & Orchestration gets zero.

Common ground Both documents share the same philosophy: assume breach, remove implicit trust, and verify continuously. Much of their practice overlaps too. ▸ They complement existing security, not replace it. Both treat zero trust as an addition to existing security and cyber hygiene. ▸ They migrate incrementally. 800-207 describes a long hybrid period of zero trust and perimeter defenses; the CSI sets priorities with 26 of 84 activities. ▸ Inventory comes first. Users and accounts, devices (NPEs), applications and databases must be known before policy can be written. ▸ They rely on attribute-based dynamic access.

PBAC/ABAC, MFA, per-session authentication and least privilege are shared tools. ▸ Micro-segmentation blocks lateral movement. The CSI's aim to "wrap legacy assets in protective enclaves" is close to 800-207's enclave-based deployment model. ▸ Third-party access is a key risk. 800-207's example is outside providers who maintain smart heating and lighting systems; the CSI points to vendor, OEM, system integrator and maintenance remote access. ▸ Observe first. 800-207's reporting-only mode and the CSI's passive-first verification reflect the same thinking. ▸ Automated actors are an attack surface.

800-207 warns about AI and other software agents in ZTA administration; the CSI warns about the new risks that come with adopting SI. Where they diverge The biggest difference is what each puts first. The CSI puts availability and safety first; 800-207 aims for a balance of security, availability, usability and cost. That one difference drives the rest.

Dimension NSA CSI NIST SP 800-207 Remote access Recommends VPN, phishing-resistant MFA and PAM Remote assets should not need to backhaul through a VPN (network requirement 8, Section 3.4.1) Architecture components The PE/PA/PEP model and the trust algorithm are not used (only generic "enforcement points" are mentioned); centered on product categories such as AD, PAM, EDR PE, PA, PEP, trust algorithm and control/data plane separation are central Threats to ZT infrastructure itself Not treated as a topic of its own Covers subversion of the decision process, DoS, stolen credentials and insiders, reliance on proprietary solutions, and NPEs in administration Automation No Automation pillar activities; automated policy changes only after human approval (5.4.1) Assumes dynamic reconfiguration, for example via SDN and intent-based networking Protecting data in transit Availability and reliability as well as confidentiality, integrity and authenticity; encryption alone is not enough All communication secured for confidentiality, integrity and source authentication Patching Assumes patches may be impossible; compensating controls, risk-based remediation, documented exceptions Assumes assets are monitored and patched as needed, for example through CDM Migration method Priority list only Step-by-step procedure, RMF mapping, tuning phase The split on VPNs reads less as a contradiction than

A model built on reliable connectivity and, for remote sites, a cloud-hosted policy engine does not transfer cleanly to OT. Strengths and limits The CSI is actionable but structurally thin; 800-207 is structurally sound but does not know OT. Each fills the other's gaps. NSA CSI: strengths ▸ Activity numbers and outcomes are spelled out, so it converts directly into a checklist or roadmap. ▸ It assumes OT realities: unpatchable assets, limited maintenance windows, care around Level 0/1 devices. ▸ It treats vendor, OEM and integrator remote access as a major risk and calls for mediation through PAM or controlled gateways with session recording and real-time oversight.

▸ Its guidance is concrete: remove default credentials, separate view and change levels on controllers, disable unused logic, keep engineering workstations for OT use only and in locked locations. NSA CSI: limits ▸ It does not discuss what happens when the policy decision infrastructure fails or is compromised, a critical gap in OT. ▸ It is AD/DC-centric and hard to apply as-is to OT without Active Directory. ▸ It mixes in military-specific items such as B/C/P/S (Base/Camp/Post/Station) segmentation. ▸ Some activities are loosely mapped to the text. Logging guidance for engineering workstations and HMIs, for example, is tied to the DLP activity (4.4.1). ▸ Cite it with care.

Activity labels alternate between "OT ZT" and "ZT OT", reference [15] gives a different EO 14144 title from the body, and it cites SP 800-82r3, still the latest final revision, though NIST released a draft r4 on 21 September 2026. NIST SP 800-207: strengths ▸ PE, PA, PEP and the seven tenets are the industry's shared vocabulary, useful for design, procurement and proposals. ▸ It explains four deployment models and the trust algorithm in a technology-neutral way. ▸ It analyzes threats to zero trust infrastructure itself. ▸ Appendix B candidly lists gaps in the ecosystem. NIST SP 800-207: limits ▸ It barely addresses availability-first, unpatchable, real-time control environments.

▸ Its remote-site use cases lean on a cloud-hosted policy engine and reliable connectivity. ▸ Written in 2020, it does not reflect today's AI or SI threats. ▸ It offers no prioritized list of controls; its only sequencing advice is to start with a low-risk business process. If AI attacks, should AI defend? Read together, the two documents point to one answer: fast judgment, approved action. Use AI to accelerate detection and analysis, but keep humans in control of any action that touches a physical process. AI on the attack side is already in the threat picture.

The CSI describes SI-enabled adversaries finding unknown vulnerabilities, automating exploit development, generating convincing social engineering, coordinating attacks on many targets at once and optimizing paths through cyber-physical environments. Long-dwell campaigns like Volt Typhoon, which start in IT and pivot to OT, are the kind of playbook that this speed would sharpen. AI on the defense side is a new attack surface. The CSI warns that bringing SI into OT can introduce new risks and attack surfaces alongside the efficiency gains. 800-207 flagged the same problem back in 2020.

AI and software agents that interact with the policy engine may authenticate at a lower bar than humans, such as an API key instead of MFA. An attacker who tricks an agent into acting can get it to do things the attacker is not privileged to do. False positives and false negatives from automated enforcement can also degrade security posture. So the CSI did not drop automation; it tethered it. Automation does appear among the 26 activities: automated auditing (1.7.1), automated configuration management (2.6.2), and EDR automated responses decided only after system analysis (2.7.1).

But the one activity that lets automation change segmentation policy, 5.4.1, reads "automated policy changes are enabled following human approval." In OT, a wrong automatic block can be as damaging as an attack. A pump stops, a valve closes, a ship loses propulsion. The message is to place human approval at the point where an AI decision crosses into the physical world. Zero trust in the age of AI means treating AI as just another subject. 800-207 calls the entities that request access subjects, whether people or non-person entities. An AI agent needs an identity, least privilege per session, and actions that are logged and verified.

That is why the CSI stresses continuous verification across both human and non-human identities. Zero trust at sea The faster AI makes decisions, the more it matters where those decisions are executed and who approves them. A ship exposes that question more sharply than almost any other environment. Fittingly, the CSI explains micro-segmentation with the image of bulkheads in a ship. Policy decisions must be made onboard. For enterprises with remote branches, 800-207 describes hosting the policy engine and administrator as a cloud service. But satellite links drop. If losing the link locks the crew out of propulsion or navigation systems, that is not security; it is an outage.

The policy decision function belongs onboard, and its behavior when the shore link is lost must be defined at the design stage. For safety-related systems, fail-safe criteria must be set alongside it. Fit the reality of no AD. Much shipboard OT runs without Active Directory. The CSI's AD/DC hardening should be applied as local account life-cycle management, removal of shared accounts and minimization of privileged accounts. Translate military terms into maritime ones. The CSI's B/C/P/S segmentation can be reread as tiered segmentation across fleet, vessel and shore. The CSI approach to remote access is the realistic one.

That means VPN plus PAM, phishing-resistant MFA, session recording and time-bound approval. The gap with 800-207's no-backhaul principle can be explained as a choice that reflects OT reality. Keep automatic blocking behind human approval. An automatic block during a voyage is itself a safety risk. The CSI's choice to allow automated policy changes only after human approval carries even more weight at sea. Putting it to work The most effective approach is to use three layers: 800-207 for the design language, the CSI for the order of execution, and IACS UR E26/E27 for the mandatory baseline. ▸ Split the roles.

Write architecture and proposals in 800-207 terms; build detailed items and priorities from the 26 CSI activities. Zero trust is not an E26/E27 requirement, so position it accurately as a beyond-compliance maturity roadmap. ▸ Map to E26/E27. Start with the CSI activities where the fit is clear: asset inventory (2.1.1, 3.1.1), zones and segmentation (5.3.1, 5.4.1), remote access (1.2.2, 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 1.5.1), and network and endpoint monitoring (2.7.1, 7.1.2). ▸ Link to test stages. The CSI's rule of passive verification first and active testing only in approved maintenance windows lines up with the shipbuilding test stages used in industry practice (FAT, HAT, SAT).

Confine active testing of Level 0/1 devices to the shipyard stage. ▸ Follow 800-207 for the migration procedure. Move through actors, assets, processes, policies, solution selection, reporting-only deployment and expansion, and fill each stage's scope with the 26 CSI activities. ▸ Start with whoever provides remote maintenance. The CSI names vendor, OEM and integrator remote access as a common vector in confirmed OT intrusions. A provider that first puts PAM, session recording, time-bound approval and phishing-resistant MFA in place becomes a verified third party in the shipowner's eyes. ▸ Don't overstate applicability. The CSI is written primarily for U.S.

NSS, DoW and the Defense Industrial Base. For commercial shipping, cite it as current U.S. government OT practice guidance. For shipyards in the defense supply chain, such as U.S. Navy MRO, it can serve as a direct reference. Closing thoughts NIST published SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, six years ago. The 2026 CSI answers where legacy OT should begin while AI accelerates attacks, and it ties automated policy changes to human approval. The remaining question sits where the CSI is silent and 800-207 leaves only an open research question. Whether a decision comes from AI or from a person, who makes the policy call, and where, on a ship that has lost its link to shore?

Any discussion of zero trust for maritime cybersecurity in the age of AI has to start there. This article is a personal reading of two public documents. Mappings and maritime applications are the author's interpretation, not an official position of any regulator or classification society. Sources · NSA, Hardening Department of War (DoW) Critical Operational Technology (OT) Environments with Zero Trust (ZT) Principles , U/OO/6070841-26, Ver. 1.0, October 2026 · NSA, Press release: NSA Releases Zero Trust Guidance for Protecting Operational Technology Systems , 8 October 2026 · NIST, SP 80

posts.t: How Can a Statement That a Function Exists Be Converted into Verifiable Evidence?
c: How Can a Statement That a Function Exists Be Converted into Verifiable Evidence? Article 7 of a 12-Part Series on UR E27 Strategies for Marine Equipment Suppliers ※ The product examples, document numbers, and identifiers described in this article are illustrative examples created to explain how a verifiable UR E27 Evidence Package can be structured. Blue Horizonist (Lew) Maritime & Cyber Security Consultant · ISP Consultant The previous article explained that the object of approval or conformity verification is not simply a product name, but a specific product Baseline combining Hardware, Software, Firmware, Interfaces, security settings, and conditions of application.

Once the product Baseline has been established, the next step is to organize the Evidence so that the classification society and shipyard can verify how the product addresses the UR E27 requirements. At this stage, equipment manufacturers often make the following statement. "This function has already been implemented in the product." In conformity verification, however, merely claiming that a function exists is not enough. The manufacturer should be able to answer the following questions. In which product Baseline is it implemented? Which requirement is the function intended to address? What specific control has been implemented in the product to address the requirement?

Under which settings and conditions does the function operate? Where can it be verified in the design documents and manuals? What test results demonstrate that it actually operates as intended? Which parts depend on security controls outside the product? Can the existing Evidence still be used if the product or its settings change? An Evidence Package is therefore not merely a collection of related documents submitted in large quantities. It is a structured body of substantiating material that links the applicable requirements, product design, settings, test results, and operating conditions so that the reviewer can trace the basis for the conformity decision.

This article examines how to link the Product Description, Hardware/Software Inventory, Network Diagram, Interface List, Hardening Guide, management procedures, and test results to the Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix, and how to build a verifiable Evidence Package without unnecessarily increasing the volume of documentation. ※ In this article, Evidence is used as an inclusive term covering design documents, configuration information, setting records, procedures, test procedures, test results, and approval records that explain or demonstrate product conformity.

The names and scope of the actual submission documents may vary according to the applicable classification society's Rules and Guidance and the project-specific submission requirements. 1 The Purpose of Evidence Is to Enable a Decision, Not Merely to Provide an Explanation Good Evidence is different from material that simply describes a product in detail. Product literature is intended to communicate features and benefits, whereas conformity Evidence should enable the reviewer to determine the following. Does the requirement apply to the product? What control has been implemented in the product to address the requirement?

Is the control implemented through product functionality, product Configuration, the manufacturer's internal procedures, or the vessel-wide security architecture? Does the design description match the actual product Configuration? Has operation of the control been confirmed through testing? Are unmet elements and external dependencies clearly managed? For example, even if the Product Description states that "the product provides user authentication," the reviewer will have difficulty determining conformity without the following information.

Access paths to which authentication applies User types and roles Functions permitted for each role Method for handling Default accounts Password configuration criteria Restrictions applied after failed login attempts Responsibility for creating, modifying, and deleting accounts Related setting screens or Configuration Test procedures and test results The quality of Evidence is determined not by the number of pages, but by whether the reviewer can confirm how the requirement has been addressed and verified without having to make additional assumptions.
2 Claims, Design, Configuration, and Test Results Should Be Distinguished The first step in organizing Evidence is to distinguish among the following four elements.

Category What It Confirms Example Conformity Claim The requirements and scope that the manufacturer considers satisfied "Administrator functions are restricted to authorized accounts." Design Evidence How the control is implemented through the product structure and functions User role structure, authentication flow, and privilege Matrix Configuration Evidence Which settings are applied to the delivered Configuration Default-account change record, Password Policy, and active-account list Test Evidence Whether the designed control actually operates Test result showing that an ordinary user is denied access to the administrator menu None of these four elements is normally sufficient on its own.

A design document does not show whether the setting was applied to the delivered product, while a Screenshot alone does not explain which requirement was tested or why. Even if a test passed, the applicability of its result must be reassessed if the tested Version differs from the delivered Version. For example, demonstrating the conformity claim that "USB use is restricted" requires at least the following links.

Design Evidence: Permitted purposes, users, and approval process for USB use Configuration Evidence: USB storage blocking or allowlist settings Test Evidence: Results showing that ordinary USB devices are blocked and only approved devices are permitted Procedure Evidence: Inspection and usage-record procedures for USB devices used during maintenance In this way, multiple types of Evidence should complement one another in demonstrating a single requirement. 3 The Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix Is the Center of Traceability, Not Merely a Document List The Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix is not a table that simply lists related document names for each requirement.
It is a management tool that connects applicability, implementation method, responsible party, verification method, and result in one traceable flow. In practice, it may include the following fields.

Field Information to Be Recorded Requirement ID Identifier of the applicable Rule or requirement Requirement Summary Core intent of the requirement Applicability Applicable, partially applicable, not applicable, or subject to separate agreement Applicability Basis Basis for the applicability decision Control Allocation Product functionality, product Configuration, manufacturer's internal procedures, or vessel-wide security architecture Design Implementation Specific control implemented in the product Design Evidence Related design document and Section Configuration Evidence Setting value, Configuration Record, or Checklist Verification Method Review, analysis, test, or witnessed test Test Reference Test Procedure and Test Case ID Result Reference Test result, Log, Screenshot, or Record Responsible Party Equipment manufacturer, shipyard, System Integrator, owner, or other party Dependency Dependency on an external system or operating condition Status Satisfied, partially satisfied, not satisfied, under discussion, or not applicable Remark Limitations, compensating controls, and follow-up actions If the Matrix contains only document names, the reviewer must search through dozens of pages to find the relevant information.

Whenever possible, the document number, Revision, Section, Figure, Table, and Test Case ID should therefore be specified. For example, instead of writing "Account management requirement—refer to User Manual," the reference can be made more specific as follows. Design Evidence: SEC-DD-001 Rev.2, Section 4.3, User Role and Authentication Configuration Evidence: SCG-001 Rev.1, Section 3.2, Account Configuration Verification Method: Functional Test Test Reference: STP-001, TC-AC-01~05 Result Reference: STR-001, Appendix B, Screenshots AC-01~05 With this level of traceability, the reviewer can move directly from the requirement to the relevant design and test results.

4 One Item of Evidence May Support Multiple Requirements, but Each Link Must Be Explained Separately There is no need to create a separate description document for every requirement merely to avoid omissions. A single Network Diagram, User and Privilege Matrix, or Software Update procedure may support several requirements. Even when the same document is referenced, however, the basis for linking it to each requirement must be specific. For example, a Network Diagram may support several different assessments.

Identification of the product's external Interfaces Confirmation of Network boundaries Confirmation of remote access paths Confirmation of communication paths to upper-level systems Confirmation of Security Log transmission paths Confirmation of Backup storage locations Confirmation of the responsibility boundary with the vessel-wide security architecture It is not sufficient to state "refer to the Network Diagram" for every requirement. For a remote access requirement, the remote access path and control points should be identified. For a Log requirement, the Log Source and receiving system should be indicated.

For a Network segregation requirement, the connections between Zones and the applicable boundary controls should be identified. Reusing a document is not the same as referring to it ambiguously. The number of documents may be reduced, but the substantiation for each requirement should not be omitted. 5 An Evidence Package Can Be Organized Efficiently in Three Layers An Evidence Package may be organized into the following three layers to support efficient review. ① Decision and Traceability Layer This layer enables the reviewer to understand the scope of application and the overall conformity status.

Submission document list Product Baseline identification information Approval or verification Scope Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix List of unmet requirements and compensating controls Project-specific Deviation list External dependencies and responsibility allocation table ② Design and Management Layer This layer explains how the requirements have been implemented in the product and how that state is maintained.

Product Description Hardware/Software Inventory Network Diagram Interface List Port, Protocol and Service List User and Privilege Matrix Security Event List Hardening Guide Backup and Restore Procedure Software Update Procedure Vulnerability Management Procedure Remote Access Procedure Configuration and change management records ③ Verification and Results Layer This layer demonstrates that the design and settings have actually been implemented and operate as intended.

Test Plan Test Procedure Test Configuration Test Record Screenshot Log Configuration Export Checksum or Hash Nonconformity and corrective-action records Retest results Classification society or shipyard witness records With this structure, the reviewer can first determine the overall status from the Matrix and then move progressively to the necessary design documents and test results. It is easier to review and manage changes than when all material is placed in one oversized document.

6 The Product Description Should Describe the Verification Target, Not Serve as a Product Brochure The Product Description should give priority to information needed for conformity verification rather than to product benefits or general features. At a minimum, it should address the following.

The product's purpose and onboard functions The product's major components The product Baseline and applicable Models Major Hardware and Software Architecture The product's internal functional structure Connections to external systems User types and maintenance methods Software Update and Backup methods Whether remote access is included Product boundaries and external dependencies Overview of major security functions Items excluded from the approval or verification scope For example, it is not sufficient to state that "the Machinery Monitoring System monitors the condition of machinery equipment." The product's actual role and potential impact should be described more specifically.

"This system collects operating data and Alarm information from Sensors and PLCs in the Engine Room and displays them on the Operator Station. It does not transmit control commands to upper-level systems during normal operation; however, users with administrator privileges can modify Alarm setpoints and communication settings through the Engineering Station. The system is connected to the vessel Automation Network via Ethernet, and remote access is disabled by Default." A description of this kind enables the product's functions, access privileges, Interfaces, and potential impact of compromise to be assessed together.

7 The Hardware/Software Inventory Should Be the Common Reference Point for the Product Baseline and Evidence Part 6 addressed the components of the product Baseline. This section therefore focuses on how the Inventory should be linked to other Evidence rather than repeating what the Inventory should contain. Each Inventory item should be assigned a unique identifier. For example, a Server may be identified as HW-001, a Switch as HW-005, an Application as SW-001, and PLC Firmware as FW-003. Using the same identifiers in the Network Diagram, Interface List, vulnerability review records, and test procedures improves traceability across documents.

For example, the following links can be established. HW-005: Internal managed Switch SW-012: Firmware installed on HW-005 IF-007: Interface between HW-005 and the vessel's upper-level Network PPS-014~018: Ports, Protocols, and Services permitted on IF-007 CFG-009: Hardening settings for HW-005 TC-NW-04: Test confirming that unnecessary management Services are disabled VR-023: Known-vulnerability review result for SW-012 This structure makes it easy to identify the Interfaces, settings, and tests associated with a particular component. The Inventory then becomes a common reference point for the Evidence Package rather than merely an asset list.

8 The Network Diagram and Interface List Serve Different Purposes A Network Diagram provides an intuitive view of the overall connection structure and security boundaries, but becomes difficult to read if every communication detail is placed in a single drawing. Conversely, an Interface List is well suited to recording detailed information but does not show the overall structure at a glance. The roles of the two documents should therefore be distinguished as follows. Document Primary Purpose Information to Include Network Diagram Visual confirmation o

posts.t: Rereading IACS UR E26/E27 Through the NSA Guidance
c: Zero Trust for OT in the AI Era: Rereading IACS UR E26/E27 Through the NSA Guidance Read clause by clause, E26/E27 already contain much of what NSA asks for. The difference lies elsewhere: where ships place trust, how they answer machine-speed attacks, and when their rules stop checking. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Introduction IACS UR E26/E27 already contain much of what NSA's new OT Zero Trust guidance asks for. The real difference is not a missing clause. It is where each document places trust, how each responds to attacks that move at machine speed, and when each stops checking.

Trust boundary, not missing clauses Legitimate entry via vendor sessions Graceful degradation over automation Certified at delivery, attacked in service Physical presence as identity On October 8, 2026, the US National Security Agency released a Cybersecurity Information Sheet (CSI), "Hardening Department of War (DoW) Critical Operational Technology (OT) Environments with Zero Trust (ZT) Principles." It was written for defense OT, but its core problem, adding security around legacy equipment that is hard to replace, is exactly the problem ships face. The reason NSA is pushing OT Zero Trust now is AI.

The document says adversaries are using AI ("super intelligence" in its wording) to automate reconnaissance, accelerate exploit development and attack many targets at once. It also warns that organizations bringing AI into OT operations are creating new attack surfaces. Ships are no exception: remote maintenance, shore-linked performance management and AI-based condition monitoring keep adding connections, while the people and time available to respond at sea stay the same. I read the NSA document against the original texts of E26 Rev.1 and E27 Rev.1. This post is about what that comparison means, not just what it counts.

What the NSA document asks for The core message is "wrap the equipment, don't replace it." DoW's Zero Trust for OT guidance defines 84 activities; NSA picked 26 that can be implemented now, favouring non-intrusive compensating controls that wrap legacy assets in protective enclaves without intrusive hardware modifications. They are grouped under ten measures, from securing remote access and inventorying assets to segmentation, hardening controllers and engineering workstations, and verifying controls safely. Two details matter for ships.

NSA names remote access by vendors, OEMs, integrators and maintenance personnel as a common vector in confirmed OT intrusions, deserving the same or greater scrutiny as internal access. And it explains micro-segmentation with the image of "bulkheads in a ship." The overlap is real, and it is the starting point Measured clause by clause, the overlap is large. Of NSA's 26 activities, E26/E27 substantively require 6 and partly require 13; only one, the CTI community activity (7.5.2), has no counterpart at all. In the other direction, 30 of the 36 clause units I listed for E26 (83%) and 45 of E27's 58 items (78%) connect to at least one NSA activity.

Some Zero Trust principles are written into E26 almost verbatim. E26 4.2.4.3.6 restricts raised privileges to the moments they are needed, using expiring privileges and one-time-use credentials, sets default privileges for new accounts as low as possible and calls for audits against privilege accumulation. E26 4.2.1 lets only explicitly allowed traffic cross a security zone boundary. E27 2.4 and 5.2 e) cover compensating countermeasures and the risks of not patching. Complying with E26 already takes a ship part of the way to Zero Trust. The interesting question is what the overlap hides. The numbers say the two documents ask for similar things.

They do not say the two documents rest on the same assumptions. Four differences in assumption explain almost every partial match and every conflict I found. Insight 1: The gap is where the trust boundary sits Look at where E26/E27 apply their strongest controls. Multi-factor authentication is mandatory only for access from or via untrusted networks (E26 4.2.6.3.2, E27 #31). Limits on unsuccessful login attempts apply only to untrusted networks (E27 #33). Cryptography is mandatory only for wireless and untrusted networks (E27 #17, #21, #38). Segmentation is drawn at security zones (E26 4.2.1). Each of these is reasonable on its own.

Together they describe a perimeter model: the ship's own network is the trusted side, and the hard checks sit at the edge. Zero Trust starts from the opposite premise, that location grants nothing. The weak point of a perimeter is not the attacker who breaks through it but the one who is let in. E26 already requires that remote access be explicitly accepted by a responsible role on board (4.2.6.3.1). That is a good control, but it is a gate, not continuous verification. Once a vendor session has been accepted, the session is inside.

Shared accounts are allowed (the note to 4.2.4.3.5 says unique identification is not required), HMIs in physically controlled areas may skip authentication (4.2.4.4.1), and E26 does not require separation between devices inside a zone. This is why NSA's emphasis on vendor and OEM access matters for ships. The vector NSA highlights is the one that crosses the ship's trust boundary legitimately. When attackers can move through a network faster with AI, the time between "accepted at the gate" and "reached a controller" is exactly where a perimeter model offers the least. What follows.

The useful upgrade is not more gate controls but verification after the gate: session-bound and time-limited privileges for remote access, a short and justified list of authentication-exempt HMIs, and segmentation that does not stop at the zone boundary. Insight 2: Ships cannot answer machine-speed attacks with machine-speed response If attacks move at machine speed, the natural Zero Trust answer is defence at machine speed. NSA's guidance goes that way: EDR with prioritized automated responses for both the operational IT and process control environments (2.7.1), and segmentation policies that change automatically once a human has approved them (5.4.1). E26 deliberately goes the other way.

Any intrusion detection system must be passive, must not activate protection functions that may affect the performance of the system, and must be qualified by the system's supplier (4.3.1.3). Modifications in operation follow the management of change process of UR E22. Security measures must not adversely affect the availability of essential systems (E27 2.3). This is not caution for its own sake. On a ship at sea, an automated response that isolates the wrong controller is not an IT ticket; it can mean losing propulsion or steering, with no outside help available.

NSA itself shares part of this instinct: it prioritizes passive verification and allows active testing only in approved maintenance windows without disturbing Level 0/1 devices. So how does a ship close the speed gap? E26's answer is not faster detection but graceful degradation. Essential functions must remain operable locally, independently or manually (4.4.2, linked to SOLAS II-1 Reg.31), systems must be able to fall back to a minimal risk condition (4.4.4), and the ship must be able to back up, restore, shut down in a controlled way and roll back (4.5.2, 4.5.3). None of these appear in the NSA guidance, which concentrates on keeping attackers out and limiting their spread.

NSA buys time by stopping the attacker sooner. E26 buys time by letting the ship keep sailing while the attack is handled. What follows. Split by layer. Automated response belongs on the operational IT layer (servers, engineering workstations), detect-only on the process control layer, and every automated policy change should be recorded as a change under MoC. The investment that matters most at sea is not the fastest detection tool but tested manual operation and recovery.

Insight 3: E26 certifies a ship at delivery; Zero Trust assumes a ship under attack in service Most of E26's verification is attached to milestones: the design documents, the factory acceptance test, commissioning tests, then annual and special surveys. In operation, E26 does require the owner to keep the test procedure and measures up to date against new threats and vulnerabilities. But it asks for this through procedures and documents checked at surveys, not through continuously running capabilities. The NSA activities that E26 covers least are the continuous ones. The only complete gap is a cyber threat intelligence community (7.5.2).

Automated configuration management (2.6.2) has no direct counterpart; E26 relies on supplier hardening guidance verified at testing. Dynamic, role-based access (1.2.2) appears in E26 as a principle, not as a mechanism. The consequence is a handover problem. At delivery, responsibility moves from the yard and suppliers, who built to E26, to the owner, who must run the ship for decades. The capabilities Zero Trust adds are exactly the ones that live on the owner's side of that line: threat intelligence, fleet-level monitoring and continuous configuration control. What follows. Owners should treat these as operational programmes with budgets and owners, not as newbuild specification items.

The NSA document is a credible reference for explaining why they are needed after the class certificate has been issued. Insight 4: Physical presence is used as identity, and that assumption is aging E26 allows two things that Zero Trust would not: shared accounts without unique identification, and HMIs in physically controlled areas that need no authentication at all. Both rest on the same idea. If someone is standing at the console in a controlled space, they are presumed to be authorized. At sea that idea has strong practical grounds. An engineer in an alarm situation cannot wait for a login, and a bridge console that locks at the wrong moment is a safety risk.

NSA, by contrast, asks for shared and service accounts to be identified and then migrated or decommissioned. The two positions do not have to collide. The question is how far the exemption reaches. Every exemption widens the space in which a session that came in through the gate (Insight 1) can act without being tied to a person. What follows. Keep the exemption, but keep it narrow: list each authentication-exempt HMI, record the physical-control justification for it, and review the list when systems or remote-access arrangements change.

Practical implications by stakeholder Treat E26 as the baseline and use the NSA document as a list of enhancements on top of it, chosen according to the four differences above. Stakeholder What to apply now Shipowners Build on E26's on-board acceptance of remote sessions (4.2.6.3.1) by adding time-limited privileges to remote access management in the SCSRP. Plan threat intelligence and fleet monitoring as operational programmes. Manage unpatchable equipment by linking E26 5.1.5 compensating countermeasures with E27 5.2 e) mitigations Shipyards and SIs Make IP/MAC, ports, criticality and security zone mandatory columns in the vessel asset inventory, with confidentiality controls.

Reuse ZCD conduit specifications as IDS detection baselines. Split the test procedure into construction (active) and post-delivery (passive first) Suppliers Include disabling unused controller logic in hardening guidelines (E27 5.7; NSA 3.3.1). Add USB connection events on EWs and HMIs to auditable events. Support a detect-only EDR mode for the process control layer Remote maintenance providers A PAM gateway with approval and session recording goes beyond E26's requirements and addresses the vector NSA highlights. It is the most direct answer to Insight 1 Closing Side by side, onshore OT Zero Trust and ship cyber resilience look at the same problem from different ends.

NSA weighs how to keep attackers out; E26 weighs how to keep sailing safely when they get in. As AI shortens the time between entry and impact, ships need both: verification that does not end at the gate, and the ability to keep operating when verification fails. This is a personal analysis written in a short time. Clause-level judgments are my own interpretation, not an official reading of the rules. Interpretations may differ between classification societies, so please confirm with your society before applying anything. If you spot an error or read a clause differently, I would welcome your comments. Method note I mapped in both directions.

Forward, each of the 26 NSA activities was linked to E26 sub-clauses and E27 items (Table 1 #1–#30, Table 2 #31–#41, Section 3 documentation, Section 5 SDLC) and graded Direct, Partial, Indirect or Gap. In reverse, E26 was listed as 36 clause units and E27 as 58 items, and each was checked for any linked NSA activity. Forward result: 6 Direct, 13 Partial, 6 Indirect, 1 Gap. Reverse coverage: E26 83%, E27 Table 1 77%, Table 2 91%, documentation 80%, SDLC 57%. The unlinked items are mostly Respond and Recover functions (E26 4.4.2, 4.4.4, 4.5.2, 4.5.3; E27 #20, #26–#28) and supplier development processes.

Sources · NSA, Hardening Department of War (DoW) Critical OT Environments with Zero Trust (ZT) Principles , U/OO/6070841-26, October 2026 · NSA, Press release: NSA Releases Zero Trust Guidance for Protecting Operational Technology Systems , October 8, 2026 · The White House, Executive Order 14434, Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence , September 2026 · IACS, UR E26 Cyber resilience of ships, Rev.1, November 2023 · IACS, UR E27 Cyber resilience of on-board systems and equipment, Rev.1, September 2023 Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance Owner-side maritime cybersecurity advisor covering IACS UR E26/E27 compliance, zone and conduit design, and OT/IT security architecture for commercial vessels — working across LR, ClassNK, DNV, ABS, and BV newbuilding projects.
