posts.t: Zones and Conduit Diagram: Establishing the Vessel’s Security-Zone Architecture (IACS UR E26 Compliance Series · Article 2 of 7)
c: Zones and Conduit Diagram: Establishing the Vessel’s Security-Zone Architecture From CBS allocation and network segmentation to conduit control, as-built verification and survey-cycle maintenance Woojin Lee Automation Cyber Engineering · Cyber Tech Consultant · LinkedIn · Crew Profile IACS UR E26 Compliance Series · 7 Articles 1 The CRSI Role and Six Core Deliverables 2 Zones and Conduit Diagram 3 Cyber Security Design Description 4 Vessel Asset Inventory 5 Risk Assessment for the Exclusion of CBSs 6 Description of Compensating Countermeasures 7 Ship Cyber Resilience Test Procedure ← Previous · Article 1 The CRSI Role and Six Core Deliverables Next · Article 3 · Coming soon Cyber Security Design Description Regulatory basis reviewed 5 October 2026 Primary references IACS UR E26 Rev.1; UR E27 Rev.1; UR E22 Rev.3 Corr.1 Implementation references ClassNK Guidelines Edition 1.1 and Q&A; LR publication information Supporting standards IEC 62443-3-2:2020 and IEC 62443-3-3:2013 Article 2 — Zones and Conduit Diagram.

Conceptual cover illustration. This article follows Article 1: The Cyber Resilience System Integrator and the Six Core Ship-Level Deliverables and examines the first deliverable: the Zones and conduit diagram. The Zones and Conduit Diagram, or ZCD, is the principal ship-level document used to demonstrate how computer-based systems (CBSs) are grouped into security zones, how communication is permitted within and across those zones, and how interfaces with networks outside the IACS UR E26 scope are controlled.

A reliable ZCD is not merely a network drawing: it is the controlled architectural baseline linking supplier information, vessel design, commissioning evidence and operation-phase maintenance. Key message: A compliant ZCD must represent the same in-scope CBSs as the Vessel Asset Inventory, show their zone allocation and physical locations, and agree with the communication and boundary-control design in the Cyber Security Design Description (CSDD) and the final installed vessel. It must also remain maintainable after delivery, because the Shipowner is required to keep the diagram updated and demonstrate continued management of security-zone boundaries during the operational survey cycle.

Terminology and interpretation note How This Article Uses “ZCD,” “Conduit” and Related Terms Series scope. The six core deliverables group the five document categories in UR E26 §5.1 and the test procedure in §5.2.1. The exclusion assessment and description of compensating countermeasures apply where relevant. Supplier documentation, test records and the Shipowner’s operation-phase program are also part of the compliance framework. CRSI means Cyber Resilience System Integrator in this series: a specialist performing or supporting the cyber-resilience aspects of the IACS-defined Systems Integrator function. CRSI is not a separate IACS stakeholder category.

Responsibilities follow the applicable requirements and the party’s appointment. Applicability. UR E26 Rev.1 is implemented by IACS Societies for ships within its scope contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. It may serve as non-mandatory guidance for other ships. The applicable Class Rules, implementation dates and project conditions must be identified for each vessel; the newest published edition is not automatically the applicable project edition. IACS UR E26 uses the document title “Zones and conduit diagram.” This article uses the abbreviation ZCD for readability.

UR E26 formally defines a security zone , a network segment , a logical network segment , a physical network segment and an untrusted network . It does not provide a separate formal definition of conduit or zone boundary device in Section 2. For the ZCD requirement, UR E26 expressly uses the term conduit for network communication between different security zones and for any communication between a security zone and an untrusted network. IEC 62443 uses a broader supporting concept in which a conduit groups communication channels connecting zones under a common security treatment. That IEC concept may support the engineering method, but it should not be presented as the formal IACS definition.

IACS UR E26 does not prescribe a mandatory number of ZCD sheets or require separately titled “Physical ZCD” and “Logical ZCD” drawings. Separate coordinated views are recommended for complex vessels, while a combined representation may be used where all required information remains clear, complete and acceptable to the Society. A Purdue Model overlay may also be used for explanation, but it is not an IACS requirement and does not replace the UR E26 zone and conduit decisions. IACS requirement Content expressly required by an IACS Unified Requirement. Additional or class-specific obligations are identified separately.

Class guidance Implementation explanation provided by a Classification Society, including examples of acceptable documentation or verification. CRSI recommended practice A structured engineering method recommended for consistency, traceability and lifecycle maintenance, but not presented as a standalone IACS obligation.

Contents Why the ZCD matters Regulatory purpose and mandatory content Core concepts and interpretation boundaries Roles, inputs and data ownership Zone design and segmentation Conduits and communication scope Recommended ZCD package Development and as-built lifecycle Traceability, commissioning and surveys Classification Society implementation notes Practical review appendices Conclusion 1. Why the Zones and Conduit Diagram Matters A conventional network drawing may show switches, cables, IP networks and connected equipment. A ZCD must go further by explaining the vessel’s security architecture.

It must identify the in-scope CBSs, allocate them to security zones, show the relevant physical locations, illustrate required communication relationships and make boundary-crossing communication traceable to the controls described in the CSDD. The ZCD serves three related functions: Architectural definition: it establishes the vessel-level segmentation model used to limit cyber-incident propagation and unauthorised lateral movement. Design traceability: it provides the architectural basis for the CSDD, which explains communication purpose, protocols, data flows, boundary devices and permitted traffic.

Lifecycle control: it becomes an as-built baseline that the Shipowner must maintain under Management of Change and use during the operational survey cycle. Under UR E26, all CBSs within scope are grouped into security zones with defined security policies and capabilities. Zones are either isolated or connected through means that control the communicated data, and only explicitly authorised traffic may cross a security-zone boundary. Regulatory reference: IACS UR E26 Rev.1, §§4.2.1.1–4.2.1.3. Figure 1. Security zones and controlled communication paths. The ZCD identifies the architecture; the CSDD explains the communication and boundary controls. Conceptual example only. 2.

Regulatory Purpose and Mandatory Content 2.1 Security-Zone Requirement UR E26 defines a security zone as a collection of in-scope CBSs that meet the same security requirements and are subject to an applicable access-control policy. This means that a security zone is not automatically equivalent to one Supplier system, one shipboard department, one room, one switch, one VLAN, one IP subnet or one Purdue level. Those attributes may influence the design, but the zone decision must be defensible in terms of common security requirements, trust, exposure, access policy, functional dependencies and the ability to control boundary-crossing communication.

Regulatory reference: IACS UR E26 Rev.1, §2, definition of “Security zone,” and §4.2.1.3. 2.2 Minimum ZCD Content The Systems Integrator is required to submit the ZCD and CSDD during the design phase. The ZCD must include the following information. 2.2 Minimum ZCD Content Required content Practical meaning Obligation Clear identification of security zones Each zone boundary and zone identifier must be distinguishable. Shall Simplified illustration of each in-scope CBS Each CBS must be identifiable, allocated to a zone and associated with a physical location.

Shall Reference to approved Supplier topology diagrams The vessel-level representation must be traceable to the detailed system topology approved under UR E27. Shall Network communication within a security zone Same-zone network relationships must be illustrated at a level that remains complete and traceable. Shall Network communication between different security zones Inter-zone network communication is represented as conduits. Shall Any communication between a security zone and an untrusted network Boundary-crossing communication to out-of-scope networks is represented as conduits; the CSDD must also address discrete and serial interfaces.

Shall Regulatory reference: IACS UR E26 Rev.1, §4.2.1.4.1 and §5.1.1. CRSI recommended practice Grouped Representation Must Remain Complete A complex ZCD may group same-zone communication to preserve readability, but only where the underlying communication relationships remain complete and traceable through a controlled communication register or approved Supplier topology reference. Aggregation should not conceal an undocumented path or omit a relationship needed to understand the zone policy. 3. Core Concepts and Interpretation Boundaries 3.

Core Concepts and Interpretation Boundaries Concept Status Meaning for ZCD development Security zone IACS-defined term A collection of in-scope CBSs meeting common security requirements and subject to an access-control policy. Network IACS-defined term Two or more computers communicating through a protocol over a communication medium. This definition is not limited to IP. The narrower Ethernet definition below applies to network segment . Network segment IACS-defined term An OSI Layer 2 Ethernet segment or broadcast domain in the context of UR E26. Logical network segment IACS-defined term A network segment sharing physical components with one or more other logical network segments.

Physical network segment IACS-defined term A network segment whose physical components are not shared with other network segments. Untrusted network IACS-defined term Any network outside the scope of applicability of UR E26. Conduit IACS usage; not separately defined in §2 A boundary-crossing communication relationship identified in the ZCD between different security zones or between a security zone and an untrusted network. Detailed engineering may group one or more channels under a common security treatment. Zone boundary device Implementation term used by UR E26 A device or function enforcing or mediating communication across a zone boundary.

UR E26 requires the CSDD to identify such devices but does not provide a separate formal definition in §2. DMZ Architectural pattern; not an automatic compliance designation An intermediate security zone may be used where services, trust relationships or exposure justify it. The actual assets, functions, scope and boundary controls must be defined. Interpretation boundary Inter-Zone Non-IP Communication UR E26 §4.2.1.4.1 requires network communication between in-scope zones and any communication with untrusted networks to be illustrated. “Non-IP” is not a blanket exemption: distinguish a non-IP network from a point-to-point serial or discrete interface.

ClassNK’s Edition 1.1 guidance (§4-2.2) describes same-zone and inter-zone communication in IP terms and separately addresses serial and discrete communication with untrusted networks. This is a class implementation explanation, not a universal redefinition of “network” in UR E26. For other inter-zone links, document the protocol, direction and boundary-control or isolation implications, and agree the representation with the Society. Showing boundary-crossing serial, fieldbus and discrete links is recommended to make functional dependencies visible. Communication with an untrusted network must be illustrated regardless of whether it uses IP. 4.

Roles, Inputs and Data Ownership 4.1 Stakeholder Responsibilities 4.1 Stakeholder Responsibilities Stakeholder Principal ZCD responsibility Systems Integrator Establish the vessel-wide zone model, allocate CBSs, define conduits, coordinate Supplier information, submit the ZCD, maintain it during construction and verify the as-built implementation. CBS Suppliers Provide approved CBS Asset Inventories, physical and logical topology diagrams, interface information, protocols, connected-system information and relevant security-capability documentation.

Shipyard design disciplines Provide equipment locations, network architecture, wiring and cable information, switch and firewall arrangements, redundancy information and construction changes. Shipowner Provide operational requirements, Owner-supplied equipment information, shore interfaces, remote-access requirements and applicable cyber-security policies. Classification Society Review the design, issue comments or approval status, and witness or assess relevant commissioning verification. Shipowner/Company after delivery Maintain the ZCD under Management of Change and demonstrate continued implementation during applicable surveys.

4.2 IACS Source Information and CRSI-Recommended Engineering Inputs The following table distinguishes information expressly required by IACS from structured project inputs recommended for efficient integration. Not every recommended register is a separate IACS submission. 4.2 IACS Source Information and CRSI-Recommended Engineering Inputs Input Purpose Basis Preliminary Vessel Asset Inventory Identifies candidate CBSs, network devices, security devices, Suppliers, locations and scope status. IACS UR E26/E27 CBS categorisation results Records applicability, the required UR E22 category where applicable, exclusion status and safety significance.

A combined categorisation register is a recommended format. IACS basis Register format: CRSI practice Vessel system-of-systems architecture Identifies functions, system boundaries, interfaces and dependencies. IACS UR E22 Supplier CBS Asset Inventories Provides hardware, software and interface information for vessel-level integration. IACS UR E27 Supplier physical and logical topology diagrams Provides detailed endpoints, devices, communication paths, protocols and external connections. IACS UR E27 Vessel network, wiring and equipment-location information Confirms actual physical connections, network segments, boundary devices and mandatory location data.

Design evidence Communication and interface matrix Structures source, destination, purpose, direction, medium, protocol and data-flow information. CRSI practice Zone Catalogue and Conduit Catalogue Creates controlled identifiers, policy descriptions and cross-document references. CRSI practice Owner-supplied equipment register Prevents late identification of equipment that ma

posts.t: True Delegation Is Sharing Your Judgment — Not Just Your Workload
c: The Psychology of Leadership Shaped by Success True Delegation Is Sharing Your Judgment — Not Just Your Workload When everyone on the team understands why, not just what — that's when you stop executing tasks and start building something real together. Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security I want to be honest with the team about where we are right now. Our project scope keeps growing. The roles each of you carry are getting heavier. And in the coming months, we're expecting to land several new projects — which means things will get busier before they get easier.

I've said this before, but it bears repeating: we will never compromise on the capability and attitude of the people we work with. That standard doesn't change, no matter how busy we get. But I also want to be clear about what kind of organization we're building — because I think it matters for how we approach this moment together. We are not building a conventional time-based consulting firm. We're building something different: a hybrid model that combines the operational depth of the maritime industry with the strategic discipline of consulting — purpose-built for the global shipbuilding and maritime domain. That's the vision.

And to get there, two things have to be true about how we work: Trust and Delegation. The Short Version Delegation isn't about passing work down. It's about sharing the framework of judgment — the why, the boundaries, the priorities — so people can make good decisions without waiting for approval on everything. When a leader handles everything personally, the whole team's growth hits a ceiling at that one person's capacity. That ceiling is real, and we're already starting to feel it. Building a delegation culture requires three specific habits: sharing context, clarifying decision boundaries, and making progress visible.

The shift from feedback to feed-forward is what moves a team from executing tasks to owning judgment. This isn't a policy announcement. It's a direction we build together — one conversation, one decision, one act of trust at a time. Delegation Is Not "Here, You Do This" I want to clear something up, because I think "delegation" is one of the most misunderstood words in any organization. A lot of leaders hear "delegate more" and translate that into "hand off tasks." Assign it, move on, check back later. That's not what I mean — and honestly, that kind of delegation can make things worse, not better. What I mean by delegation is something more fundamental.

It's sharing the context and framework of judgment. When I delegate something to you, I'm not just giving you a task — I'm trying to give you the same understanding I have about why this matters, how far your authority extends, and what the real priority is underneath all the details. Three Questions That Should Be Clear Before Any Real Delegation 01 Why are we doing this? — Not the surface reason, but the actual strategic purpose behind the work. 02 To what extent can you make independent decisions? — Where does your authority start and where should you bring it to the team? 03 What truly matters here? — When competing priorities pull in different directions, what's the real north star?

When these three things are clearly understood, something changes. The team stops waiting for direction on every small call. People start making decisions with confidence — not recklessly, but because they actually understand the bigger picture. That's when we move from a team that executes tasks to a team that thinks, judges, and acts with intention. (This is also why we take our time when selecting new team members. We're not just hiring for skill. We're assessing whether someone can hold this kind of judgment.) Doing It All Yourself Looks Efficient — Until It Isn't I'll be honest about something. For a while, I've been handling too much personally.

Not because I don't trust the team — but because it can feel faster in the short term. When you know something well, it's often genuinely quicker to just do it yourself than to explain it, hand it off, review it, and course-correct. I get that impulse. Most experienced leaders do. But here's the problem with that logic at scale: when a leader manages everything directly, the team's growth ceiling becomes that one person's available time and capacity. Every process that requires the leader's sign-off becomes a queue. Every decision that should be made at the working level instead waits in someone's inbox. If the team can't decide independently, every process runs through one bottleneck.

And that bottleneck is me. That's not good for anyone — including the people who need to grow. So going forward, I'm deliberately going to reduce the number of things I handle personally — and expand the space where the team can decide and act on their own. This is not me stepping back from responsibility. It's me taking a different kind of responsibility: building a team that doesn't need me to be in every room. Three Things We're Going to Do Differently Building a delegation culture isn't something that happens by announcing it. It happens through specific habits, practiced consistently over time. Here's what I want us to focus on — and I mean all of us, including me.

1️⃣ Captain Paul In our studies, reviews, and deliverable discussions, let's stop at "what we're doing" and always include "why we're doing it." When people understand the reason, they align naturally — without needing to be told what to do at every step. Context is the thing that turns a task-executor into a thinking team member. 2️⃣ Captain Paul Ambiguity about decision rights is one of the main reasons people default to asking for approval on everything — even when they could and should decide independently. Let's define this clearly for each person on the team. Where can you move on your own? Where do we need to bring it to a group discussion? Once that's clear, the hesitation goes away.

3️⃣ Captain Paul Trust isn't built by waiting for someone to prove themselves over months. It's built through visible, consistent progress — small things that accumulate into a track record. Tools like Microsoft Teams aren't just communication platforms. When we use them well, they become our shared language for transparent collaboration — the place where work is visible, progress is trackable, and no one has to guess what's happening. From Feedback to Feed-Forward One more thing I want to change about how we talk to each other. Right now, a lot of our review conversations sound like this: "This should have been done differently.

Next time, fix it this way." That kind of feedback is useful — but it's limited. It corrects behavior. It doesn't transfer judgment. What I want us to move toward is something more like: "Next time, what if we approach it from this angle — what do you think?" "On this next one, I'd like you to take the lead and make the call. I'll be here, but the decision is yours." These aren't just nicer ways to give corrections. They're fundamentally different conversations — ones that share ownership of judgment rather than just ownership of the task. That's the shift I'm asking for. It takes more time in the short term. It pays back enormously over months and years.

Let's Move Forward Together This isn't a top-down directive. It's a shared direction. We need to keep building mutual trust. That means I need to trust the team with real judgment calls — not just the easy ones. And it means the team needs to take those calls seriously, with the full weight of context behind them. Neither side can wait for the other to go first. The kind of organization we're building — specialized, hybrid, globally focused — will not get there by having one person at the center of every decision. It will get there because each member of this team develops the judgment, the confidence, and the ownership to move things forward on their own. That's what I'm working toward.

And I hope this is a conversation we keep having — one project, one decision, one honest exchange at a time. "Delegation without context is just workload transfer. Real delegation gives people a piece of your judgment — and trusts them to grow it into their own." — Captain Ethan Key Takeaways 🧭 Delegation = Sharing Judgment Handing off tasks is not delegation. Sharing the context, the decision boundaries, and the priorities — that's what actually transfers capability to the team. ⏱️ One Person's Ceiling Becomes Everyone's When the leader controls every decision, the team's growth is capped at that leader's bandwidth. Letting go isn't a risk — it's a prerequisite for scale.

💬 Feed-Forward Builds Ownership Moving from "fix it this way" to "next time, what do you think?" changes the dynamic from correction to co-ownership. That shift compounds over time. 🤝 Trust Is Built Through Visibility Consistent, visible progress — not grand gestures — is what builds real trust. Shared tools and transparent collaboration aren't overhead. They're the foundation. Captain Paul Maritime 4.0 · AI, Data & Cyber Security Maritime professional focused on the intersection of vessel operations, classification society regulations, and OT/IT cybersecurity. Writing for engineers, consultants, and operators navigating Maritime 4.0 together. LinkedIn 📅 October 2025

posts.t: Anthropic Just Pointed Frontier AI at OT and Open Source. Ships Run on Both.
c: Anthropic Just Pointed Frontier AI at OT and Open Source. Ships Run on Both. Anthropic Cyber Mission · Critical Infrastructure Defense Program · OSS Scanner · October 2026 Captain Paul Founder & Editor-in-Chief · ShipPaulJobs · October 2026 On October 8, 2026 , Anthropic launched the Anthropic Cyber Mission , ( https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-cyber-mission ) a long-term program to put its strongest AI models in the hands of defenders. It starts in two places: the operational technology (OT) behind power, water, and transportation, and the open-source software (OSS) that almost every product is built on.

The same day, its Frontier Red Team released OSS Scanner , a free, opt-in service that scans open-source projects for vulnerabilities and sends maintainers an exploit, an explanation, and a candidate patch. Shipping was not named in either announcement. It does not need to be. A modern vessel is a floating OT network, and the software inside its bridge, engine room, and connectivity equipment is full of open-source components. Both halves of this announcement land directly on our industry. This article does two things. First, it summarizes what Anthropic actually announced.

Second, it looks at OSS Scanner from a shipbuilding and offshore point of view: why we need it, how we can realistically use it, and what market it is likely to create. Ⅰ. The Announcement — Anthropic Cyber Mission at a Glance Anthropic's starting point is a frank admission. Through Project Glasswing , its earlier effort with partners to find bugs in important software, finding vulnerabilities turned out to be the easy part.

In Anthropic's own words, "verifying, prioritizing, and fixing these findings remains challenging." The Cyber Mission is built around that bottleneck, and it has two pillars: 🏭 Pillar 1 · Critical Infrastructure Defense Program (CIDP) Frontier Claude models, Anthropic engineers working on-site, and Anthropic's threat research, delivered through the trusted providers that OT operators already rely on. The focus starts with power grids, water systems, transportation networks, and government systems.

🧩 Pillar 2 · Open-Source Software (OSS Scanner) Free, regular security scans of enrolled open-source projects by Anthropic's strongest models, plus funding for the foundations and coordination groups that keep open source running. The launch also sits on a run of earlier moves that make the direction clear: 1 June 2026 — A $15M cyber defense program for US state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. Anthropic says it now supports more than half of all US states and some of the largest public infrastructure operators. 2 August 2026 — The Defender Advantage Fund (0xDAF), which funds pilot programs and keeps OSS Scanner free.

3 Early October 2026 — Project Glasswing merged into an expanded Cyber Verification Program , which gives qualifying security teams access to Claude's most capable cyber features. 4 October 8, 2026 — The Anthropic Cyber Mission, CIDP, and OSS Scanner launch together. Anthropic's forecast is worth noting: within about two years , it expects AI to favor defenders, because catching bugs before release and writing secure code from scratch will get easier. It is equally clear that the near term may not look like that . Exploiting a bug has become cheap, while verifying, disclosing, and fixing it is still slow and depends on people. Ⅱ.

Pillar 1 — Defending Critical Infrastructure Through Trusted OT Providers Anthropic describes the OT problem in terms every marine engineer will recognize. Controllers and industrial networks are built to run for decades. They often cannot be taken offline to patch , so known vulnerabilities stay open for years. The equipment is proprietary, changes are risky, and a mistake can stop a plant. Operators therefore depend on a small group of trusted providers to tell them what is exposed and which fixes are safe to apply on a running system. So instead of selling directly to every operator, Anthropic is working through those providers.

The founding partners fall into three groups: Consulting & Advisory Accenture, Booz Allen, Deloitte, PwC — the firms that run security programs for operators. Security Vendors CrowdStrike, Dragos, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks — the companies that guard business and industrial networks. Equipment Makers Hitachi, Rockwell Automation — the manufacturers that build and patch the equipment itself. One partner comment stood out for our industry. Insane Cyber pointed out that the sites needing protection most — remote substations, offshore platforms , air-gapped plants — are exactly where traditional tools and specialists cannot easily reach.

Replace "offshore platform" with "vessel at sea" and you have described the daily reality of maritime OT security. Ⅲ. Pillar 2 — How OSS Scanner Works OSS Scanner is modeled on Google's OSS-Fuzz , which has scanned open-source code with fuzzers (tools that throw huge volumes of random input at a program to make it crash) for years. The difference is that OSS Scanner uses large language models to read and reason about the code.

The numbers behind the decision explain why: 20% → 85%+ Share of vulnerabilities LLMs found on the CyberGym benchmark, from early last year to this year 29,000+ Candidate vulnerabilities found in six months — only about 6,000 could be reviewed by people ~5,000 Unverified reports already sent to maintainers who asked for everything, reviewed or not 88% Of 97 critical/high findings across 48 projects that passed expert review; only 1 was a false positive In practice, the service works like this: Opt-in Core maintainers enroll by submitting a pull request to Anthropic's GitHub repository.

Eligibility follows OSS-Fuzz-style criteria: projects with a critical impact on infrastructure and user security, decided case by case. What You Get Periodic scans by Anthropic's strongest models, including Claude Mythos . Each report has a self-contained reproducer, an explanation (often with the commit that introduced the bug), and a candidate patch where one is available. The Trade-off Reports are fully model-generated and sent without human review . That makes them fast, but some will be wrong — most often an inflated severity or a misread of the project's threat model. Anthropic expects a true-positive rate above 90%. Cost Free.

Projects without the capacity to handle raw findings keep receiving human-verified reports through Anthropic's normal coordinated disclosure process . The early feedback is strong. Maintainers from PostgreSQL, OpenSSL, wolfSSL, curl, and HotCRP reported findings they could act on almost as-is. wolfSSL said 72 of 74 reports were valid and five became CVEs. curl said the scanner found one of its worst vulnerabilities in years. Several of these libraries ship inside maritime equipment, which is where this story turns to us. Ⅳ.

Why Shipbuilding and Offshore Need This — A Ship Is OT Built on Open Source When people picture ship software, they imagine proprietary systems from a handful of maritime brands. Open the box, though, and much of what runs inside is open source.

Here is where it typically shows up on board: Shipboard Area Typical Open-Source Components Embedded controllers & gateways Embedded Linux, BusyBox, OpenSSL / wolfSSL, curl Automation & integration (IAS, PMS) open62541 (OPC UA), libmodbus (Modbus), MQTT brokers such as Mosquitto Navigation & sensor data gpsd, NMEA 0183 / 2000 parsing libraries, Signal K, OpenCPN-based tools Connectivity (VSAT, LEO terminals, routers) Linux networking stack, OpenSSH, OpenVPN / WireGuard, web management UIs Fleet data & shore platforms PostgreSQL, InfluxDB, Grafana, Node-RED That makes a ship exposed in two ways at once.

It inherits every bug in those upstream libraries, and it is the hardest place on earth to deliver the fix. Three reasons: Visibility Most owners, and many yards, cannot say which version of OpenSSL sits inside a given engine-room controller. When an upstream fix is released, nobody knows which vessels are affected. Delivery Ships sail with limited bandwidth and limited onboard IT skills. Changes to critical systems are often held for a service engineer's visit or the next dry-docking, which can be years away. Approval Under IACS UR E26 and E27, software changes to class-relevant systems go through management of change and may need class involvement.

A patch that is a five-minute job ashore can take months at sea. Anthropic itself notes that in Glasswing, months often passed between finding a bug and fixing it, and that an OT fix may have to wait until it can be safely applied to running machinery — in rare cases, for decades . Ships are the textbook case. If AI makes finding bugs nearly free while fixing them stays slow, the industries with the slowest patch cycles carry the most risk. Ours is near the top of that list. Ⅴ. How Maritime Can Actually Use It — Four Practical Paths One point first, because it is easy to get wrong: OSS Scanner is for open-source projects, not for a supplier's proprietary firmware.

A shipyard cannot enroll its own code, and an equipment maker cannot submit a closed-source alarm system. The value for maritime comes indirectly, through the open-source code that our equipment is built on. Here is how each player can capture it: Path 1 · Enroll the maritime open-source projects Projects such as open62541, libmodbus, gpsd, Signal K, and OpenCPN are small, volunteer-run, and sit directly in the path of shipboard data. Their maintainers can apply to OSS Scanner. Industry associations, class societies, or large yards can help by sponsoring maintainer time so the reports actually get triaged.

General-purpose libraries like OpenSSL and curl are already being scanned; the maritime-specific ones are the gap. Path 2 · Equipment suppliers: build an SBOM and absorb upstream fixes fast The faster upstream bugs get fixed, the more it matters whether you know you are using that code. A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — a list of every software component and version inside a product — lets a supplier match each new upstream fix to the products and vessels affected. That ties directly into the secure development lifecycle and security-update process that UR E27 asks suppliers to document, and into IEC 62443-4-1.

Path 3 · Proprietary code: use the paid and verified tracks For closed-source firmware and software, the relevant Anthropic options are Claude Security , its enterprise code scanning and patching product, and the Cyber Verification Program , which gives qualifying security teams expanded access for defensive work. Suppliers preparing E27 type approval can run these scans before the product goes to class, not after. Path 4 · Owners, yards, and class: bring maritime into the CIDP model CIDP already includes OT security vendors and equipment makers active in shipping, such as Nozomi Networks, Dragos, and Hitachi.

Maritime OT providers, integrators, and consultancies can register interest as the program expands to more sectors. The fleet-level job is to map each new vulnerability to specific vessels and E26 security zones, then rank fixes by operational risk rather than by CVSS score alone. Where to Start — Official Links Resource Who It Is For What You Do There Link OSS Scanner Path 1 · 2 Core maintainers of established open-source projects (e.g. open62541, libmodbus, gpsd) Check eligibility and the FAQ, then enroll by opening a pull request that adds projects/<project>/project.yaml to github.com/anthropics/oss-scanner. Free, periodic scans; reports arrive unreviewed.

red.anthropic.com/oss-scanner ↗ Claude for Open Source Path 1 Eligible open-source maintainers and contributors Apply for six months of Claude Max at no cost, to help triage findings and write fixes for the project. claude.com · Claude for OSS ↗ Verification Portal Path 3 Security teams and equipment suppliers securing proprietary code with Claude Apply for and manage Anthropic trust programs for your Claude usage, such as the Cyber Verification Program. Sign in with Google, email, or SSO.

portal.anthropic.com ↗ Claude Security Path 3 Suppliers and yards with closed-source firmware and software Scan a codebase for vulnerabilities, validate the findings, and review recommended patches before approving them. claude.com · Claude Security ↗ CIDP Interest Form Path 4 Critical-infrastructure defenders: OT providers, integrators, shipyards, owners, and class Register interest in the Critical Infrastructure Defense Program as it expands in 2027. claude.com · CIDP form ↗ A word of caution. OSS Scanner reports are unreviewed, and Anthropic warns that the model can misjudge severity or misread a project's threat model.

On a ship, threat model is everything: the same bug can be trivial in an isolated zone and critical in a system reachable from the satellite link. AI can find and draft the fix. A qualified engineer must still decide whether, when, and how it goes onto a running propulsion or navigation system. Ⅵ. Expected Market — Where the Money Moves When Finding Bugs Becomes Free Start with the published baseline. Market research firms put the global maritime cybersecurity market at roughly US$3.2–4.1 billion in 2024–2025 , growing at about 12% a year . ResearchAndMarkets projects US$6.55 billion by 2029; Grand View Research projects US$9.01 billion by 2033.

The forecasts differ in scope and base year, but they agree on direction. What changes with tools like OSS Scanner is not the size of the pie so much as where the money goes . When discovery becomes cheap and free, spending shifts toward the steps AI cannot yet do alone: knowing what you have, validating fixes, and getting them safely on board.

These are the segments I expect to grow: Segment What Is Sold Likely Buyers / Sellers Maritime SBOM & vulnerability intelligence Component inventories per product and per vessel, matched to new CVEs and upstream fixes Equipment makers, fleet operators / OT security vendors AI-assisted triage & patch validation Human-in-the-loop review of AI findings, test benches and digital twins to prove a fix is safe before it goes aboard Suppliers, yards / consultancies, test labs Secure remote update & lifecycle services Controlled delivery of patches over satellite links, with rollback and records for class Owners, ship managers / OEM service arms, connectivity providers Verification of AI-found fixes Independent confirmation that a change keeps E26/E27 compliance intact Owners, flag / class societies, third-party verifiers My rough estimate, not a published figure: if even 10% of maritime cyber spending moves into AI-assisted vulnerability management and patch lifecycle services, that is a niche of roughly US$400–650 million a year by 2029 , using the ResearchAndMarkets baseline.
Korean yards and equipment makers, who build a large share of the world's newbuilds, are well placed to lead it if they treat SBOM and patch delivery as part of the

posts.t: Three 2025 Ship Incidents That UR E26/E27 Alone Would Not Have Stopped: Solong, Iran's VSAT Fleet Hack, and MSC Antonia
c: Three 2025 Ship Incidents That UR E26/E27 Alone Would Not Have Stopped — Solong , Iran's VSAT Fleet Hack, and MSC Antonia A collision that was blamed on hackers before anyone could prove otherwise. A fleet-wide satellite-terminal attack that came in through a service provider. A grounding caused by satellite signals that lied. None of them lived where the class rules look hardest. Here is what each case teaches — and why the answer is attack-surface minimisation, not just compliance.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 · Oct 14, 2026 · 14 min read 🎯 Key Message Ship incidents in 2025 — including VSAT-based attacks and GNSS spoofing — exposed risks that sit beyond the scope of IACS UR E26/E27. Compliance builds the floor. A deliberate strategy to minimise the attack surface is what keeps a ship safe when the threat comes in through a door the rules never listed.

⚡ 2025 Incidents at a Glance ① Solong / Stena Immaculate ② Iranian Fleet VSAT Attack ③ MSC Antonia Date Mar 10, 2025 Mar 2025 (claimed) · Aug 2025 (second wave) May 10, 2025 Location North Sea, off the Humber / Yorkshire coast Fleet-wide (ships at sea and in port) Red Sea, Eliza Shoals near Jeddah Suspected Vector Navigation/steering "hack" (speculated) VSAT terminals via satcom service provider GNSS spoofing / jamming (RF) Impact Collision, jet-fuel fire, 1 seafarer lost External comms lost on 116 (Mar) / 64 (Aug) ships — as claimed ~7,000 TEU boxship grounded Cyber Verdict Not cyber — master convicted of gross-negligence manslaughter Cyber (claimed) — Lab Dookhtegan; not independently confirmed Cyber/EW (assessed) — Windward, Pole Star, MarineTraffic Ⅰ.

Case 1 — Solong vs Stena Immaculate : When "It Was Hacked" Cannot Be Ruled Out On the morning of March 10, 2025, the Portuguese-flagged container ship Solong struck the US-flagged product tanker Stena Immaculate while the tanker lay at anchor off the Humber estuary. The tanker was carrying Jet A-1 fuel under the US government's Tanker Security Program. The impact breached a cargo tank; aviation fuel spilled onto Solong 's bow, ignited, and set the boxship's containers alight. One Solong crew member, Able Seaman Mark Pernia, was lost and presumed dead. Within a day, the story had a cyber angle.

A senior White House official told the maritime outlet gCaptain that foul play had not been ruled out , and speculation followed that Solong might have been hacked by Russia or another hostile state. The UK government took a more cautious line: the transport minister told Parliament there was "no evidence" of foul play. The Stena Immaculate burning after the collision, with tugs fighting the fire (inset). Image: news footage, March 2025. The investigation pointed somewhere else entirely.

The UK Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) interim report found that Solong struck the tanker at about 16 knots in patchy visibility (0.25–2.0 nm), with the master as the lone watchkeeper and no dedicated lookout on either ship's bridge . At trial at the Old Bailey, the master, Vladimir Motin, argued he had pressed the wrong control while trying to take the ship off autopilot. The jury rejected his account, convicting him of gross-negligence manslaughter in February 2026; he was sentenced to six years. 🔎 Analysis — Not a Cyber Incident, But a Cyber Lesson The hacking hypothesis did not survive investigation.

But look at what happened in the first 48 hours: a government official publicly declined to exclude a cyberattack on a ship carrying military fuel. In that window, nobody could quickly prove the bridge systems were clean . That is the real takeaway. Following IACS UR E26 is meant to give a ship the ability to detect, respond and recover . In practice that means configuration baselines, integrity checks and security logs that let investigators say within hours, not months, whether autopilot, steering or ECDIS behaved as commanded. Forensic readiness is a safety capability. It protects the crew and the operator as much as it catches attackers. Ⅱ.

Case 2 — Iran's Merchant Fleet Goes Dark: A VSAT Attack at Fleet Scale In March 2025 the hacktivist group Lab Dookhtegan ("Sewn Lips") claimed it had disabled the VSAT-based communications of 116 Iranian vessels : 50 belonging to the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC) and 66 to the Islamic Republic of Iran Shipping Lines (IRISL). Both companies have been under US sanctions since 2020 for supporting the IRGC. The group said the attack was timed to coincide with US strikes on the Houthis, that ship–shore links had been severed, and that full recovery would take weeks. An NITC VLCC ( Iran Delvar ). NITC and IRISL ships were the reported targets of both 2025 waves.

Independent verification was limited. Maritime threat-intelligence firm NORMA Cyber said it found no open-source confirmation that the outage happened. It did judge the published vessel list likely authentic, noting that 105 of the 116 ships appear on the OFAC sanctions list. The group came back in August 2025 with a second, better-documented claim: 64 ships (39 tankers and 25 cargo ships) cut off. This time it described the route in. The attackers said they had compromised Fanava Group , an Iranian IT and telecom holding company that provides the fleet's satellite communications.

They published screenshots of root access on Linux-based terminals running iDirect satellite software described as badly outdated. According to an Iranian opposition researcher, they then overwrote storage partitions on the terminals, erasing logs, configurations and recovery data, after access that may have persisted since spring. NITC and IRISL have not confirmed any downtime. 🔎 Analysis — The Ship Never Saw the Attack Coming Set the geopolitics aside and this is a textbook supply-chain and service-provider compromise . The attackers did not need to breach 64 ships one at a time.

They breached the one company that manages all 64 satellite terminals, and from there reached every terminal the provider could reach. This is exactly where UR E26/E27 thins out. A commercial VSAT terminal used for business traffic and crew welfare is not a statutory system, so it is often left out of the computer-based system (CBS) inventory. UR E26 treats the satellite link as an untrusted network and requires protection at the ship's boundary. But the terminal's firmware, its remote management channel and the provider's network operations centre (NOC) all sit outside what the ship's class survey verifies. Mere compliance with E26/E27 is not enough.

Overlooking non-mandated systems such as VSAT leaves vessels dangerously exposed. Ⅲ. Case 3 — MSC Antonia : The Shoal Was Real. The Coordinates Were Not. On May 10, 2025 , the Liberian-flagged container ship MSC Antonia (IMO 9398216, ~7,000 TEU), on passage from Marsa Bashayer in Sudan to Jeddah, left its intended track and ran aground on the Eliza Shoals in the Red Sea. No one was injured. The day before, UKMTO had warned that several vessels in the Red Sea were experiencing electronic interference and GPS disruption.

Three intelligence providers, Windward, Pole Star Global and MarineTraffic , reached the same broad conclusion: the ship's GNSS position had been corrupted by spoofing or jamming. Its AIS track showed it "jumping" to false positions in the days before the grounding. The ship's systems believed it was somewhere it was not, and the bridge navigated on that belief. Windward has described the Red Sea, particularly near Sudan, as one of the world's busiest GNSS-interference hotspots. MSC Antonia aground, 10 May 2025, 08:04 UTC. Image: Pole Star Defense / Copernicus Sentinel data 2025. 🔎 Analysis — An Attack With No Network Packet GPS spoofing is simple in concept.

A transmitter broadcasts counterfeit satellite signals that are stronger than the real ones, and the receiver locks onto the fake. No firewall is crossed, no password is guessed and no malware is installed. The "intrusion" arrives through the antenna as radio energy, and the corrupted position then flows through the ship's systems as trusted data. GNSS feeds ECDIS, autopilot and track control, AIS, the VDR and even the time stamps on the ship's logs. This is why network segmentation, the backbone of UR E26/E27, does nothing against it.

The defence has to be resilience in the navigation process : GNSS receivers that can detect spoofing, cross-checks against radar, gyro/log dead reckoning and the echo sounder, alarms when sources disagree, and bridge teams trained to doubt a position that "looks right". It is a failure you can test for, before it happens on a real shoal. Ⅳ. Cross-Case Analysis — Where Was the Attack Surface? Put side by side, the three cases point to one pattern. The exposure was in places that a CBS-by-CBS compliance exercise tends to miss: the RF environment , third-party service providers , and the ability to produce evidence after something goes wrong. Case Exposed Surface Covered by UR E26/E27?

What Would Have Helped ① Solong Bridge automation (autopilot/steering) — trust surface, not an attack Partly — for ships contracted from Jul 2024; pre-2024 fleet not covered Forensic readiness: configuration baselines, security logs, a fast "cyber or not?" triage ② Iran VSAT Commercial VSAT terminal + satcom provider NOC Boundary only — terminal and provider out of scope Provider security assurance, terminal hardening and patching, backup comms path ③ MSC Antonia GNSS RF input to ECDIS / AIS / autopilot No — not a network threat PNT resilience: spoofing detection, multi-sensor cross-checks, crew drills 🔍 Cyber Intrusion Analysis Reference — MITRE ATT&CK for ICS Mapping Case / Stage Tactic Technique ② Provider → terminals Initial Access T0822 — External Remote Services · T0883 — Internet Accessible Device · T0859 — Valid Accounts ② Partition wipe Inhibit Response Function T0809 — Data Destruction · T0814 — Denial of Service ② Fleet comms lost Impact T0826 — Loss of Availability ③ GNSS spoofing Impact T0832 — Manipulation of View · T0880 — Loss of Safety · T0879 — Damage to Property ⚠️ This mapping is the author's analytical framing of publicly reported claims and assessments, not an official mapping by any government or investigating body.

Case ① is deliberately left out because the cyber hypothesis was not supported by the investigation or the court. ATT&CK for ICS has no technique for over-the-air GNSS spoofing as such; the techniques listed for Case ③ describe its effect on the operator's view and on safety, not the RF delivery method. Technique IDs were checked against the MITRE ATT&CK for ICS matrix. Ⅴ. What These Cases Mean for Owners, Managers & Shipbuilders Each incident shows a different blind spot. Together they describe four gaps that a passed UR E26/E27 survey will not reveal on its own: The asset inventory stops at the "mandated" line E26 asset inventories are built around the systems in scope.

VSAT terminals, crew-welfare networks, cloud-connected sensors and vendor gateways are often missing, yet attackers choose them precisely because nobody is watching them. Third-party providers hold the keys to the whole fleet One compromised satcom provider reached dozens of ships at once. Owners rarely audit their provider's NOC, remote-management credentials or patch practices, and charter contracts rarely require it. Navigation trusts a single, spoofable source ECDIS, autopilot and AIS consume GNSS as ground truth. In hotspots such as the Red Sea, the Gulf and the Black Sea, that assumption is no longer safe.

Few bridges run structured drills for a GNSS position that is wrong but still plausible. No evidence trail when the question "was it cyber?" is asked After Solong , speculation filled the gap that evidence should have filled. Without security logs and configuration baselines, an operator cannot quickly clear its own systems, or prove that an attacker was involved. Ⅵ. Beyond Compliance — An Attack-Surface Minimisation Strategy The common answer to all three cases is not another checklist. It is the discipline of shrinking what an adversary can touch , and making sure the ship can still navigate, communicate and explain itself when something gets through.

Strategy 01 Map Every Connection — Not Just the Mandated Ones Lesson from: Case ② (VSAT outside the CBS inventory). Actions: Extend the asset inventory to all external connections: VSAT and LEO terminals, 4G/5G routers, crew Wi-Fi, OEM remote-access boxes and cloud data loggers. Remove or disable every interface without a clear operational need. Each connection that stays must have an owner, a documented purpose and a defined zone/conduit. 📎 Related Guides: IACS UR E26 — Complete Guide to Cyber Resilience ↗ | Maritime OT/IT Firewall — Zone Segmentation ↗ Strategy 02 Harden Satcom Terminals & Hold Providers Accountable Lesson from: Case ② (provider compromise reaching the whole fleet).

Actions: Change default credentials, close unused management ports and keep terminal firmware patched. Write security obligations into satcom contracts: MFA on provider remote management, incident-notification deadlines, patch SLAs and the right to audit. Keep a backup communications path on a different provider or technology so that losing one link does not isolate the ship. 📎 Related Guides: Ship Communication Systems — Architecture & Vulnerabilities ↗ | Secure Vendor Remote Access (SVRA) ↗ Strategy 03 Build PNT Resilience Into the Bridge Lesson from: Case ③ (GNSS spoofing with no network intrusion).

Actions: Specify multi-constellation GNSS receivers with spoofing and jamming detection on new builds and retrofits. Configure ECDIS and the integrated navigation system (INS) to alarm when GNSS disagrees with radar, gyro/log dead reckoning or the echo sounder. In known interference areas, require radar-based position fixing and parallel indexing as standard practice. Run "plausible but wrong position" drills during bridge resource management training.

📎 Related Guides: MSC Antonia — A System Failure You Can Test For ↗ | Ship Navigation Systems — Complete Guide ↗ Strategy 04 Make Forensic Readiness Part of Safety Management Lesson from: Case ① (the "hacked?" question nobody could answer fast) and Case ② (logs wiped from the terminals). Actions: Keep configuration baselines for bridge and engine systems, and send security logs to storage that an attacker on the device cannot overwrite. Add a short "cyber or not?" triage step to the SMS casualty procedure so the first hours after an incident produce evidence, not speculation. Rehearse it with the company DPA and the class society.

📎 Related Guides: Ship Cyber Resilience — Complete Guide ↗ | ICS Security Ch. 7 — Security Testing & Audit ↗ Strategy 05 Treat E26/E27 as the Floor — and Extend It to the In-Service Fleet Lesson from: all three cases. Actions: On new builds, keep demanding UR E27-compliant equipment — it remains vital for securing onboard systems against cyber-induced loss of control. Then add the threats it does

posts.t: One Europe, Two Shipbuilding Strategies: The Gap Between Brussels and Athens
c: One Europe, Two Shipbuilding Strategies: The Gap Between Brussels and Athens Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Introduction: In 2026, Europe Spoke About Shipbuilding Twice In 2026, Europe gave two answers on how to rebuild its shipbuilding industry. In March, the European Commission in Brussels published its first standalone Industrial Maritime Strategy.

In July, the Greek Shipyards Association in Athens unanimously approved the "Greek Shipbuilding Manifesto 2027–2035 & Project NEXUS." Both documents start from the same crisis: global shipbuilding output is concentrated in a handful of places in Asia, and the EU's global share has fallen to about 5%. Yet their prescriptions are opposite. Brussels says, "Defend only where we can win." Athens says, "Redraw the whole board." This article looks at why the two documents differ so sharply, and what that gap means for Korean shipbuilding and for the ship cybersecurity (UR E26) market.

Brussels' Answer: "Focus Where We Can Win" The core of the EU Industrial Maritime Strategy (COM(2026) 111) is selection and concentration. It focuses policy resources on high-value segments where Europe still leads: cruise ships, naval vessels, icebreakers, research vessels, cable-laying ships and offshore wind support vessels. General-purpose container ships and ordinary cargo ships are left out. The strategy is built on three pillars.

Pillar Key measures Build, Equip & Repair Launch of an Industrial Maritime Value Chain Alliance, 'Shipyards of the Future' R&D calls, bundled public procurement with non-price and economic-security award criteria Transport & Connect Existing State aid guidelines retained, simplified ETS and FuelEU reporting Secure & Protect Expanded naval production capacity, support for dual-use ferries, investment in maritime domain awareness and cybersecurity Three horizontal initiatives on innovation, finance and skills sit on top of these. The Commission estimates that shipyard digitalisation alone will require EUR 3–7.5 billion a year. Its limits are also clear.

The strategy imposes no legal obligations on the 27 member states. The Commission itself states that it has no legal effect on ongoing or future vessel procurement. Indeed, Sweden ordered an icebreaker from a Korean shipyard, citing a price difference of about 3.8%. On ETS revenues, too, the strategy only "recommends" that member states spend them on maritime investment. Athens' Answer: "Redraw the Board" The Greek manifesto was proposed by Panos Xenokostas, president of the association and chairman of ONEX Shipyards & Technologies. Its goal is to restore the global competitiveness of Greek shipbuilding by 2034. Its demands fall into six strands. 1.

Tax and social-insurance treatment equal to ocean shipping, and fast-track entry of third-country technical staff within one month 2. Recycling EU ETS revenues back into the industry, funding a support mechanism that closes the Europe–Asia newbuilding cost gap 3. Investment tax credits of 100% for newbuilds and 50% for repairs (for Greek, European and US owners), and removal of State aid ceilings for shipbuilding hubs 4. Project NEXUS: a digital shipyard with collaborative robots, AI, and automated cutting and welding 5. Infrastructure for SMR-powered merchant ships after 2035, and preferential treatment for dual-use shipbuilding facilities 6.

Recognition of Greece as the southern pillar of European defence, a Transatlantic Shipbuilding Pact with the US, and regaining a 33% Western share of global shipbuilding The manifesto should be read as an opening negotiating position, not a policy document. But the backdrop is already real. ONEX revived the Elefsis Shipyards with US DFC funding and has formed the Project Trident strategic alliance with Hanwha Ocean. Skaramangas Shipyards has signed a surface combatant cooperation agreement with HD Hyundai Heavy Industries.

Why So Different: Five Structural Reasons In one sentence: the EU is playing defence to protect the niches it already holds, while Greece, with little left to lose, is playing offence to enlarge the game. Issue EU strategy Greek manifesto Target scope High-value niche segments 33% global share State aid Existing guidelines retained Ceilings removed entirely ETS revenues Recommends partial allocation by member states Mandatory return to industry US cooperation Barely mentioned Transatlantic Shipbuilding Pact as a core pillar Nuclear propulsion Subject to regulatory overhaul Infrastructure for SMR-powered ships after 2035 ① Different authors.

The EU strategy is the lowest common denominator of 27 countries. The Greek manifesto is a lobbying document from an industry association, written from the start on the assumption that it would ask big and be cut down. ② Different starting points. Shipyards in Italy, France, Germany and Finland are already competitive in cruise ships and naval vessels. What they need is defence. For Greek shipyards, restarted from the brink of bankruptcy, a niche strategy alone leaves almost nothing on the table. ③ State aid is the core of EU competition law. Lifting aid ceilings would trigger a subsidy race among member states.

To the established shipbuilding nations, Greece's demand sounds like a request to help raise a competitor. ④ ETS revenues belong to national treasuries. A large share of shipping ETS revenue flows into member states' general budgets. As the world's largest shipowning nation, Greece is one of the biggest payers. The logic "the money our owners paid should go to our shipyards" follows naturally. ⑤ Different geopolitical axes. The keyword of the EU strategy is strategic autonomy. Greece operates on a three-way structure of US DFC funding, agreements signed at the US Embassy, and Korean shipyards. If the EU moves slowly, Greece has already secured a bypass to deal directly with the United States.

There is a contradiction inside Greece as well. Greek owners have built their ships in Korea, China and Japan for decades. The tax credits are designed to change where they order, but whether owners will actually accept the higher cost is another matter. Opposite Directions, Three Common Denominators Although the two documents point in opposite directions, they overlap in three places. These common denominators will become reality whichever logic prevails. ▸ Digital shipyards. The EU has put forward 'Shipyards of the Future', Greece Project NEXUS. Robotics, AI and digital production management become the shipyard standard. ▸ Merging merchant and defence.

The EU talks about expanding naval production and dual-use ferries; Greece about preferential treatment for dual-use facilities. A structure in which merchant ships and naval vessels are built in the same yard is encouraged by policy. ▸ Criteria beyond price. The EU approaches this through non-price and economic-security criteria in public procurement, Greece by making "state-of-the-art specifications" a condition for support. The routes differ, but both point the same way: building cheaply alone will no longer earn the money. Implications for Korean Shipbuilding The Western shipbuilding revival is not a single bloc.

It moves along three tracks: the United States (MAP, MASGA), the core EU states (niche defence), and Greek-style re-entrants. This fracture is both a threat and an opportunity for Korea. Market Character Korea's position United States Rebuilding defence and merchant shipbuilding, leveraging allies Direct investment and MRO through MASGA Greek-style re-entrants Short of technology and capital, linked to the US Partner in design, technology transfer, equipment and MRO Core EU states Niche defence, stronger non-price criteria Risk of price advantage being neutralised; respond with non-price evidence The threat is medium-to-long term and limited.

Greek shipyard capacity can hardly threaten the VLCC or large LNG carrier markets. Competition will play out in ferries, coastal vessels, tugs, offshore wind support vessels, naval ships and MRO. The opportunity is already real. Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries are in place as technology partners of Greek shipyards. Even if the core EU states narrow the door, a channel is opening for indirect entry into the European market through Atlanticist member states. The remaining question is positioning. The manifesto's list of allies is Greece, Europe and the United States. Korea is not on it.

Whether Korea remains a technology supplier or becomes a co-production partner depends on the partnership structures being built now. A Cybersecurity and UR E26 Perspective: Requirements Grow Whichever Side Wins All three common denominators lead to expanded cybersecurity requirements. Ship cybersecurity is widening from "compliance for a single vessel" to the intersection of shipyards, supply chains and defence. 1. The E26 gap at restarted shipyards. When Greek shipyards resume newbuilding, every one of those ships falls under IACS UR E26/E27. Yards that have not built new ships for decades have no experience with CBS documentation, Zone & Conduit design, test procedures or class approval.

The know-how Korean shipyards have built in practice since July 2024 could become part of a technology transfer package. 2. A digital shipyard is itself an OT attack surface. A shipyard with collaborative robots, automated welding and digital twins lies outside the scope of E26. That territory belongs to IEC 62443 and the EU's NIS2. If design data or a digital twin is tampered with, the compromise flows straight into the integrity of the delivered ship. Security during construction (secure-by-build) remains an empty space. 3. Merchant and defence requirements coexist in one yard. Naval vessels are not subject to E26.

In a dual-use shipyard, E26 applies alongside NATO and national defence requirements. The moment a yard enters the US defence supply chain, requirements such as CMMC follow. 4. Cyber resilience becomes a qualification for getting paid. Whether through the EU's non-price procurement criteria or Greek-style subsidy conditions, cyber requirements are likely to be part of "state-of-the-art" specifications. Treating E26 as the minimum and demonstrating security above it becomes a differentiator. 5. Next on the agenda: autonomous ships and nuclear propulsion. The EU has said it will overhaul the regulatory framework for both, and Greece has called for infrastructure for SMR-powered ships.

Nuclear-powered merchant ships sit where ship cybersecurity meets nuclear facility security, an area that still has no rules. 6. Fast-track hiring increases insider risk. When a large temporary workforce with short vetting periods enters a digital shipyard, personnel security and access control become mandatory elements of the shipyard security framework. Conclusion: A Place Between the Fractures The gap between Brussels and Athens is not a passing difference of opinion but a structural fracture within Europe. The established powers defend their niches; the new entrants enlarge the game and join hands with the United States.

Korea holds the rare position of being able to partner with both sides of this fracture. Holding that position takes more than price competitiveness. Digital shipyards, dual use and non-price criteria all demand cybersecurity and compliance capability.

Over the next decade, shipbuilding orders will be decided as much by "how trustworthy" as by "how cheap." Sources · European Commission – EU Industrial Maritime Strategy, COM(2026) 111 · EU Blue Economy Observatory – Commission launches EU Industrial Maritime and Ports Strategies · ArcticToday – The EU's industrial maritime strategy · Hansa – EMIS: the gap between aspiration and reality · Container News – Greek Shipyards Association unveils manifesto · Naftemporiki – Xenokostas stresses need for a Transatlantic Shipbuilding Pact · Naval News – Hanwha Ocean partners to strengthen Greece's shipbuilding · Greek News Agenda – A new horizon for Greek shipbuilding · gCaptain – Korea–U.S.

posts.t: EU CRA Series, Part 2 of 5: The CRA in Numbers: Fines, Deadlines and the Reporting Clock
c: EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers · Part 2 of 5 The CRA in Numbers: Fines, Deadlines and the Reporting Clock Why the Cyber Resilience Act is already a business risk for suppliers to the EU market Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 It is easy to read the EU Cyber Resilience Act as a 2027 problem. It is not. The duty to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents has applied since 11 September 2026, and it covers products already on the market, not only new ones. Full application follows on 11 December 2027, about thirteen months from now.

This part sets out the figures a marine equipment maker needs to know: the fines, the reporting clock, the support period and the record-keeping duties, each with the article it comes from. EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers: the series What the CRA is and how it differs from IACS UR E26/E27 The CRA in numbers: fines, deadlines and the reporting clock (this article) From E27 evidence to CRA evidence: what suppliers must add Proving security, function and recovery by test A CRA roadmap for marine equipment suppliers 1. The Figures at a Glance Eight figures sum up what the CRA asks of a manufacturer and what failing it can cost.

€15M or 2.5% Maximum fine for the core duties Breaching the Annex I requirements or the manufacturer duties in Articles 13 and 14. Whichever is higher, using worldwide annual turnover. Art. 64(2) 24h · 72h Early warning, then notification Counted from when the maker becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident. Art. 14(2), 14(4) 14 days · 1 month Final report 14 days after a fix is available for a vulnerability; one month after the notification for an incident. Art. 14(2)(c), 14(4)(c) 5 years Minimum support period Set to the expected time in use, and at least five years unless the product is expected to be used for less. Art.

13(8) 10 years Security updates stay available Each update issued in the support period remains available for at least 10 years or the rest of the support period, whichever is longer. Art. 13(9) 10 years Keep the documentation Technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity, for 10 years after placing on the market or the support period, whichever is longer. Art. 13(13) 11 Sep 2026 Reporting already applies Including for in-scope products placed on the market before 11 December 2027. Art. 71(2), 69(3) 11 Dec 2027 Full application Essential requirements, conformity assessment and CE marking for products placed on the market from this date. Art. 71(2) 2.

Three Tiers of Fines Article 64 sets maximum administrative fines in three tiers. Each Member State lays down its own penalty rules within these ceilings, and the amount in a given case depends on the nature, gravity and duration of the breach and on the size and market share of the company. Breach Maximum fine (whichever is higher) Basis Essential requirements (Annex I) and manufacturer duties (Arts. 13, 14), including reporting €15 million or 2.5% of worldwide annual turnover Art. 64(2) Other obligations, such as those of importers and distributors, the EU declaration of conformity, CE marking and conformity assessment procedures €10 million or 2% Art.

64(3) Incorrect, incomplete or misleading information given to notified bodies or market surveillance authorities on request €5 million or 1% Art. 64(4) One exemption worth knowing. Micro and small enterprises cannot be fined for missing the 24-hour early-warning deadline alone (Art. 64(10)(a)). The 72-hour notification, the final report and every other duty still apply to them in full. Fines are not the only consequence. A market surveillance authority can also require corrective action, or the withdrawal or recall of a product from the EU market.

For an equipment maker, being taken off a shipyard's approved-vendor list because a product cannot legally be supplied may cost more than the fine itself. 3. The Reporting Clock Article 14 runs two parallel tracks. Both are filed through the single reporting platform run by ENISA (Art. 16), and go at the same time to the CSIRT designated as coordinator and to ENISA. Step Actively exploited vulnerability (Art. 14(1)–(2)) Severe incident affecting product security (Art.

14(3)–(4)) 24 hours Early warning, naming where known the Member States in which the product is available Early warning, including at least whether the incident is suspected to be unlawful or malicious 72 hours Vulnerability notification: the product, the general nature of the exploit and vulnerability, measures taken and measures users can take Incident notification: the nature of the incident, an initial assessment, measures taken and measures users can take Final report No later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available: description, severity, impact, any known malicious actor, details of the fix Within one month of the incident notification: detailed description, severity and impact, likely root cause, mitigation applied The manufacturer must also inform the affected users, and where appropriate all users, about the vulnerability or incident and the measures they can take, where appropriate in a machine-readable format (Art.

14(8)). When does the 24-hour clock start? The Commission's guidance of 27 July 2026 ( summary ) adds practical detail, as summarised by KOTRA Brussels and law-firm notes: Question Reading in the guidance Which products? Every in-scope product already on the market, including products whose support period has ended From when? From the moment the manufacturer, after an initial check, has reasonable certainty that a vulnerability is actively exploited or an incident is severe, not from the first rumour Anything retroactive? No. Problems the manufacturer knew about before 11 September 2026 do not have to be reported To whom?

ENISA and the coordinating CSIRT at the same time, through the single reporting platform, and the affected users (all users where needed) Why this matters at sea. The clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, wherever that awareness comes from. Equipment installed on ships in service, possibly years ago, is covered if it is in scope (Art. 69(3)). A maker that has no channel for crews, superintendents or owners' security teams to report a suspected exploit may learn of it late, and a report that reaches the maker through an unclear route can start the 24-hour clock before anyone inside knows who should act.

The other direction, whether the maker's notice actually reaches the shipowner and the ship, is examined in detail in Julius Shin's article Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner? 4. Five Years of Support Against a 25-Year Ship The support period is the maker's promise to handle vulnerabilities and deliver security updates. Article 13(8) says it must reflect the time the product is expected to be in use, taking into account user expectations, the nature of the product and the support periods of third-party components that provide core functions, and that it must be at least five years. What the guidance adds on support periods.

The end date of the support period has to be made known when the product is bought, and users should be told when it ends where possible. If a substantial modification extends the expected life of a product, the support period has to be recalculated, though it is not reset automatically. Models that differ only in colour or size can share one risk assessment. That creates a gap specific to shipping. Ships commonly trade for 25 years or more, while the operating systems and libraries inside marine equipment are often supported for far less. Three questions follow for every product: 1 What period can we justify?

A shipyard or owner may reasonably expect equipment to be used for much longer than five years, and the declared period has to be defensible against that expectation. 2 Can we keep that promise? If the embedded OS or a key library loses vendor support first, the maker still owes fixes for the declared period, so it needs a replacement path for those components. 3 What happens after it ends? Owners will still run the equipment. Isolation, compensating controls and a replacement plan have to be agreed with the shipyard and owner, ideally at the design stage.

Add the duties to keep each security update available for at least ten years and to keep the technical documentation for at least ten years, and the CRA becomes a commitment of a decade or more for every product line, not a one-off approval. 5. How Ready Are Companies? Korean figures suggest most companies have not started.

A July 2026 survey of 108 online members of Security World and Boannews , reported in Security World 's August 2026 issue, found: 13% know the CRA well and are already preparing; about six in ten have not started 54.6% say the biggest obstacle is a lack of information and guidance 5+ months expected minimum per product for certification, at an estimated KRW 150–200 million per engagement for consulting and testing The same report puts Korea's ICT exports to the EU at USD 13.4 billion in 2025, 17.2% of all Korean exports to the EU, which is the exposure these numbers sit against.

Other governments are moving at different speeds: Country Response reported Japan Aligning its own IoT security label (JC-STAR) with CRA requirements Taiwan A support programme for exporters' CRA readiness from May 2026 United States Reworking its consumer IoT label (Cyber Trust Mark); any link to the EU undecided China No national-level response reported These are survey and press figures, not official statistics, but the direction is clear: the main barrier is not money but knowing what to do. For marine suppliers that argues for an early gap assessment rather than waiting for the harmonised standards. 6.

What the Numbers Mean for a Supplier Now Read together, the figures turn into a short list of things to have in place, and when. By when What to have in place Driven by Now (already due) A way to receive vulnerability and incident reports, a named person who decides within hours whether something is actively exploited, access to the single reporting platform, and a list of which products are on the EU market and where Art. 14, 69(3) Early 2027 Scope and class decided for each product; gap analysis against Annex I using existing E27 evidence; a declared support period per product with its reasoning Art.

13(8), 32, Annex I Mid 2027 Fixes and additional tests complete; a notified body booked where the product's class requires one Art. 32 11 Dec 2027 Technical documentation, SBOM, EU declaration of conformity and CE marking ready for every product placed on the market from this date Arts. 13, 28, 30, Annex VII The middle rows are suggested planning milestones, not legal deadlines. They work back from December 2027 and allow for the time notified bodies may need once demand rises. Part 3 looks at the evidence work behind the second row in detail. ※ Figures are taken from the text of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847.

National penalty rules, implementing acts on reporting and Commission guidance continue to be published; check the latest official sources before relying on any figure for a specific case. ⚓ Captain Paul's Take The headline figure is the €15 million fine, but the number I would put on a supplier's wall is 24 hours . A fine is a risk; the reporting clock is already running, for products sold years ago as well as new ones. Most marine equipment makers have no 24-hour security desk, and building one takes longer than writing a procedure. The second number is the support period. Five years is the floor, not the answer.

A supplier that declares a period it cannot honour has simply moved its risk into the future. One that declares an honest period, explains it and agrees with the yard what happens afterwards gives the owner something it can plan around. Primary sources: Regulation / body Type Link EU CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Arts. 13, 14, 16, 32, 64, 69, 71) EUR-Lex View text ↗ Commission CRA guidance, 27 July 2026 (summary) Law-firm summary Read ↗ ENISA (runs the single reporting platform) Website enisa.europa.eu ↗ Related reading: EU CRA Series, Part 1: What the Cyber Resilience Act Is and How It Differs From IACS UR E26/E27 Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner?

(Julius Shin) One Ship, Three Layers: Unifying NIS2, CRA, and IACS UR E26 Captain Paul (In Sung Lee) Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · CRSI Specialist Maritime 4.0 · shipyard-side experience in maritime cybersecurity and IACS UR E26/E27 compliance, writing at the intersection of AI, data, and ship cyber resilience. 💼 LinkedIn ↗

posts.t: NIST Now Counts Ships as OT — An E26 Practitioner Reads SP 800-82r4 Section 2.5.4
