posts.t: SHIP25 Clause 23 Cyber Security — Reading a Newbuilding Clause That Governs the Yard, Not the Ship, From the Owner's Side
c: SHIP25 Clause 23 Cyber Security — Reading a Newbuilding Clause That Governs the Yard, Not the Ship, From the Owner's Side The first stand-alone cyber clause in a Norwegian standard newbuilding contract. It governs the shipyard, not the ship. Why the yard's cyber posture is still the owner's problem, and where it meets the cyber security of the vessel being delivered. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity On 9 October 2025 the Norwegian standard form shipbuilding contract was revised for the first time in 25 years, and SHIP25 arrived with a stand-alone cyber security clause.

Read the text and one thing is plain: Clause 23 addresses the shipyard's cyber risk during the build, not the cyber resilience of the ship being delivered . This article reads the clause sub-clause by sub-clause, then asks the question that follows: why should an owner care about the yard's cyber posture at all, and where does it meet the cyber security of the ship?

Governs the yard's Digital Environment E26/E27 sit in Clause 2.3, not Clause 23 12-hour early warning → NIS2 24h Liability cap 0.25% of contract price Audit right, or an independent report 4 points where yard and ship meet Introduction — a revision after 25 years, and four new compliance clauses On 9 October 2025 the Norwegian Shipowners' Association and the Norwegian Shipbuilders (formally the Norwegian Shipbuilders Sales and Marketing Organization) released SHIP25 , the standard form shipbuilding contract that replaces SHIP 2000.

Endorsed by the Federation of Norwegian Industries (Norsk Industri), the form grew out of a revision project started in 2024 and was negotiated with Nordisk Defence Club advising the owners' side and Wikborg Rein advising the builders' side. (Schjødt; Gard/Nordisk/Wikborg Rein) The skeleton of SHIP 2000 is kept, but nineteen Roman-numbered articles became twenty-five Arabic-numbered clauses, and four compliance clauses were added: safety and human rights (Clause 21), anti-bribery (Clause 22), cyber security (Clause 23), and export controls and sanctions (Clause 24). (Schjødt; Thommessen) This article deals with one of them, Clause 23 CYBER SECURITY.

The full text is published as a PDF by the Norwegian Shipowners' Association (rederi.no); Clause 23 runs from page 40 to 42. To state the conclusion first: this clause addresses the shipyard's cyber risk during the build period, not the cyber resilience of the ship being delivered . So why should an owner care about the yard's cyber posture at all? The second half of this article answers that question, tracing where the yard's cyber security meets the cyber security of the delivered ship. 1. The nature of the clause: it governs the yard's "Digital Environment", not the ship The first key to reading Clause 23 is a pair of definitions in Clause 1.

Digital Environment : information technology systems, operational technology systems, networks, Internet-enabled applications or devices, used for the provision of the Builder's deliverables and/or services to the Buyer under the Contract, as well as the data contained within such systems. (SHIP25 Clause 1(w)) Cyber Security Incident : an event that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of a Digital Environment or the information the Digital Environment processes, stores or transmits and which actually or potentially affects the Builder's obligations under this Contract or the Vessel.

(SHIP25 Clause 1(p)) The Digital Environment is the IT and OT systems, networks, Internet-enabled applications and devices "used for the provision of the Builder's deliverables and/or services to the Buyer", together with the data inside them. That means the electronic project room where drawings circulate, the yard's production OT, and the networks connecting subcontractors. The navigation and machinery control systems that will be installed on the ship are not the centre of this definition. The cyber resilience of the delivered ship is handled by a different route.

Clause 2.3.1 requires the vessel, including its machinery, equipment and outfitting, to be designed, engineered and constructed in accordance with the rules of the named classification society, and to comply "without conditions or recommendations". Since IACS Unified Requirements UR E26 (the ship) and E27 (on-board systems and equipment) apply as class rules to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024, E26/E27 compliance becomes a builder's obligation through this clause. (ABS Regulatory News 14/2023; ClassNK) Nowhere in Clause 23 do the words E26, E27, or the cyber resilience of on-board systems appear. Miss this and you will overstate what the clause does.

Clause 23 — the yard Project room and design servers Yard production OT Subcontractor and Hull Yard networks Data inside those systems Clause 2.3 + Specification — the ship Class rules, without conditions IACS UR E26 (ship) IACS UR E27 (systems and equipment) Owner's added requirements The trigger for the clause was the change in how drawings are approved. Clause 4.1.2 requires the builder to grant the buyer electronic access to the drawings, with the buyer returning approval or comments within 14 working days of access and notice.

BAHR describes this as the drawing approval process now being "assumed to be by way of electronic communication (project room or otherwise)", and summarises the purpose of the new cyber provision as meeting the IMO Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Risk Management and EU Directive 2022/2555 (NIS2). (BAHR) Thommessen assisted the working group with drafting and quality assurance of the clause. (Thommessen) 2. The core obligations: 23.1 to 23.7 Clause 23 has nine sub-clauses. Six place obligations on the Builder (23.1, 23.2, 23.4, 23.5, 23.6, 23.7), two on the Buyer (23.3, 23.8), and one sets the liability cap (23.9).

Sub-clause Content Practical meaning 23.1 Taking into account the degree of exposure, cost of implementation, the builder's size and the likelihood and severity of incidents: (a) implement reasonable, appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures in compliance with the IMO Guidelines and applicable law, and maintain them; (b) have response plans and procedures; (c) regularly review and keep records A proportionality standard, not an absolute one. A small yard and a large yard are not held to the same level 23.2 Reasonable endeavours to ensure any Hull Yard, Subcontractor or other third party implements measures as in 23.1.

The builder remains responsible for their acts and omissions as if its own An endeavours obligation, but the outcome sits with the builder . Reflects the Norwegian practice of subcontracting hulls 23.4 On becoming aware of an incident, without undue delay and at the latest within 12 hours , submit an early warning to the buyer.

Thereafter provide reasonable assistance for the buyer's mandatory notification under NIS2 Article 23 or its national implementation Designed to leave the owner half of its 24-hour NIS2 early-warning window 23.5 (a) promptly take steps to mitigate and resolve; (b) provide contact details, an initial assessment of severity and impact, and where available the indicators of compromise (IoC); assist in mitigating effects on the Vessel Notable that IoC sharing is written into the contract 23.6 To the extent incidents affect the Vessel, keep sharing information that subsequently becomes available A follow-on duty that triggers only where the ship is affected 23.7 On reasonable notice and subject to confidentiality, provide information demonstrating compliance.

The buyer, or a third-party auditor it appoints, may audit at the buyer's expense . As an alternative the builder may, at its own expense , provide a report from an independent auditor both parties accept. Trade secrets and other customers' information are excluded; information is governed by the builder's NDA and Clause 20. The buyer may pass results to its supervisory authority An audit right exists, but its scope and cost are carefully bounded The wording of 23.1 is close to a transcription of NIS2 Article 21(1).

Article 21(1) requires in-scope entities to take "appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures", and directs that proportionality take account of the entity's degree of exposure, its size, and the likelihood and severity of incidents . (NIS2 Article 21(1)) The opening of 23.1, "the degree of the Builder's exposure to risks, the cost of implementation, the Builder's size and the likelihood of occurrence of Cyber Security Incidents and their severity", is the contractual version of that sentence. It does not make the yard a NIS2 entity. It flows the supply-chain requirement of Article 21(2)(d) down by contract, on the assumption that the owner is one. 3.

The balance points an owner should check This is not an owner-friendly clause so much as a negotiated clause that balances both sides . Three points deserve attention. The liability cap is low The Builder's liability for a breach or series of breaches of this Clause 23 shall never exceed a total of 0.25% of the Original Contract Price, unless such breach is proven to have resulted solely from the gross negligence or wilful misconduct of the Builder's leading personnel. (SHIP25 Clause 23.9) On a USD 100 million vessel the cap is USD 250,000. The only exception is gross negligence or wilful misconduct of the builder's leading personnel , proven to be the sole cause.

Negligence by shop-floor staff or subcontractors does not lift the cap. The same 0.25% structure appears in Clause 21.8 (safety and human rights), so cyber was not singled out; the design applies across the new compliance clauses. Schjødt makes the same point: the obligations under the new provisions are largely placed on the builder, and SHIP25 operates with specific caps on liability for several of them. (Schjødt) For comparison, the BIMCO Cyber Security Clause 2019, written for insertion into a wide range of maritime contracts, defaults to a cap of USD 100,000 if the blank is not filled, with the same sole-cause gross negligence or wilful misconduct exception.

(BIMCO) SHIP25 swapped an absolute figure for a percentage of contract price but kept the structure. The owner has obligations too Clause 23.3 requires the buyer to familiarise itself with the builder's implemented measures after the date of contract and to notify the builder without undue delay if it identifies deficiencies. A deficiency not notified becomes harder to complain about later. Clause 23.8 requires the buyer to compensate the builder for all reasonable costs of providing information under 23.7, including documented personnel time and materials. The audit is at the buyer's cost, and so is the builder's time spent responding to it.

The audit is bounded Clause 23.7 grants an audit right and at the same time excludes access to the builder's trade secrets, other customers' information and anything not relevant to the audit's purpose, reserving the builder's right to restrict or redact. The builder may also substitute a report from an independent auditor. In practice a yard is likely to take that option, and the negotiation point becomes which auditor, and against which standard (ISO/IEC 27001, IEC 62443 and so on), both parties will "accept". 4.

Background: NIS2 alignment and the number twelve Article 23 of NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) requires in-scope entities to submit an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, an incident notification within 72 hours , and a final report within one month of the notification. (NIS2 Article 23(4)) Annex I, the sectors of high criticality, lists under water transport "inland, sea and coastal passenger and freight water transport companies, not including the individual vessels operated by those companies", managing bodies of ports, and VTS operators.

(NIS2 Annex I) A medium or large EU-based shipowner is therefore an in-scope entity, and if a yard-side incident affects its services, the shipowner is the one who must report. Shipyards themselves are not in the Annex. Incident at the yard → Yard aware → 23.4: early warning to owner ≤ 12h → Owner assesses → NIS2 Art. 23: owner's early warning ≤ 24h The 12 hours in 23.4 is half of that 24. If the yard notifies within 12 hours, the owner has 12 left. The number also matches the BIMCO 2019 clause, which requires contact details within 12 hours of the original notification.

(BIMCO) The contract gives no explicit rationale, but reading it as a figure worked back from the NIS2 deadline is the natural interpretation. One point about Norway itself. Norway is an EEA member, not an EU member, so NIS2 is transposed into Norwegian law only after it has been incorporated into the EEA Agreement. Some commentaries describe the Digital Security Act (digitalsikkerhetsloven) in force since 1 October 2025 as NIS1-based, with NIS2 transposition still to come; others present it as the NIS2 implementation, so secondary sources disagree.

(RISMA; Copla; Cyberday) Either way, the fact that SHIP25 cites NIS2 Article 23 directly reflects the reality that this form is widely used between Norwegian owners and foreign yards, and that EU entities within an owner's group may be in scope. The words "or its national implementation" in 23.4 point the same way. 5. Why the yard's cyber security is the owner's problem: four points where it meets the ship That Clause 23 governs the shipyard rather than the ship does not mean the clause has nothing to do with ship cyber security. The opposite is true. A large part of a ship's cyber security is decided at the yard and built inside the yard's systems .

Here are four points of contact that explain why the yard's cyber posture matters to the owner. Point 1 — Design data is a map of the ship's attack surface During the build, the yard's Digital Environment accumulates the general arrangement, electrical and network diagrams, equipment lists and configuration values. The vessel asset inventory and zone and conduit design that UR E26 calls for, and the topology diagrams and security capability documents that E27 suppliers submit, first exist in the yard's project room and design servers.

(ABS Regulatory News 14/2023) These documents are class-approval deliverables, and to an attacker they are also reconnaissance that stays valid for the 25 years after delivery : which system sits on which network, and where the remote-access paths are. This is not hypothetical. In 2018 the Australian shipbuilder Austal disclosed that an intruder had accessed staff contact details and ship design drawings , attempted to sell material online and tried to extort the company. Austal explained that the drawings were routinely distributed to customers and fabrication subcontractors and were neither sensitive nor classified, thou

posts.t: SQL Injection | Maritime Cyber Learning
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 10 of 7 · Course Index → SQL Injection In-band SQLi · Blind SQLi · Union-based Extraction · Error-based · Parameterised Queries · Input Validation · ORM · WAF — one of the longest-lived and most consistently exploited vulnerability classes in web applications.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain what SQL Injection is and why it occurs, describe the main SQLi variants (in-band, blind, out-of-band), demonstrate conceptually how a Union-based injection extracts data, explain why parameterised queries are the definitive fix, describe supporting controls (input validation, ORM, WAF), and identify which maritime web applications present the highest SQLi risk.

SQL Injection first appeared as a documented vulnerability in 1998 and has remained on the OWASP Top 10 list — the canonical ranking of the most critical web application security risks — virtually every year since the list was created in 2003. Despite being thoroughly understood and trivially preventable, SQLi continues to power major data breaches. Its persistence is a function of developer unfamiliarity, deadline pressure, and legacy code that has never been modernised. The attack exploits a single fundamental mistake: treating user-supplied input as part of an SQL command rather than as data.

When an application constructs a database query by concatenating a user's input directly into the query string, an attacker can inject SQL syntax that changes the logic of the query, extracts data the attacker should not see, modifies records, or even drops tables entirely. Maritime applications relevant to SQLi include Fleet Management Systems (FMS), Port Management Information Systems (PMIS), crew management portals, vessel tracking dashboards, and the administrative backends of any web-based tool that stores voyage or compliance data in a relational database.

A successful SQLi attack against a fleet database could expose crew personal data, voyage history, cargo manifests, and access credentials. 1. Why SQL Injection Happens — The Root Cause Consider a login form.

When a user enters their username admin and password mypassword , a vulnerable application might build the database query by string concatenation: VULNERABLE — string concatenation query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + username + "' AND password='" + password + "'" RESULT WITH NORMAL INPUT SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' AND password='mypassword' ATTACKER INPUT: username = admin'-- SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='admin' -- ' AND password='anything' → The -- comments out the rest. Authentication is bypassed entirely. The attacker logs in as admin. The single quote ' closes the string in the SQL syntax.

The double-dash -- begins an SQL comment that makes the database engine ignore everything that follows. The attacker's input changed the query's logic. 2. SQLi Variants — What Attackers Can Do SQL Injection Types In-band — Error-based The database returns error messages that reveal schema details — table names, column names, data types. The attacker crafts inputs that trigger informative errors and reads the database structure from the responses. In-band — Union-based SQL's UNION operator combines results from multiple SELECT statements.

An attacker appends a crafted UNION SELECT to retrieve data from other tables — credentials, email addresses, private records — which appear alongside the normal query results in the application's response. Blind — Boolean-based The application shows no data in its response but behaves differently based on whether a condition is true or false (e.g. displays a result versus a blank page). The attacker asks true/false questions and reads data one bit at a time from the behavioural difference. Slow but functional when no errors or data are returned. Blind — Time-based The attacker injects SQL that causes the database to delay its response (e.g. SLEEP(5) in MySQL) if a condition is true.

By measuring response time, data is extracted without any application-level feedback. No errors, no data — just timing. Out-of-band Data is exfiltrated through an out-of-band channel (DNS or HTTP callbacks) rather than the main application response. Less common; requires the database server to have outbound network access. Used when blind techniques are too slow. 3. Defences — How to Prevent SQL Injection Defence Layers — Priority Order 🔒 1. Parameterised Queries (Prepared Statements) — Primary Defence Parameterised queries separate SQL code from data.

The query template is sent to the database engine first, and user input is passed as parameters that are treated purely as data — never interpreted as SQL syntax. A single quote in a parameterised query is stored as a literal character, not as a string delimiter that changes query logic. SECURE — Parameterised Query (Python/psycopg2 example) cursor.execute( "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username=%s AND password=%s", (username, password) ) No matter what the user enters, the database never treats it as SQL syntax. This eliminates SQLi completely at the query level. 🛡️ 2.

ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) ORMs (SQLAlchemy, Hibernate, ActiveRecord, Django ORM) generate parameterised queries by default, removing the need to write raw SQL. Applications built on mature ORMs are largely protected from SQLi as long as developers do not bypass the ORM to write raw query strings. 🔍 3. Input Validation (Defense-in-Depth) Validate that input conforms to expected type, length, and character set before passing it to any database query. A vessel IMO number field should accept only 7-digit integers; a username field should accept only alphanumeric characters. Reject input that fails validation. This is not a substitute for parameterised queries but reduces the attack surface.

🌐 4. WAF (Web Application Firewall) A WAF inspects HTTP requests and blocks patterns matching known SQLi signatures (UNION SELECT, OR 1=1, SLEEP(), etc.). WAFs reduce noise from automated SQLi scanning tools and provide a detection and blocking layer. They should not be considered a substitute for secure code — an attacker with application knowledge can often craft bypass payloads that evade WAF signatures. 4. Maritime Context — Which Applications Are at Risk?

Maritime Applications — SQLi Risk Profile Application Risk Level Data at Risk Fleet Management Systems HIGH Crew PII, voyage records, maintenance logs, certification data Port Management Information Systems HIGH Cargo manifests, berth scheduling, vessel call data Crew Management Portals HIGH Passport/STCW data, contracts, payroll records, contact details Vessel Tracking / AIS Web Portals MEDIUM Position history, route data (potential cargo intelligence) Compliance Reporting Portals MEDIUM MARPOL/ISM inspection records, audit findings, non-conformities ✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 During E26 CRSI assessments, web application security is frequently the weakest layer.

Fleet management and crew management portals are often developed by specialised maritime software vendors or in-house teams whose primary expertise is operational, not cybersecurity. SQL Injection vulnerabilities in login forms, search functions, and filter parameters are not uncommon findings. The impact in a maritime context can extend well beyond the database itself. Crew records in a compromised fleet database expose STCW certification details, home addresses, next of kin contacts, and passport numbers — a significant data protection liability.

Worse, credentials extracted from the database can provide access to other systems if password reuse is present — which, in the absence of a password management policy, it very often is. Practical assessment note: Testing for SQLi does not require sophisticated tooling. A single quotation mark entered in a search field or URL parameter that produces a database error message is sufficient evidence of vulnerability. All web-facing application inputs should be reviewed for injection risk, and vendor-supplied applications should be assessed or their security assurances documented before deployment.

✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 10 SQL Injection occurs when user input is concatenated into SQL queries, allowing attackers to change query logic. In-band SQLi (error-based, union-based) extracts data directly through the application response; blind SQLi infers data from application behaviour or timing. Parameterised queries (prepared statements) are the primary, definitive defence — they separate code from data at the database protocol level. ORMs provide parameterised queries by default; WAFs and input validation are additional layers, not substitutes for secure code.

Maritime fleet management, port management, and crew management systems are high-value SQLi targets with significant data protection consequences. A single quote in an input field producing a database error is a red flag requiring immediate remediation. ▶ Next — Lesson 11 Lesson 11 — Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) examines another injection vulnerability class — but targeting the user's browser rather than the server's database. We explore Reflected, Stored, and DOM-based XSS, how malicious scripts steal cookies and credentials, and the Content Security Policy (CSP) controls that prevent script execution.

posts.t: IACS UR E26/E27: Two Years of Survey Practice — A Class Surveyor’s Inside View
c: IACS UR E26/E27: Two Years of Survey Practice — A Class Surveyor's Inside View Class survey is shifting its centre of gravity from verifying physical objects to verifying system behaviour. Kyle (Kyu-Oh Choi) Electrical Team Manager, RINA · Plan Approval & Type Approval ※ This article reflects the author's personal experience and views, and does not represent the official position of any classification society. All examples have been generalized and reconstructed so that no specific project can be identified.

Introduction — "Who Actually Reviews This Diagram?" In the second half of 2024, just after IACS UR E26/E27 entered into force, this was the question I heard most often from shipyard design engineers: "We are told to submit a Zones and Conduits Diagram — but who at the classification society reviews it, and against what criteria?" To be honest, at the time we were still building the answer ourselves. The URs, first published in April 2022 and later superseded by revised versions incorporating industry feedback, apply to ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. Two years have now passed. This article is not another clause-by-clause explainer.

Instead, it looks at how survey practice inside classification societies has actually changed over those two years, from a surveyor's point of view. There is no shortage of guidance addressed to equipment suppliers and shipyards. What the "reviewing side" has gone through — and what has genuinely settled into routine — is far less visible. 1. A New Shelf in the Plan Approval Office The first place to change — and the quietest — was Plan Approval. Before UR E26/E27, class plan approval revolved around physical systems: hull, machinery, electrical.

Today, every newbuilding project arrives with a set of cyber deliverables on the formal submission list: the Zones and Conduits Diagram, the Vessel Asset Inventory, the Cyber Security Design Description (CSDD), and the Ship Cyber Resilience Test Procedure. Documents that were initially treated as "reference material" have become critical-path deliverables — nothing moves forward without their approval. The change in review practice is even more telling. In the early months, review was essentially a check that the documents existed .

Two years on, it looks quite different: Zone boundaries are cross-checked against the actual network configuration — switches, firewalls, serial-to-Ethernet conversion points — using wiring diagrams and system drawings. The Vessel Asset Inventory is reconciled against the UR E27 Type Approval status of listed equipment and against the shipyard's purchasing specifications. Mismatches here are still far from rare. For every security capability stated in the CSDD, reviewers now ask whether it is a "manufacturer's catalogue phrase" or an "actually configured setting" — and raise comments accordingly.

In one sentence: the axis of review has shifted from the existence of documents to the consistency between documents . And almost without exception, consistency breaks down exactly where responsibility between shipyard, equipment supplier, and shipowner is ambiguous. 2. The Competency Map of the Surveyor Profession Is Being Redrawn The second change is about people. The traditional class surveyor comes from naval architecture, marine engineering, or navigation. UR E26/E27, however, brought the language of cybersecurity — security capabilities, access control, network segmentation, patch management — onto the survey scene.

In the first months, this showed most clearly in Plan Approval: cyber deliverables were a document type the review desks had simply never handled, and early reviews were, frankly, slow and difficult. That bottleneck has largely been cleared. Societies invested in internal training and — just as importantly — recruited and reinforced dedicated cybersecurity specialists within their plan approval organizations. Two years on, reviewing UR E26 deliverables and UR E27 Type Approval documentation is no longer a struggle; it has become a routine, properly staffed function, and plan approval itself now proceeds without particular difficulty. The honest remaining concern sits elsewhere: on board .

Attending surveyors — whose professional formation is hull, machinery, and electrical — still find it demanding to verify cyber items at the quay and during trials: reading a network diagram against the physical installation, or judging whether a witnessed test genuinely demonstrates what the procedure claims. This is the part of the transition that is still under way. But the direction is clear — OT network fundamentals have entered the surveyor training curriculum, standardized checklists and test procedures are maturing, and experience is accumulating survey by survey. The gap on board is real, but it is closing; I see it as a matter of time rather than a structural flaw. 3.

FAT and Commissioning — From Document Checks to Demonstrated Testing The third change is in the act of surveying itself. UR E26 requires a Cyber Resilience Test Procedure spanning construction, commissioning, and the vessel's operational life. In the early days, the cyber items at FAT (Factory Acceptance Test) witnessing were, frankly, a formality — little more than signing the relevant page of the test procedure. Not anymore. A few examples of what is actually performed at recent witness surveys: Verifying on the physical equipment that unused ports — physical and logical — are deactivated as stated in the procedure.

Confirming that default credentials have been changed and that role-based access separation exists as configured settings, not just as text. Witnessing scenario tests of fail-safe behaviour: whether essential functions are maintained under network failure or abnormal traffic conditions. Requiring a live demonstration that backup and restore procedures actually work, rather than accepting them on paper.

There is one situation surveyors encounter over and over: the case where "the documents are perfect, but the ship is different." A temporary bridge connection that does not appear on the approved Zones and Conduits Diagram; a remote access path left open for commissioning convenience; an undocumented laptop connection point. These come not from malice but from the inertia of the construction site. This is why recent practice has converged on a simple habit: not "document review here, physical inspection there," but walking on board with the approved diagram in hand . 4.

UR E27 Type Approval — From Bottleneck to Market Order For UR E27, the past two years can be summarized in two words: congestion, then relief. Immediately after entry into force, Type Approved equipment was scarce. Shipyards could not find approved products, suppliers did not know what to prepare, and Type Approval queues built up at class review desks. In that first year, the recurring problem was rarely technical capability — it was documentation . Security capabilities were often genuinely implemented, but the test reports to demonstrate them did not exist; secure development lifecycle (SDLC) practices existed on the shop floor but had never been written down.

Two years on, the approved-products lists of the major societies have grown visibly. What is interesting is the market effect this created: shipyard procurement teams now ask about UR E27 Type Approval status at the RFQ stage . From a surveyor's chair, this means the regulation has started working not through the survey hall but through purchasing practice . The gap between prepared and unprepared suppliers will only widen from here. 5. Divergent Interpretations Between Societies — and Convergence One of the hardest things for shipyards and owners in the early period was that requirement levels differed subtly from one classification society to another.

The same UR, yet one society demanded a particular template while another accepted alternative supporting evidence in lieu. For this reason, even stranger is the fact that some equipment manufacturers hold both an exemption statement and an E27 type approval certificate. I would call this less an embarrassment than an inevitable rite of passage for any new regulation. Over two years, as question-and-answer cases accumulated and IACS-level clarifications and individual societies' guideline revisions followed, the spread has clearly narrowed.

The change I feel most directly: in meetings with shipyard engineers, we now spend less time arguing " is this really a requirement " and more time discussing " how will you demonstrate it ." That is what a maturing regulation sounds like. 6. Blind Spots Emerging at Delivery — Owner-Supplied CBS and the Interface Grey Zone As of 2026, the first generation of UR E26 ships is only now beginning to be delivered. And as delivery surveys get underway, a problem that was invisible at the plan approval stage is surfacing at the quay: the boundary of applicability — specifically, the grey zone around owner-supplied Computer Based Systems (CBS) .

A newbuilding carries a fair number of systems procured directly by the owner, outside the shipbuilding contract: performance monitoring systems, fleet management solutions, communication and satellite equipment, cargo-specific systems. The problem is that these systems occupy an awkward position in the UR E26 deliverable structure. On survey, we repeatedly find them either excluded from the shipyard's Vessel Asset Inventory and Zones and Conduits Diagram altogether, or dismissed with a single annotation: "Owner's Scope." If these systems stood alone, the issue would be simple. They do not.

Owner-supplied systems ultimately interface with the shipboard network — pulling navigation data, collecting machinery data, sometimes touching control systems. The moment they connect, the approved zone boundaries and security architecture are disturbed. And the contract contains no answer to who designs, and who demonstrates, the cyber resilience of that connection point. At delivery surveys, this plays out as a classic three-way standoff.

The shipyard says: "outside our supply scope, therefore outside our deliverables and our test scope." The owner says: "integration is the shipyard's job." And the classification society is not a party to either contract — it must verify the cyber resilience of the ship as a whole . A structural mismatch — the regulation is written per ship, while responsibility is split per contract — and this is precisely the part that currently remains unresolved between class and shipyard on multiple projects , often surfacing only just before delivery and being patched over under schedule pressure, sometimes ending in outstanding items or conditional arrangements.

What I can say as a surveyor is this: the grey zone will not be closed by regulatory interpretation. It will be closed only when integration, documentation, and testing responsibility for owner-supplied CBS is explicitly allocated at the contract stage. A project whose shipbuilding contract and owner-supply purchase specifications contain no UR E26/E27 responsibility clauses is very likely to relive this same conflict at delivery. 7. When the System Integrator Is the Shipyard — Concerns Over an Expertise Gap Intertwined with the grey zone is another structural issue.

The UR E26 framework presupposes a System Integrator (SI) — a role responsible for designing and demonstrating the cyber resilience of the ship as a whole. In practice, on a majority of newbuilding projects, this role is taken not by a specialist integration firm but by the shipyard itself . Shipyard design and production organizations are world-class shipbuilding engineering organizations — but they are not cybersecurity organizations. The gap shows up in two places: the deliverables, and the test floor. First, document quality .

The CSDD and the integrated test procedures the shipyard must produce as SI too often amount to a compilation of the documents submitted by individual equipment suppliers. Each system-level document stands on its own — but the ship-level security architecture that should run through them, such as how inter-zone communication is governed overall or how trust relationships between systems are designed, is described nowhere. The reviewer is handed a document in which the sum of the parts never becomes a whole. Second, inexperienced test execution . Integration-level cyber resilience testing requires personnel who understand the purpose of each test item and can design and run the scenarios.

What we encounter at witness surveys instead: test setups not prepared, leaving the attendance idle; test operators following the procedure text keystroke by keystroke without being able to explain what the result means; failed items simply retested repeatedly with no root-cause analysis in between. This is not a failing of individuals. It is the failing of a structure that assigns the SI role without the specialist staffing and organization the role demands. To be fair, not every shipyard fits this description. Some have stood up dedicated teams and brought in external specialists, raising their game quickly.

Across the industry as a whole, however, the gap between the customary arrangement of "SI = shipyard" and the cyber expertise the SI role actually requires has not yet been closed — and there is growing concern that this gap will translate into variance in delivery quality. Whether shipyards internalize this capability or establish a working collaboration model with specialist SIs is one of the key things to watch in the newbuilding market over the next two to three years. 8. Remaining Homework — A Surveyor's List Beyond the grey zone and the SI capability gap discussed above, several unresolved items remain visible from the field. First, boundary questions.

Projects sitting at the edge of the applicable ship types and sizes, and practical enquiries around the contract-date criterion, keep coming. How far the new requirements should reach in conversions and retrofits of existing ships is a question we will face more and more often. Second, people. Across the entire industry, professionals who understand both OT and cybersecurity are in short supply. This bottleneck belongs to shipyards, equipment suppliers, and shipowners as much as to class — and, paradoxically, it is the single clearest opportunity for engineers looking to enter the maritime sector today.

Closing — The Nature of the Survey Itself Is Changing If the past two years had to be compressed into one sentence, it would be this: class survey is shifting its centre of gravity from verifying physical objects to verifying system behaviour. Steel plate thickness is settled the moment it is measured. Cyber resilience is not a property fixed at delivery — it is a state that must be maintained across the vessel's entire life. UR E26/E27 was the first attempt to translate that state into something surveyable , and the past two years have been about making tha

posts.t: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks | Maritime Cyber Learning
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 9 of 7 · Course Index → Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks ARP Spoofing · SSL Stripping · Rogue Access Points · Session Hijacking · TLS and Certificate Validation · HSTS · VSAT and Port Wi-Fi Interception — attacks that intercept communications silently between two parties.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain what a Man-in-the-Middle attack achieves, describe ARP spoofing and how it enables local network interception, explain SSL stripping and how it downgrades secure connections, describe rogue access point attacks, explain how TLS, certificate validation, HSTS, and certificate pinning defend against MitM, and identify the specific MitM risks in maritime satellite and port Wi-Fi environments. Imagine two people exchanging sealed letters through a courier.

A Man-in-the-Middle attack is the equivalent of that courier secretly opening every letter, reading it, potentially modifying the contents, resealing it, and delivering it as if nothing happened. Neither sender nor recipient knows the interception is occurring. In digital communications, a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack positions the attacker between two communicating parties — a client and a server, two internal systems, or a vessel and a shore-based management platform — in a way that intercepts, reads, and potentially modifies the traffic passing between them. The communicating parties continue to believe they are communicating directly with each other.

MitM attacks can target Confidentiality (reading credentials and data), Integrity (modifying data in transit — for example, changing an invoice's bank account number), and even Availability (if the attacker drops packets rather than forwarding them). They are particularly relevant in shared network environments — hotel Wi-Fi, port facilities, coffee shops — where multiple users share the same network segment. For maritime professionals, the attack surface includes port Wi-Fi networks used by crew members with company laptops, VSAT satellite links, and shore-to-ship communication channels used for operational data exchange.

This lesson examines the technical mechanisms and the defences — primarily TLS — that make modern MitM attacks much harder to execute than they once were. 1. ARP Spoofing — Intercepting Local Network Traffic ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is used on local networks to map IP addresses to MAC (hardware) addresses. When Device A wants to send data to Device B on the same local network, it broadcasts an ARP request: "Who has IP address 192.168.1.10?" Device B responds with its MAC address. ARP is stateless and unauthenticated — any device can send an unsolicited ARP reply claiming any IP address.

ARP Spoofing (ARP Poisoning) exploits this: the attacker sends forged ARP replies to both the victim and the network gateway, claiming that the attacker's MAC address corresponds to the IP address of the other party. Both devices update their ARP cache with the false mapping and begin sending traffic to the attacker, who forwards it to the real destination. Neither party knows the traffic is being routed through a third machine. ARP Spoofing — What the Attacker Intercepts Unencrypted HTTP traffic — usernames, passwords, session tokens, form data submitted to non-HTTPS sites.

DNS queries — allowing the attacker to observe which domains the victim is resolving (and potentially redirect them via DNS spoofing). Email traffic on unencrypted SMTP/IMAP connections — full email content including attachments. Internal application traffic — if applications use unencrypted internal protocols (Telnet, FTP, older industrial protocols). Session cookies — if not protected by the Secure and HttpOnly flags, allowing session hijacking. Countermeasures: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches validates ARP packets against a trusted DHCP database — preventing spoofed ARP replies from being accepted.

Static ARP entries for critical systems, and network segmentation that limits the shared broadcast domain, also reduce ARP spoofing risk. 2. SSL Stripping and Rogue Access Points 🔓 SSL Stripping SSL Stripping (Moxie Marlinspike, 2009) is a technique that downgrades a secure HTTPS connection to an unencrypted HTTP connection without the victim noticing. When a positioned MitM intercepts a victim's HTTP request that would redirect to HTTPS, it fetches the HTTPS version from the real server itself, but serves the plain HTTP version to the victim. The victim sees no security indicator because the browser's address bar shows HTTP — but thinks the connection is working.

This allows the attacker to read all traffic in cleartext even though the real server is using TLS. HSTS Defence: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) tells browsers to always use HTTPS for a domain, refusing HTTP connections entirely. Combined with preloading, HSTS prevents SSL stripping on known domains. 📶 Rogue Access Point (Evil Twin) An attacker sets up a wireless access point with the same SSID (network name) as a legitimate network — a port facility's "PortWiFi_Free" or a ship's crew Wi-Fi. Devices may automatically connect to the stronger signal. All traffic through the rogue AP passes through the attacker's device before reaching the internet.

This is trivially accomplished with a laptop and a wireless adapter running hostapd. No hacking tools required — the attack creates a standard Wi-Fi hotspot. Maritime risk: Crew members connecting to "free Wi-Fi" at ports with company laptops may expose corporate credentials, VPN configurations, and email contents to an attacker in the terminal or on the quayside. 3. TLS and Modern MitM Defences TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the primary defence against MitM on internet communications.

TLS provides: (1) encryption — all data in transit is encrypted, so even if intercepted, it cannot be read without the session keys; (2) authentication — the server presents a digital certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), allowing the client to verify it is communicating with the real server, not an impostor; (3) integrity — MAC (Message Authentication Code) values detect any tampering with data in transit. MitM Defence Layers TLS 1.3 Current TLS standard. Removes weak cipher suites, mandates forward secrecy (PFS — each session uses unique keys so past sessions cannot be decrypted even if the private key is later compromised).

All new services should use TLS 1.3; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated. Certificate Validation Browsers validate the server's TLS certificate against the trusted CA store. A certificate signed by an unknown or untrusted CA produces a browser warning. Users who click through certificate warnings are bypassing the MitM defence entirely. HSTS HTTP Strict Transport Security instructs browsers to always connect via HTTPS, even if the user types http://. Prevents SSL stripping. Combined with the HSTS preload list (browsers ship with a list of HSTS-enabled domains), this provides protection on first visit.

Certificate Pinning Mobile and desktop applications can pin a specific certificate or public key — refusing to connect if the server presents any other certificate, even a legitimately CA-signed one. Prevents attacks that use rogue CA certificates. Used in banking apps and high-security applications. VPN for Untrusted Networks A VPN tunnels all traffic through an encrypted channel before it leaves the device, preventing local network interception (including rogue APs and ARP spoofing). All company devices connecting to external networks (port Wi-Fi, hotel, satellite) should use a corporate VPN.

✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 During E26 CRSI assessments, the topic of crew device security at ports consistently surfaces as an area requiring immediate attention. In interviews with crew members, it is common to find that officers regularly connect company laptops to port-provided Wi-Fi networks to access email, upload voyage reports, or communicate with the operator — without any VPN or network protection. Some ports in high-risk regions operate Wi-Fi infrastructure that is unsecured or monitored by parties with interests in the vessel's voyage data, cargo information, or crew details.

An officer connecting to a rogue AP — or even a legitimate but poorly secured port Wi-Fi — with a company device and no VPN protection is exposing corporate communications and potentially OT network access credentials. The policy requirement is straightforward: all company devices must connect through a corporate VPN before accessing any company systems, regardless of the underlying network. "I'm at a trusted port" is not a security posture. The VPN must be configured as always-on, not user-optional. This single policy, consistently enforced, eliminates the local network interception risk regardless of what network the device happens to be connected to.

✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 9 MitM attacks intercept communications between two parties without either knowing — targeting confidentiality, integrity, and potentially availability. ARP Spoofing positions the attacker as the gateway on a local network, allowing interception of all unencrypted traffic. SSL Stripping downgrades HTTPS to HTTP so the attacker can read cleartext traffic even when the server supports TLS. Rogue Access Points (Evil Twin Wi-Fi) allow attackers to intercept all traffic from devices that connect — trivially deployed in port environments. TLS 1.3, HSTS, certificate validation, and certificate pinning are the primary technical defences against MitM.

Never click through browser certificate warnings — they indicate a potential MitM attack or a serious misconfiguration. Always-on VPN on company devices is the most effective single policy for maritime crew using external networks at ports. ▶ Next — Lesson 10 Lesson 10 — SQL Injection introduces one of the most persistent and well-documented web application vulnerabilities. We examine how improperly handled database queries allow attackers to extract, modify, or delete data by embedding malicious SQL code in user input — and how parameterised queries and input validation eliminate this vulnerability class.

posts.t: Ship Cyber Rules Find Their Way Back to the Shipyard — What Korea's Maritime Safety Act Amendment Asks of Global Shipbuilding
c: Ship Cyber Rules Find Their Way Back to the Shipyard — What Korea's Maritime Safety Act Amendment Asks of Global Shipbuilding A Korean bill on diagnosing the cyber safety of ships in service never mentions shipyards. What the state will measure is what the yard integrated, documented and delivered. A global comparison of who regulates the yard, and how. Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : https://www.linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Introduction — The bill does not mention shipyards On 18 September 2026 a partial amendment to Korea's Framework Act on Maritime Safety (Bill No. 2221467, sponsored by Rep.

Song Ok-joo and eleven others) was filed at the National Assembly. The statement of reasons on the Assembly's bill information system is short. Electronic chart use and ship-shore networks such as Starlink are expanding, cyber risk is growing with them, and so the bill creates a legal basis for the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries to diagnose maritime cyber safety, evaluate the actual state of it, and establish and implement cyber safety measures (a new Article 12-2).

(National Assembly bill information system) Bill 2221467, filed 18 Sep 2026 Yard = systems integrator until delivery Four routes back to the yard Only the EU names shipbuilding in cyber law IMO stays non-mandatory to 2028 Delivery documents are the asset Shipyards appear nowhere in this bill. It governs the operational phase, and the party it empowers is the state. This article reads it as a shipbuilding matter anyway. In 2025 China took 63% of new orders by compensated gross tonnage and Korea 21% (Clarksons data as reported by eworldship and cited by SCMP), and UNCTAD states that 91% of ships completed in 2025, in gross tonnage terms, were built in China, the Republic of Korea or Japan.

The cyber resilience of the world fleet is decided, in practice, in the design offices and commissioning berths of three countries. When one of them says the state will diagnose the cyber safety of ships in service, the question is who built the thing being diagnosed. The text of the bill itself had not been published at the time of writing. This article therefore does not assess the wording of the article. It starts from what the statement of reasons says. Part 1 — What the bill actually does Press reports say current law has no provision for state-level diagnosis and response. That is half right.

The Framework Act on Maritime Safety already defines "maritime cyber safety" in Article 3(6) and, in Article 4(2), requires the state and local governments to establish and implement policies for, among other things, maritime cyber safety management. The gap comes after that. The Act has no provisions on diagnosis, evaluation or incident notification. That gap has been filled by a ministerial notice, the Guidelines on Maritime Cyber Safety Management (MOF Notice No. 2023-74, currently No. 2024-52). Article 4 says the Minister "may establish and implement" measures.

Article 5 says the Minister "may conduct" a diagnosis or evaluation of ships and companies and "may request" the shipowner to correct weaknesses found. Article 17 requires shipowners to notify the Minister "without delay" when a cyber attack causes, or threatens to cause, a marine casualty. The notice applies to ships and companies that operate a safety management system under Article 46 of the Maritime Traffic Safety Act. (Korea Law Information Center) The statement of reasons and Articles 4 and 5 of the notice have the same structure. Until the text is published this cannot be stated as fact, but the bill reads as one that lifts the Minister's existing powers from a notice into statute.

The ministry also said, in its 31 October 2024 plan to strengthen maritime cyber safety, that it would enact a law, targeted to take effect in 2027, covering cyber safety management systems for private shipping companies and ships and a security certification scheme for ships and equipment. (MOF press release) The present bill is the step before that: the state measures first. The phrase shipbuilders should note is the later one, security certification for ships and equipment.

Part 2 — Why this is a shipyard matter: what gets diagnosed is what the yard delivered IACS UR E26 (Cyber resilience of ships) Rev.1 identifies four stakeholders: shipowner, systems integrator, supplier and classification society. It defines the systems integrator as follows. "Until vessel delivery, this role shall be taken by the Shipyard unless an alternative organization is specifically contracted/assigned this responsibility." (IACS UR E26 Rev.1, section 2) Until delivery, the party responsible for the ship's cyber resilience is the shipyard unless a contract says otherwise.

At delivery the yard hands the owner the suppliers' documentation and everything it produced itself (section 5): the zones and conduit diagram, the cyber security design description, the vessel asset inventory, any risk assessment for excluded computer based systems, and the test procedure. After delivery the owner maintains these and must have its own Ship cyber security and resilience program approved before the first annual survey. What would a state look at when it diagnoses a ship in service? Whether an asset inventory exists, how the network is segmented, how remote access is controlled. That is the documentation and configuration the yard produced at the design stage.

An operational-phase law returns to the yard by four routes. 1. The delivery package becomes the yardstick. Unless a new standard is written, the nearest measure is the set of E26 deliverables and the controls listed in the IMO guidelines. The quality of the delivery package becomes the owner's diagnostic result. 2. The gap between existing ships and newbuildings becomes visible. E26 and E27 are mandatory only for ships contracted for construction on or after 1 July 2024. An evaluation will put numbers on how different older ships are, and that leads to retrofit demand and to class notations for ships in service (the Korean Register's CSMS notation is one example). 3.

The certification scheme already announced targets ships and equipment directly. If the law planned for 2027 does include certification of ships and equipment, yards and equipment makers become the regulated parties. How that certification relates to IACS type approval is the key question. 4. Owners raise their newbuilding specifications. An owner who is asked the same questions by a state diagnosis, by vetting and by charterers will pass that burden to the yard through the specification and the contract. The bill regulates the ship in service. What it measures was delivered by the shipyard.

Part 3 — What shipyards already carry: the systems integrator under UR E26/E27 Duties during construction E26 does not only ask for documents. It places security duties on the integrator during the building period. The integrator "shall ensure that malware protection is kept updated during the construction phase" (4.2.3.4.2) and "shall prevent unauthorised access to the CBSs during the construction phase" (4.2.4.4.2). Communication with untrusted networks may only be enabled temporarily (4.2.6.4.2), and use of physical interface ports must be controlled (4.2.7.4.2).

At commissioning, after other commissioning activities are complete, the cyber resilience test is carried out with the class surveyor present. The risk these clauses address is documented. The industry Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships v5 list as a vulnerability the fact that automation systems are often "integrated by shipyards with minimal regard to cyber issues", and describe a newbuild dry bulk ship delayed from sailing for several days by a virus in its ECDIS, at a cost in the hundreds of thousands of US dollars.

Collecting supplier documentation UR E27 requires suppliers to produce an asset inventory, topology diagrams, a description and test procedure of security capabilities, security configuration guidelines, secure development lifecycle documents and more, and to deliver the approved versions to the systems integrator (section 6.2). Type approval is voluntary, and even with type approval a ship-specific step remains: "This classification process is ship-specific and shall result in a System certificate." (section 6) For every hull the yard must gather approved documents from dozens of suppliers and reflect them in the vessel asset inventory.

Bottlenecks that have surfaced ▸ Japan : On 9 July 2024 the Japan Maritime Daily reported, under a headline about last-minute orders for dozens of ships in response to the IACS cyber rules, that Japanese yards had brought contracts forward ahead of the application date. ▸ China : At the 2024 Maritime Cyber Security Forum in Fuzhou (reported on the website of the China Association of the National Shipbuilding Industry), a speaker from the Shanghai Merchant Ship Design and Research Institute raised added equipment cost, type approval of onboard systems and responsibility at annual survey as issues, together with ways to address them.

CCS reported that between January and November 2025 it served nearly 100 equipment makers and completed more than 60 capability verifications and more than 210 low-risk assessments. ▸ Suppliers : In an April 2026 article ABB observed that "vendors may need to secure multiple approvals because classification societies do not recognize each other's cyber security certificates" and that integration practices are likely to vary between shipyards.

▸ Owner-supplied equipment : ClassNK's guidelines note that owner-supplied network devices are often installed in the final stages of construction, that information about them has commonly not been shared with the integrator at the design stage, and that if they fall within scope they are subject to the commissioning survey. ▸ First mandatory ships : The two "world's first" cyber-notation vessels delivered by VARD in 2025 were contracted in 2023, ahead of the mandatory date. No class society announcement of the first mandatory-scope delivery was found. Given normal building periods, deliveries of ships contracted after July 2024 are only now becoming routine.

Readiness in numbers According to the 2025 Thetius, CyberOwl and HFW report (14 interviews and 142 survey responses; shipyards are a subset, so the yard sample is small), only 17% of shipyards feel they have adequate in-house cyber security expertise and 64% say they lack understanding of how to deliver vessels that are secure by design. Owners are no further ahead. Only 32% include cyber security in their newbuild teams, and one in six understands what to look for at handover.

In DNV's Maritime Cyber Priority 2024/25 (489 respondents), 41% said cyber security is not typically involved in procurement, falling to 27% among shipbuilding and yard professionals, which DNV attributes to UR E26/E27. Contracts have not caught up. The same Thetius report says, citing HFW, that "issues arising out of E26 and E27 are not making it into the contracts of newbuilds", and states that E26 has made cyber resilience at the design stage an essential factor in seaworthiness.

Part 4 — Global ship cyber security compliance: four layers Product layer — class enforces, IMO stays non-mandatory The only cyber standard that applies as a mandatory requirement to newbuildings and their equipment worldwide is IACS UR E26/E27, and every IACS member implements the same requirements. The Korean Register did so through its Guidance for Cyber Resilience of Ships and Systems, ClassNK through Part X of its steel ship rules and accompanying guidelines, CCS through its Guidelines for Ship Cyber Security (2024, with a 2025 edition since), DNV through Cyber secure (Essential), and BV through NR659. The integrator definition is the same across them.

The Korean Register says the role is performed by the shipyard until delivery unless contractually assigned elsewhere. ClassNK says "Except when contracted or designated otherwise, this is the shipyard." On the IMO side everything is guidance. MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 is now at Rev.4 (28 May 2026), and its paragraph 4.2 lists UR E26 and E27 as additional standards. FAL 50 and MSC 111 agreed to develop a goal-based, non-mandatory Maritime Cyber Code with a 2028 target (DNV), and the MASS Code adopted in May 2026 also starts as non-mandatory.

Corporate layer — who regulates the shipyard as a company The same questions were put to the leading shipbuilding nations by order and output share, plus the EU and the United States. Question China Korea Japan EU United States General law placing cyber duties on the yard as an entity The Cybersecurity Law places multi-level protection and incident reporting duties on every network operator, shipyards included. Nothing names shipbuilding. The critical information infrastructure regulation lists the defence science and technology industry but not shipbuilding None found.

National core technologies in shipbuilding carry protection duties under the industrial technology protection law (anti-leakage) Ship parts are designated critical products. Certified suppliers are "recommended" to take cyber measures, with an incident reporting Q&A NIS2 Annex II covers NACE 30 manufacturing, which includes 30.1 building of ships No sector-specific duty in force found. CIRCIA incident reporting rules are pending.

CISA's Critical Manufacturing Sector includes commercial ship manufacturing (a designation, not a duty) Naval and defence trigger The CII regulation names the defence science and technology industry (designation of individual yards not confirmed) Defence Technology Security Act None found Not researched DFARS 7012 and NIST SP 800-171.

CMMC Phase 2 suspended in July 2026 according to law firm commentary State support for yard and equipment cyber None found Technical and cost support for small equipment makers seeking IACS certification (2024 plan) No cyber-specific support found No yard-specific programme found None found Cyber in autonomous ship law Trial rules include network security requirements (secondary source) Autonomous ship act lists "security" of ship-shore data exchange in safety evaluation Safety guidelines include a cyber security section None found None found "None found" means this research did not confirm it, not that it does not exist. The picture is still clear.

Within the scope researched, the EU is the only jurisdiction whose cyber statute names shipbuilding as a regulated sector. General cyber laws, such as China's Cybersecurity Law, bind yards like any other company but do not single them out. NIS2 Annex II 5(f) covers NACE division 30, "Manufacture of other transport equipment", and NACE 30.1 is "Building of ships and boats". EU yards above the medium-sized threshold are candidate important entities, with risk management duties and 24-hour and 72-hour incident reporting. The same directive, when it comes to shipping

posts.t: DoS and DDoS Attacks | Maritime Cyber Learning
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 8 of 7 · Course Index → DoS and DDoS Attacks Denial of Service · Distributed DoS · Volumetric · Protocol · Application-layer attacks · Botnets · Amplification · Scrubbing · Maritime port and communication system risk — attacks targeting Availability, the third pillar of the CIA Triad.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can distinguish DoS from DDoS attacks, classify DDoS attack types (volumetric, protocol, application-layer), explain how botnets are used to generate attack traffic and how amplification attacks multiply that traffic, describe the maritime risk areas most exposed to availability attacks, and outline the primary DDoS mitigation approaches including CDN offloading and scrubbing centre services. In October 2021, the Port of Houston in Texas was targeted by a cyberattack that caused disruption to the port authority's IT systems.

While attribution and the full extent of the attack were not fully disclosed publicly, it highlighted what security professionals had long warned: port authorities and maritime logistics systems are increasingly targets for attacks designed to cause operational disruption rather than data theft. Among the most straightforward forms of such disruption is the Denial of Service attack. Unlike ransomware or data theft — which require sophisticated persistence and lateral movement — a DoS or DDoS attack has one simple objective: make a system, service, or network unavailable to its legitimate users. It targets Availability — the A in the CIA Triad.

For maritime operations, availability is not an abstract security concern. When a port's vessel traffic management system (VTMS) is unavailable, berth scheduling fails. When a ship's satellite communication system is overwhelmed, crew welfare, voyage management, and emergency communication all degrade simultaneously. When a shipping company's freight booking portal goes offline during a peak shipping window, the operational and financial impact is immediate. This lesson examines how DoS and DDoS attacks work technically, why DDoS is difficult to defend against using perimeter controls alone, and what mitigation strategies exist. 1. DoS vs DDoS — What's the Difference?

A Denial of Service (DoS) attack originates from a single source — one attacker, one machine, one connection. The attacker sends traffic or requests at a volume or in a format that the target system cannot handle, causing it to slow down, crash, or become unreachable. Early DoS attacks were simple: flood a server with more packets than it can process. Single-source DoS is now relatively easy to defend against — block the source IP and the attack stops. A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack coordinates traffic from thousands or millions of sources simultaneously.

Because the traffic comes from diverse IP addresses across multiple countries and ISPs, blocking individual sources is impractical. The aggregated bandwidth of the attack can exceed what the target organisation's upstream internet connection can absorb — meaning the attack is effective even before it reaches the target server. Three Categories of DDoS Attack Volumetric Overwhelm the target's bandwidth with raw traffic volume. Measured in Gbps or Tbps. Examples: UDP Flood, ICMP Flood, DNS Amplification, NTP Amplification. Scale: Largest attacks have exceeded 3 Tbps. A 1 Gbps internet connection is overwhelmed by a modest volumetric attack.

Protocol Exhaust network infrastructure resources (firewalls, load balancers, routers) by exploiting weaknesses in layer 3/4 protocol behaviour. Examples: SYN Flood, Ping of Death, Smurf Attack. SYN Flood: Sends thousands of TCP SYN requests without completing the handshake, filling the server's connection table until it cannot accept new connections. Application Layer Targets web application resources at layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). Mimics legitimate user traffic so it is harder to filter. Examples: HTTP Flood (GET/POST), Slowloris, RUDY, DNS Query Flood.

Slowloris: Opens many HTTP connections and keeps them alive with partial requests, exhausting the server's connection pool without high bandwidth. 2. Botnets and Amplification — How DDoS Scales The power of DDoS comes from scale. A single attacker cannot generate terabits of traffic. DDoS achieves this through two mechanisms: botnets and amplification . 🤖 Botnets A botnet is a network of compromised devices — PCs, servers, IoT cameras, routers, maritime satellite terminals — that have been infected with malware placing them under attacker control. The attacker (the "bot herder") commands all devices simultaneously to send traffic to the target.

The Mirai botnet (2016) demonstrated the IoT dimension: it compromised hundreds of thousands of internet-connected cameras and DVRs using default credentials, generating a 1.2 Tbps attack against Dyn DNS that took down Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, and many other major services. Maritime risk: Vessel-connected IoT devices (CCTV, HVAC sensors, cargo monitoring) with default credentials can be recruited into botnets without the ship operator's knowledge. 📡 Amplification Attacks Amplification exploits protocols where a small request generates a large response.

The attacker spoofs the victim's IP address as the source and sends small requests to thousands of open servers — all of which send large responses to the victim. DNS Amplification: A 60-byte DNS query can generate a 3,000-byte response — an amplification factor of 50x. NTP Amplification (using the monlist command) can reach amplification factors of 556x. The attacker generates 100 Mbps of outbound traffic but the victim receives 5.5 Gbps. Defence: Network operators implement BCP38 (source address validation) to block spoofed traffic; DNS and NTP servers should be configured to prevent amplification. 3.

Maritime Systems at Risk from Availability Attacks Maritime Availability Attack Surface Port Management Systems VTMS (Vessel Traffic Management), Terminal Operating Systems (TOS), and port community systems are internet-connected and handle time-critical berth scheduling, cargo handling, and customs documentation. Outage even for hours causes cascading delays across the supply chain. Fleet Management Portals Web-based fleet management, voyage planning, and freight booking systems are externally accessible and targeted by attacks when competitors, state actors, or hacktivists wish to disrupt a shipping company's operations.

Satellite Communications VSAT and LEO satellite terminals can be overwhelmed or jammed at the radio layer. While jamming is not a cyber attack in the traditional sense, satellite service denial impacts vessel communications, crew welfare systems, and remote monitoring simultaneously. AIS & GMDSS Systems AIS (Automatic Identification System) data feeds to third-party tracking sites and coast guard systems can be targeted. AIS jamming and spoofing are distinct from DDoS but share the outcome: degrading situational awareness for vessel traffic in a region.

Shipyard & Classification Systems Design systems, approval workflows, and certification databases — if unavailable — halt new construction projects and compliance processes. Ransomware groups have targeted shipyards specifically for this leverage. 4. DDoS Mitigation Strategies DDoS mitigation cannot rely on perimeter firewalls alone — if the attack traffic exceeds the upstream bandwidth capacity, the connection is saturated before it reaches the firewall. Effective mitigation requires services positioned upstream of the target's internet connection.

☁️ CDN / Anycast DDoS Protection Services like Cloudflare, Akamai, and AWS Shield use anycast routing to distribute attack traffic across globally distributed nodes. Each node absorbs a fraction of the total attack volume. The legitimate origin server is never directly exposed to the raw attack traffic. 🔄 Upstream Scrubbing Centres ISP-level DDoS mitigation services redirect attack traffic to scrubbing centres — high-capacity filtering infrastructure that distinguishes malicious from legitimate traffic and forwards only clean traffic to the target. Requires BGP routing agreements with the ISP.

🚦 Rate Limiting & Traffic Shaping For application-layer attacks that do not saturate bandwidth, rate limiting (restricting requests per IP, per session, per endpoint) can prevent server resource exhaustion. Web Application Firewalls (WAF) can identify and block HTTP flood patterns. 📋 Incident Response Plan A pre-agreed DDoS response playbook — including contacts at the ISP, scrubbing provider, and internal escalation tree — reduces response time from hours to minutes. Maritime operators should include DDoS scenarios in their cyber incident response exercises.

✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 In E26 CRSI assessments, DDoS typically ranks lower than ransomware and phishing in the threat prioritisation discussions — partly because it does not result in data theft and partly because maritime operators see it as something that happens to internet companies, not shipping companies. This is a mistake that is becoming increasingly expensive. The maritime sector's increasing digitisation — online freight booking, real-time vessel tracking, electronic documentation, web-based port clearance systems — has made availability a genuine operational dependency.

A shipping company that cannot accept freight bookings for 12 hours during peak season because its portal is under DDoS attack suffers direct revenue loss, customer relationship damage, and potential regulatory reporting obligations under cyber incident reporting rules. The simplest actionable step for maritime operators is to ensure that externally accessible web services are behind a CDN or DDoS mitigation provider. The cost of a Cloudflare or Akamai subscription is modest compared to the operational cost of even a short availability outage. This should be a baseline requirement for any internet-facing service in a maritime organisation's digital infrastructure.

✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 8 DoS (single source) and DDoS (distributed, multiple sources) attacks target Availability — the A in CIA Triad. Three DDoS categories: Volumetric (bandwidth flooding), Protocol (state table exhaustion), Application-layer (HTTP/HTTPS flood). Botnets (infected IoT/PC networks) and amplification (exploiting UDP protocols like DNS/NTP to multiply traffic) are how DDoS achieves massive scale. Maritime systems at risk include port VTS/TOS, fleet management portals, satellite comms, and AIS data feeds. Perimeter firewalls cannot stop volumetric DDoS — upstream CDN, anycast distribution, and ISP scrubbing services are required.

DDoS incident response plans — with pre-agreed ISP/scrubbing contacts — must be prepared before an attack, not during one. ▶ Next — Lesson 9 Lesson 9 — Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Attacks examines how attackers intercept communications between two parties — neither of whom realises the interception is happening. This includes ARP spoofing, SSL stripping, rogue access points, and how TLS certificate pinning provides defence. The maritime dimension covers VSAT interception risk and unsecured port Wi-Fi environments.
