posts.t: EU CRA Series, Part 5 of 5: A CRA Roadmap for Marine Equipment Suppliers
c: EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers · Part 5 of 5 A CRA Roadmap for Marine Equipment Suppliers From scoping to a running vulnerability desk: six steps, the right kind of help, and a checklist Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 The first four parts explained what the EU Cyber Resilience Act is, what it costs to get wrong, what E27 evidence still lacks and how to prove behaviour by test. This last part puts it in order: six steps a marine equipment supplier can follow between now and 11 December 2027, how to choose the kind of outside help that fits, and a checklist to measure progress.

EU CRA for Marine Equipment Makers: the series What the CRA is and how it differs from IACS UR E26/E27 The CRA in numbers: fines, deadlines and the reporting clock From E27 evidence to CRA evidence: what suppliers must add Proving security, function and recovery by test A CRA roadmap for marine equipment suppliers (this article) 1. Two Starting Points Where a supplier starts depends on the product's stage and on what the company can do itself.

Product still in development Product finished, needs to show conformity Typical situation Security functions still need to be designed and built in, so help is needed with requirements, design and implementation The company can develop and fix its own product, but needs help interpreting the CRA and judging and proving how well it meets it Main activities Define security requirements and review the design; build and improve the security functions; design and run tests and analyse defects; prepare procedures, technical documentation and assessment Check scope, product class and existing evidence; gap analysis and risk assessment per requirement; plan improvements and tests; review results; prepare procedures, technical documentation and assessment Result Security built into the product from modification through to conformity Conformity established for a product the company develops itself 2.

Six Steps to December 2027 STEP 1 Inventory and scope List every product and variant sold into the EU. Mark MED items as out of scope (Art. 2(4)). Note which are already on the market: Art. 14 reporting already applies to them. Record: product list with scope decision STEP 2 Class and route Decide each product's class (default, Annex III Class I or II, Annex IV) and the conformity procedure. Book a notified body early where one is needed. Record: class and procedure per product STEP 3 Gap diagnosis Map existing E27 evidence against Annex I (Part 3). Mark each requirement covered, partly covered or not covered.

Record: cross-mapping matrix and task list STEP 4 Fix and test Close gaps in the product and the process; run the security, function and recovery tests (Part 4); retest after fixes. Record: test reports per version STEP 5 Document and declare Technical documentation (Annex VII), SBOM, support period, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking. Record: technical file, DoC STEP 6 Run it Keep the PSIRT, CVD contact, 24-hour reporting, update releases and regular reviews going for the whole support period. Record: advisories, reports, review records Step 6 is not the last thing to do; parts of it are already due.

A supplier that has nothing else in place should set up the reporting and vulnerability intake side of step 6 first, because Article 14 has applied since 11 September 2026 (Part 2). 3. Who Does What Around the Supplier The CRA puts the duties on the manufacturer, but the shipyard and owner shape whether they work in practice.

Party Role in making the CRA work for a ship Equipment supplier Meets its CRA duties; declares the support period; provides the DoC, update policy and security contact; notifies users of exploited vulnerabilities and fixes Shipyard / system integrator Asks for CRA status, DoC, SBOM availability and support period at the RFQ stage; links supplier evidence to the E26 vessel asset inventory and design documents Shipowner / manager Builds supplier notices into its own incident and patch processes; plans for equipment whose support ends before the ship's life does How supplier notices actually reach the ship, and the contract clauses that close the gaps, are covered in Julius Shin's article Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner?
4. Choosing the Right Kind of Outside Help Most marine equipment makers will use some outside support. It helps to know which kind of question each type answers.

Type of support The question it answers What it typically includes Conformity diagnosis and improvement "Which requirements apply to our product, and what do we need to add?" Scope and class review, review of existing evidence, gap analysis and risk assessment per requirement, improvement plan, help with procedures, technical documentation and assessment Security, function and recovery testing "Can we prove by actual behaviour that the product meets the requirements and that our fixes worked?" Unauthorised access, malformed traffic and load tests; checks that functions survive and recover through update or communication failures; defect analysis and retest after changes An in-house test environment "What do we need to test ourselves every time a product or version changes?" Product-specific test connections, reproduction of operating signals and measurement; repeatable scenarios with logging and reporting; procedures, training and maintenance Before engaging anyone, the supplier should have its product list and existing evidence in hand.

The scope of development, fixes, tests and documentation can only be agreed once both sides know what already exists. 5. A Ten-Point Checklist 1 We know which of our products and variants are on the EU market, and which are MED items. 2 Each in-scope product has a class and a chosen conformity procedure. 3 We can receive vulnerability reports through a published contact, and someone owns them. 4 We can decide within hours whether a vulnerability is actively exploited, and file an early warning within 24 hours. 5 Each product has a machine-readable SBOM linked to vulnerability data. 6 Our E27 evidence is mapped against Annex I, with every gap assigned to an owner.

7 Security, function and recovery tests exist for each product, with records per version. 8 Each product has a declared support period with written reasoning, and a plan for when it ends. 9 Security updates are signed, verified on install, tested for recovery, free of charge and kept available for at least ten years. 10 Technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity will be ready, and kept for at least ten years. ※ Harmonised standards, implementing acts and Commission guidance under the CRA continue to be published. Review this roadmap against the latest official EU sources before each step.

⚓ Captain Paul's Take Over five parts, one idea has run through the series: E27 asks whether a system was secure when the ship was delivered; the CRA asks whether the maker is still looking after it. The technical work overlaps a great deal. The real change is organisational: someone in the company has to own a product's security for as long as it is supported. Suppliers that start with that ownership, and build the documents and tests around it, will find December 2027 manageable. Suppliers that start with the documents will find the reporting clock catches them first.

Primary sources: Regulation / standard Type Link EU CRA, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 EUR-Lex View text ↗ IACS UR E27 Rev.1 (Sep 2023) PDF Download PDF ↗ CRA requirements–standards mapping PDF Download PDF ↗ Related reading: EU CRA Series, Part 1: What the Cyber Resilience Act Is and How It Differs From IACS UR E26/E27 Does CRA Vulnerability Reporting Reach the Shipowner? (Julius Shin) One Ship, Three Layers: Unifying NIS2, CRA, and IACS UR E26 Captain Paul (In Sung Lee) Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · CRSI Specialist Maritime 4.0 · shipyard-side experience in maritime cybersecurity and IACS UR E26/E27 compliance, writing at the intersection of AI, data, and ship cyber resilience.

posts.t: Ransomware & the Cyber Kill Chain | Maritime Cyber Learning
c: 📚 Series Maritime Cybersecurity Learning Roadmap | PART 2 Lesson 7 of 7 · Course Index → Ransomware & the Cyber Kill Chain How ransomware encrypts systems and demands payment · The Kill Chain framework · Double extortion · Maritime OT risk · Backup strategy and recovery — the attack lifecycle that now threatens vessel operations globally.

Captain Paul Maritime Cybersecurity · IACS UR E26/E27 September 2026 🎯 Lesson Objective After this lesson you can explain how ransomware encrypts data and extorts victims, walk through the seven stages of the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain, describe how ransomware attacks have been used against maritime operators, explain double extortion and why paying the ransom is not a recovery strategy, and outline the backup and recovery architecture that provides the most effective resilience against ransomware. In June 2017, the NotPetya malware began propagating across global corporate networks. Within hours, A.P.

Møller-Mærsk — one of the world's largest container shipping companies — had 45,000 PCs wiped, 4,000 servers destroyed, and 2,500 applications offline. Every terminal in every major port the company operated went dark. The company was forced to reinstall the entire IT infrastructure from scratch, using only one domain controller recovered from a data centre in Ghana that happened to be offline during the attack. Total losses: approximately USD 300 million. Operations across 76 ports were disrupted. NotPetya was technically a wiper disguised as ransomware — it was designed to destroy, not to collect ransom.

But it illustrated with devastating clarity what a destructive malware campaign can do to global maritime logistics. Since then, true ransomware — malware designed to encrypt files and demand payment for the decryption key — has become one of the most significant threats to maritime operators, port authorities, and shipyards worldwide. This lesson explains how ransomware works, how the Cyber Kill Chain framework helps defenders understand the full attack lifecycle, and what the maritime sector's specific vulnerabilities are. Most importantly, it addresses the question that every organisation facing ransomware eventually asks: should we pay? Ransomware rarely begins as ransomware.

It begins as an email attachment, a phishing link, or an unpatched vulnerability — entry points covered in this series. Understanding the Kill Chain is understanding where defences can interrupt the attack before encryption begins. 1. How Ransomware Works Ransomware is malware that encrypts files on the infected system — and often across the network — making them inaccessible to the owner. The attacker holds the decryption key and demands payment (usually in cryptocurrency) in exchange for it. The encryption used by modern ransomware is typically strong asymmetric or hybrid cryptography (RSA-2048 or AES-256 + RSA) — without the key, recovery is practically impossible.

Ransomware has evolved significantly. Early ransomware in the early 2010s was largely opportunistic — spread via mass email campaigns, targeting individual users, demanding small payments. Modern ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operations are run like professional criminal enterprises, with dedicated developer teams, affiliate networks, negotiation specialists, and customer support for victims who want to pay. Ransomware Technical Execution — What Happens After Infection 1 Initial Access & Execution Ransomware reaches the system via phishing attachment, malicious link, exploit of an unpatched vulnerability, or RDP brute force.

The malware executable runs and begins its operation quietly, often sleeping for minutes or days to avoid immediate detection. 2 Command & Control (C2) Connection The malware connects to the attacker's Command & Control server to receive the encryption key material and instructions. This C2 connection is an opportunity for detection — network monitoring that identifies unusual outbound connections can catch this step. 3 Discovery & Lateral Movement Modern ransomware scans the network for accessible shares, databases, backup systems, and domain controllers. It uses built-in Windows tools (living-off-the-land: PsExec, PowerShell, WMI) to spread to other systems.

Attackers may spend days or weeks in the network before triggering encryption — finding all valuable targets and disabling backups first. 4 Data Exfiltration (Double Extortion) Before encrypting, modern ransomware groups exfiltrate sensitive data — crew records, financial documents, contracts, technical drawings, strategic plans. This provides a second extortion lever: "pay the ransom or we publish your data online." This is double extortion, and it means ransomware is now also a data breach. 5 Shadow Copy & Backup Destruction Before encrypting, ransomware deletes Windows Volume Shadow Copies (VSS) and any accessible backups.

This is why backups on network-attached storage accessible from the infected systems are often destroyed along with primary data. Offline or immutable backups are the critical protection here. 6 Encryption Files are encrypted using strong symmetric encryption (AES-256) with the symmetric key itself encrypted by an asymmetric public key held by the attacker (RSA-2048 or higher). The victim's files are renamed with a new extension. A ransom note is dropped in every directory. 7 Ransom Demand & Negotiation The ransom note directs the victim to a Tor-hosted negotiation portal. Demands range from tens of thousands to tens of millions of dollars in Bitcoin or Monero.

Payment does not guarantee decryption — some groups take payment and disappear; others provide a slow or partial decryptor. Law enforcement increasingly monitors ransom payments. 2. The Cyber Kill Chain — Mapping the Full Attack Lifecycle The Cyber Kill Chain was developed by Lockheed Martin in 2011, adapted from the military concept of a kill chain (the process required to identify and engage a target). In cybersecurity, the Kill Chain describes the sequential stages a threat actor must complete to achieve their objective. The key insight is that breaking any link in the chain prevents the attack — defenders do not need to stop all seven stages, only one.

Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain — 7 Stages # Stage Ransomware Context Defender Opportunity 1 Reconnaissance Attacker researches target org: identifies employees (LinkedIn), email format, exposed services (Shodan), unpatched systems. Reduce public exposure; monitor for scanning activity; use threat intelligence. 2 Weaponisation Attacker prepares the delivery: crafts phishing email, embeds ransomware in a document macro, or configures an exploit kit. Limited control at this stage — preparation happens off-site. Focus on next stages. 3 Delivery Phishing email delivered; malicious attachment or link sent; or exploit delivered via web drive-by.

Email security (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), anti-phishing gateway, URL filtering, attachment sandboxing. 4 Exploitation User opens the malicious document; macro runs; or a software vulnerability (unpatched RDP, VPN, Log4Shell) is exploited. Patch management; disable macros; endpoint protection (EDR); least privilege. 5 Installation Ransomware dropper installs the main payload; establishes persistence via registry run keys, scheduled tasks, or services. EDR behavioural detection; application whitelisting; privileged access management. 6 C2 (Command & Control) Ransomware establishes encrypted C2 channel; receives encryption keys, updates instructions; may be maintained for days or weeks.

Network detection (NDR); DNS filtering; egress monitoring; zero-trust network access. 7 Actions on Objectives Lateral movement, data exfiltration, backup destruction, then encryption. Ransom note dropped. Network segmentation (limits lateral movement); immutable backups; incident response plan. The Kill Chain also underpins the MITRE ATT&CK framework — a more granular taxonomy of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that security operations centres use to map detected activity to known attack patterns and threat actor groups. ATT&CK is the practical implementation of Kill Chain thinking at operational depth. 3.

Maritime-Specific Ransomware Risk The maritime sector presents a distinctive risk profile for ransomware for several reasons that compound the standard corporate threat: 🚢 Operational Continuity Pressure A vessel in transit or at port cannot simply "shut down and recover." Port slot windows are fixed; charter party obligations have financial penalties for delays; vessel management systems (VMS) and port management systems (PMS) are time-critical. This time pressure makes maritime operators more likely to pay the ransom quickly. 🔧 OT/IT Convergence Modern vessels run integrated IT/OT networks.

If a ransomware infection spreads from an administrative PC to the ship network, it may reach systems that control ballast, cargo, propulsion, or navigation — not because those OT systems are the target, but because of insufficient segmentation between IT and OT networks. 📡 Remote & Satellite-Connected Vessels at sea rely on satellite communications for IT connectivity. Patch management, endpoint detection updates, and incident response all depend on bandwidth-constrained links. Remote IT support during a ransomware incident at sea is severely limited compared to a shore-based office.

🏗️ Supply Chain Exposure Port terminals, shipyards, ship chandlers, and classification society systems all interact with vessel systems. A ransomware attack on a port operator can halt container handling even if the shipping company's own systems are clean. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack demonstrated this supply chain impact pattern. 4. Should Organisations Pay the Ransom? This question has no universal answer, but the security community, law enforcement (FBI, INTERPOL, NCSC), and regulators have increasingly aligned on a firm position: paying the ransom is not a recovery strategy .

Here is why: No guarantee Approximately 20% of organisations that pay the ransom do not receive a working decryption key, or receive a key that only partially restores data. Ransomware groups are criminal enterprises with no contractual obligations. Funding future attacks Payment funds the ransomware group to develop more sophisticated tools and attack more organisations. The maritime sector's willingness to pay makes it a preferred target. Re-infection risk Organisations that pay are re-attacked within 12 months at a rate of approximately 80%, because the root cause of the initial infection was not remediated. Paying does not address the access vector or the lateral movement capability.

Data still published Under double extortion, some groups publish exfiltrated data regardless of whether the ransom is paid — particularly when a higher profile victim can generate publicity for the group. Legal risk OFAC (US Treasury) has issued guidance that paying ransom to sanctioned entities — which some ransomware groups are — can constitute a sanctions violation, exposing the paying organisation to regulatory action. ✅ The Only Reliable Recovery Strategy Maintain tested, offline (or immutable cloud) backups using the 3-2-1 rule : 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite and offline (air-gapped or immutable object storage).

Backups must be tested regularly — an untested backup is not a backup. Recovery time objectives (RTO) must be defined and practiced in tabletop exercises before an incident occurs. ✍️ Author Insight — From the Field Captain Paul · Maritime Cybersecurity Consultant · IACS UR E26/E27 One pattern that emerges consistently during E26 CRSI assessments is the backup verification gap. Companies maintain backups — that much is usually true.

But when asked "when did you last test restoring from your backup?" the honest answer is often "we haven't." Or: "we test the backup process, but not the restoration." Or: "the backup runs to a NAS share on the same network segment." The painful reality is that a backup connected to the same network segment as the infected systems will be encrypted along with everything else. Modern ransomware groups specifically target backup systems as a priority — knowing that eliminating recovery options increases the pressure to pay. If the backup share is visible from the infected machine, it will be encrypted.

The single most impactful recommendation from a ransomware resilience perspective is this: implement at least one backup copy that is genuinely inaccessible from the primary network — either offline (tape, external drive in a safe) or immutable object storage (S3 Object Lock or equivalent) that cannot be deleted or overwritten by credentials on the primary network. Every maritime operator should be able to answer: "if every system on our corporate network was encrypted tonight, what is the maximum amount of data we would lose and how long would restoration take?" If that question cannot be answered, the backup strategy needs work.

✅ Key Takeaways — Lesson 7 Ransomware encrypts files using strong cryptography (AES-256 + RSA) and demands payment for the decryption key. Modern ransomware groups operate as professional criminal enterprises (RaaS), with negotiation teams and affiliate networks. Double extortion — exfiltrate data before encrypting, then threaten publication — makes ransomware also a data breach. The Cyber Kill Chain has seven stages; breaking any one stage prevents the attack. Defenders have opportunities at every stage. Maritime ransomware risk is elevated by operational continuity pressure, IT/OT convergence, satellite link constraints, and supply chain interdependencies.

Paying the ransom is not a recovery strategy: no guarantee of decryption, funds future attacks, high re-infection rate. Offline or immutable backups tested via regular restoration exercises are the most effective ransomware resilience measure. ▶ Next — Lesson 8 Lesson 8 — DoS and DDoS Attacks examines attacks that target the Availability pillar of the CIA Triad. A Denial of Service attack does not steal data or install malware — it makes systems unavailable. We examine how volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks work, how botnets amplify attack traffic, and the specific risk DDoS poses to port management and vessel communication systems.
