posts.t: The Next Maritime Transformation: A Call to the Global Consulting Industry
c: Maritime Transformation · Insight Captain Paul The Next Maritime Transformation: A Call to the Global Consulting Industry Maritime is changing. Consulting must change. Talent must change. Maritime Transformation Maritime Consulting AI · Data · Cyber Resilience IACS UR E26/E27 📚 In This Article Part I — Maritime Is Changing · Sections 1–4 Part II — Consulting Must Change. Talent Must Change. · Sections 5–10 Part III — Let's Build It Together · Sections 11–22 Maritime is changing. Consulting must change. Talent must change. The maritime industry is entering a transformation unlike anything we have seen before.

For decades, maritime competitiveness was largely defined by: Engineering Shipbuilding Operational Excellence Cost Scale But the competitive landscape is changing. 🚢 The modern vessel is becoming a connected cyber-physical system . 🏗️ The modern shipyard is becoming a digital engineering and data-driven manufacturing environment . 🤖 AI is entering design, engineering, operations and decision-making. 🛡️ Cybersecurity is becoming part of ship safety and operational resilience. ⚖️ Regulation is increasingly shaping technology architecture. 📊 And data is becoming a strategic asset. The boundaries between maritime, engineering, software, AI, cybersecurity and consulting are disappearing.

This creates a fundamental question: Who will lead the next Maritime Transformation? PART I Maritime Is Changing The industry, the consulting market, and the leader this transformation needs 1. The Maritime Industry Is Becoming a Technology Industry A ship is no longer simply a physical asset. It increasingly consists of: Ship Engineering + OT + IT + Connectivity + Cloud + Data + AI + Automation + Cybersecurity + Regulation This convergence changes the nature of the industry. 🛡️ IACS UR E26/E27 Embedding cyber resilience into the ship lifecycle. 🧭 IMO · Autonomous & Remotely Operated Ships Pushing maritime toward new operational and regulatory models.

🤖 AI Moving from experimentation toward practical applications. 🔧 Transformation Agenda Digital twins, predictive maintenance, autonomous navigation, AI-assisted engineering and intelligent operations are becoming part of the industry's transformation agenda. The question is no longer "Will maritime adopt AI?" The question is "How will maritime redesign its operating model around AI, data and cyber resilience?" 2. A New Consulting Market Is Emerging This transformation creates a new consulting opportunity.

Traditional consulting could often be represented as: Traditional Strategy → Technology → Implementation Maritime Transformation requires something broader: Maritime Transformation Strategy → Engineering → Data → AI → Cybersecurity → Regulation → Architecture → Implementation → Continuous Assurance This is no longer a single consulting practice. It is an ecosystem. And this is where the capabilities of global consulting firms become highly relevant. 🧠 McKinsey · BCG · Bain Bring deep strategy and transformation capabilities. 🏛️ PwC · EY · KPMG · Deloitte Bring broad capabilities across technology, cyber, risk, data, AI, implementation and assurance.

💻 Technology Companies Bring platforms and infrastructure. ⚓ Class Societies Bring technical and regulatory assurance. 🚢 Shipyards & Shipowners Bring engineering and operational reality. 💡 The opportunity is to connect these capabilities. 3. But There Is a Bigger Question The consulting industry has excellent methodologies. It has global networks. It has experienced partners and consultants. It has enormous amounts of research and market intelligence. But transformation ultimately depends on people . So the question becomes: Who can actually understand this new maritime environment well enough to lead it? Someone who understands only strategy ? Not enough. Someone who understands only AI ?

Not enough. Someone who understands only cybersecurity ? Not enough. Someone who understands only shipbuilding ? Not enough. The next generation requires something different. 4. The New Maritime Transformation Leader We believe the future leader will combine: Deep Expertise with Cross-Domain Integration This person can understand: Shipbuilding and Cybersecurity OT and AI Data and Regulation Technology and Business Strategy and Execution This person is not simply a generalist. And not simply a specialist. They are a: Maritime Transformation Integrator They understand enough of multiple domains to connect specialists while retaining meaningful technical depth in their own field.

This capability will become increasingly valuable. PART II Consulting Must Change. Talent Must Change. Talent models, organization design, the role of consulting, AI and Practitioner Intelligence 5. The Problem With Yesterday's Talent Model Can the talent and organizational models that created yesterday's success create tomorrow's transformation? The answer may not always be yes. Traditional organizations have often been structured around practices: Strategy Technology Cyber Data Risk Industry This model worked because clients could often separate their problems into projects. But today's maritime transformation problems increasingly cross these boundaries.

The client does not experience "This is a Cyber problem." or "This is an AI problem." The client experiences "We need to transform our ship, shipyard, fleet or organization." That is one problem. 6. Past Success Must Not Become Tomorrow's Constraint This does not mean existing high-performing professionals are no longer valuable. Quite the opposite. Their experience is essential. The challenge is to combine that experience with new capabilities.

Existing experts should be connected with: 🤖 AI specialists 🛡️ Cybersecurity engineers 📊 Data scientists 💻 Software engineers ⚓ Maritime practitioners ⚖️ Regulatory experts 🧭 Transformation leaders The objective is not Old Talent vs New Talent It is Experience + Technology Depth + Breadth Specialization + Integration Human Judgment + AI 7. Organizations Must Change Along With Talent Recruitment alone will not solve the problem. Organization design must change as well. Instead of organizing transformation strictly by internal departments, organizations need to increasingly organize around industry problems and outcomes .

For Maritime Transformation, that could mean bringing together, from the beginning: Ship Engineering + AI/Data + Cybersecurity + OT + Regulation + Business Strategy + Implementation 💡 The organizational structure should follow the problem. Not the other way around. 8. Consulting Has a New Responsibility This is where the role of consulting firms becomes particularly important.

Consulting should not simply answer: "What should the client do?" It should help answer: ❓ "What is changing?" ❓ "Why is it changing?" ❓ "What does it mean for this industry?" ❓ "What are the risks?" ❓ "What capabilities are required?" ❓ "How can it actually be implemented?" ❓ "How can the client sustain the transformation after consultants leave?" The role of consulting is therefore evolving from: Advisor → Interpreter → Integrator → Transformation Partner → Capability Builder 9. AI Makes This Responsibility Even Greater AI is changing consulting itself. This means information itself is becoming less scarce.

AI can increasingly produce Research · Analysis · Reports · Code · Presentations · Summaries · Knowledge retrieval What becomes more valuable Judgment · Context · Experience · Systems Thinking · Industry Knowledge · Accountability · Execution AI can generate an answer. But someone still needs to determine: Is this answer appropriate for this vessel , this shipyard , this architecture , this regulation and this business ? That is where human expertise becomes more valuable, not less. 10. This Is Why Practitioner Intelligence Matters There is a type of knowledge that cannot be easily obtained from market reports: Practitioner Intelligence. 🔍 What actually happens during ship design ?

🔍 Where does E27 become difficult? 🔍 How do shipyards interpret cyber requirements? 🔍 Where do engineering and procurement disconnect? 🔍 What happens during FAT and SAT ? 🔍 How does cyber resilience become operational? 🔍 Where does AI encounter real-world maritime constraints? These are questions answered by people who have actually experienced the industry. ⚓ And this is where ShipPaulJobs has a distinctive role. PART III Let's Build It Together ShipPaulJobs, the global consulting community, and a new model of collaboration 11. Meet the ShipPaulJobs Crew ShipPaulJobs has deliberately brought together practitioners from different parts of the maritime transformation ecosystem.

Our contributors bring experience and perspectives across: Shipbuilding Ship Design Maritime Engineering Shipboard OT/IT Cybersecurity IACS E26/E27 IMO & Maritime Regulations AI Data Analytics Generative AI Cloud DevSecOps Automation Autonomous Systems Digital Shipyard Cyber Resilience Technology Consulting Maritime Transformation This diversity is intentional. ⚓ Meet the ShipPaulJobs Crew → 12. We Are Not Building Another Blog ShipPaulJobs is being built as something broader: Maritime AI & Cybersecurity Intelligence.

A practitioner-driven knowledge platform connecting: Knowledge + Experience + Technology + Regulation + People + Business Our ambition is to transform practical experience into structured industry knowledge. And eventually: Knowledge → Intelligence → AI-enabled Intelligence → Decision Support → Transformation 13. The People Behind the Knowledge Are the Real Asset Articles are only the visible layer. Behind every meaningful article is: Experience Research Engineering Analysis Judgment Field Knowledge Continuous Learning That is why the ShipPaulJobs Crew matters. We are not trying to create a community where everyone thinks alike.

We are building a community where different expertise can interact. 💡 Because transformation happens at the intersection. 14. From Specialists to Connectors The next generation of maritime professionals must increasingly become connectors . A person who can discuss: Discuss… …with Ship Design an engineer E26/E27 a class expert OT Security a cyber architect AI a data scientist Digital Transformation an executive Business Value a CEO This combination is rare. And it is precisely the capability that the next Maritime Transformation requires. 15.

Why We Are Speaking to Global Consulting Firms This message is directed to the global consulting community — to McKinsey, BCG, Bain, PwC, EY, KPMG and the broader ecosystem of global consulting, technology and professional services organizations. You have Global Scale Strategy Transformation Methodologies Technology Ecosystems Executive Relationships Implementation Capabilities Industry Research ShipPaulJobs is building Maritime Practitioner Intelligence Cross-Domain Expertise Emerging Technology Insight Cybersecurity Knowledge AI/Data Capability Regulatory Intelligence Practitioner Networks 💡 These capabilities are complementary. 16.

We Are Not Asking You to Replace Your Model We are asking you to extend it. The future may not be Consulting Firm vs Practitioner Community It can be Consulting Firm + Practitioner Community Global consulting firms can bring scale. Practitioners can bring reality. Technology companies can bring platforms. Class societies can bring assurance. Shipyards can bring engineering. Shipowners can bring operational requirements. Universities can bring research. Together, these capabilities can create a new Maritime Transformation ecosystem . 17.

A New Model of Collaboration Imagine: Consulting Strategy + Practitioner Intelligence + Maritime Engineering + AI/Data + Cybersecurity + Regulatory Intelligence + Technology Platforms + Operational Experience This can create transformation programs that are not only strategically compelling , but technically credible and operationally executable . That is the opportunity. 18. The Responsibility of the Industry The future should not be defined simply by More AI More automation More digitalization The objective should be Safer ships More resilient operations Better engineering Better decisions Higher productivity Stronger competitiveness Responsible innovation Technology is the means.

Transformation is the process. Sustainable maritime competitiveness is the goal. 19. A Message to Consulting Leaders The question is not whether your organizations already have talented people. They do. The question is: Are your talent and organizational models optimized for the problems your clients will face five or ten years from now? If the answer is uncertain, now is the time to experiment. ➤ Recruit unconventional profiles. ➤ Build cross-domain teams. ➤ Bring practitioners into transformation programs. ➤ Connect engineers with strategists. ➤ Connect AI with cybersecurity. ➤ Connect regulation with architecture. ➤ Connect shipbuilding with software.

➤ And create new career paths for people who can cross these boundaries. 20. ShipPaulJobs Is Ready to Collaborate We believe the people required to lead this transformation are already emerging. Some are engineers. Some are cybersecurity professionals. Some are AI specialists. Some are consultants. Some are researchers. Some are industry veterans. Some are technology entrepreneurs. But they share one characteristic: They can connect what others see separately. That is the capability we are building. 21.

We Invite You to Work With Us If you are working on: Maritime AI Digital Shipyard Cybersecurity Cyber Resilience IACS E26/E27 AI Transformation Autonomous Ships Maritime Data OT Security Digital Engineering MASS Maritime Regulatory Transformation Future Maritime Operating Models we would like to talk. Not because we believe one organization has all the answers. But because we believe the most difficult problems require the best people to work together. 22. Let's Build the Future Together The next Maritime Transformation will not belong to one consulting firm. It will not belong to one technology company. It will not belong to one shipyard. It will not belong to one class society.

It will be built by an ecosystem. An ecosystem where: Strategy meets Engineering AI meets Cybersecurity Data meets Operations Technology meets Regulation ShipPaulJobs wants to be part of that ecosystem. And we invite the global consulting industry to build it with us. ⚓ The Next Generation Starts With People The maritime industry is changing. Consulting must change. Talent must change. Organizations must change. And the way we collaborate must change. The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most technology. They will be those with the people capable of understanding how everything connects. Maritime. Engineering. AI. Data. Cybersecurity. Regulation. Business.

Execution. This is the capability we are building at ShipPaulJobs. Let's Build It Together. We are opening the door to collaboration with: Global Consulting Firms Shipyards Shipowners Class Societies Technology C

posts.t: Anti-Heeling: When One Sensor Moves Hundreds of Tonnes
c: Anti-Heeling: When One Sensor Moves Hundreds of Tonnes How a system no regulation demands ends up holding one of the most direct physical authority paths on a ship Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Engineering Intelligence · System Anatomy An anti-heeling system is not required by any regulation. It exists because cargo work demands it. And yet it holds one of the shortest paths on a ship between a single sensor reading and hundreds of tonnes of water in motion — with no human approving each step. This is a typology-level anatomy of that system under the Interaction–Authority–Physical Effect model.

The analysis unit is not the interface but the interaction, and the classification is drawn from the equipment families the system is built from rather than from any one vendor's implementation. Authority sits upstream. Physical contact sits downstream. Treating the highest authority value as a risk score gets both ends wrong. Part I — Engineering 1. Why this system exists When forty-foot containers land in sequence on one side of a bay, when vehicles file up a PCTC ramp, when a crane slews a heavy lift outboard, all of these operations produce the same side effect. The work itself heels the ship. The problem is not that the ship heels. The problem is that when it heels, the work stops.

Gantry cranes have rail gradient limits. Ramps stop accepting vehicles when the contact angle goes out of range. Slewing cranes lose rated capacity the moment a list develops. Cargo work is priced by the hour, and halting operations for every list correction puts that cost straight onto the schedule. Single-side loading / crane slewing / ramp work | v Heel develops | +--> Cargo equipment operating limits exceeded --> work stops | +--> Stability margin eroded ------------------> safety reserve reduced | v Without correction, the operation does not work An anti-heeling system solves this by actively transferring ballast water between port and starboard heeling tanks.

Water moves from the low side to the high side, the moment is offset, and the hull stays upright without pausing the operation. This is where the character of the system is set. Anti-heeling exists not because a rule demands it, but because the work requires it. That is exactly why the source workbook records its requirement origin as design-dependent VERIFIED . No SOLAS provision requiring anti-heeling on general merchant ships was identified in this research INFERRED ; the basis for fitting one comes from what the ship carries and how it handles it.

And yet this unmandated system holds one of the shortest physical authority paths on the vessel — because a single inclinometer reading is translated into pump start without any per-event human approval. The work itself creates the heel. Anti-heeling offsets the moment while cargo operations continue — it does not remove the cause. Transfer runs from the low side to the high side. 2. What the system does At system level, anti-heeling runs a five-step closed loop. [MEASURE] heel angle + port/stbd tank levels | [DECIDE] compare against setpoint -> correction needed? direction? target volume?

| [SELECT] choose transfer path (from which tank to which tank) | [ACTUATE] align valves -> start pump (or blower, on air-driven designs) | [RE-MEASURE] confirm heel change -> stop on target | +------------------- loop -------------------+ One distinction must be made immediately. Anti-heeling is not a static stability device. It does not increase GM and it does not improve the righting arm curve. If anything it works the other way, introducing free surface effect that reduces stability. Working practice carries the same distinction in its vocabulary. Heel is a temporary inclination caused by an external force, and the vessel returns upright when that force is removed.

List is a permanent inclination arising from weight distribution TYPICAL . Anti-heeling is designed, as its name says, to correct heel — but in service it also pushes back the list created by uneven loading. When that distinction blurs, operation slides into continuously offsetting a symptom while leaving the cause in place. A ship whose anti-heeling never stops running usually has a cargo plan problem, not an equipment problem. 3. Core functions and operating modes Mode Who decides Where the human stands Manual Operator Commands direction, timing and volume directly Automatic Controller Monitors only.

No per-event approval Semi-auto (product-dependent) Controller proposes, operator accepts An approval gate exists Automatic mode is governed by its setpoint. Vendor documentation across several suppliers repeats the same figures: correction begins around ±1.5° of heel , and the initiation setpoint itself is adjustable across roughly 0.04°–5° depending on the product TYPICAL . Read that as a specification and move on, and you miss the point of this article. A setpoint is a parameter, parameters can be changed, and the act of changing one has a name — A3 CONFIGURE. 4. How the system works The answer to "how does anti-heeling work" is not a single program.

The result is produced by a combination of four things: the inclinometer reading, the tank levels, the setpoints and control parameters, and the actual state of valves and pumps. Engineering note — the thing you protect is not one executable The program can be intact and a changed setpoint will change behaviour. Program and setpoint can both be intact and a wrong inclinometer reading will make the system act precisely, in precisely the wrong direction. And if valve position feedback disagrees with reality, the console displays normal while the water goes somewhere else. What must be protected is not the executable but the entire set of inputs that manufacture the decision.

Part II — Composition 5. What the system is made of In the workbook's component breakdown this system decomposes into five components, and those five belong to five different typologies — one clean layer each, with no overlap.

Purdue Typology Equipment family Authority (out) Physical effect CBS (E26) L2 — supervisory TYP-B04 HMI / operator console / panel A4 · A3 · A1 P3 P2 P1 Y — list separately L1 — control TYP-B07 PLC / controller / control unit A4 · A5 · A2 P4 P3 P2 Y — list separately L1 — sensing TYP-B01 Process transmitter / sensor A1 · A2 P1 P2 P3 N L0 — process TYP-A04 Shutoff / isolation valve A0 P4 (P5 subset) N L0 — process TYP-C01 Centrifugal pump A0 P4 N All five carry an evidence grade of TYPICAL — these are typology-level determinations inherited from equipment-family research, not measurements taken from a specific vessel.

Read as one line each: the console receives human intent, the controller manufactures the decision, the transmitter supplies the raw material for that decision, the valve sets the path, and the pump moves the water. Supervisory, control, sensing and actuation — exactly one layer apiece. Two things in that table are worth pausing on before we unpack the layers. The bottom two rows carry zero outbound authority and the maximum physical effect , and neither of them is a CBS candidate. Section 11 returns to why that combination is the normal case rather than an anomaly. 6. Typology profiles L2 — HMI / operator console (TYP-B04).

Programmable, networked, and in the workbook all instances are CBS candidates to be listed separately. These are workstation-class devices running application software on a general-purpose or embedded OS. The family's principal authority is A4 COMMAND and A3 CONFIGURE toward its controller — and A3 is quieter than A4 but outlives it. L1 — PLC / controller (TYP-B07). All workbook instances sit at Purdue L1-control. This is not the sensing layer; it is the layer that drives final elements directly. Closing a continuous regulation loop is A5 CONTROL; discrete orders such as pump start/stop are A4 COMMAND. Both codes coexist inside one controller. L1 — Process transmitter (TYP-B01).

An important split lives here. A passive sensing element and a microprocessor-based transmitter are different devices. The latter can be re-ranged and diagnosed remotely over HART. Because the workbook records the network interface only as "likely", whether this system's instrument link is plain 4-20 mA or carries HART is not established INFERRED . L0 — Valve (TYP-A04) and pump (TYP-C01). Neither is programmable, neither is networked, and neither is an E26 CBS candidate. A valve body opens when pilot hydraulics arrive and closes when they are cut. A pump turns when power arrives and stops when it is removed. Neither interprets any information.

Key distinction — component count is not a measure of cyber relevance Of this system's five components, only two are E26 CBS candidates. The other three — transmitter, valve, pump — are not. Yet the physical work of moving water is done entirely by those three, and the two CBS candidates move no water at all. Inventory size and physical contact are different axes, and overlaying them misreads both. 7. Where the supply boundary falls In the workbook, all five components of this system sit within the parent package. On the component list, no independent control cubicle exists.

Vendor product documentation describes a different typical composition: main control cabinet, remote operator panels, tank level sensors, motor starters for pumps and valves, PLC, and inclinometer TYPICAL . Two of those do not appear as independent items in the workbook's five rows — the main control cabinet and the motor starter . The inventory trap What actually holds physical authority is not the pump but the starter panel that energises it, and the logic lives in the control cabinet. Both are absorbed into the parent package and appear on no component row. Build an E26 asset inventory mechanically from component rows and a CBS that should have been listed separately disappears entirely.

The signal to watch for is explicit in the data: a CBS candidacy of "list separately" combined with a supply boundary of "within parent package". The supply boundary is a trust boundary for reasons that have nothing to do with where a firewall sits. It is a trust boundary because administrative ownership, privilege and update path all change at that line. If the package vendor commissions, tunes and updates its own cubicle, that access should not be labelled with the name of a connection method — "remote access" — but modelled as the acts it makes possible: A3 CONFIGURE, A6 ADMINISTER, A7 UPDATE_EXECUTABLE. 8.

Architecture patterns Real topology varies by ship, and the available data does not settle it. Three conceptual patterns are offered; none is asserted as the answer. [A] Standalone dedicated inclinometer -> dedicated PLC -> dedicated valves & pumps | +--(status display only)--> IAS Character: control authority is closed inside the package. Local attack surface. [B] IAS-Integrated dedicated inclinometer -> dedicated PLC -> valves & pumps |<--> IAS (display, alarms, history, mode change) Character: display and alarms leave for the IAS, and mode-change authority now also exists at the IAS console.

[C] Ballast-Integrated inclinometer -> PLC -> shared ballast valves & pumps |<--> IAS / ballast control Character: anti-heeling and ballast operation divide authority over the same physical resources. Misbehaviour on one side can directly obstruct work on the other. Typical architecture — disclaimer These three patterns are conceptual models, not the implementation of any particular ship or product. Actual arrangement is established only by vendor documentation, P&IDs and the vessel's own wiring diagrams. Statements below of the form "this system holds A5 CONTROL" are used only where they hold across patterns A through C. Part III — Authority and Physical Effect 9.
What information and commands flow through it Writing "data is exchanged" ends the analysis before it starts. Separate them.

What flows Kind Direction Heel angle Information Transmitter → controller Port/stbd tank levels Information Transmitter → controller Pump run / trip status Information Starter → controller → console Valve position feedback Information Limit switch → controller → console Mode change Command Console → controller Initiation setpoint and limits Parameter Console / service tool → controller Pump start / stop Command Controller → starter Valve open / close Command Controller → solenoid Without the third column this table is useless — because information and commands travel the same links, and authority differs by direction. 10.

What authority does each connection carry Source → Destination Observe Provide info Configure Command Control Admin Update exec Transmitter → controller · Y · · · · · Controller → transmitter Y · ? · · · ? Controller → valve & pump · · · Y Y · · Controller → IAS · Y · · · · · Console → controller Y · Y Y · · · Vendor service tool → controller Y · Y · · Y Y Vendor service tool → console Y · Y · · Y Y Valve & pump → controller · Y · · · · · Key distinction — connectivity is not authority The inclinometer is wired to the controller. But the authority the inclinometer exercises over the controller stops at A2 PROVIDE_INFORMATION. It commands nothing.

In the other direction the controller holds A1 OBSERVE, and on a HART-class transmitter that may extend to A3 CONFIGURE through remote re-ranging — except that the source data records the network interface only as "likely", so whether that path exists here is not established. We do not write that it exists, and we do not write that it does not. The columns worth staring at are the right-hand three. The only rows carrying Admin and Update Executable are the vendor service paths , not the operating paths. And those persist after the interaction ends — logic and firmware do not disappear on the next scan cycle.

The controller typology's doctrine puts it in one sentence: changing an interlock limit can be more consequential than a runtime command. Without sending a single order, quietly widening the initiation setpoint and the transfer volume limit leaves the machine to run itself into the dangerous region. 11.

Can the system affect the physical process Interaction Authority Physical effect Human gate Security significance Transmitter → controller A2 P1 SUPERVISION False value contaminates the decision Console → controller A3, A4 P2 EXECUTION No physical quantity changes; operating state does Controller → valve & pump A4, A5 P3 / P4 SUPERVISION (auto) Physical contact of the automatic loop Valve operation A0 P4 (subset P5) — Directly opens and closes fluid flow Pump operation A0 P4 — Actually transfers the water Vendor tool → controller A3, A6, A7 P3 (persistent) AUTHORIZATION Behaviour change that outlives the session Key distinction — A0 outbound and P4 hold at the same time The valve's and the pump's outbound authority is A0 NONE.
They order nothing; they hold no logic, no setpoint, no state machine. And y

posts.t: Crude Oil Washing: The System That Rules Built
c: Crude Oil Washing: The System That Rules Built Five component rows, four typologies, and a safety case the system does not own Julius Shin Maritime Technical Consultant · Shipboard Cybersecurity & Compliance - LinkedIn : linkedin.com/in/abysstoinfinity Engineering Intelligence · System Anatomy Crude oil washing is one of the few shipboard systems whose existence is written directly into an international convention. MARPOL Annex I Regulation 33 requires it on every crude oil tanker of 20,000 tonnes deadweight and above delivered after 1 June 1982, and IMO Res. A.446(XI) specifies clause by clause how it must be designed, operated and verified.

Read those rules in the order they were actually made, however, and something unusual appears: the system was permitted only because a different system had already made it safe. In the bill of materials COW is five rows — two valves, one machine, one pressure instrument, one control panel. Three of those rows hold no firmware, no network port and no accounts, and those same three rows perform the entirety of the physical action inside the tank. The one row that holds all of the software never touches crude oil. Counting components and counting risk are two different jobs here. Key point COW does not own its own safety case.

The inert atmosphere that makes it permissible to spray crude oil at high pressure inside a cargo tank is produced, measured and alarmed by the inert gas system, and COW’s obligation under A.446 §6.6 is only to confirm the value and stop if it is out of limits. You can collapse this system’s safety case without touching a single COW component. Connectivity is not authority — and in this system the most violent physical action of all carries none. What follows is a typology-based analysis of SYS-012 in four parts: what the system is for and how it works, what it is made of, what authority and physical effect each of its connections carries, and what security follows from that.

Statements are tagged with the evidence grade of the typology doctrine they rest on, and nothing is asserted above that ceiling. Part I — Engineering 1. Why This System Exists Crude oil does not leave a cargo tank clean. Long after the pumps have started drawing air, a sticky layer of wax and asphaltene remains on the tank walls, the girders, the stringers and the bottom plating. Class and P&I material puts the quantity of this clingage at around 1,000 tonnes for a VLCC, though it varies widely with tank structure and crude properties, so the figure is better read as an order of magnitude than as a number.

Typical (UK P&I Club, Carefully to Carry — bulk oil cargo shortage claims.) The problems it creates are not one but three. The first is commercial . What the owner and charterer contracted for is the delivery at the discharge port of what was loaded at the load port, and oil stuck to the tank is cargo that was not delivered. The physical origin of ship–shore difference and of ROB (remaining on board) disputes sits here. The second is operational . Crude carriers ballast into some of their cargo tanks. Put seawater into a tank that still holds residue and that seawater becomes oily ballast, which has to go somewhere before the next load port.

The third is environmental , and it is where regulation enters. The traditional way of handling oily ballast was Load-on-Top: water-wash, collect in the slop tank, let it settle, decant the water from above. That reduces the total discharged. It does not eliminate the discharge. Crude cargo discharged | v Clingage remains on tank steel | +--> Cargo not delivered -> ship-shore difference / ROB dispute | +--> Ballast into dirty tank -> oily ballast -> operational discharge to sea | +--> Sludge accumulation -> tank entry, manual removal, occupational risk That is the engineering problem.

But the route by which COW — the solution — became standard equipment on merchant ships follows the order of accidents and rules, not the order of engineering. Reverse that order and you will misread the system's entire safety case. Between 12 and 30 December 1969, three VLCCs of about 210,000 DWT — Marpessa , Mactra and Kong Haakon VII — were severely damaged by cargo tank explosions. Marpessa sank on the ballast leg of her maiden voyage and two crew members died; the other two survived with much of their main decks blown away. Verified All three were cleaning empty cargo tanks at the time.

The intensive research the owners launched concluded that the high-pressure water jets then in standard use were building up electrostatic charge inside the large cargo tanks as they struck the steel, and that in a space full of hydrocarbon vapour this discharged as a spark. Verified The response was to fill the cargo tanks with inert gas during cleaning, and that became today's mandatory inert gas system (IGS). Then in February 1978 the TSPP Conference (International Conference on Tanker Safety and Pollution Prevention) convened by IMO adopted the 1978 Protocol , which amended MARPOL 73 and brought COW inside the rules.

Verified New crude tankers above 20,000 DWT were required to fit COW; existing tankers above 40,000 DWT had to choose between segregated ballast tanks (SBT) and COW, with clean ballast tanks permitted during the transition. The clause number at adoption was Annex I Reg. 13(6) ; after the 2004 wholesale revision of Annex I, the operative provision is MARPOL Annex I Regulation 33.1 — every crude oil tanker of 20,000 tonnes deadweight and above delivered after 1 June 1982 shall be fitted with a cargo tank cleaning system using crude oil washing.

Verified 1969 Water washing in a gas-filled tank -> static discharge -> 3 VLCC explosions | v 1970s Inert gas system mandated (O2 kept low inside cargo tanks) | v [precondition now exists] 1978 TSPP Protocol -> COW required as cargo-tank cleaning method | v 1979 Res. A.446(XI) -> design, operation and control specification | v 1982+ MARPOL Annex I Reg. 33 / Reg. 35 -> installation + operation obligations The order matters. COW could only become a rule after the inert atmosphere had already been secured as a precondition. Spraying crude oil at high pressure is not electrostatically more benign than spraying water.

The only reason it is permitted is that the inside of the tank is not a combustible atmosphere — and that fact is produced not by COW but by IGS. We return to it in section 14, but the COW system does not own its own safety case , and that structure is the single most important fact in analysing it. 2. What the System Does The function of COW is defined in one sentence: spray the crude oil currently being discharged, at high pressure, onto the internal surfaces of the cargo tank, so that clingage dissolves and leaves with the cargo stream. Every peculiarity of this system is contained in that definition. There is no dedicated washing medium. There is no dedicated storage.

In principle there is not even a dedicated pump — the discharge of the cargo pumps is branched off. Much of the piping is shared with the cargo system. IMO Res. A.446(XI) §4.1.2 requires the COW system to be a permanent installation, independent of the fire main, while explicitly allowing parts of the cargo system to be incorporated provided the requirements are met. Verified Figure 1. COW has no operating window of its own. The medium is the cargo, drawn from the cargo pump discharge, and the inert atmosphere that makes the operation permissible is produced by IGS — another system. Three of the verifications required by IMO Res. A.446(XI) sit outside the instrumentation path altogether.
The system-level functional decomposition looks like this.

Function Content Owner F1 Supply the medium Branch cargo pump discharge into the COW main, hold the specified driving pressure Cargo pumps ( external ) + COW line valves F2 Distribute Route the medium per tank or tank group, isolate the rest COW supply isolation valves F3 Apply Fixed machines strike the walls on a defined pattern (vertical arc + rotation) COW machines F4 Recover Strip the dissolved oil off the tank bottom back into the cargo stream Stripping system ( external ) F5 Monitor Indicate driving pressure, machine operation, stripping rate, level Pressure instrumentation + control panel F6 Sequence Advance the programme according to the approved manual COW control panel + person F7 Verify the precondition Confirm tank oxygen and pressure are within limits, stop if not Person (information from IGS) Note that F1 and F4 belong to external systems , and that the information source for F7 is also external.

What COW actually owns is F2, F3, F5 and F6 — which is why only five component rows in the bill of materials are attributed to it. 3. Core Functions and Operating Modes COW has no operating window of its own. It is performed inside the discharge operation itself , while the cargo is flowing out. That fact defines its modes. Top wash. While the level in the tank is still high, the machine arc is restricted to the upper sector, cleaning the structure and shell exposed above the liquid surface. There is no point spraying below the surface, so the arc programme follows the level down. Bottom wash. Once the level is low enough, the arc extends downward to cover the bottom and lower structure.

This is the phase in which the stripping load is heaviest. Single-stage / multi-stage. Depending on what the approved manual specifies, the full arc is swept in one pass or the work is divided into several stages that track the falling level. Either way, the mode is not a free parameter but an item in an approved procedure . MARPOL Annex I Reg. 35.3 requires the COW system to be operated in accordance with the Operations and Equipment Manual, except where the cargo is unsuitable. Verified Ballast-voyage preparation. Reg. 35.2 requires a sufficient number of cargo tanks to be crude oil washed before each ballast voyage so that ballast water is put only into tanks that have been washed .

Verified In other words, which tanks get washed is decided not by the convenience of the washing operation but by the ballast plan for the next voyage . The COW programme is logically coupled to cargo and ballast planning — and that coupling is the path by which the propagation chain in section 13 reaches a regulatory outcome. Verification modes. A.446(XI) requires separate acts that confirm the result and the functioning of the equipment.

§4.2.10 requires visual confirmation, after COW and before water washing, that the tank is essentially free of clingage and deposits, and sets the oil content of the departure ballast at not more than 0.00085 by volume as the criterion of stripping effectiveness. §4.2.12 requires deck-mounted machines to have a means of indicating rotation and arc movement from outside the tank . §4.2.13 accepts, for submerged machines, external indication, characteristic operating sound, or periodic verification at intervals of not more than six uses or twelve months. §4.4.4 requires hand dipping facilities at the aftermost point of the tank and at three other locations.

Verified Every one of those verification items is something a human being does with their eyes, ears and hands . The clauses were drafted two decades before the concept of cyber security existed, and yet the result is that this system carries out-of-band integrity verification mandated by rule , independent of any instrumentation signal. Section 12 returns to that property. 4. How the System Works The washing result — how clean the tank actually got — is not the output of any single piece of equipment. It is a product of several physical quantities.

Wash effectiveness = f( driving pressure [pump discharge, throttled at COW line] x nozzle throughput [machine size, nozzle bore] x arc programme [vertical sector + rotation, per stage] x machines run simultaneously [hydraulic balance limit] x tank geometry [shadow from girders, stringers, bulkheads] x stripping rate [must exceed wash throughput] x crude properties [wax / asphaltene content, temperature] ) subject to O2 <= 8 vol% and positive tank pressure [external precondition] A.446(XI) puts a quantitative constraint on each term of that product.

§4.2.8 requires that the area shadowed from direct impingement not exceed 10% on horizontal surfaces and 15% on vertical ones — meaning the arrangement, number and arc of the machines has to be verified together with the internal geometry of the tank. §4.4.3 requires the stripping arrangement to remove oil at 1.25 times the total throughput of the machines running simultaneously — a physical inequality stating that oil must be taken off the bottom faster than washing puts it there.

§4.3.3 requires the system to remain operable with one pump out of service ; §4.1.3 requires pressure relief to discharge to the pump suction side; §4.1.9 requires the piping to be tested at 1.5 times working pressure after installation. Verified ENGINEERING NOTE — the thing to protect is not one executable. Of the variables that determine COW performance, the ones that live in software are the arc programme, the step sequence, and the range settings of the pressure instrumentation. Driving pressure is set by the pump and valve opening; nozzle throughput by machined dimensions; shadow by the structural drawing of the tank; stripping capability by pump specification.

Imagining compromise of this system purely as "changing the control programme" misses half of it. The cheaper route is not to change the physical quantity but to change what people believe the physical quantity to be . Change the range of one pressure instrument and the wash fails without a single valve moving incorrectly — and the failure stays hidden until somebody enters the tank and looks. That is scenario 1 in section 16. The physical chain resolves as follows.

Cargo pump discharge -> COW main line -> COW supply isolation valve (per tank group) -> COW line valve -> Fixed tank washing machine (deck-mounted or submerged) -> High-pressure crude jet -> Tank steel surface -> Clingage dissolved -> Falls to tank bottom -> Stripping suction -> Back into cargo discharge line -> Ashore [monitoring] COW line pressure transmitter -> COW control panel -> CCR mimic [verification] External rotation/arc indicator (A.446 4.2.12) -> Operator eye [precondition] IGS -> O2 <= 8 vol% + positive pressure (A.446 6.6) -> Operator decision Part II — Composition 5. What the System Is Made Of Viewed as a component list, COW is five rows. But listing five rows is not analysis.

Which typology each row belongs to is what determines its authority, its physical effect and its attack surface — and each typology already carries confirmed doctrine. [Table 1] Typology Composition Typology Equipment kind Components Purdue CBS (UR E26) Evidence TYP-A04 Shutoff / isolation valve 2 — COW supply isolation valves, COW line valves L0 — physical process N Typical TYP-A05 Mechanical machine / tool 1 — COW machines L0 — physical process N Typical TYP-B02 Pro

posts.t: Should TA, SoC, and SoF Be Treated as Equivalent Options? - UR E27 Response Strategies (5/12)
c: Should TA, SoC, and SoF Be Treated as Equivalent Options? Article 5 of a 12-Part Series on UR E27 Strategies for Marine Equipment Suppliers ※ The product, system, and project examples described in this article are illustrative examples created to explain how UR E27 conformity demonstration routes should be selected and applied. Blue Horizonist (Lew) Maritime & Cyber Security Consultant · ISP Consultant In the previous article, we examined how to break UR E27 requirements down into detailed, independently verifiable requirements and allocate them across product functionality, product Configuration, the manufacturer’s internal procedures, and the vessel-wide security architecture.

The resulting Requirement–Design–Evidence Matrix enables equipment manufacturers to distinguish between what the current product already satisfies and what requires further development, Configuration changes, testing, or consultation with relevant stakeholders. The answer is not simply a matter of choosing between three certificate names — it requires understanding what needs to be confirmed and which route best fits the actual supply situation. At this stage, many manufacturers ask the following question: “Does our product need TA, or can we address the requirement through an SoC or SoF?” This question requires caution.

TA, SoC, and SoF should not be regarded as three parallel certification routes used consistently by all classification societies. IACS UR E27 defines the Cyber Resilience requirements that onboard systems and equipment must satisfy, but the assessment process and the titles of the documents issued may differ according to each classification society’s Rules and approval scheme. The decision should therefore not begin by selecting a document called TA, SoC, or SoF. The manufacturer should first determine which of the following situations applies: 1 Type Approval is required for a product with the same Baseline that will be supplied repeatedly across multiple projects.

2 The conformity of an individual product or system Configuration supplied to a specific vessel must be verified on a project-specific basis. 3 It is necessary to confirm, based on the product’s intended purpose and specifications, whether the product is exempt from UR E27 or whether application is non-mandatory. The manufacturer should then confirm which procedure, document title, and Evidence the relevant classification society requires for that situation. This article distinguishes among TA, project-specific conformity verification, and confirmation of exemption or non-mandatory application, and explains how to select an appropriate approach for an actual project.

※ The terminology, issuance conditions, and validity of SoCs and SoFs may differ among classification societies. In particular, the SoF described by ClassNK in relation to UR E26/E27 is used to confirm that a product’s intended purpose and specifications meet the conditions for exemption or non-mandatory application. It should therefore not be understood as a general UR E27 conformity certificate or a simplified alternative to TA. 1 First Distinguish the ‘Type of Certificate’ from ‘What Needs to Be Confirmed’ The matters that an equipment manufacturer may need to have confirmed can be divided into three broad categories.

① Repeatable Conformity of a Standardized Product This applies when a product with the same Hardware, Software, Firmware, and principal security functions is intended to be supplied repeatedly to multiple vessels. In this case, Type Approval based on a defined product Baseline may be considered. ② Conformity of a Project-Specific Supply Configuration This applies when a base product exists, but customer-specific Software, Gateways, Interfaces, or remote access functions are added, causing the actual supply Configuration to differ from one project to another. Individual design review and testing may then be required for the product or system Configuration supplied to the specific project.

Some classification societies may issue a Statement of Compliance or another form of confirmation based on such a review. However, the title “SoC” and its conditions of issuance are not applied consistently by all classification societies. ③ Exemption from UR E27 or Non-Mandatory Application This applies when it is unclear whether a product falls within the scope of UR E27, or when confirmation is required as to whether its intended purpose and specifications meet the conditions for exemption or non-mandatory application. ClassNK states that it may issue a Statement of Fact in such cases. This SoF does not confirm that the product satisfies all UR E27 requirements.

It confirms that the product’s intended purpose and specifications meet the conditions for exemption or non-mandatory application. Unless these three situations are distinguished, TA, SoC, and SoF may be incorrectly compared as higher and lower levels of certification. 2 TA, SoC, and SoF Do Not Form a Single Hierarchy TA, SoC, and SoF are sometimes understood as the following hierarchy: TA → Highest level SoC → Intermediate level SoF → Minimum level In practice, however, they should not be viewed as a vertical hierarchy because each document may address a different subject and purpose.

Category General Meaning What to Confirm for UR E27 TA Type Approval for a defined product Configuration Approved product Baseline, requirements, test scope, and conditions of validity SoC A document title that may be used by a classification society to confirm conformity with specified Rules or requirements Issuing classification society, assessment target, applicable Rules, project scope, and product scope ClassNK UR E26/E27 SoF Confirmation that a product qualifies for exemption or non-mandatory application Product purpose and specifications, basis and conditions for exemption or non-mandatory application Statements such as “We will obtain an SoF instead of TA” or “SoF is a lower level than SoC” may therefore be inaccurate.

In particular, ClassNK’s UR E26/E27 SoF is not an alternative certificate that reduces the scope of conformity demonstration. It is a document confirming whether the requirements need to be applied in the first place and should not be compared with TA or project-specific conformity verification on the same basis. 3 The First Route: Type Approval for Repeatedly Supplied Products TA is generally most valuable when the same or a sufficiently similar product will be supplied repeatedly across multiple projects. However, the fact that the product name remains unchanged does not automatically make it suitable for TA. The product Baseline subject to approval must be clearly defined and maintained.

At a minimum, the product Baseline should include: Hardware Model, Part Number, and Revision OS, Firmware, and Application Version Third-Party Software and major components User-account and privilege structure Network Interfaces Ports, Protocols, and Services Security Log functionality Backup and Restore functionality Whether remote access functionality is included Default security Configuration Installation Image and Checksum Related manuals and test procedures For example, if the same Machinery Monitoring Gateway is supplied to dozens of vessels each year and the only project-specific differences are IP addresses and connected systems, TA may allow the manufacturer to reuse common product functions and Evidence.

Conversely, if the sales proposal specifies Application Version 3.2, production installs Version 3.1, and the service team later applies Patch 3.3 onsite, the approval target itself becomes unclear. In this situation, establishing the product Baseline and Configuration-management system may need to take priority over applying for TA.

A manufacturer preparing for TA should be able to answer the following question: “How will we ensure that the product tested today and the products manufactured and delivered in the future continue to maintain the same approved Baseline?” 4 The Value of TA Comes from Reusing Evidence, Not Merely Holding a Certificate The economic value of TA depends less on the certificate itself than on whether the design and test Evidence obtained during approval can be reused in subsequent projects.

If the product Baseline is maintained, the following materials may be reusable across multiple projects: Product architecture and functional description Hardware and Software configuration list Internal product Interface specification User-role and privilege Matrix List of Ports, Protocols, and Services Security Event list Secure Configuration and Hardening Guide Software Update and integrity-verification method Product-level Backup and Restore procedure Vulnerability-management and customer-notification procedures Product security-function test procedures and results The following materials, however, are likely to require project-specific preparation or verification: Vessel-specific Network Diagram Actual IP addresses and connected systems Firewall Rules configured by the shipyard Integration with the vessel-wide Remote Access Gateway Integration testing with the central Log Server and NTP Server Testing of customer-specific Applications Vessel-wide Backup and recovery plan Shipowner’s operational procedures TA therefore does not eliminate every project-specific review or integration test.

It reduces the need to repeat verification of common product elements within the approved scope, but it does not automatically demonstrate the product’s actual integration with the vessel-wide security architecture. 5 The Second Route: Project-Specific Conformity Verification of the Actual Supply Configuration Not every product can be defined through one stable Baseline. Even when the same basic Platform is used, the actual supply Configuration of a package system may differ substantially from vessel to vessel.

For example, the following elements of a Cargo Control System may vary by project: Quantity and Model of PLCs and Remote I/O Tank and Valve Configuration HMI screens and operational Logic Server and Workstation Configuration Third-Party Gateways and Switches Interfaces with upper-level systems Remote Access method Security Log integration Backup scope and recovery method Although the product name remains the same, such a system may undergo significant design changes in every project. If it is difficult to include the complete system within one fixed TA scope, verifying conformity against the project-specific supply Configuration for a particular vessel may be more realistic.

Project-specific verification does not reduce the amount of Evidence that must be prepared. The following matters must still be clearly defined and verified: Hardware and Software actually supplied UR E27 requirements applicable to the project Product functionality and product Configuration Dependencies on the shipyard’s integrated security architecture Responsible party for each requirement Design documentation and Configuration Records Test procedures and test results Unmet requirements and compensating controls Consistency between the delivered and tested Configurations The key distinction between TA and project-specific verification is not whether Evidence is required.

It is whether that Evidence belongs to a standardized product repeatedly supplied to multiple projects or to the specific supply Configuration of one project. 6 SoC Should Be Used Only After Confirming the Classification Society’s Issuance Scheme Statement of Compliance is generally used as the title of a document confirming conformity with specified Rules or requirements. UR E27, however, does not establish SoC as a universal alternative applied consistently by all classification societies.

An equipment manufacturer should therefore not decide in advance that “we will obtain an SoC because we do not have TA.” The following matters should first be confirmed with the classification society responsible for the project: Does the classification society issue an SoC for products or systems subject to UR E27? Is the SoC issued for a standardized product, an individual product, or a project-specific system? Which UR E27 requirements are assessed? Does the assessment include design review, product testing, or both? Does it also examine the manufacturing process or quality-management system? Is the SoC valid only for a particular vessel or project? Can it be reused in subsequent projects?

Is reassessment required if the product Version or Configuration changes? Will the shipyard and classification society accept it as the required Evidence of conformity? Even where the same SoC title is used, differences in Scope and conditions can result in different levels of applicability. Any explanation of an SoC should therefore identify the issuing classification society, assessed product, applicable Rules, assessment scope, and limitations. 7 The Third Route: Confirmation of Exemption or Non-Mandatory Application Not every Computer-Based System is assessed in the same manner under UR E27.

Depending on the product’s intended purpose, specifications, and relationship with vessel functions, it may be necessary to assess whether exemption or non-mandatory application is appropriate. The important point is that an equipment manufacturer should not independently declare, “This product is not important and is therefore excluded.” Its functions, connections, and potential impact of compromise should first be analyzed, followed by consultation with the System Integrator, shipyard, and classification society.

ClassNK states that an SoF relating to UR E26/E27 may be issued in the following two situations: To confirm that the intended purpose and specifications of a Computer-Based System qualify for exemption from UR E26/E27 To confirm that mandatory application of UR E26/E27 is not required for a Computer-Based System with the intended purpose and specifications concerned ClassNK also states that issuance of such an SoF is not mandatory. ClassNK’s SoF should therefore be understood not as a certificate confirming compliance with every UR E27 requirement, but as a means of formally documenting a determination regarding applicability. 8 What Must Be Explained When Applying for a ClassNK SoF?
Submitting only the product name will not be sufficient to confirm exemption or non-mandatory application.

At a minimum, the following information should be prepared so that the classification society can assess the product’s intended purpose and specifications: Product name, Model, and Version Intended onboard use Functions performed or supported by the product Connected vessel systems Network and other Interfaces Communication direction and information exchanged Whether the product executes control commands Vessel functions affected by a product failure Possibility of incorrect information or commands Possibility of compromise spreading to other systems Maintenance and Software Update paths Technical rationale for exemption or non-m
